units.la: ILLVSTRIBVS AC GENEROSIS D. MAVRI- TIO & ERNESTO, fratribus germanis, comiti- bus in Dietz, Dominis in Lisberg & Bicken- bach, &c. Dominis suis humili obser- uantia colendis, S.
units.tr: To the illustrious and noble lords Maurice and Ernest, German brothers, counts of Dietz, lords of Lisberg and Bickenbach, etc., their lords to be honoured with humble respect: greetings.

units.la: ERIT fortasse qui miretur, cur hoc Compendium Physices uel à parente meo piæ memoriæ sit conscriptum, uel nunc à me edatur. Is itaque rationem paucis accipiat. Ac primùm quidè ad parentè quod attinet, nō ignorauit ille, quàm utilia essent bonarũ artiũ & philosophiæ studia, quamq; scitu necessaria ijs qui in maioribus, ut uocãt, facultatibus cũ fructu uersari cupiunt. Quapro-pter cũ ex animo simul agnosceret, neminè sibi soli natũ esse, sed ortus nostri partè sibi patriã uendicare, partè parentes, partè amicos, ut est præclarè à Platone dictũ: cumq; sciret, homines hominum causa (ut Stoicis placet) esse generatos, ut ipsi inter se alij alijs prodesse possint: totis sanè uiri[?]s in hoc incubuit,ut si nō de omnibus, de plurimis certè bene mererētur. Quare nō solūm publicè in hac schola nostra sacrosanctam Theologiā ea qua debuit fide & diligētia est professus,uerūm etiam iuuentutē priuatim erudiendā suscepit,eamq; piè & sobriè philosophari docuit:idq; non sine magnorū uirorū exemplo. Nam & Origenes multos cū in Sacris literis, tum in externa quoq; philosophia instituit. Ad philosophicas disciplinas etiā quotquot ingeniōsos uidebat induxit, illisq; Geometriā & Arithmeticā & reliquas liberales artes tradidit.Et cōtra hæreses quæ apud philosophos erant,etiā commentarios philosophorū produxit, illosq; exposuit,cōmentandoq; singula eorū confi derauit, ita ut apud gentiles quoq; magnus philosophus prędicaretur.Multos etiam ex idiotis ad liberales artes induxit,asserēs plū rimam ex illis cōmoditatem ad sacrarum literarū contemplationē & supelleƈtilē relaturos,unde & sibiipsi exercitiū mundanarū ac philosophicarū disciplinarū necessarium futurum duxisset.Hæc namq; disertē Eusebius lib.6. Eccl.hist.cap.18.de Origene tradit. Quod autem parens meus philosophiæ partes præcipuas uel in cōpendium redegit,
units.tr: Perhaps someone will wonder why this Compendium of Physics was written by my father of blessed memory, or why it is now published by me. Let him accept the reason in a few words. As far as my father is concerned, he was not unaware how useful the study of the liberal arts and philosophy is, and how necessary to know for those who wish to engage profitably in the so-called higher faculties. Therefore, since he acknowledged from his heart that we are not born for ourselves alone, but that our country claims a part of our birth, our parents a part, our friends a part, as Plato said splendidly; and since he knew that men are born for the sake of men (as the Stoics hold), so that they may be of service to one another, he devoted himself wholeheartedly to this, so that if not to all, at least to very many he might be of benefit. For this reason he not only professed sacred theology publicly in this our school with the faithfulness and diligence it deserved, but also took on the teaching of young people privately, and taught them to philosophise piously and soberly; and he did this not without the example of great men. For Origen instructed many, both in Sacred Letters and also in secular philosophy. He also brought to the philosophical disciplines all whom he saw to be gifted, and taught them geometry, arithmetic and the other liberal arts. And against the heresies that were among the philosophers, he also brought forward the commentaries of the philosophers, expounded them, and by commenting on each of them examined them, so that he was proclaimed a great philosopher even among the Gentiles. He also led many of the unlearned into the liberal arts, asserting that they would bring very great advantage to the contemplation and understanding of the sacred letters, whence he himself also judged that the practice of worldly and philosophical disciplines would be necessary for him. For Eusebius clearly records these things about Origen in Book 6 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 18. As for the fact that my father either reduced the principal parts of philosophy to a compendium,

units.la: uel Leuib.& perspicuis explicauit cōmentarijs (ut in Ethicis est uidere, quæ & ipsa, patris mei Annotationibus illustrata,cū stu diofis, si hunc libellū ipsis gratum animad* uertero, breui cōmunicabo) præteritis intricatis & perplexis aliorū quæstionibus & disputationibus: in eo quoque iuuentutis ratione habuit, cuius ingenium nequaquā obtundendum esse existimauit rebus plus subtilitatis quàm utilitatis habentibus. Deinde hoc quoq; cōsilio id fecit,ne adolescentes in inferioribus illis studijs consenescerent:sed principijs perceptis, ijsq; quæ maximè sunt necessaria, & suum in communi uita usum habent, ad altiora quoque difcenda animum adijceret. Non displicuit ei hoc Neoptolemi Erniani, qui philosophari sibi ait necesse esse,sed paucis: Nam omnino,inquit,haud placet. Quam sententiam Gellius interpretatus,degustandum ex philosophia censet, non in eam ingurgitandum: libro 5. Noctium Att.cap.16.
units.tr: or explained them in plain and clear commentaries (as can be seen in the Ethics, which, illustrated with my father's annotations, I will shortly make available to students, if I see that they welcome this little book), setting aside the intricate and perplexing questions and disputations of others: in this too he took account of the young, whose intellect he judged should not be blunted by matters having more subtlety than usefulness. Moreover, he did this with the further purpose that young people should not grow old in those more elementary studies, but, once the principles had been grasped, and those things which are most necessary and have their own use in common life, should apply their minds also to learning higher things. The saying of Neoptolemus of Ennius did not displease him, who said that one must philosophise, but only a little: "For not at all," he says, "is it pleasing." Gellius, interpreting this opinion, holds that one should taste philosophy, not gorge oneself on it: Book 5 of the Attic Nights, chapter 16.

units.la: Cæterūm de me nihil dicam aliud, quàm quòd morem tandem gerendum ac gratificandum studiosis arbitratus sum,qui sæpe à me petiuerunt, ut quæ à parente conscripta essent philosophica opuscula, non quidem ut ederentur,sed tamen ut plurimis prodesfent,publicarem & in lucem ederem. Vobis vero,illustres ac generosi comites,hunc patris mei charissimi laborem dedicare volui, primum quidem, ut meam erga vos observantiam hoc qualicunq; argumento testarer. Deinde vero, quod eorum quae damus lectionem vobis hac sané aetate vestra neq; iniucundam, neq; infructuosam fore putaui. Postremo,quod hoc Opusculum gratius fore studiosis existimaui, si sub amplissimi nominis vestri patrocinio ederetur. Quapropter vehementer rogamus, Illustres ac Generosi Domini comites, ut haec qualiacunque eo quo mittimus animo accipiatis. Bene in Christo Iesu valete,& me meosq; commendatos habete. Marpurgi, 7 idus Septemb. Anno 1 5 6 8.
units.tr: As for myself, I will say nothing else than this: that I have at last judged it right to comply with and gratify the students, who have often asked me to publish and bring to light the philosophical little works written by my father, not indeed that they be issued for sale, but so that they might benefit very many. To you, illustrious and noble counts, I wished to dedicate this labour of my dearest father, first indeed so that I might attest my respect for you by this token, whatever its worth. Then, because I thought that the reading of these things would be neither unpleasant nor unprofitable for you in this your present age. Lastly, because I judged that this little work would be more welcome to students if it were published under the protection of your most distinguished name. Therefore we earnestly ask, illustrious and noble lords and counts, that you accept these things, such as they are, in the spirit in which we send them. Farewell in Christ Jesus, and hold me and mine commended to you. Marburg, 7 Ides of September, in the year 1568.

units.la: Quid est Physice?
units.tr: What is Physics?

units.la: Est pars philosophiæ, cōplectens scientiam de natura, & naturaliū corporum motu, principijs, causis, effectibus, officijs, partibus, accidentibus.
units.tr: It is a part of philosophy, embracing the knowledge of nature and of the motion, principles, causes, effects, functions, parts and accidents of natural bodies.

units.la: Quomodo differt Physice ab Ethice & Logice?
units.tr: How does Physics differ from Ethics and Logic?

units.la: Ethice quidem de moribus ac vitæ institutione, Logice de sermone, atq; omni orationis facultate, ab Physice de rerum natura disserit.
units.tr: Ethics indeed treats of morals and the ordering of life, Logic of speech and every faculty of discourse, while Physics treats of the nature of things.

units.la: Quod est subiectum Physices?
units.tr: What is the subject of Physics?

units.la: Corpus naturale mobile.
units.tr: A mobile natural body.

units.la: Quid vocas corpus naturale?
units.tr: What do you call a natural body?

units.la: Corpus naturale est substantia corporea, composita ex materia prima & substantiali, cui etiam inducta fit certa forma.
units.tr: A natural body is a corporeal substance, composed of prime and substantial matter, into which a certain form is also introduced.

units.la: Quid intelligis per corpus mobile?
units.tr: What do you understand by a mobile body?

units.la: Quod motui & mutationi est obnoxium. Ac motum quidem intellige mutationem secundum substantiam, aut secundum accidens. Secundum substantiam,quando generatur uel corrumpitur: secūdum accidens,quando augetur uel minuitur in quantitate:quando item alteratur,uel uariatur in qualitate, loco,tempore,&c.
units.tr: That which is subject to motion and change. By motion understand change either in substance or in accident. Change in substance occurs when a thing is generated or corrupted; change in accident occurs when it is increased or diminished in quantity, and likewise when it is altered or varies in quality, place, time, and so on.

units.la: Quid est natura?
units.tr: What is nature?

units.la: Est principium & causa motus & quietis in re naturali, cui primum per se, & non per accidens inest. Ita Aristoteles lib.2. Physicorum.
units.tr: It is the principle and cause of motion and rest in a natural thing, in which it inheres primarily and per se, and not per accidens. So Aristotle, Physics book 2.

units.la: Quo ordine, quæ ad hanc philoso- phiæ partem pertinent, ve- niunt explicanda?
units.tr: In what order are the things that pertain to this part of philosophy to be explained?

units.la: Primo quidem loco considerare oportet in genere principia universalia, causas, motum, nec non ipsius motus, quo corpus naturale mobile movetur, accidentia & circumstantias. Nulla existit res in natura, in qua hæc non spectentur in initio. Huc autem pertinent lib.8. Aristotelis, inscripti De auscultatione Physica.
units.tr: First of all, one must consider in general the universal principles, the causes, motion, and also the motion itself by which the mobile natural body is moved, together with its accidents and circumstances. There is no thing in nature in which these are not looked at at the outset. To this belongs the eighth book of Aristotle, entitled The Physical Hearing (De auscultatione physica).

units.la: Secundo considerare oportet quæ ex principijs oriuntur: horum autem cum alia sint simplicia, alia compositá, par est, de simplicibus tractatio præcat. Quamobrem de cœlo, quod est corpus simplex, deque eius motu locali, forma, partibus, effectis, accidentibus, quinetiam de elementis, quæ similiter sunt corpora simplicia, necessario disputationes instituuntur. Atqui hæc omnia diligentissimè persequitur Aristoteles quatuor lib.De cœlo & mundo.
units.tr: Second, one must consider the things that arise from the principles. Since some of these are simple and others composite, it is fitting that the treatment of the simple things come first. Therefore it is necessary to set out discussions concerning the heaven, which is a simple body, and its local motion, form, parts, effects and accidents, and also concerning the elements, which likewise are simple bodies. Aristotle pursues all of these most diligently in the four books On the Heavens and the World.

units.la: Tertiò consideranda sunt corpora composita, eaq; ante omnia in genere quidem, id est, ut ea sunt ex elementis composita, atq; secundum formas aut qualitates mouentur aut mutantur. Secundum formas quidem, ut quomodo generantur uel corrumpuntur: secundum qualitates, ut quomodo augetur uel minuuntur. De huiusmodi autem motu scu mutatione diffusè Aristoteles duobus libris De generatione & corruptione.
units.tr: Third, composite bodies must be considered, and first of all in general, that is, insofar as they are composed of elements and are moved or changed according to forms or qualities. According to forms, as to how they are generated or corrupted; according to qualities, as to how they are increased or diminished. Aristotle treats this kind of motion or change at length in the two books On Generation and Corruption.

units.la: Quartò considerare oportet composita in specie, & primò quidem mixta, imperfecta: cuius generis sunt meteora, quorum motus, causæ, effectus, accidentia, cognitu sunt necessaria. Quamobrem rectè sequuntur libri 4. Aristotelis meteorologici.
units.tr: Fourth, one must consider composite things in particular, and first of all the mixed and imperfect ones. Of this kind are the meteors, whose motion, causes, effects and accidents must be known. Hence rightly follow the four books of Aristotle's Meteorology.

units.la: Quintò considerare oportet corpora composita, mixta, perfecta. Cumq; perfectorum alia sint animata, ut homo, brutū, planta: alia uerò inanimata, ut lapides, metalla: profectò si quis dicere uelit de animatis (quæ ordine naturæ digniora sunt inanimatis) opus est præmittat nonnulla in genere de principio uitali omnium animatorum corporum, hoc est, de ipsa anima. Hinc ergo fit, quòd apud Aristotelem tres lib. de Anima, alijq; affines libelli sequuntur. Hæc ferè ex Simplicio, necnon ipso Aristotele in initio Meteororum: atque hunc ordinem sequicum oportet in discendo, qui uolet in Physicis serió proficere.
units.tr: Fifth, one must consider composite bodies that are mixed and perfect. Since some of the perfect bodies are animate, such as man, beast and plant, and others inanimate, such as stones and metals, certainly if anyone wishes to speak of the animate (which in the order of nature are more worthy than the inanimate), he must first premise some general matters concerning the vital principle of all animate bodies, that is, concerning the soul itself. Hence it is that in Aristotle three books On the Soul follow, and other related little treatises. These things are drawn almost from Simplicius, and also from Aristotle himself at the beginning of the Meteorology; and whoever wishes to make serious progress in the Physics must necessarily follow this order in learning.

units.la: Quo ordine, quae ad hanc philosophiae partem pertinent, explicanda, breuius & succinctius in tabulam digesta. Principia & connexa, de quibus in libris octo. In rerum naturalium [?] principia, cognitione discenda sunt, Ex principijs orta: quorum alia sunt, Simplicia: Caelum, 1 & 2 libro. Elementa, 3 & 4 libro. Communi ratione insunt generationi secundum formas & qualitates, de quib. in lib. duobus de generatione & corruptione. Composita: in quib. alia sunt Mixta imperfecta, de quibus in lib. quatuor meteororum. Propria ratione insunt unicuique: Mixta perfecta: e qui-bus alia sunt, sed horum rursus alia sunt Animata, & propter haec subiiciuntur tres lib. de anima. Inanimata.
units.tr: The order in which the things pertaining to this part of philosophy are to be explained, set out in a table more briefly and succinctly. The principles and connected matters, of which there are eight books. The principles of natural things are to be learned by knowledge; the things arising from the principles are: of which some are simple: the heaven, book 1 and 2; the elements, book 3 and 4. They inhere in generation by a common reason according to forms and qualities, concerning which in the two books On Generation and Corruption. Composite: among which some are mixed and imperfect, concerning which in the four books of the Meteorology. They inhere in each by its own reason: mixed and perfect, of which some are animate, and on account of these the three books On the Soul are subjoined. Inanimate.

units.la: Quis est usus seu finis Physices?
units.tr: What is the use or end of Physics?

units.la: Multiplex. Primò, cognitio de natura rerum paulatim deducit homines ad cognitionem Dei & rerum diuinarum: quod Apostolus quoque innuit ad Rom.1. Obseruantes enim rerum naturalium admirabilem productionem, conseruationem atq; usum, excitantur ad magnificè & rectè sentiendum de Dei potentia, bonitate, sapientia, &c.
units.tr: It has many uses. First, knowledge of the nature of things gradually leads people to knowledge of God and divine things, which the Apostle also hints at in Romans 1. For those who observe the admirable production, preservation and use of natural things are stirred to think magnificently and rightly of God's power, goodness, wisdom, and so on.

units.la: Secundò conducit hæc doctrina ad confirmandas bonas mentes in honestis opinionibus: veluti de mundi gubernationibus à Deo, de prouidentia Dei, de causis medijs atq; ordinarijs multorum effectuum naturalium. Ex aduerso multum confert ad consutandas falsas opiniones, tam philosophorum quàm hæreticorum. Epicurei negabant Dei prouidentiam (quos huius disciplinæ contemptus in varios errores, teste Cicerone, pertraxit.) Stoici ponebant fatum, atq; alligabant Deum secundis causis. Hæretici item non pauca admiscuerunt doctrinæ religionis, hausta de philosophia naturali: itaque neq; discutere neq; refutare horum placita poterit quisquam, nisi qui partem hanc philosophiæ attigerit.
units.tr: Second, this teaching helps to confirm good minds in sound opinions: for example, concerning God's governance of the world, God's providence, and the intermediate and ordinary causes of many natural effects. On the other side, it contributes much to refuting false opinions, both of philosophers and of heretics. The Epicureans denied God's providence, and (as Cicero testifies) their contempt for this discipline drew them into various errors. The Stoics posited fate and bound God to secondary causes. Heretics, too, have mixed not a few things into the doctrine of religion that they drew from natural philosophy; so no one will be able to discuss or refute their positions unless he has studied this part of philosophy.

units.la: Tertiò, multa etiam sunt in ecclesiasticis contra uerfijs tractata à sanctis patribus, quæ requirut hominem in hac parte philosophiæ uersatum. Extant apud Augustinum, Hieronymum, aliosq; antesignanos Ecclesiæ permultæ & graues & perplexæ disputationes, de anima, de origine animarum, de voluntate atq; arbitrio nostro, denique de tota hominis cognitione.
units.tr: Third, many matters debated within the Church have been treated by the holy Fathers, and these require a person versed in this part of philosophy. Among Augustine, Jerome, and the other forerunners of the Church there are very many weighty and intricate disputations on the soul, on the origin of souls, on the will and our free choice, and finally on the whole knowledge of man.

units.la: Quarto, Quisquis item Ethicen cupit addiscere, debet ex hac parte prius didicisse quaedam de anima eiusq; potentijs seu facultatibus: quod animadvertere licet apud Aristotelem in Ethicis libro 1. 2. 3. 6.
units.tr: Fourth, whoever also desires to learn ethics ought first to have learned from this part certain things about the soul and its powers or faculties; this can be observed in Aristotle's Ethics, books 1, 2, 3 and 6.

units.la: Quinto, Sed nullum est scriptorum genus, sive poetas, sive philosophos, sive oratores consideres, in quo non occurrunt aliqua de partibus universi, de caelo, de terra, de aquis, item de causis naturalibus aut voluntarijs, aut concurrentibus, aliisq; eius generis: item de homine, de partibus hominis, de anima, corpore, atque singularum partium facultatibus & actionibus. Ergo ad hos quoque scriptores intelligendos perquam necessarium est Physicen aggredi.
units.tr: Fifth, there is no kind of writing, whether you consider poets, philosophers or orators, in which there do not occur some matters concerning the parts of the universe, heaven, earth, waters, likewise concerning natural causes, whether voluntary or concurring, and other things of this kind; likewise concerning man, the parts of man, the soul, the body, and the powers and actions of each part. Therefore, to understand these writers too, it is extremely necessary to take up Physics.

units.la: Sexto, Ars medica tota ex hac parte philosophiae deriuatur. Quae medici tradunt de elementis, eorundemq; qualitatibus, de temperamentis, de humoribus, de actionibus eorundem, de mutationibus seu alterationibus in corpore humano, de simplicium effectis ac viribus, sine Physicis intelligi nequeunt.
units.tr: Sixth, the whole medical art is derived from this part of philosophy. What physicians teach about the elements and their qualities, about temperaments, humours, their actions, about changes or alterations in the human body, and about the effects and powers of simples, cannot be understood without Physics.

units.la: Septimo, Sed & quibuscunq; artibus mechanicis vehementer prodest, utpote in quibus subinde opus est est rerum, quarum in ijsdem artibus præcipuus est usus, naturam, uim atq; effectus, penitus explorare.
units.tr: Seventh, it is also of great benefit to all the mechanical arts, since in them there is constant need to explore thoroughly the nature, force and effects of things, of which the principal use lies in those same arts.

units.la: Octauo & postremò, Etiamsi neq; in Theologia, neq; in medicina, neq; in ullo omnino doctrinæ genere grauiori uersari liberet: tamen ingens uoluptas, quam in uniuscuiusque animo suggerit rerum naturalium cognitio & contemplatio, merito excitare omnes deberet ad hanc parte philosophiæ perdiscendam.
units.tr: Eighth and finally, even if one had no wish to engage in theology, medicine, or any weightier kind of learning at all, the great pleasure that the knowledge and contemplation of natural things brings to each person's mind should rightly stir everyone to learn this part of philosophy.

units.la: Hactenus hæc quasi prolegomena.
units.tr: So far these things, by way of prolegomena.

units.la: PRIMA PARS PHYSI- CES, de Principijs.
units.tr: FIRST PART OF PHYSICS, on Principles.

units.la: Explana argumentum octo librorum Aristotelis de Principijs, seu de Auscultatione physica.
units.tr: Explanation of the subject matter of Aristotle's eight books on Principles, or on Physical Hearing.

units.la: GEneratim quidem sic habet. Sicut in unaquaq; disciplina quædam principia seu loci communes proponuntur, quos tenere oportet, antequam ad altiora fiat progressus (uidemus namque in artibus mathematicis, item in Theologia & Iurisprudentia cæterisq; id fieri) ita in philosophia naturali sunt quidam loci communes scitu pernecessarij omnibus qui exactè cupiunt aliquando de quarumcunq; rerum naturis disputare. Hi igitur in illis octo libris explicantur.
units.tr: Generally speaking, it is as follows. Just as in every discipline certain principles or commonplaces are laid down, which must be grasped before progress is made to higher matters (for we see this happening in the mathematical arts, and likewise in theology, jurisprudence and the rest), so in natural philosophy there are certain commonplaces that are most necessary to know for all who wish to dispute accurately about the natures of any things whatever. These are therefore explained in those eight books.

units.la: Sunt autem huiusmodi: Quot & quæ sunt natü/ ralium rerum principia? quæ & quàm multiplices sunt, earumq; causæ? quid est, & quomodo fit motus seu transmutatio in rebus naturalibus? quot sunt species motus, quænam ei contraria? Quæ quidem semper primo loco considerari debere, manifestum est.
units.tr: Such are the following: How many and what are the principles of natural things? How many kinds are there, and how manifold are they, and what are their causes? What is motion, or change, in natural things, and how does it come about? How many species of motion are there, and what are their contraries? That these must always be considered first is clear.

units.la: Speciatim autem hoc ordine Aristoteles progreditur. Quoniam oportet uolentem de rebus naturalibus disputare, primo loco scrutari earundem principia & causas, ideo Aristoteles lib.1. disserit de rerum naturalium principijs, quæ & quot ea sint exponens: secundo libro de earundem causis & causarum uarietate. Cæterum quia principia ipsa debent esse mobilia (neq; enim principium sine actione, neq; actio sine motu potest intelligi) & natura ipsa definitur principium motus & quietis: adhæc, in omnibus adeo rebus naturalibus, siue cum generantur uel corrupuntur, siue cum alia ratione mutantur, debet quædam motus ratio considerari: ideo statim lib.3. de motu orationem quoq; instituit, eaq; tractat quæ de illo opportune dici queant. Hinc adjecit nonnulla, quæ in motu, tanquam ei connexa (ac proinde in consideratione rerum naturalium observanda) expendi propter multas causas solent. ea sunt: infinitum, locus, uacuum, tempus. Ac de infinito quidem disputat lib.3, de loco autem & contrario eius vacuo, item de tempore agit toto libro quarto. Libro quinto redit ad institutum de mo-tu, & plenius eius proprietatem, quatenus in rerum principijs versatur, discutit. Tribus libris sequentibus, 6.7 & 8 inquā, diligentissimè, quicquid de motu in quaestionem venire posset, exequitur, eodem fere pacto, quo alias solet themata simplicia magno artificio tractare. Quamobrem Aristoteles ipse primos quinq; libros solitus est De principijs & naturales appellare, tres vero ultimos De motu simplici-citer, testatibus id apud Themistium Adrasto, apud Simplicium Andronico, Theophrasto, Eudemo. Sed ad ea quae libro primo Aristotelis continentur, transeamus.
units.tr: In particular, Aristotle proceeds in this order. Since one who wishes to discourse about natural things must first search out their principles and causes, Aristotle in the first book discusses the principles of natural things, explaining what they are and how many. In the second book he treats of their causes and the variety of causes. But because the principles themselves must be mobile (for a principle cannot be understood without action, nor action without motion), and because nature itself is defined as the principle of motion and rest, and furthermore, because in all natural things, whether they are generated or corrupted, or changed in some other way, some account of motion must be considered, he therefore next, in the third book, sets out a discussion of motion, and treats of those things which can fittingly be said about it. Hence he added certain things which are customarily examined, for many reasons, as connected with motion (and so to be observed in the consideration of natural things). These are: the infinite, place, the void, and time. He disputes about the infinite in the third book; he treats of place and its contrary, the void, and likewise of time, throughout the whole fourth book. In the fifth book he returns to the subject of motion and examines more fully its properties, insofar as it belongs to the principles of things. In the three following books, the sixth, seventh and eighth, I say, he most diligently works through whatever about motion could come into question, in much the same way as he usually handles simple topics with great skill. Wherefore Aristotle himself used to call the first five books On Principles and natural books, and the last three On Simple Motion, as Themistius reports on the authority of Adrastus, and Simplicius on the authority of Andronicus, Theophrastus and Eudemus. But let us pass on to what is contained in the first book of Aristotle.

units.la: Quot sunt rerum principia?
units.tr: How many principles of things are there?

units.la: Unum tantum est principium rerum omnium, tam naturalium quam supernaturalium, Deus videlicet Opt.Max. Unde Plato sic Deum alicubi definit: Deus est mens aeterna, causa boni in natura. vel: Deus est spiritus & mens libera, segregataq; ab omni cōcretione mortali, omnia sentiens, omnia movens per vim suam illis infusam. Quae definitio ex Platonis Timaeo collecta est, atq; à Cicerone usurpata, teste Lactantio libro 2.cap.5. Propterea Physici appellant Deum principium effectiuum, rerum omnium factorem & cōditorem, primam naturam, primam causam, causam infinitam, primum motorem, primum movens, summum bonum. Atqui Deus principium quoddam est supernaturale, & rerum etiam supernaturalium. Nos vero hic ea principia inquirimus, quae naturalia & rerum naturalium proprie dicuntur.
units.tr: There is only one principle of all things, both natural and supernatural, namely God, the best and greatest. Hence Plato somewhere defines God thus: God is an eternal mind, the cause of good in nature; or: God is a spirit and free mind, separated from every mortal composition, perceiving all things, moving all things by the power infused into them. This definition is gathered from Plato's Timaeus and was used by Cicero, as Lactantius attests in book 2, chapter 5. Therefore the natural philosophers call God the effective principle, the maker and founder of all things, the first nature, the first cause, the infinite cause, the first mover, the first moving thing, the supreme good. But God is a certain supernatural principle, and the principle of supernatural things too. We, however, here inquire into those principles which are natural and are properly called principles of natural things.

units.la: Quot sunt rerum naturalium prin- cipia naturalia?
units.tr: How many natural principles of natural things are there?

units.la: Variae fuerunt philosophorum opiniones. Alij tantum posuerunt unum, alij plura: omnes autem adhuc inter se dissenserunt. Principium autem est, unde primum res quaeque naturalis fit aut constat, quod & corpori naturali inest tanquam pars substantiae eius per se, & non per accidens.
units.tr: There have been various opinions of the philosophers. Some posited only one, others several; yet all have disagreed among themselves. A principle, however, is that from which each natural thing first comes to be or consists, and which is present in a natural body as a part of its substance, per se and not per accidens.

units.la: Tabula de Principijs.
units.tr: Table of Principles.

units.la: Qui de principijs disputarunt, alij posuerunt Unum: sed hoc quidam Immobile: id autè vel Infinitum, sicut Melissus. Finitum, sicut Parmenides. Mobile: sed alij Ignem, ut Heraclitus. Aerem, ut Diogenes. Aquā, ut Thales Milesius. Medium quiddā inter aerē & aquam, siue plenū & vacuum, ut Leusippus. Terrā nemo posuit, propter eius craßitudinem. Plura: que quibusdam placuit esse Finita, caq; ant Duo: ut Plato ponens magnum & parvum, vel ut Anaximander unum & unitati repugnans: item Stoici mentem & naturam. Tria. Sic namq; Aristoteles ponit materiam, formam & privationē: ante quem & Plato posuit Deum, materiam & idaam. Hac vero forma est, quam materia induit. Quatuor, quemadmodum Empedocles constituens quatuor elementa. Vel alio numero maiore comprehensa. Infinita: sed quidam voluerunt Genere seu specie esse unum, at figura sive forma diversa, sicut Democritus ponens infinita corpora ἄτομα. Genere diversa seu contraria, sicut Anaxagoras asseruit, omnia confusa in chao quodam latuisse. Cæterum ex his omnibus opinionibus sola recepta est in scholis, quæ Aristotele habet authorem, quadq; tria astruuntur principia, Materia, Forma & Priuatio.
units.tr: Of those who have disputed about principles, some posited one. But some of these held it to be immobile, and this either infinite, as Melissus did, or finite, as Parmenides did. Others held it to be mobile: some said fire, as Heraclitus; air, as Diogenes; water, as Thales of Miletus; some intermediate thing between air and water, or a full and a void, as Leucippus. No one posited earth, on account of its thickness. Several posited a plurality, which some thought to be finite, and these either two: as Plato, positing the great and the small, or as Anaximander, the one and that which is opposed to unity; likewise the Stoics, mind and nature. Or three: for thus Aristotle posits matter, form and privation, and before him Plato also posited God, matter and idea; this form is what matter takes on. Or four, as Empedocles, positing four elements; or comprehended under some larger number. Others posited infinite principles; but some wished them to be one in genus or species, yet different in figure or form, as Democritus, positing infinite bodies, atoms [ἄτομα]; others different or contrary in genus, as Anaxagoras asserted, holding that all things lay hidden together, confused, in a certain chaos. Yet of all these opinions, only one has been accepted in the schools: the one that has Aristotle as its author, and which asserts three principles: matter, form and privation.

units.la: Quare non est ponendum unum tantum principium, idq; immobile?
units.tr: Why should one principle alone, and that immovable, not be posited?

units.la: Plures sunt rationes. Prima: Qui ita sentiunt, negant Physices principia. Ante omnia enim, quod absurdissimum est, negant entium multitudinē. Neque enim potest intelligi aliquod principium, quin id simul alicuius vel aliquorū principium existat: nam sui ipsius principiū esse nequit. Quare unum & solitarium principium qui statuunt, contra naturam loquuntur. Intellige autē physicos hic loqui de principio formali & materiali, non de efficiente.
units.tr: There are several reasons. First, those who think this way deny the principles of physics. Above all, and this is most absurd, they deny the multitude of beings. For no principle can be understood that does not at the same time exist as the principle of some thing or things, since a thing cannot be its own principle. So those who posit one solitary principle speak against nature. Here I understand the physicists to be speaking of the formal and material principle, not the efficient one.

units.la: Secunda: Negant motum seu transmutationem: cum tamen generari aut corrumpi, aut quouis modo alterari aliquid citra motum, sit secundum physicos impossibile. Ista igitur principia physices, entium, inquam, multitudinem, & motum, quando illi euertunt, quis contra hos disputet?
units.tr: Second, they deny motion or change, although it is impossible, according to the physicists, for anything to be generated, corrupted, or altered in any way without motion. When they overturn these principles of physics, the multitude of beings (I mean) and motion, who will dispute against them?

units.la: Tertia: Argumenta quibus nituntur suam opinionem de uno et immobili principio stabilire, sunt vitiosa, tam in materia quam in forma. Neq; difficile est Dialecticis perito ea diluere, Primo enim Melissus errat, dum probare conatur, illud unum principium immobile esse infinitum.
units.tr: Third, the arguments on which they rest their view of one immovable principle are faulty, both in matter and in form. Nor is it difficult for someone skilled in dialectic to refute them. First, Melissus errs when he tries to prove that this one immovable principle is infinite.

units.la: Si ens factum est, inquit, habet principium.
units.tr: "If what is made," he says, "has a beginning."

units.la: Atqui factum non est: ergo principium non habet.
units.tr: "But what is eternal has no beginning" (and he means: nothing is made). "Therefore it has no beginning."

units.la: Deinde infert: Si caret principio, igitur infinitum est. Respondetur, in hac argumentatione duo vitia concurrere: primum in forma. Argumentatur namque a negatione antecedentis ad negationem consequentis: cum in syllogismo hypothetico argumentari oportet a negatione consequentis ad negationem antecedentis, hoc pacto:
units.tr: Then he infers: "If it has no beginning, then it is infinite." The reply is that two faults meet in this argument, the first in form. For he argues from the denial of the antecedent to the denial of the consequent, whereas in a hypothetical syllogism one ought to argue from the denial of the consequent to the denial of the antecedent, thus:

units.la: Si ens factum est, habet principium.
units.tr: If what is made has a beginning.

units.la: Atqui principium non habet: ergo factum non est.
units.tr: But it has no beginning; therefore it was not made.

units.la: Secundo, quando postea infert, Si caret principio, igitur infinitum est: peccatum committitur in materia. Nam in priore consequente, cum infert, Ens factum non est, igitur principium non habet: vox Principii accipitur pro principio temporis. In posteriore autem consequente, quando adiicitur, Si principium non habet, igitur est infinitum: nomen Principii accipitur pro principio rei, quo quidem infinitum caret. Distinguere autem inter principium temporis & principium rei oportet.
units.tr: Second, when he afterwards infers, "If it has no beginning, then it is infinite," the fault lies in the matter. For in the earlier consequent, when he infers, "What is made is not made; therefore it has no beginning," the word "beginning" is taken for the beginning of time. In the later consequent, where it is added, "If it has no beginning, then it is infinite," the word "beginning" is taken for the beginning of a thing, which indeed the infinite lacks. One must, however, distinguish between the beginning of time and the beginning of a thing.

units.la: Secundo Parmenides quoq; errat, ponens unum principium immobile, idq; finitum. Primo enim concedamus per hypothesin iuxta mentem ipsius Parmenidis, τὸ ὂν sive ens significare tantum unum[?]: at quæstio est, utrum τὸ ὂν[?] tantum unum significas, aut subsistentiam tantum significet, aut accidens tantum? Si dicis, tantum significare accidens: tum sequitur, quòd necessariò significabit etiam aliquod subiectum in quo hæreat. Non enim potest accidens de se ipso prædicari, sed de alio cui inest: alias oportet dare, accidens consistere sine subiecto: vel concedere, quòd ens esset non ens: quod profectò absurdissimum est. Si dicis, tantùm significare substantiam: tum tollentur necessariò omnia accidentia, ac proinde neq; quantitas neq; qualitas illi conuenit. Quòd si autem neque quantitas neque qualitas illi conuenit, certè neq; finitum constituetur. Secundò: Rationes quas Parmenides pro se adfert, conflatæ sunt ex argumentationibus non minus uitiosis, quàm erant ipsius Melissi. Manifestum igitur ex his omnibus euadit, haud posse fieri, ut principium unum constituatur, idq; immobile, & aut finitum, aut infinitum.
units.tr: Second, Parmenides too errs, positing one immovable principle, and that finite. For first, let us grant by hypothesis, according to the mind of Parmenides himself, that [τὸ ὂν] or being signifies only one thing. But the question is whether [τὸ ὂν] signifies only one thing, or signifies only substance, or only accident. If you say it signifies only accident, then it necessarily follows that it will also signify some subject in which it inheres. For an accident cannot be predicated of itself but of another in which it inheres; otherwise we must allow that an accident exists without a subject, or concede that being is non-being, which is certainly most absurd. If you say it signifies only substance, then all accidents will necessarily be removed, and consequently neither quantity nor quality belongs to it. But if neither quantity nor quality belongs to it, then certainly it will not be constituted as finite. Second, the reasons which Parmenides brings forward in his own support are made up of arguments no less faulty than those of Melissus himself. It is clear, therefore, from all these points, that it cannot come about that one principle is established, and that immovable, and either finite or infinite.

units.la: Quare non ponendum unum prin- cipium, idq; mobile?
units.tr: Why should one principle, and that movable, not be posited?

units.la: Hi quidem qui posuerunt unum principium mobile, magis physice, quàm Parmenides & Melissus, loquuti sunt, quando motum in natura concedunt: atqui in eo errant, quòd unum tantùm principium definiunt. Reuinci autem & confutari ijsdem possunt rationibus, quæ contra Parmenidem & Me-lissum lissum ad destruendum unitatem principij sunt allata. Sequitur ergo ex his, necessario plura debere poni rerum naturalium principia.
units.tr: Those indeed who have posited one movable principle have spoken more physically than Parmenides and Melissus, in that they concede motion in nature. But in this they err, in that they define only one principle. These, however, can be refuted and confuted by the same arguments which were brought against the unity of the principle by Parmenides and Melissus. It follows from these points, therefore, that of necessity several principles of natural things must be posited.

units.la: Si ponenda sunt principia plura, quare non infinita?
units.tr: If several principles must be posited, why not infinite ones?

units.la: Sciendum ante omnia, eorum qui posuerunt plura principia eaq; infinita, diuersas fuisse sententias. Omnes quidem secuti sunt communem omnium naturaliter loquentium sententiam, quòd uidelicet ex nihilo nihil fiat. Quamobrem constituunt, omnia prius simul extitisse. Verùm in duobus dissenserunt. Primùm, quòd alij quidem, ut Anaxagoras, dixerùt extitisse omnia in quodam confuso chao: alij uero, ut Democritus, extitisse omnia in aliquo principio materiali, nempe aqua, uel igne, uel aere, uel aliquo quod inter hæc medio modo se haberet. Secundò dissenserunt de modo productionis rerum naturalium. Nam illi quidem, Anaxagoram habentes ducem, iudicarunt res fieri seu produci per congregationem & segregationem. Isti uero existimarunt, res produci per alterationem siue condensationem & rarefactionem. His ita expositis, non est dissicile probare, quòd principia infinita constitui nequeant. Sit ergo hæc prima ratio: De infinitis non potest haberi scientia: Igitur si principia sunt infinita, nulla de iis scientia habebitur: quamobrem inanis erit omnis de tota hac re suscepta disputatio. Secunda ratio fluens ex praecedenti: Si de principiis non potest haberi scientia, igitur nec de iis quæ ex principiis constant. Compositum enim videmur haud posse scire, quamdiu ignoramus, ex quibus & ex quot illud constet. Fuerit autem perabsurdum afferere, de compositis non haberi scientiam. Plura quidem argumenta Aristoteles profert in medium, præcipuè contra Anaxagoram: sed nobis satis est unum argumentum proposuisse, atq; ostendisse, qua methodo in disputando Aristoteles ingrediatur.
units.tr: First of all it must be understood that among those who posited several principles, and these infinite, there were differing opinions. All indeed followed the common opinion of all who speak naturally, that from nothing nothing comes to be. Hence they hold that all things existed together beforehand. But they disagreed on two points. First, some, like Anaxagoras, said that all things existed in a certain confused chaos; others, like Democritus, said that all things existed in some material principle, namely water, or fire, or air, or something which stood in a middle state between these. Second, they disagreed about the mode of production of natural things. For those who took Anaxagoras as their leader judged that things come to be or are produced by aggregation and segregation. The others, however, held that things are produced by alteration, or condensation and rarefaction. With these points set out, it is not difficult to prove that infinite principles cannot be established. Let this, then, be the first argument: there cannot be knowledge of infinite things; therefore if the principles are infinite, no knowledge of them will be had, and so all disputation undertaken on this whole matter will be vain. The second argument, following from the previous one: if there cannot be knowledge of principles, then neither of those things which consist of principles. For we seem unable to know a compound while we are ignorant of what it consists of, and how many things. Moreover, it would be utterly absurd to assert that there is no knowledge of compounds. Aristotle brings forward many arguments, chiefly against Anaxagoras; but for us it is enough to have set forth one argument and shown the method by which Aristotle proceeds in disputing.

units.la: Sunt igitur constituenda principia plura & finita?
units.tr: Are there therefore several finite principles to be posited?

units.la: Maximè. Atque hi recto iudicio fuerunt præditi, qui plura posuerunt, & apud hos veritas inueniri potest. Convenit autem inter hos omnes de principiorum proprietatibus: atqui de numero principiorum non convenit.
units.tr: Most certainly. Indeed, those who posited several principles were endowed with sound judgment, and among them the truth can be found. Moreover, all of them agree about the properties of principles; but they do not agree about the number of principles.

units.la: Quot sunt principiorum proprietates?
units.tr: What are the properties of principles?

units.la: Quatuor. Prima: Principia rerum naturalium debent esse contraria: etenim res naturales per generationem producuntur, quæ sanè aliud nihil est, quàm de contrario in contrarium transitio. Nam non quodlibet agere in quodlibet, neque quodlibet pati à quolibet aptum natum est: sed determinatum à determinato, & contrarium à contrario. Sicut nō ex qualibet materia in artificialibus potest quælibet res confici, sed ex ea tantùm res fit, quæ ut huiusmodi fiat, idonea est. Quamuis quibus ex contrarijs res fiant, & quæ contraria in rerum productione corrumpantur, nos non semper possumus intelligere.
units.tr: There are four. The first: the principles of natural things must be contrary to one another. For natural things are produced by generation, and generation is nothing other than a transition from one contrary to another. For it is not the case that anything can act upon anything, or that anything is naturally apt to be acted upon by anything; rather, what is determinate acts upon what is determinate, and a contrary upon a contrary. Just as in artificial things not every material can be made into every thing, but only that material which is suitable for becoming such a thing. Yet which contraries things come from, and which contraries are destroyed in the production of things, we cannot always understand.

units.la: Secunda: Non fiunt ex alijs. Si enim ex alijs fierent, quomodo intelligerentur esse principia: nam ipsamet alia haberent principia.
units.tr: The second: they do not come from other things. For if they came from other things, how would they be understood to be principles? For those other things would themselves have principles.

units.la: Tertia: Non fiunt ex alterutris, siue ex se invicem. Nam contrarium in sui contrarij substantiam transfire nequit.
units.tr: The third: they do not come from one another, that is, from each other mutually. For a contrary cannot pass over into the substance of its contrary.

units.la: Quarta: Omnia fiunt producunturq; ex ipsis: aliâs namq; principia dici non possent, nisi juxta naturam relatiuorum essent aliquarum rerum principia: sicut nec pater potest quispiam dici, nisi respectu alicuius filij. Hæ tres postremæ proprietates declarant confirmantq; primam, quod nimirum principia necessum sit contraria existere.
units.tr: The fourth: all things come to be and are produced from them. For otherwise they could not be called principles, unless, according to the nature of relatives, they were the principles of some things, just as no one can be called a father except in relation to some son. These three last properties declare and confirm the first, namely that principles must necessarily exist as contraries.

units.la: Quot igitur sunt principia?
units.tr: How many principles, then, are there?

units.la: De numero, ut diximus, inter philosophos nō convenit, quando alij plura, alij pauciora constituunt.
units.tr: Concerning the number, as we have said, there is no agreement among the philosophers, since some posit more and others fewer.

units.la: An non rectè constituitur unum principium?
units.tr: Is it not correct to posit one principle?

units.la: Minimè. Nam principia rerum naturalium debent esse contraria: quâ de re omnes, ut diximus, consentiunt. Atqui unum non est sibi contrarium. Contrarietas namque ut minimum inter duo conslstit[?]. Igitur non potest unum tantum principium constitui.
units.tr: Not at all. For the principles of natural things must be contrary, and on this point all agree, as we have said. But one thing is not contrary to itself. For contrariety consists at minimum between two. Therefore only one principle cannot be posited.

units.la: An'non rectè constituuntur duo principia?
units.tr: Is it not correct to posit two principles?

units.la: Ne id quidem. Nam quicquid generatur, id ex aliqua tanquam subiecta materia generetur necessum est: atqui contraria ex se mutuo non generantur: igitur propter duo contraria requiritur quoddam tertium, quod subiectū sit, nec non materiæ patientis vicem subeat. Quod cum ita sit, duo principia nequaquam sufficiunt.
units.tr: Not even that. For whatever is generated must necessarily be generated out of some underlying matter as a subject; but contraries are not generated from one another; therefore, on account of two contraries, there is required some third thing that is the subject and takes the place of the matter which undergoes change. Since this is so, two principles by no means suffice.

units.la: Quare non constituuntur quatuor principia, aut plura?
units.tr: Why are four or more principles not posited?

units.la: 1. Rationes sunt in promptu. Prima: Generatio rerum potest perfici, dato uno principio materiali ad patiendum, & duobus formalibus ad agendum: igitur quando generatio rerum perfici potest per tria, frustra adhibebutur quatuor. Frustra adhibentur plura, ubi sufficiunt pauciora.
units.tr: 1. The reasons are at hand. The first: the generation of things can be accomplished, given one material principle to undergo change and two formal principles to act; therefore, when the generation of things can be accomplished through three, four are employed in vain. Several are employed in vain where fewer suffice.

units.la: 2. Secunda: Si ponerētur quatuor principia, oporteret duabus primis contrarietatibus duo addere subiecta, ut videlicet unicuiq; subiecto in transmutatione una responderet contrarietas. Atqui hoc pacto non una, sed diversæ res naturales confuso quodam modo generarentur. Ergo non est opus quatuor principia constituere. Tertia: Si plura considerentur principia quàm tria, necessum foret plures constituere primas contrarietates. Sed istud est impossibile: igitur & illud ex quo sequitur.
units.tr: 2. The second: if four principles were posited, it would be necessary to add two subjects to the first two contrarieties, so that each subject would correspond to one contrariety in the change. But in this way not one but different natural things would be generated in a certain confused manner. Therefore there is no need to posit four principles. The third: if more than three principles are considered, it would be necessary to posit several first contrarieties. But this is impossible; therefore that from which it follows is also impossible.

units.la: Sufficient ergo ad transmutationem rerum naturalium tria principia: duo, inquam, contraria, eademq; agētia: deinde unum subiectum, idq; patiens. Plura vero ponere, superuacaneum est.
units.tr: Therefore three principles suffice for the transmutation of natural things: two, I say, contraries and acting in the same way, and then one subject, which is passive. To posit more, however, is superfluous.

units.la: Primam contrarietatem intellige, quæ spectatur in primo genere, videlicet substātia. Porrò cum Aristoteles conetur ex probabiliter dictis eruere veram aliquam sententiam, intelligemus probabiliter quoque dici, quòd in substantijs sit una quædam prima contrarietas, rursumq; quòd in substantijs nulla sit contrarietas. Si enim cōsideretur substantia ipsa per se, nihil est ei contrarium: si vero cōsiderentur formales differentiæ in genere substantiæ, tum sanè contrarietas aliqua in ijs inuenitur. Quo pacto substantia corporea contraria est substantiæ incorporeæ, quas duas differentias substantia in se complectitur.
units.tr: Understand the first contrariety as the one observed in the first genus, namely substance. Furthermore, since Aristotle attempts to draw out some true opinion from probable statements, we shall understand that it is also probably said that in substances there is a certain first contrariety, and again that in substances there is no contrariety. For if substance itself is considered in itself, nothing is contrary to it; but if the formal differences within the genus of substance are considered, then certainly some contrariety is found among them. In this way corporeal substance is contrary to incorporeal substance, these two differences which substance embraces within itself.

units.la: Hactenus igitur relatæ sunt aliorum de numero principiorum opiniones, eademq; sic satis confutatæ. Reliquum est, ut certa tandem sententia habeatur.
units.tr: Thus far, then, the opinions of others concerning the number of principles have been related, and in this way they have been sufficiently refuted. It remains that a certain opinion be finally held.

units.la: Propositio. Quot igitur sunt principia naturalia?
units.tr: Proposition. How many, then, are the natural principles?

units.la: Sit hæc propositio, certam complectens, iuxta Aristotelis mentem, sententiam: Ex ijs quæ dicta sunt cōficitur, cum neq; unum principium sufficiat, neq; duo, deinde non opus sit ponere quatuor aut plura: rectè definiri, tria esse principia rerum naturaliū, & neq; plura neq; pauciora.
units.tr: Let this proposition, containing a certain doctrine according to the mind and opinion of Aristotle, be stated: From what has been said it follows that, since neither one principle suffices, nor two, and then there is no need to posit four or more, it is rightly defined that there are three principles of natural things, and neither more nor fewer.

units.la: Confirmatio. Quare tantum tria sunt, & quænam illa sunt?
units.tr: Confirmation. Why are there only three, and what are they?

units.la: Quia in quarumcunq; rerum naturalium productione tria inter se distincta cōcurrunt ut necessaria & sufficientia. Sunt autem hæc, materia, forma, & priuatio.
units.tr: Because three things, distinct from one another, concur as necessary and sufficient in the production of any natural thing. These are matter, form, and privation.

units.la: Quomodo demonstras considerari in productione rerum, materiam?
units.tr: How do you show that matter is to be considered in the production of things?

units.la: Duabus rationibus. Prima: Omne quod fit, aut fit simpliciter, id est, efficitur substantia: aut fit non simpliciter, id est, acquirit quoddā accidēs. Sed neutro horum modorū aliquid fit, nisi præstò sit materia, seu nisi aliquid subijciatur. Igitur ad productionem rerum naturalium necessaria est materia. Minor probatur. Nam si quid fit simpliciter, aliquid quidem necessario subijcitur: quandoquidem forma aduenire non potest, nisi ubi subiecta est materia: forma semper præexhibet materiam. Si aliquid autem fiat non simpliciter, tum multò magis oportet subiectum seu materia aliqua ut adsit. Reuera enim accidens acquiri nullum potest, nisi adsit subiectum Atum[?] in quo hæreat. Accidens sine subiecto non consistit.
units.tr: By two arguments. First: everything that comes to be either comes to be simply, that is, it is made into a substance, or it comes to be not simply, that is, it acquires some accident. But neither of these modes of coming-to-be happens unless matter is present, or unless some subject is underlying. Therefore matter is necessary for the production of natural things. The minor premise is proved thus. If something comes to be simply, some subject must necessarily underlie it, since a form cannot arrive except where matter is already there: form always presupposes matter. If something comes to be not simply, then much more must some subject or matter be present. For indeed an accident cannot be acquired unless a subject is there in which it may inhere. An accident does not subsist without a subject.

units.la: Secunda probatio per inductionem: Eorum quæ fiunt,
units.tr: A second proof by induction: of the things that come to be,

units.la: Quædam fiunt μετασχηματίσεα[?], transfiguratione, sicut æs transfiguratur in poculum.
units.tr: some come to be by change of shape [μετασχηματισμός], by transfiguration, as bronze is transfigured into a cup.

units.la: Quædã fiunt προσθέσεα[?], additione, sicut fluuius fit ex multis riuis.
units.tr: some come to be by addition [πρόσθεσις], as a river is formed from many streams.

units.la: Quædam fiunt ἀφαιρέσεα[?], id est ablatione, veluti cum ex lapide sculpitur Mercurius.
units.tr: some come to be by subtraction [ἀφαίρεσις], that is, by removal, as when a Mercury is carved out of stone.

units.la: Quædam fiunt συνθέσεα[?], id est compositione, sicut fit domus omnibus partibus simul compositis.
units.tr: some come to be by composition [σύνθεσις], as a house comes to be when all its parts are put together at once.

units.la: Quædam fiunt ἀλλοιώσεα[?], id est alteratione, sicut ea quorum materia alteratur, siue per naturam, siue per artem.
units.tr: some come to be by alteration [ἀλλοίωσις], that is, by change, as those things whose matter is altered, whether by nature or by art.

units.la: Atqui in his omnibus modis quibus aliquid fit, semper consideratur quoddam subiectum, adeoq; materia. Igitur in quarumcunq; rerum naturaliū productione, necessum est subiectum aliquod seu materia intelligatur. Porrò illud subiectum unum quidem est numero, specie tamen seu ratione non est unum. Enimuerò si seorsim spectetur subiecti rudis materia, tum unum quoddam intelligitur: sin consideretur ut nondum est induta forma, non intelligetur unum, sed duo. Quod similitudine declaratur. Sit homo qui fieri debet ex non Musico Musicus. hic homo per se quidem consideratus, est unum quoddam numero: atqui secundum rationem seu speciem, est duo, id est, & homo, & non Musicus.
units.tr: But in all these ways in which something comes to be, some subject, and therefore matter, is always considered. Therefore in the production of any natural thing, some underlying subject or matter must necessarily be understood. Moreover, that subject is indeed one in number, but it is not one in kind or in concept. For if the raw matter is considered by itself, then one thing is understood; but if it is considered as not yet clothed with form, then it is understood not as one but as two. This is made clear by an example. Let there be a man who is to become a musician out of a non-musician. This man, considered in himself, is one thing in number; yet according to concept or kind he is two, namely both a man and a non-musician.

units.la: Quomodo demonstras conside- rari in productione rerum formam?
units.tr: How do you show that form is to be considered in the production of things?

units.la: Necessario cum res naturales producuntur, spectatur secundo loco illud quod ex transmutatione, seu per ipsam transmutationem fit, atq; inducitur: veluti cum rudi massae argillae inducitur forma poculi vel matulae, item ex homine nō Musico fit Musicus. Quod autem hoc pacto inducitur, non alio nomine rectius appellaverimus, quàm formae: quae quidem ipsa subiectum seu materiam informat, expolit, absoluit, & per eam unum subiectum ab altero distinguitur.
units.tr: Necessarily, when natural things are produced, there is observed in second place that which comes about through the change, or by the change itself, and is introduced: as when the form of a cup or a jug is introduced into a lump of raw clay, or when a non-musician becomes a musician. What is introduced in this way we could call by no name more fittingly than form. Form itself gives shape to the subject or matter, refines it, completes it, and by it one subject is distinguished from another.

units.la: Quomodo demonstras considerari in productione rerum natura- lium privationem?
units.tr: How do you show that privation is to be considered in the production of natural things?

units.la: Necessario ubi inducitur forma, spectatur privatio eius quod ante formam inductum fuerat, eodem modo quo massa argillae, dum fit urceus, definit esse rudis & informis massa: itemq; homo dum fit Musicus, definit esse non Musicus: & truncus quando fit statua, definit esse truncus. Vbi accesserit forma, subiectum definit esse informe. Estq; formae plane contraria privatio.
units.tr: Necessarily, where a form is introduced, the privation of what was there before the form is observed, in the same way that a lump of clay, while it becomes a jar, ceases to be a raw and shapeless mass; and a man, while he becomes a musician, ceases to be a non-musician; and a trunk of wood, when it becomes a statue, ceases to be a trunk. Once the form has arrived, the subject ceases to be formless. And privation is plainly the contrary of form.

units.la: Hæc tria igitur, ὕλη, μορφὴ, στέρησις, id est, materia, forma, priuatio, cum in omni rerum naturalium productione concurrant, planū fit, eadem ipsa recte numerari tria principia rerum naturalium.
units.tr: Therefore, since these three, ὕλη, μορφή, στέρησis [ὕλη, μορφή, στέρησις], that is, matter, form, and privation, concur in every production of natural things, it is plain that these same three are rightly counted as the three principles of natural things.

units.la: Quomodo igitur tria hæc principia inter se distinguuntur?
units.tr: How, then, are these three principles distinguished from one another?

units.la: Materia & forma intelliguntur rerum naturalium principia per se: quia uidelicet intrinsecè res naturales constituunt, earundemq; absoluunt substantiam. Priuatio uerò tantum per accidēs est principium, utpote quæ rei naturalis substantiam non absoluit: imò ut substantia absoluatur, oportet ipsam disparere, nec potest manere, sicut manet materia atque forma. Hinc quoq; constat, quomodo principia sint ut duo, quomodo item ut tria, quomodo ut contraria. Duo quidem per se, subiectum inquam & forma: tria uerò per accidēs, nempe subiecta materia, & duo contraria, forma uidelicet & priuatio: contraria autem quomodo sint, ex supra dictis patet.
units.tr: Matter and form are understood to be principles of natural things in themselves, because they clearly constitute natural things from within and complete their substance. Privation, however, is a principle only by accident, inasmuch as it does not complete the substance of a natural thing; rather, for a substance to be completed, privation must itself disappear, and it cannot remain, as matter and form remain. Hence it is also clear in what way the principles are two, in what way three, and in what way contraries. Two in themselves, namely the subject and the form; three by accident, namely the underlying matter and the two contraries, form and privation. How they are contraries, however, is plain from what was said above.

units.la: Confutatio. Obiectio prima ad euertendum materiam.
units.tr: Refutation. First objection, to overthrow matter.

units.la: Veteres quidam negauerunt, quicquam generari aut corrumpi: ac proinde materiam siue subiectum sustulerunt. Vsi autem sunt hoc argumento: Omne quod fit, aut fit ex ente, aut ex nõ ente: Neutrum est dicendum: igitur nihil fit, nihil generatur siue corrumpitur. Minor probatur: Ex ente quidē non potest aliquid fieri: posset ex eo alterari, sed non fieri aliquid, quia iam ammodo id tale est. Similiter ex non ente non potest aliquid fieri: nam ex nihilo nihil fit. Igitur minor probata relinquitur. Quare nihil etiam generatur siue corrumpitur.
units.tr: Certain ancients denied that anything is generated or corrupted, and therefore they did away with matter or subject. They used this argument: everything that comes to be comes to be either from being or from non-being. Neither is to be said. Therefore nothing comes to be; nothing is generated or corrupted. The minor premise is proved thus: indeed nothing can come to be from being; it could be altered from it, but something could not come to be, since it is already such. Likewise nothing can come to be from non-being, for nothing comes from nothing. Therefore, the minor premise having been proved, the conclusion remains. Hence nothing is generated or corrupted either.

units.la: Dilutio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Prima dilutio. Distinguo: Fit aliquid ex non ente, non quidem simpliciter (hoc enim foret absurdissimum, & contra communem sententiam, Ex nihilo nihil fit) sed per accidens. Ubi namque forma non adest, sed privatio tantum (quae revera est non ens) ibi quaedam forma inducitur. Hic autem omnino fit aliquid ex non ente, non quidem quatenus nihil est (secundum materiam,) sed quatenus nō est hoc (secundum formam videlicet.) Ad eundem modum fit aliquid etiam ex ente, non quidem simpliciter, sed per accidens. Quemadmodum namque per medicum fit simpliciter medicina, sed per accidens fit etiam domus, quando videlicet qui medicus est aedificat: ita ex eo quod est simpliciter, fit aliquid, sed tātum per accidens: ut ex animali fit animal, non autem simpliciter, id est, non quatenus illud est animal, sed quatenus praeter id quod animal est, ad productionem animalis operatur.
units.tr: First reply. I distinguish: something comes from non-being, not indeed simply (for that would be most absurd and contrary to the common opinion that out of nothing nothing comes), but accidentally. For where form is not present, but only privation (which in truth is non-being), some form is there introduced. Here, however, something comes altogether from non-being, not indeed insofar as it is nothing (with respect to matter), but insofar as it is not this (namely with respect to form). In the same way something also comes from being, not simply but accidentally. For just as through a physician medicine comes simply, but a house also comes accidentally, namely when the one who is a physician builds, so something comes from what simply is, but only accidentally: as an animal comes from an animal, not simply, that is, not insofar as it is an animal, but insofar as, besides being an animal, it works toward the production of an animal.

units.la: Secunda dilutio: Duplex est ens, item duplex non ens. Quoddam actu, ἐνεργείᾳ: quoddam potentia, δυνάμει. δυνάμει[?]. Itemq; ex ente actu non fit aliquid simpliciter, sed tantum per accidens: ex ente potentia fit aliquid simpliciter. Nam ex materia per se fit aliquid, quæ quidem est non ens, quatenus uidelicet non est illud quod fieri debebat. Ex non ente potentia, nihil potest fieri. Quomodo enim ex eo quod nec potentia quidem est, fiat aliquid actu?
units.tr: Second reply: being is twofold, and non-being is likewise twofold. One is actual [ἐνεργείᾳ], another is potential [δυνάμει]. Likewise, from actual being nothing comes simply, but only accidentally; from potential being something comes simply. For something comes through itself from matter, which indeed is non-being, insofar namely as it is not that which was to be made. From potential non-being nothing can come. For how can something come actually from what is not even potentially?

units.la: Obiectio secunda ad euertendum priuationem.
units.tr: Second objection against overthrowing privation.

units.la: Nulli ueteres recesfuerunt priuatione inter principia, idq; hac de causa. In materia siue subiecto, quando illud per se consideratur, antequam forma aliqua accesserit, comprehenditur & ipsa priuatio, adeoq; materia et priuatio sunt plane unum numero. Atqui quæ hoc pacto coniuncta sunt, atq; unum sunt numero, absque re ab inuicem separantur. Igitur priuatio à materia distingui non debet. Si autem non distinguuntur, quomodo constituunt diuersa principia?
units.tr: None of the ancients has put privation among the principles, and for this reason. In matter or subject, when it is considered in itself before any form has been added, privation is also comprehended, and so matter and privation are plainly one in number. But things that are thus conjoined and are one in number are not separated from each other in reality. Therefore privation ought not to be distinguished from matter. But if they are not distinguished, how do they constitute different principles?

units.la: Dilutio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Sunt quidem materia & priuatio unum numero seu subiecto, attamen distingui debent ratione, quamobrem diuersa quoq; agnoscentur principia. Quòd autem ratione distinguantur, perspicuum est.
units.tr: Matter and privation are indeed one in number or subject, yet they must be distinguished in concept, and so they are also to be acknowledged as different principles. That they are distinguished in concept is evident.

units.la: Materia est non ens per accidens, priuatio est non ens per se & simpliciter.
units.tr: Matter is non-being accidentally; privation is non-being per se and simply.

units.la: Materia pertinet ad rei substantiâ, atq; absoluit substantiâ: de priuatione autem nihil tale dici potest.
units.tr: Matter belongs to the substance of a thing and completes its substance; but nothing of the kind can be said of privation.

units.la: Materia simul cum forma est causa generationis rerum, atque se habet veluti mater: privatio vero non facit ad generationem rerum, sed magis quodammodo studet impedire, laboratque ad interitum, & se habet veluti noverca.
units.tr: Matter together with form is the cause of the generation of things, and it stands as a mother; privation, however, does not contribute to the generation of things, but rather in some way strives to hinder it, and labours toward destruction, and stands as a stepmother.

units.la: In rerum productione materia cum ipsis rebus permanet: privatio nequaquam, sed aboletur. Nam simul atque forma advenerit, actum de privatione est.
units.tr: In the production of things, matter remains with the things themselves; privation by no means does, but is abolished. For as soon as form has arrived, privation is done away with.

units.la: Si materia & privatio essent idem ratione, tum profecto, quemadmodum materia appetit formam, tanquam diuinum quiddam & ad perfectionem sui faciens: ita privatio quoque formam appeteret. Atqui istud est falsum: igitur et illud ex quo sequitur. Quod autem privatio non appetat forma, sic probatur. Advenien-te forma, perit privatio, ut ante dictū est. Itaque si privatio appeteret formam, tum appeteret sane sui ipsius interitum. Quo quid absurdius dici queat? Igitur ex his perspicuum evadit, privationem necessario distingui a materia. Iam vero si privatio distinguitur a materia, consequitur, quemadmodum materia est unum principium separatum, ita privationem quoque unum principium separatum agnosci debere. Quod confirmatur etiam hac ratione. Notum est, quod materia appetit formam, ad sui nimirum perfectionem, sicut & foemina appetit virum, sicut insuper omne quod defor-me est me est appetit pulchritudinem. Quo dato, sic ratiocinamur: Quod est causa efficiens cur materia appetat formam, id merito inter principia numerabitur. Atqui privatio est eiusmodi: igitur privatio iure unum inter principia numerabitur. Minor nihil habet obscuritatis. Cum enim privatio sit carentia formae, necnon imperfectionem significet, propter ipsam movetur materia, ut perfici absoluique desideret. De maiore nullus scrupulus residet.
units.tr: If matter and privation were the same in concept, then surely, just as matter desires form as something divine and conducive to its own perfection, so privation too would desire form. But that is false, and therefore so is that from which it follows. That privation does not desire form is proved thus. When form arrives, privation perishes, as was said before. So if privation desired form, it would surely desire its own destruction. What could be said more absurd? Therefore it is clear from these things that privation must necessarily be distinguished from matter. Now if privation is distinguished from matter, it follows that just as matter is recognized as one separate principle, so privation too ought to be recognized as one separate principle. This is confirmed also by the following reasoning. It is known that matter desires form for its own perfection, just as the female desires the male, and likewise everything deformed desires beauty. Given this, we reason thus: whatever is the efficient cause why matter desires form will rightly be counted among the principles. But privation is of this kind; therefore privation will rightly be counted among the principles. The minor premise has no obscurity. For since privation is the lack of form and signifies imperfection, matter is moved on account of it, so that it longs to be perfected and completed. Concerning the major premise there is no doubt.

units.la: Hactenus disputatio de rerum naturalium principiis, quot uidelicet & quaenam ea sint. Sequitur nunc de rerum naturalium causis.
units.tr: So far the discussion of the principles of natural things, how many and what they are. Now follows the discussion of the causes of natural things.

units.la: DE CAUSIS. Quare nunc agendum de causis?
units.tr: CONCERNING CAUSES. Why must we now treat of causes?

units.la: Quod multae res naturales non tantum a natura, verum etiam ab aliis causis producuntur atque subsistunt. A natura quidem sunt elementa, ignis, aer, aqua, terra, animalia, animalium partes, plantae et huiusmodi: ab aliis vero causis sunt domus, tectus, vestitus, &c. Siquidem haec ab arte sunt huiusmodi. Secundo, tum videmur uniuscuiusque rei naturam percipere, quando non solum principia, verum etiam causas eius habemus exploratas. Quamobrem physici interest, etiam causas quae in generatione, corruptione, omnique mutatione rerum naturalium concurrunt, prudeter inuestigare.
units.tr: Because many natural things are produced and subsist not only by nature but also by other causes. By nature are the elements, fire, air, water, earth, animals, parts of animals, plants and the like; by other causes are houses, roofs, clothing, etc., since these are made by art. Second, we seem to grasp the nature of each thing when we have explored not only its principles but also its causes. Therefore it is of interest to the natural philosopher to investigate prudently also the causes that concur in the generation, corruption and every change of natural things.

units.la: Quid est causa?
units.tr: What is a cause?

units.la: Est propter quod aliud est: vel est res antecedens, quam effectus aliquis sequi potest. Atq; aliquando latius patet causa quàm principium, cum principium tantùm de materia & forma prima accipiatur: causa vero nō tantùm de ijsdem, verùm etiā de materia & forma secunda, deque accidentibus. Quamuis re ipsa principium naturale & causa naturalis distingui vix possunt, testante id Aristotele in Metaphysicis.
units.tr: It is that on account of which something else exists, or it is an antecedent thing which some effect can follow. A cause is sometimes understood more broadly than a principle, since a principle is taken only as prime matter and form, whereas a cause includes not only these but also secondary matter and form, and accidents. Yet in fact a natural principle and a natural cause can scarcely be distinguished, as Aristotle testifies in the Metaphysics.

units.la: Quotuplex est causa?
units.tr: How many kinds of cause are there?

units.la: Duplex: Naturalis & non naturalis. Cum enim omnes res aut per naturam sunt, aut per alias causas, veluti vel artem, vel casum, recte primo loco haec causarum diuisio ponitur.
units.tr: Two: natural and non-natural. For since all things exist either through nature or through other causes, such as art or chance, this division of causes is rightly placed first.

units.la: Quomodo natura est causa?
units.tr: How is nature a cause?

units.la: Natura, ut initiò diximus, definitur principium et causa motus ac quietis, in eo in quo est primò & per se, & non secundum accidens. Atqui illa quidem naturam habent, quæ ex naturis (materia inquam & forma) constant, atq; principium sui motus habent in se ipsis: qua quidem ratione omnia subiecta dicuntur naturam habere. Secundum naturam sunt non solùm subiecta illa, verùm etiam quæ subiectis proprie coueniunt. Ignis igitur, substantia quædam est atq; subiectum, naturam habens: motus autem ille, quo ignis tendit sursum, secundum naturam est.
units.tr: Nature, as we said at the beginning, is defined as the principle and cause of motion and rest, in that in which it is primarily and of itself, and not accidentally. Now those things have a nature which consist of natures (I mean matter and form) and have in themselves the principle of their own motion; and in this sense all subjects are said to have a nature. Not only those subjects are according to nature, but also those things which properly belong to subjects. Fire, therefore, is a certain substance and subject, having a nature; and that motion by which fire tends upward is according to nature.

units.la: Quotuplex est causa naturalis?
units.tr: How many kinds of natural cause are there?

units.la: Duplex: Materia & Forma. Ac de materia quidem, quòd ipsa sit natura, itemq; causa rerum naturalis, hunc in modū probatur: Quod facta rei transmutatione, aut corruptione, semper manet, atq; est principium motus, id eiusdem rei est natura. Atqui talis plane est in rebus habentibus in se principium motus, subiecta materia. Igitur materia est natura, ac proinde & causa: siquidē natura est principium & causa, ut ante audiuimus.
units.tr: Two: matter and form. That matter itself is nature, and so also a natural cause of things, is proved in this way: whatever remains through every change or corruption of a thing and is the principle of motion, is the nature of that same thing. But clearly such a thing is, in those things which have in themselves the principle of motion, the underlying matter. Therefore matter is nature, and consequently also a cause, since nature is principle and cause, as we heard before.

units.la: De forma uero, quòd ipsa quoq; sit natura, ideoque & causa, hac ratione demonstratur: Quemadmodum se habet forma in rebus artificialibus, ita quoque ease habet in rebus naturalibus. Atqui res artificiales non intelliguntur perfici, nisi ubi accesserit forma, quinetiam à forma sortiuntur appellationem. Lignum namq;, postquam inducta ei est forma, & propter inductam formam hanc uel illam, uocatur lectus, sedes, aut statua, &c. Igitur res naturalis à forma potissimum habet ut subsistat, necnon à forma appellationem trahit. Hoc autem si datur, consequitur sane, ipsam formam esse rei naturam, ideoq; & causam. Item: Per formam res naturalis est actu, per materiam uero res naturalis tantum est potentia. Atqui res unaquæq; tum præcipuè dicitur existere,quādo est actu. Igitur forma per quam res præcipuè existit, est natura: atq; adeò magis est natura quàm materia, quandoquidem per formam res quæq; naturalis absoluitur.
