Ergo comprobatum relinquitur,quòd tam materia,quàm forma,sint natura rerum, ac proinde etiam causæ rerum naturales. Huc verò pertinet quod semel dictum est, materiam & formam esse principia per se atq; Entia, priuationem verò tantùm esse principium per accidens atque non Ens. Ex quo intelligi potest, priuationem non posse eodem modo dici natura & causam naturalem rerum, quomodo materia & forma sunt natura & causa.
units.tr: That form too is nature, and therefore also a cause, is demonstrated by this reasoning: as form stands in artificial things, so it also stands in natural things. But artificial things are not understood to be perfected unless form has been added; indeed they receive their name from their form. For wood, once a form has been introduced into it, and on account of the form introduced, whether this or that, is called a bed, a seat, or a statue, and so on. Therefore a natural thing has its subsistence chiefly from its form, and draws its name from its form as well. If this is granted, it follows certainly that form itself is the nature of a thing, and therefore also its cause. Again: through its form a natural thing is in act, but through its matter a natural thing is only in potency. But each thing is said to exist most properly when it is in act. Therefore the form through which a thing chiefly exists is nature; and so it is more nature than matter, since through form each natural thing is completed. Hence it remains proved that both matter and form are the nature of things, and consequently also natural causes of things. To this pertains what has been said once before, that matter and form are principles per se and beings, while privation is only a principle per accidens and not a being. From this it can be understood that privation cannot be called nature and natural cause of things in the same way that matter and form are nature and cause.

units.la: Vtrum Physicus & Mathematicus eo- dem pacto considerant formas rerum naturalium?
units.tr: Do the physicist and the mathematician consider the forms of natural things in the same way?

units.la: Confiderat quidem physicus corpora, necnon formam in corporibus: similiter verò & mathematicus confiderat corpora, & in iisdem formam ex punctis, lineis & superficiebus constantem. deinde physicus disserit de corporibus cœlestibus, Sole, inquam, & Luna, ac de toto cœlo, earundemq; forma, magnitudine & motu: idem verò facit & mathematicus, imprimis Astrologus. Attamē quamuis hac in parte tum physicus, tum mathematicus conueniant, longè tamen diuersa ratione in iisdem rebus uersantur. neq; enim alienum est, de eadem re in diuersis disciplinis disseri, alijs tamen atque alijs de causis.
units.tr: The physicist indeed considers bodies, and also the form in bodies; and similarly the mathematician considers bodies, and in them a form made up of points, lines and surfaces. Then the physicist discourses about the heavenly bodies, the Sun and Moon, I mean, and about the whole heaven, and their form, magnitude and motion; and the mathematician, especially the astrologer, does the same. Yet although the physicist and the mathematician agree in this respect, they deal with the same things in very different ways. For it is not out of place for the same thing to be discussed in different disciplines, but for different reasons.

units.la: Primò igitur physicus considerat formas in rebus naturalibus, sed coniunctas materiæ, necnon ut ad motum proprie tendunt. Mathematicus autem sic in solam formam est intentus, ut neq; de materia, neq; de motu cogitet: imò verò hæc ipse prorsus excludit, atq; intellectu à forma separat.
units.tr: First, then, the physicist considers forms in natural things, but as joined to matter, and as they properly tend toward motion. The mathematician, however, is so intent on form alone that he thinks neither of matter nor of motion; indeed he altogether excludes these and separates form from them in the intellect.

units.la: Secundò: Physicus quando definit res aliquas na-turales, semper adiungit quæ materiam atq; motum aliquo modo declarant: veluti si definit arborem, ait constare eam radicibus, trunco, ramis, ligno, item producere etiam fructus, flores, &c. e quibus illa exprimunt materiam, hæc motum. Mathematicus verò in suis definitionibus ne meminit quidem materiæ aut motus: & quamuis formæ faciat mentionem, ulterius tamen non progreditur.
units.tr: Second: when the physicist defines any natural things, he always adds those things which in some way make clear the matter and the motion. For example, if he defines a tree, he says that it consists of roots, trunk, branches and wood, and also that it produces fruits, flowers, and so on; of which the former express the matter, the latter the motion. But the mathematician in his definitions does not even mention matter or motion; and although he makes mention of form, he does not proceed further.

units.la: Tertiò: Physicus longè aliter demonstrationes instituit quàm mathematicus. Ille enim demonstrationes sumit ex materia, motu, atq; iis quæ rem naturalem consequuntur: hic verò ab Arithmetica ac Geometria, id est, partim ex numeris, partim ex figuris, subtiles demonstrationes mutuatur.
units.tr: Third: the physicist sets up demonstrations in a very different way from the mathematician. For the former takes his demonstrations from matter, from motion, and from those things which follow a natural thing; the latter, however, borrows subtle demonstrations from arithmetic and geometry, that is, partly from numbers and partly from figures.

units.la: Perspicuum igitur euadit, physicum longè aliâ ratione formas considerare, quàm id facit mathematicus. Ac physici quidem proprium est officium, in explicatione materiæ ac formæ versari. Cui namq; incumbit disputare de natura, eiusdem etiam interest de materia & forma (quando constat utramque esse naturam, differre.
units.tr: It therefore becomes plain that the physicist considers forms in a very different manner from the mathematician. And indeed it is proper to the physicist's office to be occupied in explaining matter and form. For whoever undertakes to discourse about nature is also concerned with matter and form, since it is agreed that both are nature, and differ.

units.la: Quæ est secunda diuisio causarum?
units.tr: What is the second division of causes?

units.la: Causæ plurimum in omnibus rebus considerari solitæ, enumerantur quadruplices. Prima causa ex qua, siue materialis, ex qua uidelicet aliquid fit.
units.tr: Causes that are usually considered in all things are listed as four. The first is the cause from which, or material cause, that is, that from which something is made.

units.la: 2. Sic æs causa est statuæ. Secunda causa secundum quam, siue formalis, à qua nomen rei unicuique inditur. Forma æri inducta, est causa cur nominetur statua
units.tr: 2. Thus bronze is the cause of a statue. The second is the cause according to which, or formal cause, from which the name of a thing is given to each thing. The form impressed on the bronze is the cause why it is called a statue

units.la: 3. tua, uel clypeus, uel statua Mercurij. Tertia causa à qua, uel per quam, siue efficiens, nempe cuius operatione aliquid perficitur. Ita qui dat consilium, aut sua manu collaborat, est causa efficiens: ut artifex est causa rei per artè effectæ.
units.tr: 3. or a shield, or a statue of Mercury. The third cause is that by which, or through which, namely the efficient cause, by whose operation something is brought about. Thus one who gives advice, or works with his own hand, is an efficient cause, as a craftsman is the cause of a thing made by skill.

units.la: 4. Quarta causa propter quam, siue finalis, adeoq; cuius gratia aliquid fit: ut deambulatio, detractio sanguinis, est causa sanitatis, & sanitas est illarum causa finalis.
units.tr: 4. The fourth cause is that for the sake of which, or final cause, that is, the purpose for which something is done: as walking, or bloodletting, is the cause of health, and health is the final cause of those.

units.la: Hæ causæ sunt principes, quæ in omnibus prope rebus, & non tantum naturalibus, uerum etiam artificialibus, quinetiam in omnibus prope quæ contemplationi aut actioni sunt subiecta, primo loco considerandæ ueniunt.
units.tr: These causes are the principal ones. They must be considered first in almost all things, not only natural but also artificial, and indeed in almost everything that is subject to contemplation or action.

units.la: Da regulas de harum causa- rum usu.
units.tr: Give rules on the use of these causes.

units.la: 1. Alienum non est, unius eiusdemq; rei plures simul mul causas existere. veluti æreæ statuæ causa est æs, similiter & ipse artifex: sed non eodem modo. Nam illud quidē causa est ut materia, hic vero ut efficiēs.
units.tr: 1. It is not out of place for several causes of one and the same thing to exist at once. For example, the cause of a bronze statue is the bronze, and likewise the craftsman himself; but not in the same way. For the former is a cause as matter, the latter as efficient.

units.la: Hæ causæ possunt sibi invicē esse causæ, tametsi diverso respectu. Deambulatio est causa sanitatis: & vice versa, sanitas est causa deambulationis. Sed ibi deambulatio se habet ut causa efficiens, sanitas vero ut causa finalis: hic autem sanitas se habet ut causa efficiens deambulationis.
units.tr: These causes can be causes to one another, though in different respects. Walking is the cause of health, and conversely health is the cause of walking. But there walking stands as the efficient cause and health as the final cause; here, however, health stands as the efficient cause of walking.

units.la: Eadem causa potest esse causa contrariorum effectuum, idq; rursus diversa ratione. veluti gubernator præsens, vel diligens, est causa cur structur nauis: absens vero aut negligens, causa est cur ea pereat.
units.tr: The same cause can be the cause of contrary effects, again in different ways. For example, a helmsman who is present and diligent is the cause of the ship's being well built; but when he is absent or negligent, he is the cause of its perishing.

units.la: Quæ est tertia divisio causarum?
units.tr: What is the third division of causes?

units.la: Causarum etiam sub eadem specie contentarum alia est propinquior, seu prior, etiam imperans dicta, estq; ea quæ præcipuè operatur: alia remotior seu posterior, aliàs obsequens, quæ non agit ut præcipua, sed tantùm huic cooperatur. Itaque sanitatis causa efficiens propinquior est medicus, remotior seplasiarius vel similis quispiam, iussu medici aliquid ægroto parans.
units.tr: Among causes contained under the same kind, one is nearer or prior, also called commanding, and it is the one that works principally. Another is more remote or posterior, also called subordinate, which does not act as the principal but only cooperates with it. So the nearer efficient cause of health is the physician, and the more remote is the apothecary or someone similar, who prepares something for the patient at the physician's command.

units.la: Quæ est quarta divisio cau- sarum?
units.tr: What is the fourth division of causes?

units.la: Causa quædam est per se, quædam per accidens. Sculptor est causa statuæ per se: at Polycletus, idēq; Musicus vel robustus, est causa statuæ per accidens. Potest enim fieri statua, etiamsi Polycletus eam non formaret, præterea etiamsi Polycletus non esset Musicus vel robustus. At citra operam sculptoris non potest fieri. Causa per se est causa propinquior, causa per accidens est remotior.
units.tr: One cause is per se, another per accidens. The sculptor is the per se cause of a statue; but Polycletus, who is also a musician or a strong man, is the per accidens cause of the statue. For a statue can be made even if Polycletus did not shape it, and even if Polycletus were not a musician or a strong man. But it cannot be made without the sculptor's work. A cause per se is the nearer cause; a cause per accidens is the more remote.

units.la: Quæ est quinta diuisio causarum?
units.tr: What is the fifth division of causes?

units.la: Quædam causa est actu, quædam potentia. Causa actu est, quæ nunc agit: ut qui præsenti tempore ædificat, est causa ædificij actu. At faber otiosus, est causa ædificij potentia tantum: quandoquidem nunc non agit, sed ad agendum tempore opportuno est idoneus.
units.tr: Some cause is actual, some potential. A cause is actual when it is now acting: as one who is building at the present time is the actual cause of a building. But an idle builder is the cause of a building only potentially, since he is not now acting but is fit to act at a suitable time.

units.la: Causæ actu, sunt simul cum suis effectibus, & cum ijsdem simul esse desinunt. Causæ vero potentia, neque sunt simul cum effectibus, neque cum illis esse desinunt.
units.tr: Actual causes exist together with their effects, and cease to exist together with them. Potential causes, however, neither exist together with their effects nor cease together with them.

units.la: Da regulas de harum causa- rum usu.
units.tr: Give rules on the use of these causes.

units.la: 1. Quando de causis rerum fit quæstio, eundum est per omnes causarum species, & eousque progrediendum, donec ad ultimam & proximam causam deuenitur, hoc pacto: Cur hic ædificat? Quia ædificator est. Cur ædificator? Quia præditus ædificandi habitu. Non est quo longius progrediaris.
units.tr: 1. When a question arises about the causes of things, one must go through all the kinds of causes and proceed until one arrives at the last and nearest cause, in this way: Why is this man building? Because he is a builder. Why a builder? Because he has the habit of building. There is no further you need go.

units.la: 2. Si quis roget de uniuersalibus effectibus, reddere decet causas uniuersales: sin de particularibus essectibus, stibus,causas particulares. Præterea si de effectibus actu quæstio est, respondebitur per causas actu existentes: sin de effectibus potétia, respondebitur per causas potentia.
units.tr: 2. If someone asks about universal effects, it is fitting to give universal causes; but if about particular effects, particular causes. Moreover, if the question concerns actual effects, the answer will be given through causes actually existing; but if it concerns potential effects, the answer will be given through potential causes.

units.la: Súntne aliæ adhuc causæ?
units.tr: Are there any other causes besides these?

units.la: Sunt,ut plurimorum fert opinio: nimirum Fortuna & Casus.ab his namq; multa quodammodo fieri putantur.
units.tr: There are, as the opinion of most people holds: namely Fortune and Chance, for many things are thought to happen in some way from these.

units.la: An fit fortuna uel casus?
units.tr: Does fortune or chance occur?

units.la: De hac quæstione tres cōmemorātur opiniones.
units.tr: Three opinions on this question are recorded.

units.la: Prima fuit eorum, qui Casum aut Fortunam, ac proinde ijsdem quicquam fieri simpliciter negarunt. Mouebantur autem hisce duabus rationibus.
units.tr: The first was of those who denied outright that Chance or Fortune exists, and therefore that anything happens by them. They were moved by two reasons.

units.la: Omnium eorum quæ dicuntur fieri uel casu uel fortuna, inueniuntur aliæ certæ ac definitæ causæ. Igitur casu & fortuna nihil fit. Antecedens ita probabant: Cum quis casu siue fortuna dicitur inuenire amicum in foro, causa cur inuenerit definita hæc est, Quòd uidelicet ad forum se contulerit, deliberata uoluntate, ac negotij alicuius peragendi gratia: deinde, quòd alter quoq; eodem propter aliquod negotium aduenerit. Quare nihil huiusmodi casu aut fortuna, sed omnino aliam ob causam fit.
units.tr: Of all the things said to happen either by chance or by fortune, other certain and definite causes are found. Therefore nothing happens by chance or fortune. They proved the antecedent thus: when someone is said to find a friend in the marketplace by chance or fortune, the definite cause of his finding him is this: that he went to the market of his own deliberate will, for the sake of carrying out some business; then, that the other also came there for some business. Therefore nothing of this kind happens by chance or fortune, but altogether for another cause.

units.la: Vetustissimi Philosophi de causis rerū differentes, fortunæ & casus inter causas haud meminerunt.
units.tr: The most ancient philosophers, discussing the causes of things, made no mention of Fortune and Chance among the causes.

units.la: Sed nullo negotio hæ rationes euertuntur. Nam casu & fortuna multa fieri palàm est. Etiamsi enim causa quaedam definita reddi possit, cur quis forum (ut in exemplo proposito haereamus) adierit, nimirum quod negotij aliquid perficere habuerit in animo: non tamen simul causa redditur, cur amicum ibi repererit. Quocirca fortunam, sive casum, necessum est concedere. Deinde, quod veteres casum et fortunam inter causas non numerarunt, id non sufficit ad comprobandum, quod casus et fortuna non sint. Quin potius arguuntur illi insciitiae atque negligentiae, qui de his agere praetermiserunt. Atque haud dubie possunt posteri aliqua nosse deprehendere, quae veteres ignorarunt. Dies diem docet. Quamuis nonnulli etiam ex veteribus, in quibus Empedocles, de fortuna disseruerunt. Liquet igitur ex his, errare eos qui casum et fortunam prorsus tollunt.
units.tr: But these arguments are overturned with no difficulty. For it is plain that many things happen by chance and fortune. Even if some definite cause can be given for why a man went to the market (to stay with the example proposed), namely that he had something in mind to accomplish in his business, yet at the same time no cause is given for why he found his friend there. Therefore we must concede fortune, or chance. Further, that the ancients did not count chance and fortune among causes is not enough to prove that chance and fortune do not exist. Rather, those who neglected to treat of these things are charged with ignorance and carelessness. And without doubt later generations can discover and know some things that the ancients did not know. Day teaches day. Also, some of the ancients, among whom was Empedocles, discussed fortune. It is clear, then, from these points that those are mistaken who altogether remove chance and fortune.

units.la: Secunda opinio: Quidam senserunt, omnia casu et fortuna fieri, adeoque ipsum cœlū casu voluit: deinde de et haec inferiora omnia similiter casu provenire. Revincuntur autem illi duabus rationibus.
units.tr: The second opinion: some held that all things happen by chance and fortune, and so the heaven itself was willed by chance; then these lower things likewise come about by chance. They are refuted by two reasons.

units.la: Prima: Testatur experientia, animalia, plantas, atque id genus, a definitis causis provenire. Neque enim ex quolibet semine nascitur quaelibet res: verum ex semine oliuae oliua, ex homine homo, atque ita deinceps. Igitur inferiora haec non fortuito, sed a definitis causis proveniunt. Quod si autem ne inseriora quidem ista proveniunt fortuito, quanto minus concedemus, coelum & sublimiora illa fortuito agi voluiq;?
units.tr: First: experience testifies that animals, plants, and the like arise from definite causes. For not every thing is born from any seed: from an olive seed an olive, from a man a man, and so on. Therefore these lower things come about not by chance but from definite causes. But if these lower things do not come about by chance, how much less shall we grant that heaven and those higher things are driven by chance and will?

units.la: Secunda: Tametsi in inferioribus his quaedam fortuna seu casu conspiciantur euenire: attamen in coelo nihil fortuito euenit, uerum omnia quaordinatissime & perpetua immutabiliq; ratione ibi geruntur. Quamobrem asserere, uel coelum uel inferiora haec omnia casu aut fortuna consistere, absurdum est.
units.tr: Second: although in these lower things some things are seen to happen by fortune or chance, yet in heaven nothing happens by chance, but all things there are carried on in the most orderly, perpetual, and unchangeable manner. Therefore to assert that either heaven or all these lower things stand by chance or fortune is absurd.

units.la: Tertia opinio: Quidam prudentiores dixerunt, fortunam esse quidem causam, sed humanae menti inexploratam, utpote in qua diuinum quiddam latere uideatur. Quocirca nonnulli, teste Satyrico, fortunam inter numina collocauerunt. Nullum numen (inquit) habes, si sit prudetia: sed te Nos facimus fortuna Deam coeloq; locamus.
units.tr: The third opinion: some wiser men said that fortune is indeed a cause, but one unexplored by the human mind, since something divine seems to lie hidden in it. Therefore some, as the satirist testifies, placed Fortune among the deities: "You have no deity," he says, "if there is prudence; but we make Fortune a goddess and set her in heaven."

units.la: Conclusio: Igitur ex his ad propositam quaestionem habeatur, fortunam siue casum esse.
units.tr: Conclusion: From these points, the answer to the question proposed should be taken to be that fortune or chance exists.

units.la: Christiane loquendo fortuna reuera locum non habebit. Nam quicquid fortuito euenire creditur, certas id habet causas, in Dei prouidentia positas, utpote quae non tantum intenta est rebus humanis uniuersaliter, uerum etiam singulis speciatim. Quod uerba Christi arguunt, ubi & passeres Deo curae esse, & singulos capitum nostrorum esse numeratos capillos, ac ne unum quidem ex his sine bona Dei uoluntate in terram cadere, affirmat.
units.tr: Speaking as a Christian, fortune will in truth have no place. For whatever is believed to happen by chance has certain causes, placed in God's providence, which is concerned not only with human affairs in general but also with each individual in particular. The words of Christ prove this, where he affirms both that sparrows are a care to God, and that the hairs of our heads are all numbered, and that not even one of them falls to the ground without the good will of God.

units.la: Quid est fortuna?
units.tr: What is fortune?

units.la: Videamus imprimis quibus modis aliqua fiant.
units.tr: Let us first see in what ways things come about.

units.la: 1. Prima diuisio eorum quae a natura fiunt: Quaedam fiunt semper & certo modo, quaedam crebro, quaedam raro.
units.tr: 1. The first division of things that come about by nature: some happen always and in a fixed way, some often, some rarely.

units.la: 2. Secunda diuisio: Alia fiunt ob certum finem, veluti quae natura, intellectu, aut voluntate fiunt: alia nequaquam fiunt ob certum finem.
units.tr: 2. The second division: some things happen for a fixed end, as those that come about by nature, by intellect, or by will; others do not happen for any fixed end at all.

units.la: 3. Tertia: Quaedam fiunt certo agentis propositu, quaedam fiunt praeter propositum agentis.
units.tr: 3. The third: some things come about by the agent's settled purpose, and some come about beyond the agent's purpose.

units.la: 4. Quarta: Causarum alia est per se causa, alia per accidens. Ex his animadverti potest, quae tribui fortunae recte queant, & quomodo eadem definiri debeat. Fortuna igitur est causa per accidens eorum quae raro fiunt, neque ob certum finem, & in habentibus propositum sive deliberationem. Et eventus fortuitus recte definitur eventus rarus praeter consilium & spem hominis, vel cuiuslibet efficientis. Exempla fortuitorum quotidie sunt obvia. Fortuitum est, si quis fodiens in horto, & fortasse fierere aliquid volens, thesaurum invenit.
units.tr: 4. The fourth: of causes, one is a cause in itself, another a cause by accident. From these points it can be seen which things can rightly be attributed to fortune, and how fortune ought to be defined. Fortune, then, is the accidental cause of those things that happen rarely, not for a fixed end, and in beings that have a purpose or deliberation. And a fortuitous event is rightly defined as a rare event beyond the counsel and expectation of a human being, or of any agent whatever. Examples of fortuitous events are everywhere to be seen every day. It is fortuitous if someone, digging in a garden and perhaps wanting to do something else, finds a treasure.

units.la: Quotuplex est fortuna?
units.tr: How many kinds of fortune are there?

units.la: Duplex. Bona, quae εὐτυχία dicitur, qua uidelicet aliquid boni contingit. Mala, ἀυτυχία, quando malum contingit.
units.tr: Two. Good fortune, which is called eutychia [εὐτυχία], when some good befalls someone. Bad fortune, dystychia [δυστυχία], when some evil befalls.

units.la: Quomodo differt fortuna a casu?
units.tr: How does fortune differ from chance?

units.la: Casus latius patet quam fortuna. Quicquid enim fortuna fit, idem & casu fit: at non econtrario.
units.tr: Chance has a wider range than fortune. For whatever happens by fortune also happens by chance, but not the reverse.

units.la: Fortuna tantùm in ijs spectatur, quæ possunt ratione atq; ex proposito agere. Quocirca homines proprie fortunatos atq; fœlices appellant. Casus uero consideratur tum in animalibus rationis expertibus, tum in rebus inanimatis. Cuius generis est, si equus, qui aliquandiu oberrauit in sylua, ad fontem excurrens reddit ad suum dominum:item tripes e sublimi deiectus cadit stans in pedes, ut insidere quisquam commodè possit.
units.tr: Fortune is considered only in those things that can act by reason and from purpose; hence people are called properly fortunate and happy. Chance, however, is considered both in animals lacking reason and in inanimate things. Of this kind is the case of a horse that has wandered about in a wood for some time and, running to a spring, returns to its master; likewise a three-legged stool thrown down from a height that falls standing on its feet, so that someone can sit on it conveniently.

units.la: Ad quam speciem causarum in fecunda diuisione positarum casus & fortuna referuntur?
units.tr: To which of the kinds of causes set out in the second division are chance and fortune referred?

units.la: Ad causam efficientem. Quamuis quia sunt tantùm causæ per accidens, posteriores erunt natura & uoluntate, quæ sunt causæ per se efficientes. Hæc de fortuna & casu hactenus.
units.tr: To the efficient cause. Although, because they are only causes by accident, they will be posterior to nature and will, which are causes efficient in themselves. So much for fortune and chance.

units.la: Sùntne plures causarum species principales, præter 4 illas fecunda diuisione enumeratas?
units.tr: Are there more principal kinds of causes than those four enumerated in the second division?

units.la: Minimè opus est plures constituere. Comprehenduntur namq; illis omnia quæ ad quæstiones de causis respondere apte possint. Cum enim quatuor his modis, omnis de causis quæstio proponi solet, nempe, Ex quo, Per quid, A quo, & Cuius gratia, plenè ostendunt quatuor illæ species, quomodo ad singulas respondeatur. Ad quæstionem Ex quo, adfertur
units.tr: There is no need to set up more. For all those things that can aptly answer questions about causes are comprehended under them. For when every question about causes is usually put in these four ways, namely, From what? By what? By whom? and For whose sake? those four kinds fully show how each question is answered. To the question From what? is assigned

units.la: materia: ad quæstionem Per quid, forma: ad quæstionem A' quo, efficiens: ad quæstionem Cuius gratia, finis. Atque physici quidem interest, ubiq; diligenter inuestigare has causarum species, ut rerum naturas perdiscat. Quinetiam quoties res postulat, demonstrationes appositas atque evidentes concinnat physicus per easdem causas. Itaq; sufficient quatuor illæ species, quod tribus rationibus iam ostendimus.
units.tr: matter; to the question By what? form; to the question By whom? the efficient cause; to the question For whose sake? the final cause. And it is indeed the business of the natural philosopher to investigate everywhere carefully these kinds of causes, so that he may learn the natures of things. Moreover, whenever the matter requires it, the natural philosopher constructs appropriate and evident demonstrations through these same causes. Therefore those four kinds are sufficient, as we have already shown by three arguments.

units.la: Quomodo comparantur causæ in- ter se, siue quænam est omnium præstantissima?
units.tr: How do the causes compare with one another, or which of all is the most excellent?

units.la: Causa finalis præstat omnibus. Nam omnes res naturales propter finem fiunt, atque ipsa natura propter finem operatur. Confirmatur id aliquot rationibus.
units.tr: The final cause excels all others. For all natural things come about for an end, and nature itself works for an end. This is confirmed by several arguments.

units.la: 1. Omnia quæ fiunt, aut fiunt casu, aut propter finem (quæcunque enim eueniunt præter intentionem finis, ea casu euenire par est concedamus.) Atqui impossibile est, ea quæ fiunt semper & frequenter, euenire casu. Igitur ea quæ fiunt semper uel frequenter, fiunt propter finem. His uero addamus: Omnia quæ fiunt secundum naturam, ea fiunt semper & frequenter. Igitur omnia quæ fiunt secundum naturam, propter finem fiunt.
units.tr: 1. Everything that comes about either comes about by chance or for an end (for whatever happens beyond the intention of an end, we must concede, happens by chance). But it is impossible that things which come about always or frequently happen by chance. Therefore those things which come about always or frequently come about for an end. To these we add: all things that come about according to nature come about always or frequently. Therefore all things that come about according to nature come about for an end.

units.la: 2. In quibuscunque consideratur aliquis finis, in ijs & priora & consequentia omnia propter finem nem agunt. Quo dato, recte sequitur: In quibuscunque consideratur finis, ea quando finem suum nacta fuerint, absoluta sunt: & quæ finem antecedunt, eius gratia fieri intelliguntur. Atqui res naturales semper moventur, donec tales euadant, quales fieri aptæ natæ sunt: hoc est, donec finem suum sortiantur, atque ita absoluantur. Igitur quæ in rerum naturalium productione ante finem fiunt, ea propter finem fiunt. Quare natura propter finem agit.
units.tr: 2. In whatever things an end is observed, in those all the earlier and later stages act for the sake of the end. Granted this, it rightly follows: in whatever things an end is observed, those are complete when they have attained their end, and what precedes the end is understood to be done for its sake. But natural things are always moved until they become such as they are fitted by nature to become, that is, until they obtain their end and so are completed. Therefore whatever precedes the end in the production of natural things is done for the sake of the end. Hence nature acts for an end.

units.la: §. Ars quædam perficit, quæ non perficit natura: veluti domum, & multa alia artificialia. Plerunque autem in omnibus ipsa naturam imitatur: ut in fictione imaginum. Sed in his quæ fiunt arte, antecedentia omnia fiunt propter finem. Igitur & in his quæ fiunt natura, antecedentia omnia fiunt propter finem. Enimuero in utrisque, tam naturalibus quàm artificialibus, priora & posteriora similiter se habent.
units.tr: §. Some art brings to completion what nature does not: for example a house, and many other artificial things. But for the most part art imitates nature itself in all things, as in the making of images. Yet in those things which are made by art, all the antecedent steps are done for an end. Therefore in those things which are made by nature too, all the antecedent steps are done for an end. Indeed, in both natural and artificial things, the earlier and later stages stand in the same relation.

units.la: 4. Manifeste videmus, animalia atque alias etiam res, quæ neque per artem, neque per disquisitionem, neq; per deliberationem operantur, agere propter aliquem finem. Quamobrem naturam quoque agere propter finem, perspicuum est. Antecedens probatur: Nam aranæ texunt telas ad capiendas muscas. Formicæ colligunt grana in æstate, quibus se alant hyeme. Hirundines extruunt nidos de terra ad se tutandum: & plantæ producŭt folia,tegendorum fructuum gratia: eædem radices ducunt in terram ad attrahendum humidum alimentum,&c.
units.tr: 4. We plainly see that animals and other things as well, which work neither by art, nor by inquiry, nor by deliberation, act for some end. Wherefore it is evident that nature too acts for an end. The antecedent is proved thus: spiders weave webs to catch flies. Ants gather grain in summer, by which they feed themselves in winter. Swallows build nests of earth to protect themselves, and plants put forth leaves for the sake of covering their fruits; the same roots run down into the earth to draw up moist nourishment, etc.

units.la: 5. Natura dicitur de materia atq; de forma,quod & ante demonstrauimus.Atqui forma est finis generationis, atq; ad finem hunc tendit aspiratq; materia.Igitur propter finem natura agit.
units.tr: 5. Nature is spoken of with respect to matter and form, as we have also shown before. But form is the end of generation, and matter tends and strives toward this end. Therefore nature acts for an end.

units.la: Obiectio prima ad euertendum, quòd natura agat pro- pter finem.
units.tr: First objection, to overturn the claim that nature acts for the sake of an end.

units.la: Si natura ageret propter finem, tum nunquam à fine producendo deficeret.Atqui natura sæpe deficit: veluti cum intendens producere aliquod animal,producit monstrum.Igitur natura non agit propter finem.
units.tr: If nature acted for the sake of an end, then it would never fall short of producing the end. But nature often falls short: for example, when intending to produce some animal, it produces a monster. Therefore nature does not act for the sake of an end.

units.la: Dilutio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Quemadmodum in artificialibus subinde peccat artifex,neq; præstat quod intendebat: ita etiam in rebus naturalibus aliquando impedimentum aliquod obuenit, quo minus destinatus finis sequatur. Verùm hæc causa non est sufficiens, cur negetur natu-ram propter finem agere.
units.tr: Just as in artificial things the craftsman sometimes errs and does not achieve what he intended, so also in natural things some hindrance occasionally intervenes, by which the intended end fails to follow. But this cause is not sufficient to deny that nature acts for the sake of an end.

units.la: Obiectio secunda eodem pertinens.
units.tr: Second objection bearing on the same point.

units.la: Natura non deliberat,Quare neq; agit propter finem.
units.tr: Nature does not deliberate; therefore neither does it act for the sake of an end.

units.la: Dilutio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Ad agendu propter finem non necessario præit deliberatio. Nam &c in artificialibus omnia fiunt ab artifice propter finē: & tamē is non semper deliberat,nisi forte alicubi cōtingeret,ipsum propter inscitiā dubitare,quasi de arte parum esset certus.
units.tr: Deliberation does not necessarily precede acting for an end. For even in artificial things everything is made by the craftsman for the sake of an end, and yet he does not always deliberate, unless perhaps it sometimes happens that he hesitates through ignorance, as if he were not quite certain of his craft.

units.la: Recte ergo ad quæstionem propositam responsum est,Causam finalem existere omnium præstantissimam, propterea quod natura ipsa propter finem agat omnia.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, the answer to the question proposed was given: that the final cause is the most excellent of all, because nature itself acts all things for an end.

units.la: Quænam est causa præstantior post causam finalem?
units.tr: What cause is more excellent after the final cause?

units.la: Forma. Nam de rebus naturalibus à forma atq; fine spectatur simplex necessitas.
units.tr: The form. For in natural things, simple necessity is observed from the form and the end.

units.la: Quomodo in rebus naturalibus spectatur necessitas, atque aliquid dicitur necessario fieri,uel non necessario?
units.tr: In what way is necessity observed in natural things, and is something said to happen necessarily or not necessarily?

units.la: Necessitas duplex est. Prima, Necessitas simplex siue absoluta. Et hæc dependet ex causis prioribus,nempe materia, forma efficiente: ueluti cum ratione materiæ dicimus hominem necessario esse corruptibilem, quia uidelicet ex iis rebus est, quarum qualitates sunt prorsus contrariæ. Ratione formæ dicimus necessario præditum esse ratione. Facit humana forma ut ita iudicemus. Et triangulum dicimus necessario habere tres angulos æquales duobus rectis. Ratione causæ efficientis dicimus necessario diei succedere noctem, propter motum uidelicet Solis.
units.tr: Necessity is twofold. The first is simple or absolute necessity, and this depends on the prior causes, namely matter and the efficient cause. For example, when we say by reason of matter that man is necessarily corruptible, because he is made of things whose qualities are wholly contrary. By reason of form we say that he is necessarily endowed with reason; the human form causes us to judge so. And we say that a triangle necessarily has its three angles equal to two right angles. By reason of the efficient cause we say that night necessarily follows day, namely on account of the motion of the sun.

units.la: Secunda, Necessitas ex conditione siue ex suppositione, quæ dependet ex causis posterioribus. ueluti cum dicimus: Si ista fiant, tum necessario talia quoq; sequentur: Si æger sic se habet, necessario morietur. Causæ posteriores sunt, forma atque finis, quatenus finis est generationis.
units.tr: The second is necessity from condition or supposition, which depends on the posterior causes. As when we say: "If these things come about, then such things will necessarily follow too. If the sick man is in such a state, he will necessarily die." The posterior causes are the form and the end, insofar as the end is the end of generation.

units.la: His ita expositis, respondetur ad quæstionem duabus propositionibus.
units.tr: With these things thus explained, the question is answered by two propositions.

units.la: Prima propositio: Necessitas simplex non spectatur in rebus naturalibus ex materia, sed tantum necessitas ex conditione. Probatur: Nam tametsi materia est, non statim necesse est rem naturalem existere: sed è diuerso, si res naturalis sit, materia quoque ut sit necesse est. Nam si quis quærat, propter quid ignis uel similis quæpiam res naturalis existat: non satis apte respondebitur, Quia materia est. At è diuerso, si quis roget, unde ibi materia sit: rectè respondebitur, Quia ignis uel similis quæpiam res naturalis ibi est. In artificialibus ista necessitas similiter conspicitur. Nam etiamsi in loco aliquo sint ligna & lapides, non tamen necesse est, domum quoque ibi existere: uerum è diuerso, si domus est, necessum [?] quidem est, tum ligna, tum lapides ibi adesse.
units.tr: The first proposition: simple necessity is not observed in natural things from matter, but only necessity from condition. It is proved thus. Although there is matter, it is not at once necessary that the natural thing exist; but conversely, if the natural thing is, it is necessary that the matter be there too. For if someone asks why fire, or some similar natural thing, exists, one will not answer aptly, "because there is matter." But conversely, if someone asks where the matter there comes from, one will rightly answer, "because fire, or some similar natural thing, is there." In artificial things this necessity is similarly seen. For even if there are wood and stones in some place, it is not necessary that a house also exist there; but conversely, if there is a house, it is indeed necessary that both wood and stones be present there.

units.la: Secunda propositio : Necessitas simplex spectatur in rebus naturalibus à forma & fine. Probatur : Nam forma & fine existente ( est autem forma in rebus naturalibus finis , ) materia & motus materiæ ut sint aut fuerint necesse est : uerùm materia existente & eius motibus , non protinus necesse est & rem naturalem existere. In disciplinis necessitas ista similiter conspicitur . Sicut enim forma existēte,necessum est eius esse dispositiones: & non econtrario,dispositionibus existentibus, necesse est formam esse. ita in disciplinis quoq;, præmissis existentibus, necessum est esse conclusionem, & quidem ex præmissis necessarijs conclusionem itidem necessariam. Sed non econtrario, conclusione existente, necessum est esse præmissas : & conclusione necessaria,non oportet præmissas esse necessarias.
units.tr: The second proposition: simple necessity is observed in natural things from the form and the end. It is proved thus. When the form and the end exist (and in natural things the form is the end), matter and the motion of matter necessarily are, or have been. But with matter and its motions existing, it does not at once follow that the natural thing exists. This necessity is similarly seen in the disciplines. For just as, with the form existing, its dispositions must be, and not conversely (with the dispositions existing, the form must be), so too in the disciplines, with the premises existing, the conclusion must be, and indeed from necessary premises a conclusion likewise necessary. But not conversely: with the conclusion existing, the premises must be; and with a necessary conclusion, the premises need not be necessary.

units.la: Ex his omnibus manifestum iam cuadit, inter causas præcellere quidem finem, deinde uero & formam : ideoq; in rebus naturalibus has duas causas diligentissimè obseruari à physico debere.Quocirca & definitiones rerum naturalium à forma & fine potissimum ducuntur. Hæc de causis sufficiunt : superest de motu dicamus.
units.tr: From all these things it is now clear that among causes the end indeed excels, and then the form. Therefore in natural things the physicist ought to observe these two causes most diligently. Hence also the definitions of natural things are chiefly derived from form and end. These things suffice concerning causes; it remains that we speak of motion.

units.la: Quare nunc agendum est de motu?
units.tr: Why must we now treat of motion?

units.la: Tres sunt rationes. Prima: Initio diximus, subiectum huius partis philosophiae esse Ens naturale mobile. Quomodo vero intelligat quispiam, quid sit Ens mobile, nisi motus cognitionem habeat?
units.tr: There are three reasons. The first: at the beginning we said that the subject of this part of philosophy is natural mobile being. But how could anyone understand what mobile being is, unless he has knowledge of motion?

units.la: Secunda: Natura definitur principium motus & quietis. Quare quicunq; de natura volet disputare, necessario debet, quid sit motus, quaeq; ad motum pertineant, scire.
units.tr: The second: nature is defined as the principle of motion and rest. Therefore whoever wishes to dispute about nature must necessarily know what motion is, and what pertains to motion.

units.la: Tertia: Quae communia sunt omnibus rebus naturalibus, ea prius tractari par est, quam veniatur ad explicationem propriorum ac singularium. Atqui motus & quae motui sunt adiuncta, in omnium rerum naturalium productione spectantur communiter (ut enim principium non potest intelligi sine actione, ita actio sine motu.) Igitur opportunum est hoc loco de motu agamus.
units.tr: The third: those things which are common to all natural things ought to be treated before we come to the explanation of the proper and particular ones. But motion, and the things adjoined to motion, are observed commonly in the production of all natural things (for as a principle cannot be understood without action, so action cannot be understood without motion). Therefore it is fitting that we speak of motion at this point.

units.la: Quid est motus?
units.tr: What is motion?

units.la: Est actus eius quod est potentia, quatenus est mobile, vel crassius: Motus est progressus ab una forma ad aliam: est transmutatio ab imperfecto ad persectum, vel rursus a perfecto ad imperfectum. Sic generatio est actus eius quod generabile est, & quatenus generabile est. Et corruptio est actus eius quod corrumpi potest, & quatenus ipsum tale est. Augmentatio est actus eius quod augeri potest. Alteratio est actus eius quod alterabile est.
units.tr: It is the act of that which is in potency, insofar as it is mobile; or, more crudely: motion is progress from one form to another; it is a change from the imperfect to the perfect, or again from the perfect to the imperfect. Thus generation is the act of that which is generable, insofar as it is generable. And corruption is the act of that which can be corrupted, insofar as it is such. Augmentation is the act of that which can be augmented. Alteration is the act of that which is alterable.

units.la: Quare motum uocas actum?
units.tr: Why do you call motion an act?

units.la: Quia id quo aliquid fit actu, quod prius tantum erat potentia, recte dicitur quidem actus. Sed tum quidem aliquid fit actu, quando illud quod tantum est potentia, mouetur ut possit actu existere. Igitur motus est actus siue ἐντελέχεια.
units.tr: Because that by which something becomes actual, which before was only potential, is rightly called an act. Something becomes actual when that which is only potential is moved so that it can actually exist. Motion is therefore the act, or entelechy [ἐντελέχεια], of the potential.

units.la: Cur dicis actum eius quod est potentia?
units.tr: Why do you call it the act of that which is potential?

units.la: Hac de causa: Omnis actus, eius est actus in quo semper inuenitur. Atqui motus semper inuenitur in eo quod est potentia: naturaliter enim, quod potentia est, enititur ac laborat ut existat actu. Igitur motus est actus eius quod est potentia. Ad comprobationem maioris hoc esto exemplum: Lumen accipere transmittere q; actus est corporis diaphani, transparentis: quale est uitrum, aqua, &c. Huic autem corpori simul inest idem ille actus per naturam. Quod si aliunde adueniat impedimentum, quo minus lumen transmittat, id accidentarium est & extraordinarium, non naturale. Physici autem eaconsiderant, quae rei cuiq; sua natura conueniunt.
units.tr: For this reason. Every act is the act of that in which it is always found. But motion is always found in that which is potential, for by nature what is potential strives and labours to become actual. Therefore motion is the act of that which is potential. As an example of the major premise, take the receiving and transmitting of light, which is the act of a diaphanous body, one that is transparent, such as glass, water, and so on. The same act is naturally present in such a body at the same time. If some hindrance from elsewhere prevents it from transmitting light, that is accidental and extraordinary, not natural. Natural philosophers, however, consider those things that belong to each thing by its nature.

units.la: Cur dicis, Quatenus est mobile?
units.tr: Why do you say, insofar as it is mobile?

units.la: Quod si mobile seu motionis capax non esset, profecto actus motionis in eo loco nunquam haberet. In summa, Motus est quiddam inter potentiam & actum. Quod enim tantum est potentia, non movetur, sed mobile est. Quod vero actu est, similiter non movetur, sed motum est. Quod autem medio modo se habet inter potentiam & actum, ac partim quidem est potentia, partim vero est actu, id moveri debet. Sic aqua movetur, quæ cum prius potentia tantum fuerit calida, nunc incipit calorem recipere: sensim vero magis magisq; alteratur, donec dicatur actu calida. Atque huc quidem pertinent divisiones, quas Aristoteles digerit libro 3. de Auscultatione physica, cap.1. ante motus definitionem. Ea sic habent. Potentia, δυνάμεις. Eorum quae mutatur, quaedam mutantur secundum Substantiam. Quantitatē. Qualitatē. Locum. Vnde totidē sunt motus species, quot sunt res secundum quas fit motus. Antequā uero aliquid moueatur, est in potētia ad actū aut Perfectu. Imperfectu. Quare consideratur in Substantia, forma & priuatio. Quantitate, perfecta et imperfecta. Qualitate, albedo, nigredo. Loci mutatione sursum, deorsum. Eorum quæ sunt, alia Actu, ἐντελε-χείᾳ. Horum autem aliud est Substantia. Quantitas. Qualitas. Ad aliquid, vel Alterius prædicamenti. Horum autem quædam dicuntur secun-dum Excessum. Defectum. Actionem. Passionem. 4 Motium. [?] Mobile. Ex his diuisionibus percipi clarius possunt, quae de definitione motus hucusq; dicta sunt. Est autem aptissima ratio colligendi definitiones, si uariae definitiones ob oculos sint positae, in quibus species atq; differentiae congeruntur. Quod ex ijs quoque, quae ad parandam definitionem fortunae suprà sunt posita, potest intelligi. Et non tantum definitio motus, uerumetiam alia quae sequuntur, perspicua ex his euadent.
units.tr: Because if a thing were not mobile, or capable of motion, the act of motion would never be present in it. In sum, motion is something between potency and act. What is merely potential is not moving but movable; what is actual is likewise not moving but moved. What stands in a middle state between potency and act, being partly potential and partly actual, must be in motion. Thus water is moved: when before it was only potentially warm, it now begins to receive heat, and gradually and by degrees it is altered until it is said to be actually warm. To this belong the divisions which Aristotle sets out in the third book of the Physics, chapter 1, before the definition of motion. They stand thus. Potency, [δυνάμεις]. Of the things that are changed, some are changed in substance, in quantity, in quality, in place. Hence there are as many species of motion as there are respects in which motion occurs. Before anything is moved, it is in potency to act or to perfection, or to imperfection. Hence in substance one considers form and privation; in quantity, perfect and imperfect; in quality, whiteness and blackness; in change of place, upward and downward. Of the things that exist, some are in act, [ἐντελέχεια]. Of these, one is substance, quantity, quality, relation, or belongs to another category. Some of these are said to be according to excess, deficiency, action, passion, the moving, and the movable. From these divisions the points made so far about the definition of motion can be understood more clearly. Indeed the most suitable method of gathering definitions is to set several definitions before the eyes, in which species and differences are brought together. This can also be understood from what has been laid down above for preparing a definition. And not only the definition of motion, but the other things that follow will become clear from these points.

units.la: Suntne aliae definitiones motus?
units.tr: Are there other definitions of motion?

units.la: Sunt. Quidam enim ex ueteribus, imprimis Pythagorici, definiuerunt, motum esse uarietatem, seu alterationem: quandoquidem quod mouetur, semper alio atque alio modo se habet.
units.tr: There are. Some of the ancients, above all the Pythagoreans, defined motion as variation or alteration, since whatever is moved is always in one condition after another.

units.la: Alij, esse inaequalitatem: quia quod mouetur, semper magis magisq; accedit ad terminum, id est, persectionem, secundum quam actu dicitur esse tale vel tale.
units.tr: Others defined it as inequality, because what is moved always draws nearer and nearer to its end, that is, to its perfection, according to which it is said to be actually such and such.

units.la: Nonnulli motum dixerunt esse non Ens: quia nimirum quod mouetur, dum adhuc mouetur, non habet id ad quod mouetur, nondumq; obtinet formam ad quam contendit. Sed quoniam hae definitiones non ita proprie explicant naturam ipsius motus, uti prima quam posuimus, ideo merito reijcientur.
units.tr: Some have said that motion is non-being, because whatever is moved, while it is still moving, does not yet have that to which it is moving, and does not yet possess the form towards which it strives. But since these definitions do not explain the nature of motion itself as properly as the first one we have laid down, they will rightly be rejected.

units.la: Da aliam definitionem, si quam ha- bes, quae recipi possit?
units.tr: Give another definition, if you have one, that can be accepted.

units.la: Motus est actus eius quod mobile est, quatenus mobile est. Quæ definitio se habet ad primam, sicut materialis definitio ad formalem, aut sicut conclusio ad præmissas. Quo autem hæc definitio clarius intelligatur, uideamus, motus cuiusnā sit actus, mouentis'ne, an tantum mobilis. Atqui demonstrari potest, motum accidere etiam ipsi mouenti, idq; hoc pacto : Omne quod prius est potentia, post uero est actu, quodammodo mouetur. Atqui mouens inuenitur prius mouens potentia, post uero mouens actu (dictum namq; est, motum esse actum eius quod est potentia.) Igitur mouens etiam mouetur. Contingit autem id non ea ratione, qua simpliciter est mouens: sed qua mouet aliud quidpiam, quod tangendo mouetur. Hoc ipsum enim dum mouetur, fieri non poteft (quandoquidem contactu fit motus) quin illud etiam mouens simul moueatur. Siquidem corpora quibus tactus est mutuus, simul et agere & pati inter se alienum non est. His igitur ita positis, quòd ut[?] delicet mouens moueatur, recte definitur motus, quòd fit actus eius quod mobile est, quatenus mobile est.
units.tr: Motion is the act of that which is movable, insofar as it is movable. This definition relates to the first as a material definition relates to a formal one, or as a conclusion relates to its premises. To understand this definition more clearly, let us see whose act motion is: of the mover, or only of the movable. Now it can be shown that motion belongs also to the mover, and this way: everything that is first potential and afterwards actual is in some sense moved. But the mover is first a mover in potency and afterwards a mover in act (for it has been said that motion is the act of what is potential). Therefore the mover is also moved. This happens, however, not by the reason by which it is simply a mover, but by the reason by which it moves something else, which is moved by touching. For while that other thing is being moved, which cannot happen (since motion comes about by contact) without the mover being moved at the same time. Indeed, when bodies touch one another mutually, it is not strange that they both act and are acted upon at once. Therefore, with these things so laid down, that the mover is moved as well, motion is rightly defined as the act of that which is movable, insofar as it is movable.

units.la: In quo tanquam subiecto conside- ratur motus, in mouente'ne, an in mobili?
units.tr: In which does motion, as in its subject, get considered: in the mover or in the moved?

units.la: Motus in mobili est tanquam subiecto. Probatur. Cum enim motus fit actus eius quod mobile est, utiq; in mobili potissimum consideratur, etiamsi à mouente
units.tr: Motion is in the moved, as in its subject. This is proved: since motion is the act of that which is movable, it is considered chiefly in the movable, even though it is induced by some mover.

units.la: d ꝭ mouente quopiam inductus.Ac frustra quidem aget mouens,nisi ipsum mobile sit ad motu dispositum.
units.tr: And the mover would act in vain unless the movable itself were disposed to motion.

units.la: Estne unus idemq; actus & mo- uentis & mobilis?
units.tr: Is there one and the same act of both the mover and the movable?

units.la: Est, idq; hac ratione demonstratur: Quorum unum producit actum, alterum vero recipit, eorundem oportet unum eundemq; esse actum communem. Atqui moues producit actum, mobile vero eum recipit. Igitur & mouentis & mobilis unus idemq; actus communis existit. Nec dicitur mouens, nisi respectu alicuius mouentis. Licet vero actus tam mouentis quam mobilis, sit reipsa tantum unus: ratione tamen distinguuntur, ac duo actus sunt. Quandoquidem actus ut est a mouente, dicitur actio: ut vero a mobili, dicitur passio.
units.tr: There is, and this is shown by the following reasoning: of two things, one of which produces an act and the other receives it, there must be one and the same common act. But the mover produces the act, and the movable receives it. Therefore there exists one and the same common act of the mover and of the movable. Nor is anything called a mover except in relation to something moved. Although the act of the mover and that of the movable is really only one, it is nonetheless distinguished by reason, and there are two acts. For insofar as the act is from the mover, it is called action; but insofar as it is in the movable, it is called passion.

units.la: An actio & passio sunt actus reipsa diuersi, quorum unus specta- tur in agente, alter in patiente?
units.tr: Are action and passion really different acts, one of which is regarded in the agent and the other in the patient?

units.la: Actio & passio non sunt actus reipsa diuersi. Probatur. Si enim essent diuersi, tunc aut uterque constitueretur in agente, aut uterq; in patiente: aut actio quidem in agente, & passio in patiente: aut contrario modo actio in patiente, & passio in agente. Atqui nullum horum potest astrui. Igitur actio & passio non sunt actus reipsa diuersi. Minor pro-batur, batur, eundo per singula membra, quæ in maiore sunt expressa.
units.tr: Action and passion are not really different acts. This is proved: for if they were different, then either each would be located in the agent, or each in the patient; or action would be in the agent and passion in the patient; or, conversely, action in the patient and passion in the agent. But none of these can be maintained. Therefore action and passion are not really different acts. The minor premise is proved by going through the individual members set out in the major premise.

units.la: 1. Non possunt actio & passio consistere simul in agente. id enim si fieret, necesse esset, omne movens indesinenter & movere & moveri, ipsum vero patiens seu mobile nunquam moveri. Hæc autem absurda sunt.
units.tr: 1. Action and passion cannot exist together in the agent. For if they did, it would be necessary that every mover should unceasingly both move and be moved, while the patient or movable itself would never be moved. But these things are absurd.

units.la: 2. Non possunt actio & passio simul constitui in patiente. Hoc enim si daretur, omne mobile moueretur & simul moveret, movens autem esset otiosum. Quorum illud quidem perinde ridiculum est, ac si diceres: Quicunque docetur, is docetur atque etiam docet. Deinde sequeretur, idem duobus diversis motibus ad eundem movieri terminum: quod profecto fieri nequit.
units.tr: 2. Action and passion cannot be placed together in the patient. For if this were granted, every movable would be moved and at the same time would move, while the mover would be idle. The first is as ridiculous as if you were to say: whoever is taught, is taught and also teaches. Then it would follow that the same thing is moved to the same terminus by two different motions, which certainly cannot happen.

units.la: 3. Neque constitui potest actio simpliciter in agente, neque passio simpliciter in patiente. Sequeretur enim inde, omne patiens moveri, similiter & omne agens moveri: Etenim utrumque, patiens inquam & agens, haberet actum suum in potentia. Quo quidem pacto unicuique separatim, hinc videlicet moveti seu agenti, inde mobili seu patienti, duplex actio tribuetur: quod itidem absurdum.
units.tr: 3. Action cannot be placed simply in the agent, nor passion simply in the patient. For it would follow that every patient is moved, and likewise every agent is moved; for each, the patient and the agent, I mean, would have its act in potency. In this way a double action would be assigned to each separately: on one side to the mover or agent, on the other to the movable or patient. This too is absurd.

units.la: 4. Non constituetur actio in patiente, neque passio in agente. Eo enim posito, omne patiens ageret, omne vero agens pateretur. Vtrumque a ratione alienum est: atque pugnare hæc, satis declarat ipsa vocabulorum significatio. RelinRelinquitur ergo, actionem & passionem non esse actus reipsa diversos, sed unum tantum, licet distinguantur ratione seu intellectu. Quæ in contrarium possint objici, non difficile est diluere. Hæc vero ad intelligendum, quid proprie sit motus, in præsenti sufficient. Porro ad percipiendum cætera quæ de motu explicari adhuc debet, necessum est, de infinito, de loco, & per contrarium de vacuo, de tempore, quædam præmittamus.
units.tr: 4. Action will not be placed in the patient, nor passion in the agent. For if this were posited, every patient would act, and every agent would suffer. Both are foreign to reason, and the very meaning of the words sufficiently shows that they contradict each other. It remains, therefore, that action and passion are not really different acts, but only one, although they are distinguished by reason or intellect. The objections that may be raised to the contrary are not hard to dissolve. For the present, these points suffice for understanding what motion properly is. Further, to grasp the remaining things still to be explained about motion, we must first premise some things about the infinite, about place, and, by way of contrast, about the void, and about time.

units.la: DE INFINITO.
units.tr: ON THE INFINITE.

units.la: Quare nunc agendum de Infinito?
units.tr: Why must we now treat of the infinite?

units.la: PRimò: Cum hæc pars philosophiæ consideret motum, magnitudines, tempus, atque de his quæri soleat, finitáne sint an infinita: consentaneum sanè est, de infinito disputationem instituí.
units.tr: First: since this part of philosophy considers motion, magnitudes and time, and it is customary to ask about these whether they are finite or infinite, it is certainly fitting that a discussion of the infinite be undertaken.

units.la: Secundò: Quotquot ferè hactenus physici de naturalibus disseruerunt, sermonem admiscuerunt de infinito. Quamobrem tractatio de infinito præteriri à nobis nullo modo potest.
units.tr: Second: almost all the natural philosophers who have so far discussed natural things have mixed talk of the infinite into their accounts. Therefore we can in no way pass over the treatment of the infinite.

units.la: AN SIT INFINITVM?
units.tr: IS THERE AN INFINITE?

units.la: Variæ quidem rationes atq; opiniones à veteribus sunt relatæ: nos recensebimus primo loco, quæ in partem affirmativam conveniunt: secundo, quæ in partem negativam: inde conclusionem subiciemus.
units.tr: Various arguments and opinions have indeed been handed down by the ancients. We shall first recount those that agree on the affirmative side, second those on the negative side, and then add the conclusion.

units.la: Pars affirmatiua?
units.tr: The affirmative side?

units.la: Ex ijs qui non satis physice locuti sunt,
units.tr: Among those who have not spoken sufficiently physically:

units.la: 1. Pythagorici posuerunt, infinitum esse quoddam principium, non autem ut accidens alicui alteri naturæ, sed quoddam per se existens. Quocirca numerum parem & quantitates constituebant rerum substantias, utpote in quibus incrementum perpetuo considerari queat.
units.tr: 1. The Pythagoreans held that the infinite is a certain principle, not however as an accident of some other nature, but as something existing through itself. Hence they constituted the even number and quantities as the substances of things, inasmuch as increase can be perpetually considered in them.

units.la: 2. Platonici eodem modo posuerunt, infinitum esse quoddam principium, & quidem per se existens. In hoc tamen dissenserunt à prioribus, quòd ubi illi infinitum constituerunt tantum in rebus sensibilibus, & intra cœlum atq; in terra cōstitutis: hi, Platonici inquam, etiam in insensibilibus & intelligibilibus & ubiq;. Deinde illi quidem tantum parem numerum recensuerunt infinitum, Platonici verò etiam imparem.
units.tr: 2. The Platonists likewise held that the infinite is a certain principle, and indeed one existing through itself. They differed from the former in this: whereas those placed the infinite only in sensible things, and in things constituted within the heavens and on the earth, these, I say the Platonists, placed it also in insensible and intelligible things, and everywhere. Moreover, the former counted only the even number as infinite, but the Platonists counted the odd as well.

units.la: Cæterum ex ijs qui physice locuti sunt,
units.tr: But among those who spoke physically:

units.la: 1. Anaximander cum nonnullis aliis constituit infinitum esse quoddam principium, sed tanquam accidens, alicui subiecto inhærens. Itaq; aliqui posuerunt infinitum in igne ut in subiecto, aliqui in aere ut in subiecto: ipse autem Anaximander in quodam corpore medio, quod densius sit igne, & tamen subtilius aere.
units.tr: 1. Anaximander, with some others, held that the infinite is a certain principle, but as an accident inhering in some subject. Hence some placed the infinite in fire as in a subject, some in air as in a subject; but Anaximander himself placed it in a certain intermediate body, which is denser than fire and yet finer than air.

units.la: 2. Democritus posuit infinita corpuscula ἄτομα pro principijs, ex quibus omnia fierent. Illa autem simul iuncta dicebat magnitudine esse infinita: & sicut omnia ex ijs fierent, ita ipsa ex se inuicem minime conflari.
units.tr: 2. Democritus posited infinite corpuscles, atoms, as the principles from which all things are made. He said that these, joined together, were infinite in magnitude, and just as all things are made from them, so they themselves are in no way compounded from one another.

units.la: §. Anaxagoras infinita similaria ἄτομα [?] posuit, afferens omnia esse in omnibus, & omnia fieri ex omnibus, diuino autem intellectu procurari omnium ab omnibus segregationem.
units.tr: §. Anaxagoras posited infinite similar parts, asserting that all things are in all things, and all things are made from all things, but that the separation of all things from all is brought about by divine intellect.

units.la: Etsi uero omnes hi de infinito disputantes uaria pronunciarunt, tamen communi sensu omnes definierunt: Primo, Esse infinitum quoddam principium. idq; non abs re: quia si haberet principium, intelligeretur etiam habere finem: si autem haberet finem, nequaquam dici posset infinitum. Quare infinitum necessario principium esse constituitur. Secundo, Esse ingenitum et incorruptibile. quod ex eo fluit, quod constituitur esse principium. Si namq; est principium, plane oportet ingenitum quoq; & incorruptibile existat. Tertio, Quod continet & gubernet omnia. Quod quidem primi principij proprium esse uidetur. Quarto, Quod sit quiddam diuinum. Revera enim, quod ingenitum est incorruptibileq;, id diuinum quiddam esse apparet. In his igitur ueteres philosophi infinitu constituentes, inter se de infinito consenserunt, in cæteris autem aliter atq; aliter de infinito pronunciauerunt.
units.tr: Although all these men who disputed about the infinite pronounced various things, yet all defined it in a common sense. First, that the infinite is a certain principle; and this not without reason: for if it had a principle, it would be understood to have an end too; but if it had an end, it could by no means be called infinite. Hence it is necessarily established that the infinite is a principle. Second, that it is unbegotten and incorruptible. This follows from the fact that it is established to be a principle: for if it is a principle, it must plainly also be unbegotten and incorruptible. Third, that it contains and governs all things. This seems indeed to be proper to the first principle. Fourth, that it is something divine. For that which is unbegotten and incorruptible appears to be something divine. In these matters, therefore, the ancient philosophers, positing the infinite, agreed among themselves about the infinite, but in other respects they pronounced about the infinite differently and differently.

units.la: Pars negatiua.
units.tr: The negative part.

units.la: Rursus autem omnes Philosophi, qui posuerunt principia rerum naturalium et numero & magnitudine finita, ij infinito in rebus sensibilibus locum non reliquerunt, hoc est, neq; in principijs ipsis, neque in rebus quæ ex ijsdem constant.
units.tr: Again, all philosophers who have posited the principles of natural things as finite in number and magnitude have left no place for the infinite in sensible things, that is, neither in the principles themselves nor in the things that are composed of them.

units.la: Conclusio.
units.tr: Conclusion.

units.la: Infinitum esse concedimus. Quæ conclusio pluribus rationibus confirmatur.
units.tr: We grant that the infinite exists. This conclusion is confirmed by several arguments.

units.la: 1. A' consideratione temporis. Nam tempus sem[?] per fuit & semper erit: quare est infinitum. Caeterum accipi debent hæ rationes ex sententia eorum philosophorum, qui arbitrati sunt mundum fuisse ab æterno atq; æternum manere, necnon partium temporis atq; quarumuis rerum naturalium per generationem & corruptionem fieri perpetuam successionem. In qua opinione fuit ipse Aristoteles.
units.tr: 1. From the consideration of time. For time always was and always will be, so it is infinite. These arguments must, however, be taken according to the opinion of those philosophers who held that the world has existed from eternity and remains eternal, and that parts of time and of any natural things go through a perpetual succession by generation and corruption. Aristotle himself held this opinion.

units.la: 2. A' divisione magnitudinum in infinitum. Mathematici enim ponunt magnitudines quæ in infinitum augeri queant: ergo infinitum est.
units.tr: 2. From the division of magnitudes into infinity. For mathematicians posit magnitudes that can be increased to infinity; therefore the infinite exists.

units.la: 3. Ex perpetuitate generationis & corruptionis. Si non esset infinitum, non posset dici quod generatio & corruptio in infinitum durarent, sed cessare deberent: quod intelligi nullo modo potest, ex sententia videlicet veterum philosophorum, de quibus jam diximus.
units.tr: 3. From the perpetuity of generation and corruption. If there were no infinite, it could not be said that generation and corruption last into infinity; rather they would have to cease. This cannot be understood in any way, namely according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers of whom we have just spoken.

units.la: 4. Ex apparenti ratione finiti. Nam ubicunq; datur aliquod finitum, necesse est id ad aliquod aliud finiri. Atqui si eo pacto semper ab uno finito ad aliud finitum proceditur, necessum est tandem in infinitum abeatur.
units.tr: 4. From the apparent reasoning about the finite. For wherever some finite thing is given, it must be bounded by some other finite thing. But if in this way one always proceeds from one finite thing to another finite thing, it must at last come to the infinite.

units.la: 5. Ab apprehensione intellectus. Intellectus apprehendere & intelligere nunquam definit. Et quocunque finito sive secundum multitudinem, sive secundum magnitudinem dato, intellectus apprehendit aliquid addi posse. Quinetiā intellectus apprehendit extra cœlum infinitum spacium. Quocirca iudicio intellectus infinitum constituitur.
units.tr: 5. From the apprehension of the intellect. The intellect never ceases to apprehend and to understand. And to whatever finite thing is given, whether in multitude or in magnitude, the intellect apprehends that something can be added. Moreover, the intellect apprehends an infinite space beyond the heavens. Hence by the judgement of the intellect the infinite is established.

units.la: Hæ igitur rationes satis probare uidentur, infinitum esse. Reuera autem, sicut si negetur infinitum, multa absurda uidentur sequi: ita etiam dum coceditur infinitum, perplexæ inde oriuntur quæstiones. Perdifficile namque est definire, an uspiam sit reipsa infinitum: deinde, an sit substantia, an accidens. Veruntamen quando philosophi naturalis interest considerare, num sit magnitudo aliqua sensibilis infinita, nos infinitum esse in præsenti largiamur. Quam vero efficaces sint præcedentes rationes, infinitum esse probantes, sub fine huius disputationis, etiam ex ipsius Aristotelis sententia explicabimus.
units.tr: These arguments therefore seem sufficiently to prove that the infinite exists. Indeed, just as, if the infinite is denied, many absurdities seem to follow, so also, while the infinite is granted, perplexing questions arise from it. For it is exceedingly difficult to define whether anywhere in reality there is an infinite, and then whether it is a substance or an accident. Nevertheless, since it is the business of the natural philosopher to consider whether there is some infinite sensible magnitude, let us for the present grant that the infinite exists. How effective the preceding arguments proving that the infinite exists are, we shall explain near the end of this discussion, also according to Aristotle's own opinion.

units.la: QVID SIT INFINITVM. Da definitionem nominis Infiniti.
units.tr: WHAT THE INFINITE IS. Give the definition of the name "infinite."

units.la: Infinitum quatuor modis dicitur.
units.tr: The infinite is spoken of in four ways.

units.la: 1. Quod per se tale est, ut secundū naturam suam pertransiri pertrāsiri seu finiri nequeat. Quo pacto vox quoq; dicitur invisibilis, quia videri nullo modo potest.
units.tr: 1. That which is of such a nature that, by its own nature, it cannot be traversed or brought to an end. In this way the word "invisible" is also used, because it cannot be seen in any way.

units.la: 2. Quod sua quidem natura pertransiri posset: quo tamen id minus fiat, impedimetum aliunde obvenit. Ita profunditatem maris dicimus infinitam, atq; iter ad nostros antipodes infinitum.
units.tr: 2. That which in its own nature could be traversed, but which is prevented from being so by an obstacle from elsewhere. Thus we call the depth of the sea infinite, and the route to our antipodes infinite.

units.la: 3. Infinitum est, quod aptum est ut pertranseatur, minime tamen ad finem eius venitur. Sic lineà quaedam infinita potest constitui. Atque hac significatione proprie accipitur infinitum, ut præsenti seruit disputationi.
units.tr: 3. The infinite is that which is fit to be traversed, yet its end is never reached. Thus some line can be conceived as infinite. It is in this sense that the infinite is properly taken, as serves the present discussion.

units.la: 4. Infinitum dicitur aliquid vel propter additionem, quae fieri potest, ut numeri: vel propter divisionem, ut magnitudines: vel propter utrumque, ut tempus.
units.tr: 4. Something is called infinite either on account of addition, which can be carried out, as with numbers; or on account of division, as with magnitudes; or on account of both, as with time.

units.la: Da definitionem rei.
units.tr: Give the definition of the thing.

units.la: Non ita promptum est dare: tamen inuestigando conabimur aliquam invenire. Prius tamen oportet discutiamus, num Infinitum sit substātia, sive aliquid per se existens, à sensibilibus separatum: an potius sit accidens, alicui sensibili corpori actu conveniens.
units.tr: It is not so easy to give; nevertheless, by inquiring, we shall try to find one. First, however, we must examine whether the infinite is a substance, that is, something existing through itself and separated from sensible things, or rather an accident, actually belonging to some sensible body.

units.la: Est'ne Infinitum substantia per se exi- stens, atq; aliquid à rebus sensi- bilibus separatum?
units.tr: Is the infinite a substance existing through itself and separated from sensible things?

units.la: Veteres quidem illi philosophi, quos paulo ante dixi mus minus physicè locutos, arbitrati sunt, infinitum esse aliquid per se existens, à sensibilibus separatum. Atqui nullo modo potest ita habere: quod probatur duabus rationibus.
units.tr: Those ancient philosophers whom we have just mentioned, speaking less physically, thought that the infinite is something existing through itself and separated from sensible things. But in no way can it be so, which is proved by two arguments.

units.la: 1. Si erit substantia, erit utique & indiuisibile (ut enim aliquid sit diuisibile, oportet magnitudinem in eo spectari, aut multitudinem, ac proinde accidens.) Si autem est indiuisibile, non erit infinitum, aut certè tantum primo modo, de quo hic non agimus. Quare infinitum non est quiddam per se existens.
units.tr: 1. If it were a substance, it would certainly also be indivisible (for in order for something to be divisible, a magnitude or a multitude must be considered in it, and therefore it is an accident). But if it is indivisible, it will not be infinite, or at least only in the first sense, with which we are not dealing here. Therefore the infinite is not something existing through itself.

units.la: 2. Quod passio est, minus potest separari & per se existere, quàm quod subiectum est. Atqui infinitum passio est magnitudinis et numeri, quæ ipsa (magnitudo, inquam, & numerus) haud possunt separari & per se existere. Ergo multò minus infinitū potest per se existere. Nequaquam igitur infinitum est substantia, aut quiddam per se existens.
units.tr: 2. What is a passion can less be separated and exist through itself than what is a subject. But the infinite is a passion of magnitude and number, which themselves (magnitude, I say, and number) cannot be separated and exist through themselves. Therefore much less can the infinite exist through itself. Thus the infinite is in no way a substance, or something existing through itself.

units.la: Est'ne Infinitum accidens, quod actu spectari in ullo corpore sensibili uel numero potest?
units.tr: Is the infinite an accident that can actually be observed in any sensible body or number?

units.la: Non datur infinitū actu in ullo corpore uel numero. Quod probatur sex rationibus.
units.tr: Actually infinite quantity does not exist in any sensible body or number. This is proved by six arguments.

units.la: 1. A' definitione Corporis. Illud uocatur corpus, quod est circumscriptum seu determinatum superficie. Sed nullum determinatum superficie est infinitum. Igitur nullum corpus est infinitum.
units.tr: 1. From the definition of body. That is called a body which is bounded or delimited by a surface. But nothing delimited by a surface is infinite. Therefore no body is infinite.

units.la: 2. Quod non sit numerus infinitu[?]m, à ratione numeri. Omne numerabile potest numerari, ac proin de numerando pertransiri. Sed omnis numerus & omne quod habet numerum est numerabile, igitur potest etiam numerari & numerando pertransiri. Quamobrem infinitus numerus nullus est. Nam si constitueretur aliquis numerus, siue separatus, ut Mathematici ponunt, siue in rebus sensibilibus existens, infinitus: sequeretur hinc, quod etiam infinitum pertransiri poterit. hoc vero absurdissimum est, & cum definitione infiniti pugnas. Sunt autem hæ probationes logicæ, nunc addamus quasdam physicas.
units.tr: 2. That number cannot be infinite follows from the nature of number. Every numerable thing can be numbered, and so can be gone through by counting. But every number, and everything that has a number, is numerable, and so can be numbered and gone through by counting. Therefore there is no infinite number.
