For if some number were posited, whether separate, as the mathematicians hold, or existing in sensible things, and it were infinite, it would follow that the infinite could also be gone through. But this is most absurd and contradicts the definition of the infinite. These are the logical proofs; now let us add some physical ones.

units.la: 3. Omne corpus sensibile aut est copositum, aut est simplex: Atqui neutrum horum potest dici infinitum: Igitur nullum corpus sensibile est infinitum. A' sufficienti diuisione ad explicationem Minoris, quod nullum corpus sensibile compositum sit infinitum, hac ratione probatur. Quod constat ex iis quæ magnitudine aut multitudine sunt finita, id ipsum quoq; finitum sit oportet. Omne autem corpus compositum sensibile constat ex elementis, quæ sunt multitudine & magnitudine finita. Igitur omne quoq; corpus compositum finitum est. Nec potest dici, quod ex elementis unum sit infinitum, alia finita: neq; etiam, quod omnia sint infinita. Si enim illud astruas, sequitur unius infiniti elementi infinitam sore vim, ac proinde cætera nihil prorsus effi-cere: cere: unde aer infinitus ignem,aquam,terram finita opprimeret, neq; possent unquam res naturales ex illis conflari. Quamobrem ut finita,ita in omnibus quoq; proportionata elementa esse oportet.Sed neq; possunt omnia simul infinita esse, quando unum ex illis infinitum occuparet omnia, neq; alteri cuipiam ex elementis locus ullus relinqueretur:quæ fanè [?] valde absurda sunt. Quod vero nullum corpus sensibile simplex sit infinitum, hoc modo probatur.
units.tr: 3. Every sensible body is either compound or simple. But neither of these can be called infinite. Therefore no sensible body is infinite. As for the minor premise, that no compound sensible body is infinite, it is proved this way, following a sufficient division. What is finite in magnitude or in multitude must itself also be finite. But every compound sensible body consists of elements which are finite in multitude and magnitude. Therefore every compound body too is finite. Nor can it be said that one of the elements is infinite and the others finite, nor that all are infinite. For if you assert the first, it follows that the power of the one infinite element would be infinite and so the others would accomplish nothing at all: whence infinite air would overpower the finite fire, water and earth, and natural things could never be compounded from them. Therefore the elements ought to be finite and also proportionate in all respects. But neither can all of them together be infinite, since one infinite element would occupy everything, and no place would be left to any other of the elements; which is plainly very absurd. That no simple sensible body is infinite is proved in this way.

units.la: Sensibilia corpora simplicia sunt inuicem contraria: siquidem aer humidus & calidus est,ignis vero siccus & calidus,aqua autem frigida & humida,terra frigida & sicca. Iam vero si unum ex his simplicibus esset infinitum, id cætera simplicia propter inhærentem naturam pugnantem statim corrumperet perderetq;. Atq; ita unum corpus simplex existe-ret,reliqua interirent. Sed hæc ad expositionem tertij argumenti sufficient.
units.tr: Simple sensible bodies are contrary to one another: for air is moist and warm, fire is dry and warm, water is cold and moist, earth is cold and dry. Now if any one of these simple bodies were infinite, it would at once corrupt and destroy the others, because of its inherent opposing nature. And so one simple body would exist and the rest would perish. But these points are sufficient for the explanation of the third argument.

units.la: 4. Omne corpus sensibile aptum natum est, esse in aliquo loco, imo debet in aliquo loco esse. Atqui si esset corpus aliquod sensibile infinitum, non pofset loco ullo contineri: quandoquidem extra ipsum locus non esset.Igitur corpus infinitum non est.
units.tr: 4. Every sensible body that is fit and apt by nature to exist is in some place; indeed it must be in some place. But if some sensible body were infinite, it could not be contained by any place, since there would be no place outside it. Therefore an infinite body does not exist.

units.la: 5. Deinde, cum extra ipsum locus non fit,nō intelligetur posse moueri,sed semper stabit quiescetq;: quod itidem à natura alienum est.
units.tr: 5. Furthermore, since there is no place outside it, it could not be understood to be able to move, but would always stand still and be at rest; which is likewise contrary to nature.

units.la: 6. Omne corpus sensibile est in loco. Quicquid autem est in loco, terminatum est (locus quippe terminus est.) Igitur quicquid est in loco, finitum est, nullumque corpus sensibile infinitum.
units.tr: 6. Every sensible body is in a place. But whatever is in a place is terminated, for place is indeed a boundary. Therefore whatever exists is finite, and no sensible body is infinite.

units.la: Hæ sex rationes satis evidenter concludunt, nullum corpus sensibile actu infinitum dari posse.
units.tr: These six arguments conclude quite clearly that no sensible body can exist that is actually infinite.

units.la: Quomodo fit Infinitum?
units.tr: How does the infinite come about?

units.la: Si infinitum neque est substantia per se existens, neque accidens corpori alicui actu inhærens, quomodo do intelligetur finitū esse? Dicitur aliquid esse actu, aliquid vero potentia. Itaque actu quidem infinitum non est, sed potentia. Quo quidem pacto si infinitum non concederemus, multa sequerentur incommoda: quemadmodum ex supradictis, ubi infinitum esse probabatur, licet cognoscere.
units.tr: If the infinite is neither a substance existing in itself nor an accident actually inhering in some body, how can it be understood to be finite? Something is said to be actual, and something potential. So the infinite is indeed not actual, but potential. If we did not concede this, many inconveniences would follow, as can be recognised from what was said above, where it was proved that the infinite exists.

units.la: Declara quomodo Infinitum fit potentia.
units.tr: Explain how the infinite comes to be potentially.

units.la: Dupliciter intelligitur aliquid esse potētia. Primò, ut quod potētia est tandem existat actu: quemadmodum æs potentia est statua, paulo post vero fit etiam actu statua. Secundò est aliquid potentia, quando licet aliud atque aliud accedat, nunquam tamen actu completur, sed accedere adhuc semper aliud potest. Sic certamina Olympica sunt potentia, quoniam & aliquando fiunt, & fieri ampliora [?]m per possunt. Hoc igitur secundo modo existere infinitum potentia intelligimus.
units.tr: Something is understood to be potential in two ways. First, as that which is potential eventually comes to exist actually: as bronze is potentially a statue, but shortly afterwards it also becomes a statue actually. Second, something is potential when, although one thing after another is added, it is never brought to completion in actuality, but another can always still be added. Thus the Olympic contests are potential, since they both sometimes take place and can be made larger. Therefore we understand the infinite to exist potentially in this second way.

units.la: Da exempla, in quibus Infinitum po- tentia deprehenditur.
units.tr: Give examples in which the infinite is found potentially.

units.la: Infinitum potentia secundo modo deprehenditur in tempore & in generatione, item in magnitudinibus, secundum appositionem & diuisionem. His enim semper aliquid addi queat, ut actu nunquam compleantur.
units.tr: The infinite is found potentially in the second way in time and in generation, likewise in magnitudes, by addition and by division. For something can always be added to these, so that they are never completed in actuality.

units.la: Habetne Infinitum in his se eo- dem modo?
units.tr: Does the infinite behave in the same way in these cases?

units.la: Minime. In quibusdam enim conuenit infiniti ratio, in quibusdam uero plurimum distinguitur. Quare operæprecium est collationem instituamus. Primo conuenit infiniti ratio in omnibus, quòd in ijs semper aliud atque aliud accedit, idq; perpetua quadam successione. Quod in tempore, in generatione hominum, atque etiam magnitudinibus licet deprehendere. Differentia autem hæc est: Infinitum in magnitudinibus per appositionē uel diuisionem permanet cum prius accepto. Infinitum in tempore & generatione non permanet cum prius accepto, sed corrumpitur: quandoquidem aliis definientibus, siue temporibus, siue hominibus, alia tempora aliisq; homines sibi succedunt inuicem perpetua serie. Secundo conueniunt aliquo modo infinitum appositione & infinitum diuisione, rursusq; ab inuicem differunt. Conueniunt, quòd idem propemodum inter se sunt, quando ex diuisione magnitudinis accrescit multitudo, siue infinitum appositione. Quantum enim magnitudini detrahitur, tantum multitudini adijcitur. Differunt uero, quòd ubi diuisio fit distrahendo, appositio fit adijciendo: & per diuisionem quantalibet magnitudo efficitur minor, apponendo autem facimus eam maiorem.
units.tr: No. For the notion of the infinite agrees in some of them, but in others it differs greatly. So it is worth making a comparison. First, the notion of the infinite agrees in all of them, in that something always gets added to them, one thing after another, in a continuous succession. This can be observed in time, in the generation of human beings, and also in magnitudes. The difference, however, is this: the infinite in magnitudes, by addition or division, remains with what was previously taken. The infinite in time and in generation does not remain with what was previously taken but is destroyed, since, as one period or one human being is set aside, other times and other human beings succeed one another in a perpetual series. Second, the infinite by addition and the infinite by division agree in some way, and yet again differ from each other. They agree in that they are almost the same thing, when from the division of a magnitude a multitude increases, or in the infinite by addition. For as much as is taken away from the magnitude, so much is added to the multitude. They differ, however, in that where division is done by subtracting, addition is done by adding; and by division any magnitude, however large, is made smaller, whereas by adding we make it larger.

units.la: Quid est Infinitum?
units.tr: What is the infinite?

units.la: Est extra quod nihil potest accipi: ita quidam definierunt. Sed rectius contrario modo infinitum definitur, extra quod semper potest aliquid accipi. Quòd prior definitio non sit apta, probatur. Illa enim definitio deprehenditur conuenire toto & perfecto. Nam id quoque totum & persectum dicitur, cui nihil deest, & extra quod nihil potest accipi. Sic totus & perfectus homo, tota & perfecta domus, appellatur, cui nihil deest, & in quo nihil desideratur: siquidem Totum & Persectum idem prope sibi volunt. Quando autem quod hoc modo totum & perfectum dicitur, etiam est finitum, constat sane definitione hanc infinito haud congruere. Quòd posterior definitio sit apta, probatur à signo. Etenim annulos solent dicere infinitos, quòd cum quis eos circumagit, extra partem captam semper alia pars accipitur. Signum igitur est, rectè definiri infinitū, extra quod semper queat aliquid accipi. Quamuis inter infinitum & annulos hoc discriminis obseruari debet, quòd quod ubi in infinito semper aliud accipitur, quod prius non fuerit acceptum: in annulis uero idem accipitur saepius. Recte igitur infinitum definitur, extra quod semper aliquid ratione quantitatis accipi potest. Caeterum quemadmodum ante diximus, corpus sensibile infinitum actu non inuenitur. Infinitum tantum potentia spectatur in tempore & in generatione, id est, in transeuntibus: deinde in magnitudinibus secundum appositionem & diuisionem, id est, in permanentibus.
units.tr: It is that beyond which nothing can be taken; so some have defined it. But more correctly the infinite is defined in the opposite way, as that beyond which something can always be taken. That the former definition is not apt is proved as follows. That definition is found to apply to the whole and the perfect. For that is also called whole and perfect to which nothing is lacking, and beyond which nothing can be taken. Thus we speak of a whole and perfect man, or a whole and perfect house, meaning one to which nothing is lacking and in which nothing is wanting; for "whole" and "perfect" almost mean the same thing. But since what is called whole and perfect in this way is also finite, it is clear that this definition does not fit the infinite. That the latter definition is apt is proved from a sign. For people are accustomed to call rings infinite, because when someone turns them round, beyond the part grasped another part is always taken. So it is a sign that the infinite is rightly defined as that beyond which something can always be taken. Yet between the infinite and rings this difference must be observed: in the infinite, when something is always taken beyond, it is something that was not taken before; but in rings the same part is taken again and again. Therefore the infinite is rightly defined as that beyond which something can always be taken in respect of quantity. Moreover, as we said before, a sensible body is not found to be infinite in actuality. The infinite is considered only potentially, in time and in generation, that is, in things that pass away; and then in magnitudes, by addition and division, that is, in things that remain.

units.la: Declara, quomodo Infinitum spectetur in magnitudinibus & numeris se- cundum appositionem & diuisionem.
units.tr: Explain how the infinite is considered in magnitudes and numbers, by addition and division.

units.la: Infinitum secundum diuisione spectatur potissimum in magnitudinibus: infinitu uero secundum appositionem in numeris. Illud quidem manifestum hoc modo fit. Cum infinitum habeat rationem materiae, id quidem quod continetur intus, sic habet ut quaedam materia: quod autem continet, ut species siue forma. Sed & totum se habet ut forma, partes autem ut materia. Quocirca quando in magnitudinibus itur a toto ad partes per diuisionem, consentaneum est, ibi nullum existere terminum, ultra quem non licet diuisione in infinitum fieri. Verum quando per additionem itur a partibus ad totum (quod habet rationem formae continentis) consenta-neum neum est,ibi existere certa quantitate, ultra quam infinita appositio fieri nequeat. In numeris autem spectatur infinitum contrario modo, nempe per appositionem seu additionem, non autem per diuisionem. Nam per diuisionem quidem venitur in numeris ad unum aliquem numerum non amplius diuisibilem, id est, ad unitatem: sed per additionem, à quocunq; numero maiori transiri ad alium in infinitum potest.
units.tr: The infinite by division is considered chiefly in magnitudes; the infinite by addition is considered in numbers. The former is made clear in this way. Since the infinite has the character of matter, what is contained within behaves like a kind of matter, and what contains it behaves like a species or form. But the whole also stands as form, and the parts as matter. Hence, when in magnitudes we proceed from the whole to the parts by division, it follows that there is no limit there beyond which division cannot go on to infinity. But when by addition we proceed from the parts to the whole (which has the character of the containing form), it follows that there is a certain quantity there, beyond which infinite addition cannot be made. In numbers, however, the infinite is considered in the opposite way, namely by addition or adding, not by division. For by division in numbers we arrive at some one number that can no longer be divided, that is, at unity; but by addition one can pass from any larger number on to another, to infinity.

units.la: Declara quomodo Infinitum spe- ctetur in tempore & in ge- neratione.
units.tr: Explain how the infinite is considered in time and in generation.

units.la: Sequendo Aristotelem, siue eos philosophos, qui arbitrati sunt mundum esse æternum, neq; finem habituru, perfacile est id demonstrare. Vbi enim perpetua deprehenditur partium temporis, deinde quarumcunq; rerum naturalium per generationem & corruptionem successio, ibi infiniti ratio ac vis animaduerti plenissimè potest.
units.tr: Following Aristotle, or those philosophers who thought the world eternal and would have no end, it is very easy to demonstrate this. For where there is found a perpetual succession of parts of time, and then of any natural things through generation and corruption, there the nature and power of the infinite can be perceived most fully.

units.la: Sùntne solida ac rata habenda, quæ hucusq; de infinito sunt tradita?
units.tr: Are the things handed down so far about the infinite to be held as sound and established?

units.la: Adnotare hoc loco oportet, totam hanc disputationem de infinito agitatam quidem esse à ueteribus philosophis, ueru propter illos præcipuè, quorum alij ponebant principia infinita, alij certum quoddam principium, sed illud ipsum quoq; infinitum. Alias uero nullam adfert notabilem utilitatem præsens tractatio, neque opus omnino fuisset eam admiscere. Quocirca Aristoteles ad finem lib.3. veluti definire postremo loco volens, quid de infinito in uniuersum sentiendum sit, subijcit rationes, quibus argumenta illa, quæ adducebantur ad probandum quòd infinitum sit, diluuntur.
units.tr: It must be noted here that this whole disputation about the infinite has indeed been debated by the ancient philosophers, but chiefly on account of those of whom some posited infinite principles, and others a certain definite principle, but that principle itself also infinite. Otherwise the present treatment offers no notable benefit, nor would it have been necessary to introduce it at all. Hence Aristotle, at the end of the third book, as if wishing to define finally what must be thought about the infinite in general, adds arguments by which those arguments that were brought forward to prove that the infinite exists are refuted.

units.la: Ad primam igitur probationem, quæ ducebatur à consideratione perpetuitatis in tempore, respondetur, quòd tempus perinde atq; motus infinitum quidem est potentia, at non actu: quandoquidem partes temporis licet intellectu simul apprehendantur, nunquam tamen reipsa simul manent: verum una succedente, aliæ effluunt. Nulla pars temporis actu est præter τὸ νῦν [?].
units.tr: To the first proof, which was drawn from the consideration of the perpetuity of time, it is answered that time, just like motion, is infinite potentially but not actually; for although the parts of time can be grasped together by the intellect, they never in reality remain together, but one flows away as another succeeds. No part of time actually exists except the now [τὸ νῦν].

units.la: Ad secundam probationem, sumptam à diuisione magnitudinum, respondetur, neque actu neque intellectu magnitudinem ullam infinitam dari, sed tantum potentia.
units.tr: To the second proof, taken from the division of magnitudes, it is answered that no infinite magnitude is given either actually or in the intellect, but only potentially.

units.la: Ad tertiam probationem, collectam ex perpetuitate generationis et corruptionis, respondetur: Etiamsi generationes & corruptiones fieri non desinant, non tamen propterea necessum est materiam aliquam existere actu infinitam. Potest enim generatio perpetua atq; corruptio procedere etiam finita materia posita. Nam quantum materiæ res quæpiam naturalis in corruptione amittit, tantum alia rursus in generatione assumit. Corruptio unius, est generatio alterius.
units.tr: To the third proof, gathered from the perpetuity of generation and corruption, it is answered: even if generations and corruptions do not cease, it does not on that account follow that some matter must exist actually infinite. For perpetual generation and corruption can proceed even when matter is posited as finite. For as much matter as a natural thing loses in corruption, so much another thing again takes up in generation. The corruption of one is the generation of another.

units.la: Ad quartam probationem, ex apparēti ratione finiti sumptā, respondetur: Aliud est, corpus aliquod tangi, aliud finiri. Finitur corpus per se positum & solitarium, non tangitur corpus nisi alteri coniunctum. Itaque etsi omne corpus sit finitum, haudquaquam necessarium est, ab alio corpore contingatur.
units.tr: To the fourth proof, taken from the apparent reasoning about the finite, it is answered: it is one thing for a body to be touched, another for it to be finite. A body placed by itself and alone is finite; a body is not touched unless it is joined to another. So although every body is finite, it is by no means necessary that it be touched by another body.

units.la: Ad quintam probationem, ab apprehensione intellectus, respondetur: Non quicquid intellectu apprehenditur, id statim actu est. Intellectu perlustras Asiam, Aphricam, imò & cœlum ipsum penetras: non tamen in ijsdem locis es.
units.tr: To the fifth proof, drawn from the apprehension of the intellect, it is answered: not everything apprehended by the intellect is at once actual. By the intellect you survey Asia and Africa, and even penetrate the heavens themselves; yet you are not in those places.

units.la: Constat igitur, quasdam rationes ante allatas, tantum habere probabilitatis speciem, quasdam vero[?] simpliciter esse falsas, & nihil quicquam efficere ad constituendum infinitum actu. Deniq;, etiamsi negetur infinitum actu, non sequuntur ulla incommoda. Siquidem mathematici neq; egent, neq; utuntur in suis demonstrationibus ulla infinita magnitudine: sed si quam desiderant, eam finitam ponunt, quam intellectu quoq; quantam volunt apprehendunt. Prudenter igitur Aristoteles infinitum, nisi potentia, non concessit.
units.tr: It is clear, then, that some of the arguments adduced above have only the appearance of probability, while certain ones are simply false, and contribute nothing towards establishing the infinite in actuality. Finally, even if the infinite in actuality is denied, no inconveniences follow. For mathematicians neither need nor use any infinite magnitude in their demonstrations; but where they require one, they posit a finite one, which they grasp in the intellect as large as they wish. Aristotle, then, wisely conceded the infinite only potentially.

units.la: Ex his hactenus expositis, An sit infinitū, Quomodo sit, Quid sit, cognosci abundè potest: sequitur disceptatiuncula De loco.
units.tr: From what has been set out so far, it can be sufficiently known whether the infinite exists, how it exists, and what it is; there follows a short disputation about place.

units.la: Quare nunc agendum de loco?
units.tr: Why must we now treat of place?

units.la: {1}Via omnes res naturales in loco esse intelliguntur.
units.tr: First, all natural things are understood to be in a place.

units.la: {2}Quando physicus disputat praecipue de motu, atq; hic quidem secundum locum fit, necessum est loci peraeque atq; motus cognitionem habeat.
units.tr: Second, when the natural philosopher discusses motion, especially local motion, it is necessary that he have knowledge of place just as much as of motion.

units.la: AN SIT LOCVS?
units.tr: IS THERE PLACE?

units.la: Variae de hac quaestione fuerunt opiniones. Nos congeremus rationes in utramq; partem, post quas subijciemus conclusionem.
units.tr: There have been various opinions on this question. We will set out the arguments on both sides, and after them we will add the conclusion.

units.la: Pars affirmatiua.
units.tr: The affirmative side.

units.la: {1}Primum argumentum, à transpositione corporum: Corpora inuicem sibi succedunt, ita ut ubi prius fuerat aqua, ibi nunc sit aer, atq; e diuerso. Hoc autem fieri non posset, si locus in quem transferrentur corpora, non esset. Itaque locus est, et quidem aliquid diuersum ab ijs quae loco comprehenduntur.
units.tr: (1) The first argument is from the exchange of bodies: bodies succeed one another, so that where there was water before, there is now air, and vice versa. But this could not happen if there were no place into which the bodies were transferred. Therefore there is place, and indeed something different from the things that are contained by place.

units.la: {2}Secundum, à motu corporum simplicium: Motus corporum naturalium simplicium semper uergit (quando non obsistit impedimentum) ad suum locum, in quo seruatur et bene habet. Verbi gratia: Ignis et omne leue tendit sursum, terra et omne graue deorsum. Igitur locus est, et praeterea uim quandam conseruatricem eorum quae in se comprehendit, habens. Enimuero omnia naturaliter locum aliquem expetunt, quasi proprium receptaculum, adeoq; domicilium in quo conserventur.
units.tr: (2) The second is from the motion of simple bodies: the motion of simple natural bodies always tends (unless some hindrance stands in the way) to its own place, in which it is preserved and is well off. For example, fire and everything light tends upward, earth and everything heavy downward. Therefore there is place, and moreover it has a certain preserving power over the things it contains. Indeed all things naturally seek some place as their own proper receptacle, and so a home in which they may be preserved.

units.la: Tertium, à signo siue à communi loquendi con-suetudine: Veteres posuerunt vacuum, in quod corpora reciperentur, idq; locum etiam appellarunt, dicentes, locum esse vacuum, ubi nullum corpus continetur, sed contineri posset. Ergo vel hic receptus loquendi mos testatur locum esse. Dicimus autem, rationem hanc sumptam à loquendi consuetudine, quòd vacuum revera in natura dari nullum potest: loquendi tamen consuetudo obtinuit, ut vacuum nominetur, in quo nullum corpus sensibus expositum apparet.
units.tr: (3) The third is from a sign, or from common usage of speech: the ancients posited a void into which bodies might be received, and they also called this place, saying that place is a void where no body is contained but could be contained. Therefore this accepted manner of speaking also testifies that place exists. We say, however, that this argument is taken from the usage of speech, because a void can in fact exist nowhere in nature; yet the custom of speech has prevailed that we call "void" that in which no body appears to the senses.

units.la: Quartum, à pronunciato Hesiodi in 1. Theogonias. Is enim constituit ante res conditas quoddam chaos, commune omnium earum quæ post conditæ sunt rerum receptaculum, adeoq; locum. Igitur locus est, quodq; ad dignitatem eius facit, etiam ante alias res naturales, utpote quæ subsistere non potuissent, si non fuisset prius quidam locus, in quo colligerentur. Hæc argumenta ad stabiliendum partem affirmatiuam certa ac valida sunt.
units.tr: (4) The fourth is from the saying of Hesiod in the first book of his Theogony. For he sets up, before things were made, a certain chaos, the common receptacle, and so the place, of all the things that were made afterwards. Therefore place exists, and, which adds to its dignity, it exists even before other natural things, since they could not have subsisted had there not first been some place in which they might be gathered together. These arguments are sure and strong for establishing the affirmative side.

units.la: Pars negatiua.
units.tr: The negative side.

units.la: Primum argumentum: Si locus esset, necessariò aut esset corpus, aut alia à corpore natura. Atqui neutrum horum dici potest. Igitur locus non est.
units.tr: First argument: If place existed, it would necessarily be either a body or a nature other than body. But neither of these can be said. Therefore place does not exist.

units.la: Quòd locus non sit corpus, probatur. Nam cum locus & loco comprehensum simul sint, necnon loco comprehensum in loco ipso reperiatur, sanè hinc sequeretur, duo corpora simul in sese existere: quod absurdum plane. Quòd uero non sit alia natura à corpore, probatur. Nam habere tres dimensiones, longitudinis, latitudinis et profunditatis, omni et soli corpori proprium est. Atqui locus habet tres has dimensiones. Igitur locus nō est alia natura à corpore.
units.tr: That place is not a body is proved thus: since the place and the thing contained by it are together at the same time, and moreover the thing contained is found within the place itself, it would clearly follow that two bodies exist at the same time in one another, which is plainly absurd. That place is not another nature apart from body is proved thus: to have three dimensions, of length, breadth and depth, belongs to every body and to body alone. But place has these three dimensions. Therefore place is not a nature other than body.

units.la: Si locus est receptaculum corporis, necessum est sit etiam receptaculum superficici, lineæ & puncti. Eadem quippe est horum ratio. Atqui puncto non potest locus assignari, utpote quod nullam habet dimensionem. Igitur neq; lineæ neq; superficiei assignari locus potest. His autem si locus non datur, neque corporis ullum futurum est receptaculum, ac proinde neque locus erit: siquidem per se positus intelligi non potest.
units.tr: If place is the receptacle of a body, it must also be the receptacle of a surface, a line and a point, for the reasoning is the same for these. But no place can be assigned to a point, since it has no dimension. Therefore no place can be assigned to a line or a surface either. And if no place is given to these, then no place will be a receptacle of a body either, and consequently there will be no place, since it cannot be understood to exist by itself.

units.la: Omne quod est, uel est elemetum, uel aliquid ex elementis cōstans. Atqui locus neutrum horum dici potest. Igitur locus non est. Minor probatur. Etenim quod huiusmodi est, oportet sit de numero corporeorum aut incorporeorum. Atqui locus non est de numero incorporeorum: quandoquidem habet, ut dixi[?]mus, magnitudine atq; tres dimensiones. praeterea non est de numero corporeorum: probatū namq; est, eum corpus dici non posse. Igitur locus non est.
units.tr: Everything that exists is either an element or something made up of the elements. But place can be said to be neither of these. Therefore place does not exist. The minor premise is proved thus: whatever is of this kind must be among the corporeal or the incorporeal things. But place is not among the incorporeal things, since, as I have said, it has magnitude and three dimensions. Moreover it is not among the corporeal things, for it has been proved that it cannot be called a body. Therefore place does not exist.

units.la: Omne quod est, referri appositè potest ad aliquam speciem quatuor causarum, saltem respectu alicuius. Sed non potest demonstrari aliqua species quatuor causarum, ad quam locus reducatur. Neq; enim potest dici materia, neq; forma, neq; finis, neq; efficiens: quod facile potest intelligi. Igitur locus non est.
units.tr: Everything that exists can fittingly be referred to some kind of the four causes, at least in relation to something. But no kind of the four causes can be shown to which place may be reduced. For it cannot be called matter, nor form, nor end, nor efficient cause; this can easily be understood. Therefore place does not exist.

units.la: Ex sententia Zenonis: Omne quod est, id in loco est. Quare fi locus aliquid est, & ipse quoque in loco erit, deinde hic locus similiter in alio: atq; ita in infinitum progressus fiet. Atqui istud est plane impossibile. Conficitur ergo, quod locus non fit.
units.tr: According to the opinion of Zeno: everything that exists is in a place. Wherefore, if place is something, it too will be in a place, and then this place again in another, and so the process will go on to infinity. But that is plainly impossible. It follows, therefore, that place does not exist.

units.la: Omne corpus est in loco, & rursus in omni loco est corpus. Quo dato, sequitur, quod ubi ea quae in loco sunt, contigerit crescere vel decrescere, ipse quoque locus similiter crescere vel decrescere debeat. Istud autem est absurdum, cum locus fit quiddam immobile. Igitur locus non est. Caeterum auditis in utramque partem argumentis, conclusio certa retinenda est.
units.tr: Every body is in a place, and again in every place there is a body. Given this, it follows that when the things that are in a place happen to grow or shrink, the place itself must likewise grow or shrink. But this is absurd, since place is something immovable. Therefore place does not exist. Yet, having heard the arguments on both sides, a sure conclusion must be held.

units.la: Conclusio.
units.tr: Conclusion.

units.la: Pars affirmatiua retinenda est, quod uidelicet locus fit. Neq; difficile est argumenta quae in partem contrariam sunt allata, diluere.
units.tr: The affirmative part is to be retained, namely that place does exist. Nor is it difficult to dissolve the arguments that have been brought forward on the opposite side.

units.la: Ad primum argumentum respondetur, negando quod locus fit corpus. Falsum enim est, q; in loco spe stentur tres dimefiones. Sed neq; insuper erunt duo corpora simul in sese, fiue corpus in corpore. Nam cum locus sit terminus corporis continentis (quod paulo post patefiet) & dari non possit aliquod spatium corporeum medium inter extremitates corporis continentis & corporis contenti, non potest intelligi ibi esse corpus in corpore, sed tantum aliquod corpus certis terminis comprehensum.
units.tr: To the first argument, the reply is made by denying that place is a body. For it is false that three dimensions are found in place. Nor, moreover, will two bodies be in one another at the same time, or a body in a body. For since place is the boundary of the containing body (which will be made clear a little later), and no corporeal space can be given between the extremities of the containing body and of the contained body, it cannot be understood that a body is in a body there, but only that some body is comprehended within fixed boundaries.

units.la: Ad secundum argumetum: Puncto, linea, superficiei per se non potest locus assignari, sicut neque aliis accidentibus, quae subiecto cuipiam inhaerent. Neque eadem est horum ratio, quae aliorum corporum, quae undiq; à loco concluduntur.
units.tr: To the second argument: a place cannot be assigned to a point, a line or a surface considered in itself, just as neither can it be assigned to other accidents, which inhere in some subject. Nor is the reasoning the same for these as for other bodies, which are enclosed on every side by place.

units.la: Ad tertium argumentum: Locus non est elementum, vel aliquid ex elementis, sed quiddam ea ipsa circumdans atq; ambiens. Est enim extremū quiddam, sive terminus ipsorum elementorum & rerum corporearum. Et elementa ipsa loco comprehensa atq; in se invicem sita intelliguntur: ut terra in aqua, aqua in aere, et aer in æthere sive igne cœlesti. Sunt autem hæc omnia sibi invicem cognata, & mutuō sese conservāt, necnō suis extremitatibus quasi contingunt, ut alterū ad alterum sic se habeat, quemadmodum agens ad patiens, atq; diversō: unde etiā fit, ut in se mutuō transeant.
units.tr: To the third argument: place is not an element, or something made of the elements, but a certain thing that surrounds and encompasses them. For it is an outermost thing, or the boundary of the elements themselves and of corporeal things. And the elements themselves are understood to be comprehended by place and situated within one another: as earth in water, water in air, and air in the aether or heavenly fire. All these, moreover, are akin to one another and mutually preserve one another, and they touch, as it were, by their extremities, so that one stands to the other as agent to patient, and vice versa; whence it also comes about that they pass over into one another.

units.la: Ad quartum: Locus se habet ut causa efficiens et conservans, imò etiam ut finis, respectu corporis locati. Manifestum enim est, quòd locus conservat locatum, atque unumquodq; corpus natura desiderat in suo atq; idoneo esse loco.
units.tr: To the fourth argument: place stands in relation to the located body as efficient and preserving cause, and even as end. For it is evident that place preserves what is placed, and every body by nature desires to be in its own and fitting place.

units.la: Ad quintum: Locus non est in aliquo uti in loco, sed ut numerus in finito, ac terminus in eo cuius est terminus. Non enim omne quod est, in loco est, sed omne corpus sensibile.
units.tr: To the fifth argument: place is not in something in the way that a thing is in a place, but as a number is in what is finite, and a boundary is in that of which it is the boundary. For not everything that exists is in a place, but every sensible body is.

units.la: Ad sextum: Non omne corpus in loco esse diximus, sed tantum sensibile, quod proximè quoq; dictum. Itaq; caeleste corpus aut eius ultimum globum in loco esse negamus. Sed neq; oportet, aucto vel diminuto corpore contento, ipsum locum continentem augeri vel minui: siquidem locus eiusmodi est terminus, cui augeri vel minui per se non conuenit. Quamuis hoc verum est, quòd aliquando aucto vel diminuto corpore contento, ipsum corpus continens densatur aut rarescit. Si quae hic obscura sunt, ea ex sequentibus dilucidiora euadent. Tantum de quaestione, An sit locus?
units.tr: To the sixth argument: we have said that not every body is in a place, but only a sensible body, as was also said just above. Therefore we deny that the heavenly body, or its outermost sphere, is in a place. Nor is it necessary, when the contained body is increased or diminished, that the containing place itself should be increased or diminished: since place is of such a kind as a boundary, to which increase or diminution does not belong in itself. Although it is true that sometimes, when the contained body is increased or diminished, the containing body itself becomes denser or rarer. If some things here are obscure, they will become clearer from what follows. So much concerning the question, Is there a place?

units.la: QVID SIT LOCVS?
units.tr: WHAT IS PLACE?

units.la: Utrum locus sit forma, an materia?
units.tr: Is place form or matter?

units.la: Neutrum est. Quidam sanè ueteres[?] dixerunt, locum esse formam, quod hac ratione conati sunt demonstrare: Quemadmodum eorum quae sunt, quoddam dicitur Ens per se, quoddam uerò Ens per accidens: ita dicere possumus quendam locum proprium, qui primò & per se dicitur locus, veluti locus immediatè nihil praeter te continens: quendam locum communem &[?] per accidens, quo uidelicet plura corpora cōtinentur, quomodo si dicam te esse in cœlo, quia nimirum in terra existens, simul est in aëre, qui & cœlo continetur. Si igitur quod primo & per se aliquid continet, dicitur proprius eius locus, huiusmodi aut semper est terminus, ad quem res terminatur: sequitur, quod locus per se sumptus, sit rei terminus. Iam vero, cùm forma sit uniuscuiusque rei terminus, erit profectò & locus forma.
units.tr: It is neither. Certain of the ancients indeed said that place is form, and they tried to demonstrate this by the following reasoning: just as among things that exist, one is called being per se and another being per accidens, so we can say there is a certain proper place, which is said primarily and per se to be place, as for example the place that immediately contains nothing but you; and a certain common place, and per accidens, by which, namely, several bodies are contained, as when I say that you are in heaven, because, existing on earth, you are at the same time in the air, which is also contained by heaven. If therefore that which contains something primarily and per se is called its proper place, and such a thing is always the boundary to which a thing is bounded, it follows that place taken per se is the boundary of the thing. Now, since form is the boundary of each thing, place will certainly also be form.

units.la: Rursus quidam dixerunt, locum esse materiam, secuti nimirum authoritatè Platonis, qui in Timæo uisus est ita sentire. Atqui locum neque formam esse, neque materiam, pluribus rationibus perspicuis euincitur.
units.tr: Again, certain others said that place is matter, following, of course, the authority of Plato, who in the Timaeus seems to have thought so. But that place is neither form nor matter is proved by several clear reasons.

units.la: Forma & materia non separantur à re cuius sunt. Locus autem separatur à re cuius est. Etenim ubi prius fuit aër, ibi paulo post aqua, & alia deinceps corpora inuicè succedunt. Ex quo similiter manifestum fit, locum non posse dici rei cuiusphiam partem uel habitum, uel ullum omnino accidens: quandoquidem partes habitus atque accidentia à re cuius sunt, minimè separatur. Et sicut uas non est quicquam eorum quæ ipsum in se continet, ita nec locus est quicquam eorum quæ ipse continet.
units.tr: Form and matter are not separated from the thing of which they are. But place is separated from the thing of which it is the place. For where air was before, a little later there is water, and other bodies succeed one another in turn. From this it is likewise plain that place cannot be called a part or a habit of some thing, or any accident whatever; since parts, habits and accidents are not separated at all from the thing of which they are. And just as a vessel is not any of the things which it contains within itself, so neither is place any of the things which it contains.

units.la: Oportet ad illud quod locus est, aliquam fieri motionem, necnon spectari in illo has differentias, sursum ac deorsum. Atqui in materia & forma hæc differentiæ non possunt inueniri. Igitur repugnat, ut locus intelligatur materia aut forma. Si locus effet materia aut forma, sequeretur, quod ubi materia & forma cum re quapiam existerent in loco, locus quoq; in loco effet. Istud vero est absurdum. Igitur & illud ex quo sequitur.
units.tr: To that which place is, some motion must be attributed, and in it these differences are to be observed, up and down. But in matter and form these differences cannot be found. Therefore it is inconsistent that place should be understood as matter or form. If place were matter or form, it would follow that where matter and form exist together with some thing in a place, the place would also be in a place. But that is absurd. Therefore that from which it follows is also absurd.

units.la: Quando res aliqua corrumpitur, simul etiam aliquo modo corrumpuntur partes speciei ipsius. Materia autem & forma sunt partes speciei. Ergo corrupta re, simul corrumpuntur (saltem per accidens) materia & forma. Quo ita posito, sic rursus ratiocinamur: Si materia & forma corrumpuntur, necesse est ut locus quoq; (si is sit materia vel forma) corrumpatur. Atqui aliud nulla ratione potest, quod locus corrumpatur. Igitur locus materia aut forma non est. Relinquitur proinde manifestum, quod locus neque sit materia, neque forma, neque ullorum constitui vice generis in definitione loci queat. Caeterum hac ratione licebit tandem aliquam definitionem loci sive descriptionem colligere, si quot modis aliquid dicatur esse in aliquo, & utrum aliquid idem esse possit in se ipso, disquiramus.
units.tr: When some thing is corrupted, at the same time the parts of its species are also in some way corrupted. But matter and form are parts of the species. Therefore, when the thing is corrupted, matter and form are at the same time corrupted (at least per accidens). With this granted, we reason again in this way: if matter and form are corrupted, it is necessary that place also (if it is matter or form) be corrupted. But place cannot be corrupted in any way. Therefore place is not matter or form. It is thus plainly left that place is neither matter nor form, and cannot be set in the definition of place in the position of a genus of any of them. Moreover, by this line of reasoning we shall at last be able to gather some definition or description of place, if we inquire in how many ways something is said to be in something, and whether something can be in itself.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur aliquid esse in aliquo?
units.tr: How many ways is something said to be in something?

units.la: Octo. 1. Sicut pars est in toto: quo pacto dicitur digitus esse in manu.
units.tr: Eight. 1. As a part is in a whole, in which way a finger is said to be in the hand.

units.la: 2. Quemadmodum totum est in partibus. Non enim praeter partes totum esse potest.
units.tr: 2. As the whole is in its parts. For a whole cannot exist apart from its parts.

units.la: 3. Vt species in genere. Sic iustitia continetur in virtute.
units.tr: 3. As a species is in a genus. Thus justice is contained in virtue.

units.la: 4. Vt genus in specie. quo pacto virtus dicitur comprehendi in iustitia.
units.tr: 4. As a genus is in a species, in which way virtue is said to be comprised in justice.

units.la: 5. Sicut forma in materia seu subiecto, sive essentialis sit forma, sive accidentalis. Ita sanitas est in corpore secundum temperamentum frigoris et caloris bene constituto.
units.tr: 5. As form is in matter or subject, whether the form is essential or accidental. Thus health is in the body when the temperament of cold and heat is well balanced.

units.la: 6. Sicut in efficiente. Ita res Graecorum dicuntur esse in imperatore Graeciae: et dicimus aliquid esse in nobis, significates videlicet, esse id in nostra potestate.
units.tr: 6. As in an efficient cause. Thus the goods of the Greeks are said to be in the emperor of Greece; and we say that something is in us, meaning, namely, that it is in our power.

units.la: 7. Sicut in fine et plurimum expetendo. Quaquidem ratione dicimus quosdam felicitatem constituere in virtute, quosdam in opibus, quosdam in voluptate.
units.tr: 7. As in an end, and in what is most desired. In this way we say that some people place happiness in virtue, some in wealth, and some in pleasure.

units.la: 8. Sicut in uase:et generatim, sicut quod loco continetur, est in loco. Atq; hoc modo proprie quidem aliquid in aliquo esse dicitur: quandoquidem reliqui omnes modi quadam similitudine ab hoc ipso deducuntur.
units.tr: 8. As in a vessel; and generally, as what is contained by a place is in the place. In this way, properly speaking, something is said to be in something, since all the other modes are derived from this one by some likeness.

units.la: Vtrum possit aliquid idem esse in seipso?
units.tr: Can something be in itself?

units.la: Duobus modis intelligi potest aliquid esse in seipso.
units.tr: Something can be understood to be in itself in two ways.

units.la: 1. Est aliquid in seipso primo et per se, quando videlicet aliquid cum omni quod ipsius est, in se est.
units.tr: 1. Something is in itself first and through itself, when, namely, a thing is in itself together with everything that belongs to it.

units.la: 2. Est aliquid in seipso per aliud: quia uidelicet pars uel partes in ipso sunt. ueluti quādo aliquis dicitur albus uel doctus, quoniā cute albus est, & do​ctrinam habet in parte animi rationali. Inde autem totus homo albus, totus homo doctus nominatur, ratione uidelicet illius partis, in qua albedo uel doctrina consistit.
units.tr: 2. Something is in itself through another, namely because a part or parts of it are in it; as when someone is said to be white or learned, since he is white in his skin and has learning in the rational part of his mind. Thus the whole man is called white, and the whole man learned, by reason of that part in which the whiteness or the learning consists.

units.la: Ad quæstionem igitur ut respondeamus, posteriore quidē modo totum dicitur esse in seipso, priore autem illo modo nihil in seipso existere potest. Enimuero intelligi non potest, unum aliquod corpus sibi ipsi sic imponi, quemadmodum e duobus distinctis corporibus unum subinde imponitur alteri. Nec quisquam sanæ mentis dixerit, unum esse in uno, amphoram in amphora: sed bene, aquam esse in uino, & uinum in amphora.
units.tr: So, to answer the question: in the latter way the whole is said to be in itself, but in the former way nothing can exist in itself. For indeed it cannot be understood that one body is placed upon itself, as one of two distinct bodies is then placed upon the other. Nor would anyone of sound mind say that one thing is in one thing, a jar in a jar; but rather that water is in wine, and wine in a jar.

units.la: Da certam loci definitionem.
units.tr: Give a certain definition of place.

units.la: Operæprecium est, adhuc quasdam constitumus hypotheses, ex quibus quid de loco rite dici queat, propius innotescat.
units.tr: It is worth while to lay down some further hypotheses, from which what may rightly be said of place may become better known.

units.la: 1. Hypothesis: Locus eam rem continet, cuius est locus, neq; quicquam eiusdem rei est.
units.tr: 1. Hypothesis: place contains the thing of which it is the place, and is not any part of that same thing.

units.la: 2. Locus in quo aliqua res primò est, neq; maior neq; minor est re contenta, sed plane huic æqualis.
units.tr: 2. A place in which something is primarily is neither larger nor smaller than the thing contained, but exactly equal to it.

units.la: 3. Non est res contenta suo sine loco, neque locus sine re contenta, à qua tamen locum ipsum separabilem esse oportet.
units.tr: 3. A thing contained is not without its place, nor a place without the thing contained; yet the place must be separable from the thing itself.

units.la: 4. In omni loco invenitur aliqua loci differētia, nempe sursum aut deorsum: & naturaliter unumquodque corpus, quādo est extra proprium locum, omnibus viribus ad ipsum fertur, cumq; eo pervenerit, conquiescit.
units.tr: 4. In every place some difference of position is found, namely up or down; and naturally each body, when it is outside its proper place, is carried toward it with all its powers, and when it has arrived there, it comes to rest.

units.la: 5. Tenenda est & hæc partitio: Eorum quæ mouentur, alia mouentur Per se atq; actu. Per accidēs. horum tamen quaedam mouentur Etiam per se: sicut partes alicuius corporis, quæ mouentur quidem cum toto corpore per accidens, interea tamen etiā per se moueri possunt. Nullo modo per se, sed tantum per accidens: sicut albedo & scientia, quæ nunquam sanè mutant locum, nisi cum eo cui insunt.
units.tr: 5. This division too must be kept: of things that are moved, some are moved per se and actually, others per accidens. Yet some of these are also moved per se: for example the parts of a body, which are moved per accidens together with the whole body, but meanwhile can also be moved per se. Others are never moved per se but only per accidens, in no way of themselves: such as whiteness and knowledge, which never change place except together with that in which they inhere.

units.la: 6. Locus non est totum continens aliquam rem, sed tantum extremum cōtinentis. Quod probatur: nā solius extremi eius gratia aliquid dicitur esse in loco. veluti in cœlo esse diceris, quia in aere: & in ære, quia eius extremo undiquaq; comprehederis.
units.tr: 6. Place is not the whole thing containing something, but only the extremity of the container. This is proved: for something is said to be in a place for the sake of that extremity alone. Thus you are said to be in heaven because you are in the air; and in the air because you are surrounded by its extremity on every side.

units.la: 7. Ex his igitur restat inquiramus genus loci. Necessum autem est, locus sit aliquid horum quatuor, nempe aut materia, aut forma, aut spacium, aut extremum corporis continentis. Sed non potest dici, quòd sit aliquid illorum trium: relinquitur ergo, quòd sit quartum, uidelicet extremu corporis continentis. Quòd non sit forma uel materia, ante est demonstratum. Quòd item non sit spacium, probatur. Nam si esset spacium, quod est infra extremitates corporis continentis, sequeretur locum transmutari posse. Atqui istud est absurdum: igitur & illud ex quo sequitur. Maior probatur. Transmutato aliquo corpore, ueluti amphora, simul transferretur illud spacium quod est infra extremitates amphorae, cum id nunquam alibi sit, quàm ubi est amphora. Sed quod alio transfertur, commensuratur à dimensionibus eius spacij in quod transfertur. Consicitur ergo, quòd aliæ dimensiones occupant dimensiones eius spacij in quod est amphora translata, atque ita unius loci rursus erit locus alius, & huius deniq; alius, tandemq; multa loca unius corporis simul existent. Itaq; relinquitur, locum non esse spacium: quamobrem necessariò erit extremum.
units.tr: 7. From these things, then, let us inquire into the kind of place. Place must necessarily be one of four things: either matter, or form, or space, or the extremity of the containing body. But it cannot be said to be any of the first three; it remains, therefore, that it is the fourth, namely the extremity of the containing body. That it is not form or matter has been shown above. That it is not space is likewise proved. For if it were space, that which lies within the extremities of the containing body, it would follow that place could be transferred. But that is absurd, and therefore so is that from which it follows. The major premise is proved: when a body such as a jar is moved, the space that lies within the extremities of the jar would be transferred at the same time, since it is never anywhere else than where the jar is. But what is transferred elsewhere is measured by the dimensions of the space into which it is transferred. It follows, therefore, that other dimensions occupy the dimensions of the space into which the jar is carried; and thus there will again be another place of one place, and another of that, and finally many places of one body would exist at once. Therefore it remains that place is not space; wherefore it must necessarily be the extremity.

units.la: 8. Porrò ex his ipsis quæ proximè dicta sunt, quòd uidelicet locus transferri non possit, colligi potest etiam quædam differentia, nempe quòd locus sit immobilis.Nam rem contenta quidem moueri contingit:id vero quod continet, non cotingit moueri.
units.tr: 8. Furthermore, from these very things just said, namely that place cannot be transferred, there can also be gathered a certain further difference, namely that place is immobile. For the thing contained may be moved; but that which contains cannot be moved.

units.la: Ex his igitur omnibus proprietates loci cognosci possunt,definitio autem hæc recte colligetur: Locus est corporis continentis extremum, & quidem immobile primum.hoc est:Locus est superficies concava corporis rem continentis, proxima rei contentæ,cum qua moueri haud potest. Quocirca locus cum vase non male confertur.Hoc tantum differunt,quod vas per se mouetur ac defertur, locus autem manet immobilis. Atq; omnia quidem quæ sunt loci propria,possunt in data definitione spectari.
units.tr: From all these things the properties of place can be recognised, and this definition will rightly be drawn: Place is the extremity of the containing body, and indeed the first immobile one; that is, place is the concave surface of the containing body, next to the thing contained, with which it cannot be moved. Hence place is not badly compared with a vessel. They differ only in this: that the vessel is itself moved and carried along, but place remains immobile. And all the things that are proper to place can be observed in the given definition.

units.la: Declara, quomodo res aliqua fit in loco?
units.tr: In what way is a thing in a place?

units.la: Paucis propositionibus id expediri potest.
units.tr: This can be explained in a few propositions.

units.la: Omne corpus extra quod est aliud corpus continens ipsum,proprie in loco esse dicitur. Quocirca ignis,aer,terra,aqua, & omne corpus ex his conflatum,recte in loco esse dicuntur:quandoquidem alio corpore,videlicet coelo,continentur. At coelum non perinde.
units.tr: Any body outside which another body contains it is properly said to be in a place. Hence fire, air, earth, water, and every body made up of these are rightly said to be in place, since they are contained by another body, namely the heaven. But the heaven is not in the same way.

units.la: 2. Etsi vero coelum totum non sit in loco, attamen secundum diuersas partes varie quoq; in loco consistit. Prior pars huius propositionis manifesta est. Nam extra ipsum coelum nihil est. Illud vero extra quod nihil est, quomodo contineri extremo aliquo intelligatur? Altera pars similiter manifesta cuadit. euadit. Nam quædam eius partes actu in loco sunt, ut quæ seiunctæ ac separatæ attinguntur inferne à proximis orbibus circundantibus. Quædam potentia tantùm sunt in loco, nempe quæ toti continuá sunt, atq; à nullis circundantibus attinguntur. Adhæc quædam per se sunt in loco, ut eæ partes quas diximus actu in loco existere. Quædam per accidens, veluti accidetia nonnulla in partibus, et ipsum corpus cœleste ab ea parte in qua illa accidentia sunt. Item ratione inferiorum orbium, qui suo quiq; ordine sunt locati, dicitur cœlū quoq; suo loco existere. Subijcit hic Aristoteles dilutiones argumentorum, quæ allata fuerant ad probandum, locū non esse. nos eas suprà attulimus.
units.tr: 2. Although the whole heaven is not in place, nevertheless in its different parts it stands in place in various ways too. The first part of this proposition is plain: for nothing exists outside the heaven itself, and that outside which there is nothing, how can it be understood to be contained by any extremity? The second part likewise is plain enough. For some of its parts are actually in place, namely those which, separated and set apart, are touched below by the neighbouring surrounding spheres. Some are in place only potentially, namely those which are continuous with the whole and are touched by no surrounding bodies. Further, some are in place per se, such as those parts we have said are actually in place; some per accidens, as certain accidents in the parts, and the heavenly body itself in respect of that part in which those accidents are. Likewise, by reason of the lower spheres, which are each situated in their own order, the heaven too is said to exist in its place. Here Aristotle goes on to answer the arguments which had been brought forward to prove that place does not exist; we have set them out above.

units.la: Quare omne corpus naturaliter fere- tur ad suum locum?
units.tr: Why does every body naturally move towards its place?

units.la: Omne corpus contentum quandam habet συμπάθειαν cum continente. Quamobrem sicut certo quodam ordine inter se sita sunt partes illæ primipaliores uniuersi, ignis inquam, aer, aqua, terra: ita reliquæ quoq; partes rerum naturalium ex illis compositarum, simili ordine collocari semper gestiunt. Hinc igitur fit, quod omnis ignis semper eluctatur sursum, terra uero atq; omne terrenum inclinat deorsum.
units.tr: Every contained body has a certain sympathy [συμπάθεια] with its container. Therefore, just as those primary parts of the universe, I mean fire, air, water and earth, are placed in a certain fixed order among themselves, so the remaining parts of natural things, compounded out of them, always strive to be arranged in a similar order. Hence it comes about that all fire always struggles upward, while earth and everything earthy inclines downward.

units.la: Quare omne corpus naturaliter,ubi ad locum suum peruene- rit,quiescit?
units.tr: Why does every body, once it has reached its place, naturally come to rest?

units.la: Cum locus extremum sit corporis continentis, sane corpus contentum se habet ad corpus continens sicut pars ad totum, diuisa tamen. Sed pars omnis gaudet coniungi suo toto,suoq; locari ordine: atque id ubi fit,bene habet. Eadem igitur ratione,ubi res naturalis ad suum locu peruenerit,ibi gaudet quiescere,& conseruatur.
units.tr: Since place is the extremity of the containing body, the contained body certainly stands to the containing body as a part stands to a whole, though divided from it. But every part rejoices to be joined to its whole and to be placed in its order; and where this happens, it is well. By the same reasoning, therefore, when a natural thing has reached its place, there it rejoices to rest and is preserved.

units.la: Hæc de quæstionibus: An sit locus, Quid sit locus,tum Quomodo res in loco existant. Nunc autem de uacuo par est aliquid dicamus.
units.tr: These things have been said concerning the questions: whether there is place, what place is, and then how things exist in place. Now, however, it is fitting that we say something about the void.

units.la: DE VACVO.
units.tr: ON THE VOID.

units.la: Quare nunc agendum de Vacuo?
units.tr: Why must we now treat of the void?

units.la: Qva ratione Physicus disputat de loco, eadem disputabit de uacuo. Habent namq; hæc quandam inter se affinitatem.
units.tr: By the same reasoning by which the natural philosopher discusses place, he will also discuss the void, for these have a certain affinity with each other.

units.la: Quæstiones non minus agitatæ sunt à ueteribus de uacuo,atq; de loco.
units.tr: Questions about the void have been debated by the ancients no less than questions about place.

units.la: AN SIT VACVVM?
units.tr: WHETHER THERE IS A VOID?

units.la: Variæ sunt rationes in utramq; partem à philosophis allatæ.
units.tr: Various arguments have been advanced by the philosophers on both sides.

units.la: Pars negatiua.
units.tr: The negative side.

units.la: Primum argumentum à signo: Vtres inflati, non statim statim subsidunt, sed diu resistunt: quod fit, quia intus omnia plena sunt aëris. Igitur nullum est vacuū.
units.tr: The first argument is from a sign: when bellows are inflated, they do not collapse at once, but resist for a long time; this happens because everything inside is full of air. Therefore there is no void.

units.la: Secundum argumentum, itidem à signo. Clepsydræ, obdurato superiore ore, aquam per inferiora foramina non emittunt: quod similiter fit, quia aer inclusus omnia premit, quo non habente liberum meatum, neque aqua egreditur. Igitur nullum est vacuum.
units.tr: The second argument, likewise from a sign: clepsydras, when the upper mouth is closed, do not let water out through the lower holes; this likewise happens because the enclosed air presses on everything, and since it has no free passage, the water does not come out either. Therefore there is no void.

units.la: Sed hæ rationes non probant, directè vacuū non esse: verùm potius euincunt, aerem esse quiddã corporeum. Ac vulgari quidem loquendi more (quo ui delicet vacuum appellant, in quo nullum sensibile corpus continetur) probationes illæ procederent: atqui philosophicè loquendo, alia oportet via ingredi, atq; probare, non esse aliquod spacium astu separatum ab omni corpore. Itaq; nonnulli considérantes, rationes præcedentes esse parum firmas, ausi sunt vacuum constituere, rationibus moti quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: But these arguments do not prove directly that there is no void; rather, they show that air is some corporeal thing. And indeed, taken in the common manner of speaking (in which, namely, they call a void that in which no sensible body is contained), those proofs would hold; but speaking philosophically, we must take another path and prove that there is no space at all separated from every body. Therefore some, considering that the preceding arguments are rather weak, have dared to posit a void, moved by the reasons that follow.

units.la: Pars affirmatiua.
units.tr: Affirmative part.

units.la: Primum argumentum ex ratione motus: Fit motus à loco ad locum: igitur ibi est vacuum. Probatur.
units.tr: The first argument, from the nature of motion: Motion occurs from place to place; therefore there is a void there. Proof follows.

units.la: Nam si res naturalis non mouetur per vacuum, necessum est ibi aliquod corpus existat, à quo motus impediatur: Istud vero dici nequit: Igitur ibi est vacuum. Minor probatur. Si enim ibi aliquod existeret corpus, tū corpus moueretur per corpus, adeoq; duo corpora ibi simul existerent, & in paruo corpore esset maximum corpus (constans uidelicet multis paruis) denique in uno loco simul inuenirentur multa corpora aequalia & inaequalia. quae omnia absurda sunt. Itaq; uacuum constitui debet.
units.tr: For if a natural body is not moved through a void, it must be that some body exists there by which the motion is impeded. But this cannot be said. Therefore there is a void there. The minor premise is proved thus. For if some body existed there, then body would be moved through body, and so two bodies would exist there at the same time, and a greater body would be in a smaller body (namely, one consisting of many small parts); finally, many bodies, equal and unequal, would be found together in one place. All of these are absurd. Therefore a void must be posited.

units.la: Secundum argumentum, à ratione condensationis, quae in quibusdam rebus conspicitur. Compertum enim est, quod dolia tantum uini recipiant, ubi uinum inijcitur una cum utribus, quantum reciperent, si sine utribus uinum infunderetur. Atqui hoc non posset fieri, nisi in uino, sese tunc condensante & premente, esset quaedam uacuitas, utres admittens. Igitur uacuum recte asseritur.
units.tr: The second argument, from the condensation that is seen in certain things. For it is known that casks take in just as much wine when wine is poured in together with the skins as they would if the wine were poured in without the skins. Yet this could not happen unless, in the wine, which then condenses and compresses itself, there were some emptiness admitting the skins. Therefore a void is rightly asserted.

units.la: Tertium argumentum, ex naturali rerum augmentatione: Corporea augentur alimento, quod ab ipsis recipitur. Sed duo corpora non possunt esse simul in eodem loco. Igitur constituendum est, in corpore augendo esse quandam uacuitatem, in quam alimentum, & ex alimento augmentum recipitur.
units.tr: The third argument, from the natural growth of things: bodies grow by the nourishment they receive from themselves. But two bodies cannot be in the same place at once. Therefore it must be held that in the growing body there is a certain void into which the nourishment is received, and from the nourishment the growth.

units.la: Quartum argumentum, à signo: Vas cineribus plenum recipit tantundem aquae, quantum reciperet, etiamsi nulli inessent cineres. Ergo oportet in uase cineribus pleno adhuc aliquid esse uacuum, quod aquam recipiat. Quare uacuum esse concedi debet. Haec argumenta in utramq; partem sunt allata.
units.tr: The fourth argument, from a sign: A vessel full of ashes takes in just as much water as it would take if there were no ashes in it. Therefore there must still be something empty in the vessel full of ashes, which receives the water. Hence it must be conceded that a void exists. These arguments have been brought forward on both sides.

units.la: Responsio ad quaestionem.
units.tr: Response to the question.

units.la: Priusquam aliquid certi de quaestione allata definiamus, stniamus[?], uidere oportet, quid intelligatur nomine Vacui: deinde, quantum uirium habeant rationes ad partem affirmatiuam proximè allatæ.
units.tr: Before we define anything certain about the question raised, we must see what is meant by the name of void, and then how much force the arguments just brought forward for the affirmative side have.

units.la: Primùm igitur communi opinione hominum, uacuum dicitur locus, in quo nullum est corpus. Sed non rectè sic definitur. Primò, falsa est enim hominum opinio, qua putant omne ens esse corporeum, & ubi non cernunt quicquam tangibile aut corporeum, ibi nihil prorsus esse arbitrantur. Secundò, eadem definitio conuenit etiam puncto, utpote in quo nullum corpus sit. Quapropter ad uitandum hoc inconueniens, existimarunt aliqui sic perficiendam definitionem datam: Vacuum est locus, in quo nullum sit corpus tangibile, quod ve graue aut leue sit. Verùm hac definitione nihilo plus efficitur quàm priore. Falsò namque præsupponitur, omne ens esse tangibile.
units.tr: First, then, according to the common opinion of men, a void is a place in which there is no body. But this is not rightly defined. First, the opinion of men is false, by which they think that every being is corporeal, and where they perceive nothing tangible or corporeal, they suppose there is absolutely nothing. Second, the same definition also applies to a point, since in it there is no body. Therefore, to avoid this inconvenience, some have thought the given definition should be completed thus: a void is a place in which there is no tangible body, whether heavy or light. But by this definition nothing more is achieved than by the former. For it is falsely presupposed that every being is tangible.

units.la: Secundò: Vacuum iuxta Platonicos dicitur, in quo non est hoc aliquid (id est, habens certam formam) neque substantia ulla corporea. Sed ne hoc quidem pacto rectè definitur. Nam illi ipsi uacuum aiunt se habere ut materiâ: hoc uero aliquid, ut formam. Atqui cùm materia non possit separari à corporibus, uacuum autem separetur ab ijs, quomodo consistet ea definitio? Tantum igitur de nomine Vacui. Porrò rationes illæ probantes uacuum esse, parum habent ponderis, nec difficile est eas diluere.
units.tr: Second: according to the Platonists, a void is that in which there is not "this something" (that is, having a determinate form), nor any corporeal substance. But not even in this way is it rightly defined. For they themselves say that the void stands to matter, while "this something" stands as form. Yet since matter cannot be separated from bodies, while the void is separated from them, how will that definition hold? So much, then, concerning the name of void. Moreover, those arguments proving that a void exists carry little weight, and it is not difficult to refute them.

units.la: Dilutiones argumentorum allato- rum in partem affirma- tiuam.
units.tr: Refutations of the arguments brought forward for the affirmative part.

units.la: Ad primum argumentum respondetur: Non est necessarium, ut existat uacuū, propterea quòd motus est. Nam res quascunque alterari uidemus, nulla habita loci in quo sunt ratione. Deinde possunt corpora sibi mutuo in loco succeedere, inuicemq; cedere: possunt deniq; in se ipsis quadam ratione moueri, sicut aqua mouetur in aqua.
units.tr: To the first argument it is answered: it is not necessary that a void exist because there is motion. For we see things altered of every kind, without any regard to the place in which they are. Further, bodies can give way to one another in place and yield mutually; and finally they can move in some manner within themselves, as water moves in water.

units.la: Ad secundum argumentum : Condensantur quidem corpora,atq; partes secum mutuo coniunguntur: non quòd aliquæ ingrediantur spacium uacuum, sed quòd foramina quædam seu meatus impleantur crassiori corpore, in quibus erat prius corpus aliquod subtilius,quod quidem subtile corpus,quando fit cõdensatio,cedit atq; elabitur. In aqua dum congelatur, & corporibus porosis haud difficulter id deprehenditur.
units.tr: To the second argument: bodies are indeed condensed, and their parts are joined together with one another; not because some parts enter an empty space, but because certain pores or passages are filled with a denser body, in which there was previously some more subtle body; which subtle body, when condensation takes place, yields and slips away. This is easily detected in water while it freezes, and in porous bodies.

units.la: Ad tertium: Augmentatio non solùm contingit, quia aliquod corpus,alimentum uidelicet,in corpus recipitur,tanquam res à corpore distincta & separata: sed magis propter alterationem & transmutationem ipsius alimenti. Neq; enim alimentum constitui debet diuersum corpus ab eo in quo est:quandoquidem in huius ipsius conuertitur substantiam, prorsus quemadmodum ligna apposita igni conuertuntur in ignem. Huiusmodi igitur transmutatio, & per transmutationem augmentatio vacuum non constituit.
units.tr: To the third: growth does not occur only because some body, namely nourishment, is received into the body as a thing distinct and separate from it; but rather on account of the alteration and transmutation of the nourishment itself. For the nourishment ought not to be posited as a body different from that in which it is; since it is converted into the substance of that very body, just as wood placed on fire is turned into fire. Such transmutation, and growth through transmutation, therefore does not establish a void.

units.la: Ad quartum: Vas quidem plenum cinere recipit aquam, non quia vacuum ibi est, sed quia cinis & aqua simul junguntur, coalescunt, condensantur, & pars aliqua subtilior exhalatur. Argumentum condensationis huius evidens[?] est, quod cineres paululum subsidunt, deinde tantum aquae postea educi non queat, quantum prius infuderas.
units.tr: To the fourth: a vessel full of ashes receives water not because a void is there, but because the ashes and the water are joined together, coalesce, condense, and some finer part is exhaled. The argument from condensation is evident in this, that the ashes settle a little, and afterwards not as much water can be drawn off as you had poured in before.

units.la: His ita expositis, promptum est conclusionem, qua quaestioni satis fiat, colligere.
units.tr: With these things thus set out, it is easy to draw the conclusion by which the question is sufficiently answered.

units.la: Conclusio.
units.tr: The conclusion.

units.la: In rerum natura vacuum omni privatum corpore dari non potest. Quæ conclusio perspicuis aliquot rationibus probatur.
units.tr: There cannot be a void, deprived of all body, in the nature of things. This conclusion is proved by several plain arguments.

units.la: Si constitueretur vacuum, maxime quidem id fieret propter motum localem. Sed hac de causa non opus est constituere. Igitur vacuum non est. Minor probatur: Omnia corpora simplicia habent motum localem a natura: veluti ignis natura tendit sursum, aqua deorsum. Igitur natura uniuscuiusque corporis est causa motus localis, non vacuum.
units.tr: If a void were posited, it would be posited chiefly for the sake of local motion. But there is no need to posit one for this reason. Therefore there is no void. The minor is proved thus: all simple bodies have local motion from nature. Fire, for instance, tends upward by nature, water downward. Therefore the nature of each body is the cause of local motion, not a void.

units.la: Si constituatur vacuum, tollitur causa motus naturalis, & quietis naturalis. Probatur: Corpus naturale movetur ad locum suum naturalem, & quiescit in eo, quia habet quādam cum eo συμπάθειαν, neq; conuenire ei potest cum alio ab eo. Atqui si ponas corpus naturale in uacuo, cum quo illud nullam prorsus habet συμπάθειαν, tum sane corpus illud nusquam, id est, neq; sursum, neq; deorsum moueri poterit. Igitur concesso uacuo, ut uidelicet sit quasi locus quidam priuatus corpore, tollitur causa motus & quietis corporis naturalis in eo positi.
units.tr: If a void is posited, the cause of natural motion and of natural rest is removed. This is proved thus: a natural body moves to its natural place and rests in it, because it has a certain sympathy [συμπάθεια] with that place. Nor can it be joined to anything other than what it has sympathy with. But if you place a natural body in a void, with which it has no sympathy whatever, then that body will be nowhere, that is, it will be able to move neither upward nor downward. Therefore, if a void is granted, that is, a kind of place deprived of body, the cause of motion and of rest for a natural body placed in it is removed.

units.la: Imò si constituas uacuum, sequitur simpliciter motum non esse. Probatur id similitudine: Terra quiescit in medio propter similitudinem partium circumferentiæ eius, ob quam quidè similitudinem non potest moueri magis in unam partem quàm in aliam. Eadem igitur ratione si concedatur uacuum, cum in eo nullæ sint partium differentiæ, causa motus omnis tolletur. Itaq; tantum abest, ut quia motus est, conueniat constituere uacuum: ut si uacuum constituas, motum omnem plane sustuleris.
units.tr: Indeed, if you posit a void, it follows that there is simply no motion. This is proved by a comparison. The earth rests in the middle because the parts of its circumference are alike, and for this same reason it cannot be moved more toward one side than toward another. By the same reasoning, then, if a void is granted, since in it there are no differences of parts, the cause of all motion will be removed. So far is it from being the case that, because there is motion, it is fitting to posit a void; rather, if you posit a void, you will have utterly abolished all motion.

units.la: Si uacuum conceditur, tum plane omnem motum tam naturalem quam uiolentum tolli necessum est. Quod sic probo: Vacuum prohibet motum naturalem: quia, ut dictum est, in uacuo non sunt differentiæ, per quas res naturales huc potius quàm illuc, deinde sursum aut deorsum feruntur. Hinc uero sequitur: Si aufertur motus naturalis, simul quoque aufertur ac prohibetur motus uiolètus. Enimuero cū motus uiolentus tantùm sit declinatio quædam à motu naturali, necessum est, remoto isto, simul[?] removeri & illum. Ergo concesso vacuo, motus omnis tolletur. quod quidem absurdum est, & cum natura pugnans.
units.tr: If a void is granted, then all motion, natural as well as forced, must necessarily be removed. I prove it thus: a void prevents natural motion, because, as has been said, in a void there are no differences by which natural things are carried hither rather than thither, and then upward or downward. Hence it follows that if natural motion is taken away, forced motion is at the same time taken away and prevented. For forced motion is only a certain deviation from natural motion, so when the one is removed the other must be removed too. Therefore, if a void is granted, all motion will be abolished. This is plainly absurd, and contrary to nature.

units.la: Ex his omnibus manifestum fit, vacuum nullo modo constituendum esse, eo praesertim nomine quod motus fit.
units.tr: From all this it is clear that a void must in no way be posited, especially on the ground that there is motion.

units.la: Sed probat deinde Aristoteles aliquot rationibus, atq; concludit, vacuum nullo modo esse constituendum, neq; adiunctum motui, ratione velocitatis aut tarditatis, neq; per se seorsum positum, atque à motu separatū, postremò neq; etiam corporibus ullis inditum. Nos autem brevitatis causa argumenta et probationes omittimus, rati satis nos facere, quam do quem Aristoteles sequitur ordine, tenuiter commonstremus. Recte autem illud in genere dictum retinebitur, nullum dari posse spacium, quod non aere saltem refertum sit, quem quouis penetrare, atq; omnia implere, notissimum est. Nunc res postulat, ut de tempore orationem instituamus.
units.tr: But Aristotle then proves by several arguments, and concludes, that a void must in no way be posited, neither joined to motion, with respect to speed or slowness, nor set apart by itself and separated from motion, nor finally inserted into any bodies. For the sake of brevity, however, we omit the arguments and proofs, judging it enough to indicate briefly the order which Aristotle follows. It will rightly be retained in general that no space can be granted which is not filled at least with air, which is well known to penetrate everywhere and fill all things. Now the matter requires that we set out a discussion concerning time.

units.la: DE TEMPORE.
units.tr: CONCERNING TIME.

units.la: Quare nunc agendum de Tempore?
units.tr: Why must we now treat of Time?
