units.la: 1. In disputatione de motu admodum necessaria est temporis cognitio.
units.tr: 1. A knowledge of time is very necessary in the discussion of motion.

units.la: 2. Physici est investigare, an res naturales in tempore esse coeperint, tum an tempore transmutentur.
units.tr: 2. It is the business of the natural philosopher to investigate whether natural things began to exist in time, and then whether they are changed in time.

units.la: De hac quæstione uariæ fuerunt opiniones, atq; alij negarunt, alij affirmarunt. nos utriusq; partis rationes referemus.
units.tr: Opinions on this question have varied: some have denied, others have affirmed. We shall set out the arguments of both sides.

units.la: Pars negatiua.
units.tr: The negative side.

units.la: 1. Quod compositum est ex his quæ impossibile est esse, id profecto esse, siue aliquam habere substantiam, non potest. Atqui tempus est huiusmodi. Igitur tempus non est. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur: Tempus omne componitur partim ex præterito, quod iam non est, sed esse desijt: partim ex futuro, quod nondum est. Igitur partes temporis esse impossibile est: quamobrem nec tempus existet.
units.tr: 1. What is composed of things that cannot exist cannot itself exist, or have any substance. But time is of this kind. Therefore time does not exist. The major is evident. The minor is proved thus: all time is composed partly of the past, which no longer is but has ceased to be, and partly of the future, which is not yet. Therefore the parts of time cannot exist, and for this reason time itself will not exist.

units.la: 2. Vt res aliqua diuisibilis existat, oportet aliquam quoq; uel aliquas eius partes simul existere. Atqui temporis nullæ prorsus existunt partes: quandoquidem aliæ præteritæ sunt, aliæ futuræ. Igitur nec tempus quoq; est.
units.tr: 2. For any divisible thing to exist, some one or more of its parts must exist at the same time. But no parts of time exist at all, since some are past and others future. Therefore time does not exist either.

units.la: Quod si dicas, τὸ νῦν[?] esse partem temporis: atq; cum hoc consistit, etiam tempus consistere. hic rursus aliam opponunt rationem. Pars est, quæ mensurat totum, uel ex qua componitur totū. Sed tempus nequaquam componitur hac ratione ex ipso NVN C, neq; eo mensuratur. Igitur NVN C nō est pars temporis. Relinquitur ergo, tempus non esse.
units.tr: But if you say that the now [τὸ νῦν] is a part of time, and that with this it stands, then time also stands, they again raise another argument. A part is that which measures the whole, or that out of which the whole is composed. But time is in no way composed of the now, nor is it measured by it. Therefore the now is not a part of time. It remains, then, that time does not exist.

units.la: Pars affirmatiua.
units.tr: The affirmative part.

units.la: Alij dixerunt, tempus simpliciter esse, necnon id constare uno eodemq; NUNC semper manete, quo quidem ita copulentur praeteritum & futurum, ut ipsum NUNC finiat sane praeteritum, incipiat vero etiam futurum. Quod ita esse debere, nec posse aliud atq; aliud NUNC constitui, hac ratione demonstratur. Duae temporis partes diversae non possunt simul esse, nisi una contineat aliam, sicut maius tempus continet minus, & annus mensem, mensis diem: simul namq; sunt annus, mensis, dies. Sed si ponas diversa NUNC quibus tempus constabit, sane uno consistente, necessum erit statim alterum, nimirum antecedens, corrumpi: deinde & quod praesens est, oportet similiter corrumpi, atq; ita deinceps. Quod tamen est multo absurdissimum. Igitur tantum unum idemq; NUNC est, semper manens. Quod vero absurdum sit, unum NUNC post aliud corrumpi, declaratur. Ut enim aliquod NUNC corrumpatur, necessum est id in aliquo NUNC corrumpi. Atqui hoc qui fiat, non potest intelligi. Non enim corrumpebatur in quo erat. Quamdiu namq; aliquid est, non potest dici simul & semel corrumpi. Non item in quo nondum erat, non item in aliquo posteriori: alias enim oporteret constitui duo NUNC simul & semel, alterum in quo consistit, alterum in quo consistere definit. Ergo perspicuū cuadit, tempus esse, necnon ex uno eodemq; NUNC semper manente id constare.
units.tr: Others have said that time simply is, and that it consists of one and the same NOW, always remaining, by which past and future are so joined that the NOW itself certainly ends the past and also begins the future. That this must be so, and that a different NOW cannot be posited after another, is shown by this reasoning. Two different parts of time cannot exist at the same time unless one contains the other, as a greater time contains a lesser, and a year a month, and a month a day; for the year, the month and the day are together at once. But if you posit different NOWs of which time would consist, with one existing, the other, obviously the preceding one, must necessarily be destroyed at once; then what is present must likewise be destroyed, and so on in sequence. Yet this is far the most absurd. Therefore there is only one and the same NOW, always remaining. That it is absurd for one NOW to be destroyed after another is shown as follows. For any NOW to be destroyed, it must be destroyed in some NOW. But how this could happen cannot be understood. For it would not be destroyed in the NOW in which it was, since as long as something is, it cannot be said to be destroyed at the same time and at once. Nor could it be destroyed in a NOW in which it was not yet, nor in some later NOW; otherwise two NOWs would have to be posited at once and together, one in which it persists and the other in which it ceases to persist. Therefore it is clear that time exists, and that it consists of one and the same NOW always remaining.

units.la: Quamuis rursum ostendi queat, unum idemq; NVNC eo modo non satis posse consistere. Aristoteles duas adfert rationes.
units.tr: Yet it can be shown again that one and the same NOW cannot sufficiently subsist in this way. Aristotle brings two arguments.

units.la: 1. Nullius rei diuisibilis finitæ potest unus tantum esse terminus, siue sit in ea una tantum dimensio, ut in linea: siue plures, ut in superficie atq; corpore. Atqui dari potest tempus diuisibile finitum. Igitur tempus non potest poni unus tantum terminus, siue unum tantum NVNC.
units.tr: 1. Of any finite divisible thing there can be only one terminus, whether it has only one dimension, as a line, or several, as a surface and a body. But time can be a finite divisible thing. Therefore time cannot be posited with only one terminus, that is, with only one NOW.

units.la: 2. Si unum idemq; NVNC in toto tempore constituatur, sequitur illa NVNC quæ fuerut ante mille annos, simul esse cum his NVNC quæ iam sunt. Istud autem est absurdum: igitur & illud ex quo sequitur.
units.tr: 2. If one and the same NOW were posited throughout the whole of time, it would follow that those NOWs which were a thousand years ago would be at the same time as those NOWs which now are. But this is absurd; therefore that from which it follows is absurd too.

units.la: Sed ex his satis constat tépus esse. Cæterum quia rationes iam allatæ faciunt ut ambiguum sit, utrum tempus constet uno eodemq; NVNC semper manente: quid de hac re sentiendum sit, paulo post dicetur cómodius. Tátum igitur de quæstione An sit?
units.tr: But from these things it is sufficiently established that time exists. Moreover, since the arguments already brought make it doubtful whether time consists of one and the same NOW always remaining, what should be thought about this matter will be stated more conveniently a little later. So much, then, concerning the question whether it is?

units.la: QVID SIT TEMPVS? Quid est Tempus?
units.tr: WHAT TIME IS? What is time?

units.la: Variæ à ueteribus definitiones temporis sunt edita, è quibus nonnulla reprobantur.
units.tr: The ancients have put forward various definitions of time, some of which are rejected.

units.la: Da primam definitionem.
units.tr: Give the first definition.

units.la: Tempus est motus seu couersio cœli. Verum hæc definitio non est satis aptà, quod duabus probatur rationibus.
units.tr: Time is the motion or revolution of the heavens. But this definition is not altogether apt, for it is refuted by two arguments.

units.la: 1. Si conuersio cœli esset tempus, oporteret parte conuersionis eius, esse conuersione, sicut pars quoq; temporis est tempus. Sed illud est absurdum: igitur neq; tempus est.
units.tr: 1. If the revolution of the heavens were time, a part of that revolution would have to be a revolution, just as a part of time is also time. But this is absurd; therefore time is not that either.

units.la: 2. Positis pluribus cœlis, ponentur & plures conuersiones: positis pluribus conuersionibus, conficietur plura quoque esse debere simul tempora, quod rursus peræquè absurdum est.
units.tr: 2. If several heavens are posited, several revolutions will also be posited; if several revolutions are posited, several times must also be at the same time, which again is equally absurd.

units.la: Da secundam definitionem.
units.tr: Give the second definition.

units.la: Tempus est circulus ac sphæra uniuersi. Fortassis rati sunt huius definitionis authores, quod quèad modum circulus, ita tempus quoq; omnia cõtineat. Sed longè aliter res continetur tempore, aliter circulo siue sphæra. Quamobrem falsi sunt.
units.tr: Time is the circle and sphere of the universe. Perhaps the authors of this definition thought that, as a circle contains, so time also contains all things. But things are contained in time in a far different way than in a circle or sphere. Therefore they are false.

units.la: Da tertiam definitionem.
units.tr: Give the third definition.

units.la: Tempus est motus siue mutatio. Verùm ne hæc quidem definitio admittetur. Rationes sunt in promptu.
units.tr: Time is motion or change. But this definition too will not be admitted. The reasons are at hand.

units.la: 1. Omnis motus & mutatio est aut in ea tantum re quæ transmutatur, aut in loco quo transmutatio peragitur. Atqui tempus est apud omnia & ubiq;: igitur tempus non potest dici motus aut mutatio.
units.tr: 1. Every motion and change is either in that thing alone which is changed, or in the place where the change is carried out. But time is everywhere and in all things; therefore time cannot be called motion or change.

units.la: 2. Omnis mutatio & motus uelox est aut tardus. Atqui tempus neq; uelox dicitur, neq; tardum: igitur tempus non est motus uel mutatio. Minor probatur. Tardum enim & uelox describuntur ex ratione temporis. Siquidem uelox dicitur, quod breui tempore pertransit longum spacium: tardum uero, quod longiori tempore pertransit modicum spacium. Atqui tempus nullo modo describitur ex ratione temporis, neq; secundum suam quantitatem, neque secundum qualitatem. Igitur tempus neque uelox neque tardum dicitur, ac proinde neq; etiam motus est.
units.tr: 2. Every change and motion is either swift or slow. But time is called neither swift nor slow; therefore time is not motion or change. The minor premise is proved thus. For swift and slow are described from the measure of time: something is called swift because it traverses a long space in a short time, and slow because it traverses a small space in a longer time. But time is in no way described from the measure of time, neither according to its quantity nor according to its quality. Therefore time is called neither swift nor slow, and consequently it is not motion either.

units.la: Est'ne tempus prorsus sine motu, aut nihil ipsius motus in tempo- re spectatur?
units.tr: Is time altogether without motion, or is nothing of motion itself observed in time?

units.la: Non est tempus sine motu. Etenim tunc tempus intelligimus, quando uidelicet rationem apud nos inimus motus aut mutationis: adeoq; de tepore[?] non cogitamus, quin occurrat aliquid de motu. Quocirca tempus sine motu prorsus nō est. Imò uero, quando sine motu non est, atq; alterum cum altero sentitur, sane conficietur, tempus aliquid etiam ipsius motus existere.
units.tr: There is no time without motion. For we understand time only when we form in our minds the idea of motion or change; and so we do not think of time without something about motion occurring to us. Therefore time altogether without motion does not exist. Indeed, since it is not without motion, and one is perceived together with the other, it will certainly follow that time is also something of motion itself.

units.la: Quomodo spectatur motus in tempore?
units.tr: How is motion regarded in time?

units.la: Cum motus sit continuus, tempus autem sit aliquid ipsius motus, erit profectò & ipsum tempus cōtinuum. quamobrem erit motus in tempore quadam ratione continui, nimirum secundum prius ac posterius. Quemadmodū enim in magnitudine siue spacio aliquid prius est, aliquid uero posterius: ita & in motu aliquid prius est, aliquid uero posterius: ut ut autem in motu,ita quoq; in tempore. Quamuis in magnitudine quidem prius & posterius simul permanent:in motu autem,cum succedit posterius, aboletur prius.
units.tr: Since motion is continuous, and time is something of motion itself, time too will certainly be continuous. Therefore motion in time is, in a certain sense, continuous, namely according to a before and an after. For just as in magnitude or space one part is before and another part after, so too in motion one part is before and another after, and likewise in time. Although in magnitude the before and the after remain together at once; in motion, however, when the after follows, the before is destroyed.

units.la: Da quartam,eamq; certam defini- tionem temporis.
units.tr: Fourth, the certain definition of time.

units.la: Tempus est numerus ipsius motus rerum mutabilium secundum prius ac posterius. Estq; haec definitio ex praecedentibus collecta, cuius haec est sententia: Tempus est spacium deductum ex coeli Solisq; motu, quo mensuratur omnium rerum mutabilium agitatio & uicissitudo. Vocatur autem tempus numerus, non quo, sed quem numeramus, seu numerus numeratus. Numeratur quippe tempus secundum prius & posterius.
units.tr: Time is the number of the motion of changeable things according to before and after. This definition is gathered from what has gone before, and its sense is this: time is an interval drawn from the motion of the heavens and the sun, by which the activity and alternation of all changeable things is measured. Time is called a number not by which we count, but which we count, or a counted number. For time is counted according to before and after.

units.la: QVALE SIT TEMPVS.
units.tr: WHAT TIME IS.

units.la: Utrum tempus sit unum idemq; NVN C, an aliud atq; aliud NVN C?
units.tr: Is time one and the same NOW, or is it always another and another NOW?

units.la: Quando in tepore consideratur hinc prius, inde posterius, secundu successione temporis & continui motus, tunc sane recte dicimus, quod tepus sit aliud atq; aliud NVN C. Quando vero tepus consideratur in se, nulla habita ratione prioris aut posterioris, tunc est unum idemq; NVN C. Ex quo fit, quod ipsum NVN C, omne tempus mesurat. unumquodq; enim per id mensuratur, quod maxime de eo seu in eo notum est. Atqui de tempore maxime notum est ipsum NVNC: quare & tempus ipso NVNC men furatur. Et qua ratione motus cognoscitur per id quod mouetur, & motus localis per id quod loco mouetur, eadem quoq; ratione tempus mensuratur per ipsum NVNC , cum nihil certius de tempore deprehendamus quam ipsum NVNC. Ergo apte dicitur, quod tempus mefuratur uno quoda NVNC.
units.tr: When in time we consider one part as before and another as after, according to the succession of time and continuous motion, then indeed we rightly say that time is always another and another NOW. But when time is considered in itself, with no regard to before or after, then it is one and the same NOW. From this it follows that the NOW itself measures all time. For each thing is measured by that which is best known of it or in it. But of time the best known thing is the NOW; therefore time too is measured by the NOW. And just as motion is known through that which is moved, and local motion through that which is moved in place, so by the same reasoning time is measured through the NOW itself, since we grasp nothing more certain about time than the NOW itself. Therefore it is rightly said that time is measured by a certain NOW.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum uenit,quod dicitur,nihil esse temporis nisi NVNC?
units.tr: How is it to be understood that it is said there is nothing of time except the NOW?

units.la: Si non fit tempus,non erit etiam NVNC:& uice uersa,fi non fit NVNC,nec tempus quidem erit. itaque tempus & NVNC coniuncta sunt, nec alterum fine altero esse potest, non magis quam motus potest esse fine mobili.
units.tr: If time does not exist, then neither will the NOW exist; and conversely, if the NOW does not exist, neither will time exist. Thus time and the NOW are joined, and neither can be without the other, no more than motion can be without a moving thing.

units.la: Ac tempus quidem praeteritum non est,similiter tempus futurum non est:quocirca no potest aliquid temporis esse,nisi NVNC.
units.tr: Indeed past time is not, and likewise future time is not; therefore nothing of time can exist except the NOW.

units.la: Quomodo intelligendum, quod NVNC continuat & diuidit tem- poris partes?
units.tr: How is it to be understood that the NOW both connects and divides the parts of time?

units.la: Duabus rationibus fiue similitudinibus id explicatur.
units.tr: This is explained by two comparisons or likenesses.

units.la: 1. Sicut quod mouetur,unum idemq; manet in toto motu,hoc est,tam cum incipit, quam cum pergit mouere,atq; ita dat unitatem motui: interea tamen etiam distinguit motum secundum priorem & posteriorem motus partem. Sic ipsum nvn c pariter continuat tempus ac diuidit: continuat inquam, dando unitatem tempori: diuidit uero, secundum prius & posterius.
units.tr: 1. Just as that which is moved remains one and the same through the whole motion, that is, both when it begins to move and when it continues to move, and so gives unity to the motion; yet at the same time it also divides the motion into an earlier and a later part of the motion. So the NOW likewise both connects time and divides it: it connects it, I say, by giving unity to time; but it divides it according to before and after.

units.la: 2. Rursus, sicut punctum continuat lineam, nec non distinguit eandem, cum nimirum sit in ea prin cipiu unius partis, & finis alterius: eodem pacto ipsum nvn c & continuat tempus, & distinguit tempus.
units.tr: 2. Again, just as a point connects a line and also divides it, since in it is the beginning of one part and the end of another, in the same way the NOW both connects time and divides time.

units.la: Cum tempus sit numerus, utrum in tempore inuenietur minimum sicut in numero?
units.tr: Since time is a number, is a minimum found in time as in number?

units.la: Partim sic, partim non. Vt enim tempus est numerus, atque in tempore spectatur multitudo, inuenitur in eo minimum. quemadmodum in numeris minimus numerus est binarius: ita minimum tempus constitui potest momentum, uel similis portio minima. Vt uero tempus est continuum, siue ut in tempore spectatur magnitudo, non inuenitur in eo minimum: quemadmodum neque in linea secundum magnitudinem inuenitur minimum. Pleraque quaestiones hic mouentur explicandae definitionis supra posi-tae, tum etiam quaestionis An sit, gratia.
units.tr: Partly so, partly not. For insofar as time is a number, and in time multitude is considered, a minimum is found in it, just as in numbers the smallest number is two; so the smallest time can be taken to be a moment, or some similar minimal portion. But insofar as time is continuous, or as magnitude is considered in time, no minimum is found in it, just as in a line, considered as magnitude, no minimum is found. Many questions are raised here, which must be explained from the definition set down above, and also from the question whether it is, which is needed.

units.la: Quare tempus non dicitur tardum aut uelox, sed multum & paucum, breue & longum?
units.tr: Why is time not called slow or swift, but much and little, brief and long?

units.la: Verum quidem est, tempus sine motu non exi-stere stere(quod supra dictum est:)non tamen propterea tempori tribuentur tarditas vel velocitas, utpote quæ proprie conveniunt ipsi motui. Atqui dicetur tempus multum & paucum, qua videlicet ratione tempus est numerus,siue in tempore spectatur multitudo.Dicetur item breue & longum, qua ratione tempus est continuum,atq; in eo spectatur magnitudo : quo quidem pacto & linea,quoniam continua est,longa & breuis dicitur.
units.tr: It is true that time does not exist without motion, as was said above; nevertheless slowness or swiftness is not for that reason attributed to time, since these properly belong to motion itself. Yet time will be called much and little, insofar as time is a number, or insofar as multitude is considered in time. It will likewise be called brief and long, insofar as time is continuous and magnitude is considered in it; in this way also a line, because it is continuous, is called long and short.

units.la: Quomodo ubiq; est idem simul tem- pus, non autem ubiq; est idem prius & posterius[?]?
units.tr: How is the same time everywhere at once, but not everywhere the same before and after?

units.la: Idem tempus,ut est cōtinuum, mensurat quidem ubiq; omnia : cæterum ut est numerus, palam quidem est,quod in rebus tēpore existentibus non cōsiderantur eadem temporis partes secundum prius & posterius, prout diuersa est earum rerum duratio . Quod enim unius rei est posterius, id alterius rei est prius : sicut corruptio unius, est generatio alterius.
units.tr: The same time, insofar as it is continuous, measures all things everywhere. But insofar as it is a number, it is clear that in things that exist in time, the same parts of time are not considered as before and after, since the duration of those things differs. For what is after one thing is before another: the corruption of one thing is the generation of another.

units.la: An idem tempus potest redire?
units.tr: Can the same time return?

units.la: Sicut potest redire idem motus, siue eadem cœli latio, ita recurrere potest idem tempus. Sic autem stato tempore redit æstas, hyems, solstitium, bruma. Aliter uero non intelligitur redire idem tempus.
units.tr: Just as the same motion, or the same revolution of the heavens, can return, so the same time can recur. In this way summer, winter, the solstice and the winter solstice return at their appointed times. Otherwise, the same time is not understood to return.

units.la: An sicut tempore mensuratur motus, ita etiam motu mensura- tur tempus?
units.tr: Just as time is measured by motion, is motion also measured by time?

units.la: Maximè. Colligimus (exempli causa) tantam cœli partem circumuolutam: atque ita dicimus,tot abijsse horas,dies uel menses. Rursus colligimus,tanto tempore aliquid esse factum: inde autè dicimus, tantam cœli partem esse circumuolutam. Mensurāt ergo tempus & motus sese mutuò.
units.tr: Certainly. We gather (for example) that so great a part of the heavens has been revolved; and so we say that so many hours, days or months have passed. Again, we gather that something was done in so much time; and from that we say that so great a part of the heavens has been revolved. Therefore time and motion measure each other mutually.

units.la: Quomodo dicuntur res esse in tempore?
units.tr: In what sense are things said to be in time?

units.la: Res esse in tempore nihil aliud est,quàm eas tempore mensurari. Cum autem tempus sit mensura ipsius motus, deinde etiam eius quod mouetur: sequitur hinc,quòd res esse in tempore,bifariam possit intelligi.
units.tr: To be in time is nothing other than to be measured by time. Since time is the measure of motion, and then also of that which is moved, it follows from this that being in time can be understood in two ways.

units.la: 1. Sunt res in tempore, quia sunt quando etiam tempus est,siue sunt simul cum tempore.
units.tr: 1. Things are in time because they exist when time also exists, or they exist together with time.

units.la: 2. Sunt res in tempore,secundum suam uidelicet durationem, atq; ut ipsæ in sua natura perseuerant. Hoc autem secundo modo dicuntur res magis proprie esse in tempore. Ex quo fit, ut quæ res in tempore esse dicuntur, eædem in tempore pati intelligantur,necnon tempore ipso corrumpi:quando nimirum longinquitate temporis necessum est res naturales semper alterari, paulatimq; etiam deficere. Atq; hinc quidem ipsum tempus causa corruptionis rerum appellatur. Rursus autem, quæ non corrumpuntur tempore, neq; ulla ratione patiuntur, ea dicuntur non esse in tempore, sed immortalia, & incorruptibilia æternaq; nominantur. Cuius generis sunt corpora cœlestia, etc. Deus, spiritus, anima, &c.
units.tr: 2. Things are in time according to their own duration, and insofar as they persist in their own nature. It is in this second sense that things are said to be in time more properly. From this it follows that those things which are said to be in time are understood also to undergo change in time, and to be corrupted by time itself, since, clearly, through the length of time natural things must always be altered and gradually fail. And for this reason time itself is called the cause of the corruption of things. Again, however, those things which are not corrupted by time, and in no way undergo change, are said not to be in time, but are called immortal, incorruptible and eternal. Of this kind are the heavenly bodies, etc., God, spirit, the soul, etc.

units.la: An quiescentia sint in tempore?
units.tr: Are things at rest in time?

units.la: Hæc est huius quæstionis occasio: Tempus definitur esse numerus motus: quando autem additur mentio ipsius motus, ac demonstratum est proxime motum esse admodum affinem tempori, hinc meritò subit animum cogitatio etiam de quiete, ac scire quiuis desiderat, an tempori conueniat cum quiete. Respondetur autem, quod quiescentia sunt in tempore. Ac tempus quidem recte definiri potest, numerus seu mensuratio, non tantum motus, uerumetiam quietis. Nam cum quies nihil aliud sit quam privatio motus, sane qua ratione mensurabitur habitus, hoc est motus, eadem mensurabitur & privatio, hoc est quies. Sicut namque solemus dicere, motum esse in tempore, atque pronunciare quantus ille sit: ita quietem quoque esse in tempore, præterea definire quanta ea sit, convenit. Tanta quippe est quies, quantus fuisset motus, si res mobilis toto eo spacio in motu perseveraret. Hoc tamen inter motum quietemq; est discriminis, quod motum quidem mensurat tempus per se, quietem vero per accidens.
units.tr: This is the occasion of this question: time is defined as the number of motion. Since mention is made of motion itself, and it has just been shown that motion is very closely related to time, it is reasonable that the thought of rest also comes to mind, and everyone wants to know whether rest belongs to time. It is answered that things at rest are in time. And time can rightly be defined as a number or measure not only of motion but also of rest. For since rest is nothing other than the privation of motion, by whatever measure the state, that is motion, is measured, by the same measure the privation, that is rest, will be measured. For just as we are accustomed to say that motion is in time and to state how great it is, so it is also fitting to say that rest is in time and to define how great it is. Rest is indeed as great as the motion would have been, if the mobile thing had continued in motion through that whole span. There is, however, this difference between motion and rest: time measures motion through itself, but rest only incidentally.

units.la: Comprehende aliquot conclusio- nibus, quae in tempore sint aut non sint.
units.tr: Comprehend, by some conclusions, which things are or are not in time.

units.la: 1. Non sunt in tempore, quae neque moventur neque quiescunt.
units.tr: 1. Those things are not in time which neither move nor rest.

units.la: 2. Non sunt in tempore, quae nunquam aliter possunt se habere, id est, quae necessario sunt vera, etiam si tempus non esset: ut ternarium esse numerum imparem, diametrum quadrati commensurabilem esse cuicunque lateri ipsius quadrati, item Deum summe esse sapientem.
units.tr: 2. Those things are not in time which can never be otherwise, that is, which are necessarily true even if time did not exist: as that three is an odd number, that the diagonal of a square is commensurable with any side of that same square, and likewise that God is supremely wise.

units.la: 3. Non sunt in tepore, quae nunquam esse possunt.
units.tr: 3. Those things are not in time which can never exist.

units.la: 4. Cetera vero omnia, nimirum quae moveri aut quiescere possunt, quae aliter atque aliter possunt se habere: quae cum non sint, tamen esse possunt: cum sint, esse desinunt, in tempore esse dicuntur.
units.tr: 4. All other things, namely those which can move or rest, which can be now one way and now another, which, when they do not exist, can nevertheless exist, and when they exist, cease to exist, are said to be in time.

units.la: Explana proprias significationes, tum vocis NVNC: tum reliquarum vocum, quibus temporis differentiae notantur?
units.tr: Explain the proper meanings both of the word NOW and of the other words by which the differences of time are marked?

units.la: Cum ea quae sunt in tempore, diversis notentur differentijs, par est de vocibus differentias temporis notantibus, aliquid dicere: unde etiam quale tempus sit, constabit clarius.
units.tr: Since those things which are in time are marked by different differences, it is right to say something about the words marking differences of time; from this it will also be clearer what kind of time it is.

units.la: 1. NVNC, νῦν[?], accipitur duobus modis. Primo est terminus, quo praeteritum copulatur futuro, ut praeteriti quidem sit finis, futuri aut initium: secundò significat tempus propinquū praesenti NUNC, siue sit aliquandiu praeteritum, siue aliquanto post secuturum. ut: Nunc reuersus est imperator, id est, ante aliquantum tempus. Nunc ueniet nuncius, id est, hodie uel cras, siue post aliquantum tempus.
units.tr: 1. NOW, [νῦν], is taken in two ways. First, it is the boundary where the past is joined to the future, so that it is the end of the past and the beginning of the future. Secondly, it signifies a time close to the present NOW, whether it is somewhat past or will come some while later. For example: Now the general has returned, that is, some time ago. Now the messenger will come, that is, today or tomorrow, or after some time.

units.la: 2. TUNC, τότε, significat tempus aliquod determinatum, quod praecessit Nunc praesens, siue admodum diu, siue non adeo diu. ut: Tunc actum erat de Asia, cum nasceretur Alexander.
units.tr: 2. THEN, [τότε], signifies some determinate time which preceded the present Now, whether very long ago or not so very long. For example: Then it was all over for Asia, when Alexander was born.

units.la: 3. JAM, ἤδη, notat tempus paulo ante elapsum, aut paulo post secuturum. ut: Quando abijt? Iam. Quando tu abibis? Iam, hoc est, post paucas horas.
units.tr: 3. ALREADY, [ἤδη], denotes a time just elapsed, or about to come shortly after. For example: When did he leave? Already. When will you leave? Already, that is, after a few hours.

units.la: 4. MODO', uel nuper, ἄρτι, est portio temporis praeteriti, parum à praesenti distans. ut: Quando appulisti? Modò.
units.tr: 4. JUST NOW, or lately, [ἄρτι], is a portion of past time, little distant from the present. For example: When did you arrive? Just now.

units.la: 5. OLIM, seu quondam, πάλαι, tempus notat à nostra memoria ualde remotum. ut: Olim fortes fuerunt Milesij.
units.tr: 5. FORMERLY, or of old, [πάλαι], denotes a time very remote from our memory. For example: The Milesians were brave formerly.

units.la: 6. REPENTE, uel Subitò, ἐξαίφνης, notat tempus, quod ob breuitatem uix sentitur. ut: Subitò insilierunt milites armati.
units.tr: 6. SUDDENLY, or all at once, [ἐξαίφνης], denotes a time which is hardly perceived because of its brevity. For example: Suddenly the armed soldiers leapt in.

units.la: Verum'ne est, quòd in tempore omnia fiunt & corrumpuntur?
units.tr: Is it true that all things come into being and are corrupted in time?

units.la: Maxime. Cum enim motu omnia fiant & corrumpantur, motus autem mensuretur tempore, concficitur sanè, & in tempore omnia fieri & corrumpi. Propterea rectè dixerunt quidam, tempus esse sapientissimum, σοφώτατον. Recte etiam Paron Pythagoricus, tempus esse maxime rude & ignauum, ἀμαθέστατον. Nam tempus omnia invenit, docet, monstrat, efficit, tam in natura quàm in artibus & quibuscunq; rebus. Rursus, tempus inducit omnium oblivionem, omnia consumit, omnium abrumpit memoriam. Quāuis magis proprie locutus est Paron: corruptionis namq; causa tempus est per se, generationis autem causa tempus per accidens.
units.tr: Most certainly. For since all things come into being and are corrupted by motion, and motion is measured by time, it is clearly agreed that all things come to be and are corrupted in time. Therefore some have rightly said that time is most wise [σοφώτατον]. Paron the Pythagorean also rightly said that time is most rude and idle [ἀμαθέστατον]. For time discovers, teaches, shows and brings about all things, both in nature and in the arts and in whatever else there is. On the other hand, time brings on the forgetting of all things, consumes everything, and blots out all memory. Yet Paron spoke more properly: time is by itself the cause of corruption, but time is the cause of generation only incidentally.

units.la: Utrum omnis mutatio fiat in tempo- re, & omne quod movetur, mo- veatur in tempore?
units.tr: Whether every change takes place in time, and everything that is moved is moved in time?

units.la: Sic: quod probatur, 1. In omni mutatione inuenitur velocitas ac tarditas. Atqui haec ipsa describunbuntur tempore. Igitur in omni mutatione necessario tempus consideratur, siue omnis motus fit in tempore. 2. In omni motu seu mutatione consideratur prius & posterius. Atqui haec maxime sunt temporis. Igitur in omni motu seu mutatione tempus spectatur.
units.tr: So it is, as is proved: 1. In every change we find swiftness and slowness. But these very things are described by time. Therefore in every change time is necessarily taken into account; in other words, every motion takes place in time. 2. In every motion or change we consider before and after. But these belong above all to time. Therefore in every motion or change time is regarded.

units.la: Utrum tempus sit ubiq;, in coelo, ter- ra, mari, & quibuscunque rebus aliis?
units.tr: Whether time is everywhere: in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all other things?

units.la: Cum omnia haec mobilia sint (sunt autem huiusmodi, quandoquidem loco continentur) sane quatenus in iis spectatur motus, eatenus etiam spectatur ipsius motus mensuratio, ac proinde tempus.
units.tr: Since all these things are mobile (and they are of this kind, since they are contained in place), certainly insofar as motion is observed in them, so far also the measure of that motion is observed, and therefore time.

units.la: Vtrum non existente anima, quæ sola potest numerare, esset tempus, an non?
units.tr: Whether, if there were no soul, which alone can count, there would be time or not?

units.la: Tempus quidem est numerus ipsius motus. Cum autem numeratio non fiat, nisi ab anima (sola namque anima siue intellectus, principalis animæ functio, potest numerare) apparet sane, si nulla existat anima, neq; tempus posse existere. Quamuis rectius dicetur, tempus esse posse, etiamsi non sit anima, siue intellectus humanus numerans. nam neq; motus ipse, neq; rerum naturalium existentia, ab intellectu humano numerante dependet, sed potius ab intellectu diuino, qui nõ solum numerat, uerum etiam est causa efficiens motus & omnium. Quare uel solo intellectu diuino consistente, poterit & tempus esse: quemadmodum fuit quoque tempus, antequam homo conderetur.
units.tr: Time indeed is the number of motion itself. But since counting is done only by a soul (for the soul alone, or the intellect, the principal function of the soul, can count), it clearly appears that if no soul existed, time could not exist either. Yet it will be more rightly said that time can exist even if there is no soul, or human intellect, to count it. For neither motion itself nor the existence of natural things depends on the human intellect that counts, but rather on the divine intellect, which not only counts but is also the efficient cause of motion and of all things. Therefore, even with only the divine intellect existing, time could also exist, just as time existed before man was created.

units.la: Tempus cuius motus est numerus?
units.tr: Time, of which motion is the number?

units.la: Tempus definitur numerus motus, primi uidelicet & principalis, à quo & omnes alij motus deriuantur atque ordinantur, quinetiam omnes res inseriores mouentur, alterantur, generantur, corrumpuntur. Quam ob causam dici receptum est, νυνλος εἶναι τὰ ἀνθρώπινα πράγματα, id est, Circulum esse omnes res humanas. Intelligimus autè primum motum, circumuolutionem sphæræ cœlestis, seu eius cœli cœli quod primum mobile nuncupant. Hucusq; de Infinito, Loco, Vacuo, Tempore: quæ omnia motum consequuntur, & ad cognoscendam motus naturam sunt pernecessaria. nunc redire ad institutũ connenit, atq; quæ posst exposita principia & causas cœpta sunt de motu dici, eadem prosequi. Tractata autem est de motu quæstio, Quid sit: consequitur ergo, ut aggrediamur quæstionem, Quotuplex sit, siue quot species ac partes motus sint.
units.tr: Time is defined as the number of motion, namely of the first and principal motion, from which all other motions are derived and ordered, and by which all the lower things are moved, altered, generated and corrupted. For this reason it is commonly said that human affairs are a circle [κύκλος εἶναι τὰ ἀνθρώπινα πράγματα]. We understand the first motion to be the revolution of the heavenly sphere, or of that heaven which they call the first moved. So far concerning the infinite, place, the void and time: all of which follow from motion and are very necessary for knowing the nature of motion. Now it is fitting to return to our plan, and to pursue the same principles and causes which were set out and begun as concerning motion. The question of what motion is has been treated; it follows, therefore, that we take up the question of how many kinds, or what species and parts, of motion there are.

units.la: DE MOTV.
units.tr: ON MOTION.

units.la: QVOTVPLEX MOTVS, SIVE quot sunt species atque partes motus?
units.tr: WHAT IS THE KIND OF MOTION, OR WHAT ARE ITS SPECIES AND PARTS?

units.la: Quot sunt species motus?
units.tr: How many species of motion are there?

units.la: PRiusquam ad hanc responderetur quæstionem, operæprecium est nosse, quænam sint ad motum necessaria, & quomodo ea ipsa distinguantur, seu diuidantur. Quibus cognitis, procliue erit species motus recensere.
units.tr: Before this question is answered, it is worth knowing what things are necessary for motion and how those same things are distinguished or divided. Once these are known, it will be easy to list the species of motion.

units.la: Quot sunt ad omnem motum necessaria?
units.tr: What things are necessary for every motion?

units.la: Quinq;. 1. Ipsum mouens, à quo uidelicet est principium motus. Sic ignis siue igneum quiddam, est mouens ad calefaciendum.
units.tr: There are five: (1) the mover itself, from which the principle of motion comes. Thus fire, or something fiery, is the mover in heating.

units.la: 2. Mobile, seu quod mouetur: ueluti lignum, uel aliud corpus quod debet calefieri.
units.tr: (2) The mobile, or that which is moved: for example, wood, or another body that is to be heated.

units.la: 3. Tempus quo est motus: veluti hora, vel similis pars.
units.tr: (3) The time in which the motion occurs: for example, an hour, or a similar part of time.

units.la: 4. Terminus à quo motus incipit: ut à frigore, vel à non calente.
units.tr: (4) The terminus from which the motion begins: for example, from cold, or from what is not hot.

units.la: 5. Terminus ad quem motus tendit: ut ad calorem aliquem ignis actio contendit.
units.tr: (5) The terminus to which the motion tends: as the action of fire tends towards some heat.

units.la: Secundum hæc ad motum concurrentia parari possunt utiles aliquot divisiones.
units.tr: In accordance with these, several useful divisions relating to the things that concur in motion can be made.

units.la: Da primam divisionem ex ratione ipsius mobilis.
units.tr: Give the first division, taken from the nature of the mobile.

units.la: Eorum quæ transmutantur seu moventur,
units.tr: Of those things that are changed or moved:

units.la: 1. Quædam moventur per accidens: veluti cum dicimus musicum ambulare, quando nimirum homo peritus Musices ambulat.
units.tr: (1) Some are moved accidentally: as when we say that the musician walks, meaning of course that a man skilled in music walks.

units.la: 2. Quædam moventur per partes: quia videlicet in aliqua eorum parte aliquid fit. Quo pacto hominem dicimus sanari, quod oculus, seu caput, seu pulmo eius sanitatem recipiat.
units.tr: (2) Some are moved by their parts, that is, because something happens in one of their parts. In this way we say that a man is healed when his eye, or head, or lung receives health.

units.la: 3. Quædam moventur primò & per se sive proprie, idq; secundum diversas species motus: nempe secundum alterationem, si fit alterabile: secundum augmentationem, si fit augmentabile, atque ita de cæteris.
units.tr: (3) Some are moved primarily and through themselves, or properly, and this according to the different species of motion: namely, according to alteration, if a thing is made alterable; according to augmentation, if it is made capable of growth; and so on for the rest.

units.la: Da secundam divisionem ex ratio- ne ipsius movəntis.
units.tr: Give the second division, taken from the nature of the mover.

units.la: Movens dicitur tripliciter aliquid movere.
units.tr: Something is said to move in three ways.

units.la: 1. Per accidens: ut, Musicus ædificat.
units.tr: (1) Accidentally: as, the musician builds.

units.la: 2. Per partem siue propter partē: ut, homo percutit, quando hominis manus percutit.
units.tr: (2) By a part, or on account of a part: as, a man strikes when a man's hand strikes.

units.la: 3. Per se & proprie: ut, Medicus sanat.
units.tr: (3) Through itself and properly: as, the physician heals.

units.la: Da tertiam diuisionem ex ratio- ne terminorum.
units.tr: Give the third division, taken from the nature of the termini.

units.la: Potest etiam ex parte terminorum accipi aliquid in motu existens:
units.tr: Something existing in motion can also be taken from the side of the termini:

units.la: 1. Per accidens: veluti si dicam de eo quod dealbatur, mutari illud seu moueri in id quod intelligitur album: ubi accidit colori albo, ut intellectu apprehendatur, priusquam existit.
units.tr: (1) Accidentally: as if I were to say of that which is being whitened, that it is changed or moved into that which is understood as white; here whiteness belongs to the colour only so that it may be grasped by the intellect before it actually exists.

units.la: 2. Secundum partem. Aliquid ex parte terminorum in motu consideratur: veluti si dicam, id quod mutatur in albedinem, mutari in colorem. Etenim albedo tantum est coloris pars siue species quaedam. Item si de eunte Athenas dicam, adire eum Europam, cuius quidem pars quaedam Athenae sunt.
units.tr: (2) According to a part. Something is considered in motion on the side of the termini: as if I were to say that what is changed into whiteness is changed into colour. For whiteness is only a part or a certain species of colour. Likewise, if I were to say of one who goes to Athens that he goes to Europe, of which Athens is indeed a certain part.

units.la: 3. Per se & primò: ut si dicam, id quod fit album, mutari in album.
units.tr: (3) Through itself and primarily: as if I were to say that what becomes white is changed into white.

units.la: Da quartam diuisionem ex ratione ipsius temporis.
units.tr: Give the fourth division, taken from the nature of time.

units.la: Non datur: nam tempus se habet ad motum, tanquam mensura extrinseca.
units.tr: There is none: for time stands in relation to motion as an external measure.

units.la: Cuius potissimum motus constitutum est inuestigare species?
units.tr: Of which motion is it chiefly the task to investigate the species?

units.la: De motu per accidens, undecunq; fit, non dicemus: sed de motu secundum partem & per se.
units.tr: We shall not speak of motion accidentally, from whatever source it comes, but of motion according to a part and through itself.

units.la: Motus per se quot sunt species?
units.tr: How many species of motion are there through itself?

units.la: Nomen motus adhuc per se quidem generaliter accipitur, utpote quod commune est quibuscunque speciebus mutationis. Quare operæprecium est, motum rursus ita distinguere, ut certa quædam species mutationis, nomine motus intelligatur. Sunt autem tres mutationis species.
units.tr: The name "motion," taken in itself, is still understood in a general sense, since it is common to all the species of change. Therefore it is worth while to divide motion again, so that a certain definite species of change is understood by the name of motion. There are three species of change.

units.la: 1. Cum fit mutatio ex subiecto in subiectum: veluti quando aliquid mutatur ex albo in nigrum.
units.tr: (1) When change occurs from subject to subject: as when something is changed from white to black.

units.la: 2. Ex subiecto in non subiectum: quod fit, ubi transit aliquid ab esse in non esse.
units.tr: (2) From subject to non-subject: which happens when something passes from being to non-being.

units.la: 3. Ex non subiecto in subiectum, hoc est, à non esse ad
units.tr: (3) From non-subject to subject, that is, from non-being to

units.la: Ex his speciebus mutationis secunda quidè proprie notat corruptionem, tertia verò generationem (id quod quivis potest intelligere, nec difficile esset rationibus demonstrare:) quamobrem sequitur, nomine motus per se accepti proprie intelligi primam mutationis speciem, usque adeo, ut recte dici queat, motum per se esse mutationis speciem, qua fit transitio ex subiecto in subiectum. Igitur motus hoc pacto acceptus in tres diuiditur species.
units.tr: Of these species of change, the second properly denotes corruption and the third generation (which anyone can understand, and which would not be difficult to demonstrate by arguments). Therefore it follows that the name of motion taken in the proper sense means the first species of change, so much so that it can rightly be said that motion through itself is that species of change by which there is a transition from subject to subject. Motion so understood is therefore divided into three species.

units.la: 1. Est motus secundum qualitatem. 2. secundum quantitatem. 3. secundum ubi, siue locum.
units.tr: (1) It is motion according to quality; (2) according to quantity; (3) according to where, or place.

units.la: Declara, quòd tantùm secundum hæc tria prædicamenta distingui motus debeat.
units.tr: Explain why motion ought to be distinguished only according to these three categories.

units.la: Duabus rationibus id comprobatur.
units.tr: This is proved by two arguments.

units.la: 1. In reliquis prædicamentis, substantia, inquam, ad aliquid, actione, passione, spectari motus non potest, quemadmodum Aristoteles luculenter explanat: similiter neq; in istis, videlicet quando, situ, habitu, spectatur motus per se dictus: in his septem prædicamentis non spectatur motus nisi per accidens. Relinquitur ergo, quòd tantùm in tribus illis primò nominatis.
units.tr: (1) In the remaining categories, I mean substance, relation, action, and passion, motion cannot be considered, as Aristotle clearly explains; and likewise not in those others, namely when, position, and habit, is motion so called through itself considered: in these seven categories motion is considered only accidentally. It remains, therefore, that it is only in those first three named.

units.la: 2. In illis tribus tantum prædicamentis inuenitur contrarietas, quæ ad productionem motus omnino est necessaria. Igitur tres tantum species motus secundum illa tria prædicamenta enumerari debent.
units.tr: (2) Contrariety, which is wholly necessary for the production of motion, is found only in those three categories. Therefore only three species of motion according to those three categories ought to be enumerated.

units.la: Quibus nominibus proprie appellantur tres illæ distinctæ species motus?
units.tr: By what names are those three distinct species of motion properly called?

units.la: Motus qui est secundum qualitatem, communi nomine appellatur Alteratio, ἀλλοίωσις [?]. Nam alterum solemus appellare, quod differt secundùm qualitatem. Vocamus autem hic qualitates, non ut solemus dicere substantiales qualitates, sed potiùs ut sunt quædam passiones, et passibiles qualitates, nimirum ad tertiam speciem qualitatis reducendæ, siquidem in his proprie consideratur alteratio.
units.tr: Motion which is according to quality is commonly called alteration, ἀλλοίωσις. For we are accustomed to call "another" (alterum) that which differs according to quality. We here call qualities not what we are accustomed to call substantial qualities, but rather qualities as they are certain affections and affectible qualities, namely to be reduced to the third species of quality, since in these alteration is properly considered.

units.la: Motus qui est secundum quantitatem, non exprimitur uno communi nomine: sed qui tendit ad quantitatem ampliorem & perfectam, appellari potest Augmentatio, αὔξησις [?]: qui verò tendit ad quantitatem minorem & imperfectam, uocatur di minutio, φθισις.
units.tr: Motion which is according to quantity is not expressed by one common name; but that which tends to a greater and more perfect quantity can be called augmentation, αὔξησις; that which tends to a smaller and imperfect quantity is called diminution, φθίσις.

units.la: Motus qui est secundum locum, similiter non gaudet proprio nomine, nisi uelimus generaliter et improprie appellare lationem, φορα’. Siquidem illa sola proprie dicuntur ferri, quae uidelicet mouentur sic secundum locum, ut sistere seipsa non ualeant: cuiusmodi aduerti non possunt quaedam inanimata, quae a seipsis secundum locum non mouentur.
units.tr: Motion which is according to place likewise has no proper name, unless we wish to call it in a general and improper sense transference, φορά. For only those things are properly said to be carried which are moved according to place in such a way that they cannot stop themselves; of this kind some inanimate things, which are not moved according to place by themselves, cannot be observed.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur im- mobile?
units.tr: How many ways is a thing said to be immobile?

units.la: Tribus. 1. Quod nullo modo est aptum natum moueri: ut Deus. Qua ratione inuisibile quoq; dicitur, quod nullo modo aptum natum est uideri: ut sonus.
units.tr: In three ways. (1) That which is in no way apt or fit by nature to be moved: as God. In this sense also that is called invisible which is in no way apt by nature to be seen: as sound.

units.la: 2. Quod difficulter potest moueri, quod & duobus contingit modis: nimirum, cum aut non facile primum inducitur ad motum, aut postquam inductum est, lente tardeq; in motu procedit: ut testudo, homo aeger, loripes, &c.
units.tr: (2) That which can be moved only with difficulty. This happens in two ways: either when it is not easily brought to motion at first, or, once it has been set in motion, it proceeds in its motion slowly and sluggishly: as a tortoise, a sick man, a lame man, etc.

units.la: 3. Quod natum quidem est moueri, ac potest moueri: non tamen quando, ubi & quomodo debebat, mouetur. Atq; istud proprie dicitur quiescere: quies namque motui est contraria, utpote quae nihil aliud est quam priuatio motus in corpore, quod alias in tempore & loco & modo moueri aptum natum est.
units.tr: (3) That which is indeed by nature fit to be moved and can be moved, but is not moved when, where and how it ought to be. This is properly called being at rest; for rest is contrary to motion, since it is nothing other than the privation of motion in a body which is otherwise fit by nature to be moved in time, place and manner.

units.la: Súntne aliæ motus species?
units.tr: Are there other species of motion?

units.la: Sunt adhuc duæ. Alius namque est motus unus, alius est motus contrarius. Cæterum priusquam de his plenius differamus, necesse est quasdam definitiones explicari: veluti, quid sit esse simul, vel esse separatim, quid sit contingere vel contiguum esse, quid sit medium seu intermedians, quid sit continuo movens, quid sit ex ordine se habens, quid iunctum vel insequens ex ordine, quid continuum. Quas definitiones nisi quis tenuerit, disputationes sequentes non plane assequentur.
units.tr: There are yet two. For one motion is single, another is contrary. But before we treat these more fully, it is necessary to explain certain definitions: for example, what it is to be together or to be separate, what it is to touch or to be contiguous, what is the middle or intervening, what is continuously moving, what is in order, what is joined or following in order, and what is continuous. Unless one has grasped these definitions, the following disputations will not be fully understood.

units.la: Quæ dicuntur simul esse?
units.tr: What things are said to be together?

units.la: Simul sunt secundum locum, quæ videlicet continentur eodem loco primo. Est autem locus primus, uniuscuiusque rei locus proprius, quem res ipsa per naturam maxime appetit. Locus imus vel inferior, est locus primus corporis gravis; supremus vero locus, est locus primus corporis levis. Opponitur locus primus loco communi.
units.tr: Things are together in place when they are contained in the same first place. Now the first place is the proper place of each thing, which the thing itself desires most by nature. The lowest or inferior place is the first place of a heavy body; the highest place, however, is the first place of a light body. The first place is opposed to the common place.

units.la: Quæ dicuntur esse sepa- ratim?
units.tr: What things are said to be separate?

units.la: Quæ in diuersis distinctisque locis sunt.
units.tr: Those which are in different and distinct places.

units.la: Quæ dicuntur contingere vel contigua esse?
units.tr: What things are said to touch, or to be contiguous?

units.la: Quorum extrema simul sunt, adeoque secum mutuò conveniunt.
units.tr: Those whose extremities are together, and so meet one another mutually.

units.la: Quid dicitur intermedians?
units.tr: What is meant by intervening?

units.la: Quod in mutatione prius attingitur, quàm ad ultimum, quod succedere aptum natum est, perueniatur. Hic semper tria simul considerantur, nempe duo extrema, & hoc ipsum quod inter eadem consistit.
units.tr: That which is touched first in a change, before the last thing, which is naturally fit to succeed, is reached. Here three things are always considered together, namely the two extremes, and that which lies between them.

units.la: Quid est continuè moueri?
units.tr: What is it to move continuously?

units.la: Est, cum neq; ex tempore, quando fit motus, neque ex re in qua fit motus, siue per quam fit transitus motus, quicquam intermittitur.
units.tr: It is when nothing is interrupted, neither in the time when the motion occurs, nor in the thing in which the motion occurs, or through which the transition of the motion takes place.

units.la: Quid dicitur ex ordine se habens?
units.tr: What is said to be in order?

units.la: Ex ordine se habent, in quibus unum sequitur aliud ordine prius (prius inquam siue positione, siue loco, siue virtute, siue dignitate, siue cognitione) neque inter ipsa aliquid eiusdem generis seu naturæ intercedit medium.
units.tr: Those things are in order in which one follows another which is prior in order (prior, I say, either in position, or in place, or in power, or in dignity, or in knowledge), and between which there intervenes nothing of the same kind or nature as a middle.

units.la: Quid dicitur iunctum seu insequens?
units.tr: What is said to be joined or following?

units.la: Quod sic aliud quippiam sequitur, ut mutuò sese tangant, nullo prorsus medio, ne alterius quidem generis, interveniente.
units.tr: That which so follows some other thing that they touch each other mutually, with nothing at all, not even of another kind, intervening.

units.la: Quid est continuum?
units.tr: What is continuous?

units.la: Est, in quo unus idemq; fit terminus duorū sese tangentium.
units.tr: That in which one and the same thing becomes the terminus of two things touching each other.

units.la: His definitionibus breuiter expositis, licebit pergere.
units.tr: These definitions having been briefly set out, we may proceed.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur motus unus?
units.tr: How many ways is one motion said?

units.la: Tribus, sicut unum quoq; tribus modis dicitur: nempe genere, specie, numero.
units.tr: In three ways, just as "one" is also said in three ways: namely by genus, by species, and by number.

units.la: 1. Motus unus genere dicitur secundum figuras prædicamenti. Omnes enim motus, qui sunt in uno ordine prædicamenti, dicuntur unus motus genere. Sic omnis loci mutatio, est unus motus genere, quia in uno prædicamento, uidelicet Vbi. Item omnis motus augmenti & decrementi, est unus motus genere, quandoquidem in uno prædicamento Quantitatis locum habens. Omnis motus alterationis similiter unus est genere, utpote sub uno prædicamento Qualitatis.
units.tr: 1. One motion is one by genus according to the figures of the category. For all motions that belong to one order of the category are said to be one motion by genus. Thus every change of place is one motion by genus, because it falls under one category, namely Where. Likewise every motion of increase and decrease is one motion by genus, since it takes place in the one category of Quantity. Every motion of alteration is similarly one by genus, as it falls under the one category of Quality.

units.la: 2. Motus unus specie dicitur, quando non solum est unus secundum genus, sed etiam secundum speciem indiuiduam, id est, specialissimam, quæ non diuiditur in alias species subiectas. ut dealbatio, denigratio, sunt species motus alterationis, quæ non diuiduntur in alias species: omnis namque dealbatio eiusdem est speciei.
units.tr: 2. One motion is said to be one by species when it is one not only by genus but also by an indivisible species, that is, the most specific species, which is not divided into further subordinate species. Thus whitening and blackening are species of the motion of alteration that are not divided into further species, for every whitening is of one and the same species.

units.la: 3. Motus unus numero dicitur, qui aliàs simpliciter unus est: in quo quidem tria hæc simul spectari debent, nempe unum subiectum siue mobile: ut, unus homo, una planta, hic homo. Deinde una forma, secundum quam est motus: ut, una coloratio, una loci mutatio. Denique unum idemq; tempus ipsius motus,citra interpellationem. Vbi non concurrunt hæc tria simul, ibi motus unus numero non intelligitur. Exemplum huiusmodi motus esto: Vnus homo una aliqua temporis duratione ab uno morbo liberatur, ac pristinæ restituitur ualetudini. Hic tria illa simul sunt proposita, & singula ut indiuidua (quæ proprie differunt numero) expendi debent. Ex his autem manifestum fit,
units.tr: 3. One motion is one by number, which is otherwise simply called one. In this case three things must be considered together: first, one subject or mobile thing, as one man, one plant, this man. Then one form, according to which there is motion, as one coloring, one change of place. Finally, one and the same time of the motion itself, without interruption. Where these three do not come together, the motion is not understood to be one by number. Let this be an example of such a motion: one man is freed from one disease within one continuous span of time and restored to his former health. Here those three things are set before us together, and each must be weighed as an individual (which properly differ in number). From these things it becomes clear

units.la: 1. Quòd omnis motus unus sit continuus: & uiceuersa, omnis motus continuus sit unus.
units.tr: 1. That every motion that is one is continuous; and conversely, every continuous motion is one.

units.la: 2. Eum præcipuè dicendum motum unum, qui iam consummatus perfectusq; sit: sicut in aliis quoque rebus perfectum & totum ad unitatis rationem pertinet.
units.tr: 2. That motion should be called one chiefly when it has already been completed and perfected, just as in other things the perfect and the whole pertain to the notion of unity.

units.la: 3. Eum motum potius dici unum, qui sit regularis seu uniformis, quàm qui irregularis aut deformis. Potest autem irregularis motus in quacunque motus specie inueniri. Is namque motus irregularis appellatur, in quo non succedit æquis temporibus continua uelocitas. Quod solet cuenire, cum ob inordinatam[?] magnitudinem, tum ex ratione loci, tum ex parte eius rei in qua fit motus, denique ex ipsius motus inæqualitate. Tantum de altera specie motus, uidelicet motu uno: sequitur de altera specie, nimirum de motu contrario.
units.tr: 3. That motion is rather to be called one when it is regular or uniform than when it is irregular or deformed. An irregular motion, however, can be found in any species of motion. For that motion is called irregular in which continuous speed does not follow in equal times. This commonly happens, whether because of irregular magnitude, or because of the nature of the place, or on the part of the thing in which the motion occurs, or finally from the very unevenness of the motion. So much for the one species of motion, namely motion as one; there follows the other species, namely contrary motion.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur motus contrarius?
units.tr: How many ways is contrary motion said?

units.la: Quinq̃. Primus motus, quo contrarietas motuū spectatur, est in accessu ad aliquem terminum, & recessu ab eodem. Huiusmodi sunt motus ad sanitatem, & motus à sanitate.
units.tr: Five. The first motion, by which the contrariety of motions is viewed, lies in approach to some terminus and withdrawal from the same. Of this kind are motion to health and motion from health.

units.la: Secundus spectatur ex contrarietate terminorum, à quibus motus incipit.Sic contrarij sunt motus, alter ex sanitate, alter ægritudine.
units.tr: The second is viewed from the contrariety of the termini from which the motion begins. Thus motions are contrary when one is from health and the other from sickness.

units.la: Tertius motus à contrarietate terminorum, ad quos motus tendit: veluti sunt motus ad sanitatem, & motus ad ægritudinem.
units.tr: The third arises from the contrariety of the termini to which the motion tends, as motion to health and motion to sickness.

units.la: Quartus motus spectatur secundum contrarietatem termini à quo, ad terminum ad quem.Sic aduersantur motus qui ex sanitate est, & motus qui est ad ægritudinem.
units.tr: The fourth is viewed according to the contrariety of the terminus from which and the terminus to which. Thus the motion from health and the motion to sickness are opposed.

units.la: Quintus motus spectatur ex parte utrorumque terminorum. Sic opponuntur motus qui est ex sanitate ad ægritudinem, & motus ex ægritudine ad sanitatem.
units.tr: The fifth is viewed from the side of both termini. Thus the motion from health to sickness and the motion from sickness to health are opposed.

units.la: His quinque modis contrarietas in motu considerari potest.
units.tr: In these five ways contrariety can be considered in motion.

units.la: Spectatūrne in omnibus hisce modis contrarietas æquè propriè?
units.tr: Is contrariety observed equally properly in all these modes?

units.la: Non. Magis enim proprie contrarietas animaduertitur in tertio & quinto, quàm in secundo & quarto. Deinde, primus cum non exhibeat contrarietatem ratione terminorum, sed ratione accessus & recessus, paulo adhuc aliter se habet. Breuiter, secundi & quarti modi nullus est usus: tertius & quintus seruiunt ad explorandam contrarietatem mutationum, in generatione inquam & corruptione, incremento ac decremento & alteratione: primus vero proprie ad explorandam contrarietatem motuum.
units.tr: No. For contrariety is more properly observed in the third and fifth modes than in the second and fourth. Next, the first, since it does not display contrariety with respect to the termini but with respect to approach and withdrawal, stands in a somewhat different position. In short, the second and fourth modes have no use; the third and fifth serve to test the contrariety of changes, namely in generation and corruption, increase and decrease, and alteration; the first, however, properly serves to test the contrariety of motions.

units.la: Venit'ne alia contrarietas in motu obseruanda?
units.tr: Must another contrariety in motion be observed?

units.la: Maxime. Nā motui adhuc opponitur quies, quae est priuatio motus. Quamobrem quanta est contrarietas priuationis & habitus, tanta etiam erit motus & quietis. Quamuis non ita proprie & simpliciter hic inueniatur contrarietas, ut ubi motus opponitur motui.
units.tr: Most certainly. For rest, which is the privation of motion, is still opposed to motion. Therefore, as great as the contrariety of privation and habit is, so great will also be the contrariety of motion and rest, although this contrariety is not found in the same proper and simple way as where motion is opposed to motion.

units.la: Opponitúrne quies cuiuis motui?
units.tr: Is rest opposed to every motion?

units.la: Non. Indicabimus autem, cui potissimum motui opponatur.Primò quidem motui qui est ex hoc termino in suum contrarium, opponitur quies quae est in contrario: veluti motui qui est ex albo in nigrum, opponitur quies quae est in albo. Deinde motui qui est ex contrario in hoc, opponitur quies quae est in contrario: veluti motui qui est ex nigro in album, opponitur quies quae est in nigro. Vix alia ratione quies motui opponitur.
units.tr: No. We will indicate, however, to which motion rest is chiefly opposed. First, to the motion that goes from this terminus to its contrary, the rest that is in the contrary is opposed: for example, to the motion from white to black, the rest that is in white is opposed. Next, to the motion that goes from the contrary to this, the rest that is in the contrary is opposed: for example, to the motion from black to white, the rest that is in black is opposed. Rest is opposed to motion on hardly any other ground.

units.la: Opponitúrne quies quieti,sicut motus motui?
units.tr: Is rest opposed to rest, as motion is opposed to motion?

units.la: Imò, quando videlicet sunt in contrarijs terminis. Quies enim rursus eadem ratione invenitur opposita quieti,qua motus sunt oppositi sibi invicem. Quinetiam sicut motus secundū locum alius est naturalis,alius violentus, & hi sibi invicem adversantur: ita quies quoq; alia est naturalis,alia violenta, & altera alteri adversatur.
units.tr: Yes indeed, namely when they are between contrary terms. For rest is found opposed to rest on the same ground on which motions are opposed to one another. Moreover, just as local motion is partly natural and partly violent, and these are opposed to each other, so rest too is partly natural and partly violent, and the one is opposed to the other.

units.la: Est'ne quies contraria mutationi, perinde ac motui?
units.tr: Is rest contrary to change, just as it is to motion?

units.la: Nihil prohibet, quatenus in ipsis mutationibus occurrit contrarietas,eatenus etiam in quiete inveniri ex altera parte contrarietatem. Etenim spectatur contrarietas in mutationibus prorsus quemadmodum in motibus. ut enim est motus alius naturalis,alius violentus: ita mutatio quoque alia naturalis est,alia violenta. Ex quo fit,ut corruptio naturalis contraria sit corruptioni violentæ, & generationi naturali generatio violenta. Est autem generatio violeta, veluti si quis flores vel ramos faciat crescere subitò, vel alio tempore, vel aliter quàm secundum naturā crescere solent. Similiter iudicandū de augmento & decremeto,itemq; de alteratione.
units.tr: Nothing prevents this: insofar as contrariety occurs in the changes themselves, to that extent a contrariety is also found on the other side in rest. For contrariety is observed in changes exactly as it is in motions. For just as there is natural motion and violent motion, so too change is partly natural and partly violent. Hence it follows that natural corruption is contrary to violent corruption, and violent generation to natural generation. Violent generation is, for example, when someone suddenly makes flowers or branches grow, or at a time other than usual, or in a manner other than plants customarily grow according to nature. The same judgement is to be made about increase and decrease, and likewise about alteration.

units.la: Est'ne motus sursum tendens contrarius motui tendenti deorsum?
units.tr: Is upward motion contrary to downward motion?

units.la: Est plane contrarius, ac tum quidem maximè, si alter sit secundum naturam, veluti cum ignis sursum fertur: alter praeter naturam, ut cum ignis vi aliqua occurrente deorsum praecipitatur. Motus sursum tendens contrarius est motui deorsum tendenti, vel eo nomine, quod neque secundum totum, neque secundum partes sese in eodem admittunt.
units.tr: Plainly it is contrary, and most of all when the one is according to nature, as when fire is carried upward; the other is against nature, as when fire is hurled downward by some force opposing it. Upward motion is contrary to downward motion, if for no other reason, because they do not admit each other either in the whole or in the parts.

units.la: Hactenus de divisione motus in suas species: super-est ut agamus de divisione motus in partes secundum quantitatem.
units.tr: So far concerning the division of motion into its species. It remains to deal with the division of motion into parts according to quantity.

units.la: Utrum motus dividi possit in par- tes quantas?
units.tr: Can motion be divided into quantitative parts?

units.la: Maxime. Quod probatur hac inductione:
units.tr: Very much so. This is proved by the following induction:

units.la: Continuum dividitur in partes quantas. Si autem continuum dividitur in partes quantas, necessario etiam magnitudo ita dividitur.
units.tr: A continuum is divided into quantitative parts. If indeed a continuum is divided into quantitative parts, then of necessity magnitude is also so divided.

units.la: Si vero magnitudo ita dividitur, par erit & tempus sic dividi, quandoquidem eodem modo se habent: atque ut magnitudo est continua, ita tempus quoq; continuum est.
units.tr: But if magnitude is so divided, time must also be divided in this way, since they stand in the same relation: and just as magnitude is continuous, so time is also continuous.

units.la: Si vero tempus sic dividitur, conficitur & motum pari ratione dividi posse, cum tempus atq; motus coniuncta sint, alterutroq; sine altero intelligi nequeat.
units.tr: And if time is so divided, it follows that motion can likewise be divided, since time and motion are joined together, and neither can be understood without the other.

units.la: Hanc inductionem explicat Aristot. lib.6. tribus capitibus, variis adferendo singularum propositionum probationes. Nos autem omissis reliquis, tantum demonstrabimus, quae ad primam propositionem recte intelligendam sint necessaria.
units.tr: Aristotle explains this induction in three chapters of Book 6, bringing forward various proofs for each of the propositions. But we, leaving the rest aside, will only demonstrate what is necessary for rightly understanding the first proposition.

units.la: Continuum non posse dari aliquod ex indivisibilibus compositum, sic probatur:
units.tr: That a continuum cannot be composed of indivisibles is proved as follows:

units.la: 1. Si aliquod continuum, veluti linea, ex indivisibilibus, nempe punctis, esset cōpositum, oportet sane hæc puncta indivisibilia aut continua esse, aut se contingentia, aut consequenter se habentia. Atqui horum nullum dici potest. Igitur nullū dabitur continuum ex indivisibilibus compositum. Minor manifesta est ex definitionibus supra positis, & earundem applicatione ad lineæ divisionem.
units.tr: 1. If some continuum, such as a line, were composed of indivisibles, namely points, these indivisible points would have to be either continuous, or touching one another, or following one another in sequence. But none of these can be said. Therefore no continuum will be composed of indivisibles. The minor premise is clear from the definitions set out above and their application to the division of a line.

units.la: 2. Si continuum, ut (verbi gratia) magnitudo, efset ex indivisibilibus compositum, necessum[?] esset & motum, qui supra magnitudinem fieret, similiter ex indivisibilibus componi. Sed istud est absurdum: ergo & illud ex quo sequitur.
units.tr: 2. If a continuum, such as a magnitude, were composed of indivisibles, then the motion that takes place across the magnitude would necessarily also be composed of indivisibles in the same way. But this is absurd; therefore so is that from which it follows.

units.la: Patet igitur, continuum non posse dari, quod sit ex indivisibilibus compositum. Quamobrem neque motus ex indivisibilibus constare intelligetur.
units.tr: It is evident, then, that a continuum cannot exist that is composed of indivisibles. Accordingly, motion too will not be understood to consist of indivisibles.

units.la: Da divisionem motus in partes se- cundum quantitatem.
units.tr: Give the division of motion into quantitative parts.

units.la: Bifariam dividitur motus in partes quantas. uno modo ratione temporis, quo fit motus: alio modo ratione partium eius rei quæ movetur. Ac de tempore quidem his rationibus probatur.
units.tr: Motion is divided into quantitative parts in two ways: in one way with respect to the time in which the motion occurs; in another way with respect to the parts of the thing that is moved. Regarding time, it is proved on these grounds.

units.la: 1. Omnis motus est in tempore. Omne autē[?] tempus est divisibile in partes quantas, sicut supra probatum est. Ergo & motus eadem ratione in partes quantas dividetur. Relinquitur vero, ut per se notum, quod non sit in ipso NVN C, sed in tempore.
units.tr: 1. Every motion is in time. Every time is divisible into quantitative parts, as has been proved above. Therefore motion too will be divided into quantitative parts by the same reasoning. It follows, as is self-evident, that it is not in the now itself but in time.

units.la: 2. Longiore tempore longior fit motus, breviore autem tempore brevior, ut motus dicatur diuturnus aut brevis prorsus quemadmodum tempus ipsum. Ergo necessum est, motum quoq; in partes quantas dividi, perinde atq; tempus ipsum dividitur.
units.tr: 2. A motion becomes longer with a longer time and shorter with a shorter time, so that a motion is called lasting or quite brief just as time itself is. Therefore it is necessary that motion too be divided into quantitative parts, just as time itself is divided.

units.la: De motu partium eius rei quae movetur, facilis est demonstratio. Est quidem per se manifestum, omne quod movetur, posse in partes C dividi. Hoc igitur dato, sit res mobilis A ⌐——¬——¬ B, eademq; dividatur in partes, nimirum ad punctum C. hic sane quilibet intelligit, ubi totum movetur, necessario & partem utramq;, videlicet A C. & C B. moueri.Erit proinde motus divisus etiam in partes ratione rei mobilis.
units.tr: The demonstration regarding the parts of the thing that is moved is easy. It is indeed self-evident that everything that is moved can be divided into parts in quantity. Granting this, let there be a mobile thing A ⌐——¬——¬ B, and let it be divided into parts, namely at the point C. Here anyone understands that when the whole is moved, both parts, namely A C and C B, are necessarily moved as well. Motion will therefore also be divided into parts with respect to the moving thing.

units.la: Quot modis intelligitur dividi mo- tus secundum partes rei mobilis?
units.tr: In how many ways is motion understood to be divided according to the parts of the moving thing?

units.la: Duobus. 1. Ut pars post partem moveatur. Quod quidem observari non potest in ea re quae secundum se tota movetur: haec namq; semel mota, simul moventur omnes eius partes, neq; separatim quidem a toto, sed simul in ipso & cum ipso toto.
units.tr: In two ways. (1) When one part is moved after another. This cannot be observed in a thing that is moved as a whole in itself, for once such a thing is moved, all its parts are moved together, not separately from the whole but together in it and with the whole.

units.la: 2. Sicut divisio cuiuslibet accidentis quod inhæret subiecto divisibili, sumitur ex divisione subiecti, (veluti si detur totum corpus aliquod album, dividetur profecto ista albedo, quæ est accidens, prorsus quemadmodum diuiditur illud corpus cui inhærét:) ita & motus partium simul fieri intelligetur, quemadmodum fit motus totius rei mobilis.
units.tr: (2) The division of any accident that inheres in a divisible subject is taken from the division of the subject. For example, if some whole body is white, that whiteness, which is an accident, is divided just as the body in which it inheres is divided. In the same way, the motion of the parts is understood to occur together, just as the motion of the whole moving thing occurs.

units.la: Quomodo distinguitur motus secun- dum partes rei mobilis à motu secundum tempus?
units.tr: How is motion according to the parts of the moving thing distinguished from motion according to time?

units.la: Hoc pacto: Quando diuiditur motus secundum partes rei mobilis, ipsæ partes simul manent: quando vero diuiditur motus secundum tempus, tum partes non manent simul. Si tamen motus partis unius comparetur ad partem alterius, non simpliciter, sed secundum certum aliquod signum, ad quod fit motus, sanè hic motus unius partis etiam tempore præcedet motum alterius. c Sumatur (uerbi gratia) res mobilis A ⌐——⌙——⌐ B. & moueatur in G magnitudine E ⌐——⌙——⌐ F. ita ut magnitudo E G æqualis sit toti A B. manifestum fit, quòd signum G prius pertransibit C B, quàm A C. quo quidem pacto simul deprehenditur ibi motus secundum partes temporis, & secundum partes rei mobilis.
units.tr: In this way. When motion is divided according to the parts of the moving thing, the parts themselves remain together. When motion is divided according to time, the parts do not remain together. Yet if the motion of one part is compared with the motion of another, not absolutely but according to some certain sign toward which the motion is made, then the motion of one part will indeed precede the motion of the other in time. Let the moving thing A ⌐——⌙——⌐ B be taken, for example, and let it be moved through the magnitude E ⌐——⌙——⌐ F, so that the magnitude EG is equal to the whole AB.
