It is clear that the sign G will pass over CB before AC. In this way, motion is seen there at once according to the parts of time and according to the parts of the moving thing.

units.la: Potestne motus ita diuidi, ut non etiam aliæ res simul diui- dantur?
units.tr: Can motion be divided in such a way that other things are not also divided at the same time?

units.la: Non potest. Quando enim omne quod mouetur, necessum est in aliquo (quod uidelicet uel genere, uel specie distinguitur) moueri, praeterea in aliquo tempore, deniq; motus non est, nisi alicuius rei mobilis: ideo fieri non potest, quin quoties placet motum diuidere, oportet etiam alias res simul diuidere. Quinq; autem simul cum motu diuiduntur: uidelicet tempus, motus ipse, ipsum moueri, res mobilis seu quae mouetur, id in quo est motus, siue sit locus, siue qualitas, siue quantitas. necessum est ista in partes diuidi, si motum uolumus in partes diuidere.
units.tr: It cannot. For whatever is moved must necessarily be moved in something (which is distinguished either by genus or by species), and moreover in some time; and motion exists only of some moving thing. Therefore it cannot be that whenever we wish to divide motion, we do not also have to divide other things at the same time. Five things are divided together with motion: namely, time, motion itself, the being-moved itself, the thing that is moved (or the moving thing), and that in which the motion is, whether that be place, quality or quantity. These must necessarily be divided into parts if we wish to divide motion into parts.

units.la: Sed non eodem modo fit diuisio omnium eorum in quibus motus conspicitur.
units.tr: But the division of all those things in which motion is observed does not take place in the same way.

units.la: 1. Quorundam diuisio fit per se, nempe eorum quae pertinent ad genus quantitatis: ueluti in motu locali, & in augmento & decremento.
units.tr: (1) The division of some takes place per se, namely of those that belong to the genus of quantity, as in local motion and in increase and decrease.

units.la: 2. Quorundam diuisio fit per accidens, nempe pertinentium ad qualitatem: ut in motu alterationis. Neq; difficile esset plenius demonstrare, quomodo diuisiones fiant in singulis partibus enumeratis, id est, quomodo pariter diuidantur tempus & motus, deinde motus & ipsum moueri, praeterea motus & res mobilis, deniq; motus & id in quo motus peragitur: sed nos breuitatis causa praetermittimus.
units.tr: (2) The division of others takes place per accidens, namely of those that belong to quality, as in the motion of alteration. It would not be difficult to demonstrate more fully how the divisions occur in each of the parts enumerated, that is, how time and motion are divided alike, then motion and the being-moved itself, next motion and the moving thing, and finally motion and that in which the motion is carried out. But for the sake of brevity we omit this.

units.la: Hastenus de diuisione motus in partes quantas: restat ut de partium ordine aliquid adijciatur.
units.tr: So far on the division of motion into quantitative parts. It remains to add something about the order of the parts.

units.la: Utrum posit in partibus motus osten- di aliquis ordo, seu demonstra- ri pars prima?
units.tr: Whether some order can be shown among the parts of motion, or the first part be pointed out?

units.la: Priusquam directè respondeamus, quasdam propositiones præmitti necesse est.
units.tr: Before we answer directly, some propositions must be set out.

units.la: Prima propositio: Quandoquidem omne quod mutatur, ex uno termino mutatur in alium: necesse est, omne quod mutatur, quando iam mutatum consummatumq; est, esse in termino ad quem. Probatur hæc propositio: Omne quod mutatur, cum iam mutatum est, aut est in termino unde proficiscebatur, aut in termino ad quem proficiscebatur, aut in utriusque medio. Nam omnino in aliquo horum esse oportet. Atqui non est in termino unde proficiscebatur, cum mutatum esse, plane sit, ab eo termino progressum esse alio. Neq; etiam est in medio, ut in C, cum mutatum esse consummatumq; tantum contingat in B. Et cum mutatio sit continuū illud quod iam mutatū est, intelligeretur moveri ad id in quo iam ante mutatum est: quod absurdum esse, nemo non advertit. Relinquitur ergo, Omne quod mutatur, quando iam mutatum est, esse in termino ad quem. Ex quo etiam sequitur: Omne quod generatum est, cum primum generatum est, tunc vere esse: atq; econtrario, omne quod corruptum est, cum primum corruptum est, tunc esse desijsse.
units.tr: First proposition: since everything that is changed is changed from one term into another, it is necessary that everything that is changed, when it has now been changed and completed, is in the term to which it is changed. This proposition is proved thus. Everything that is changed, when it has already been changed, is either in the term from which it set out, or in the term toward which it was setting out, or in the middle between the two. For it must necessarily be in one of these. But it is not in the term from which it set out, since, having been changed, it plainly has progressed from that term to another. Nor is it in the middle, as at C, since its change and completion happens only at B. And since change is continuous, that which has already been changed would be understood to be moving toward that in which it was already changed before. This is absurd, as everyone notices. It remains, therefore, that everything that is changed, when it has been changed, is in the term to which it was changed. From this it also follows that everything that has been generated, when it is first generated, then truly is; and conversely, everything that has been corrupted, when it is first corrupted, has then ceased to be.

units.la: Secunda propositio: Tempus in quo quod mutatum est,primum mutatum est,oportet constituere indiuisibile. Indiuisibile intellige, non terminum ipsius motus,sed temporis.Probatur autem hæc propositio. c Nam si constituas tepus,uerbi gratia, A ⌐———⌝———⌐ B, in quo res primum mutata est, diuisibile: quæro abs te,aut res mutata est in A C. aut in C B, aut in toto A B? Quodcunq; dederis, probabo diuersum. Non in A C, quia cum positum sit esse primum mutatum in AB, atque A C ordine prius existat, erit sane quoddam primum prius primo:quod est absurdum. Dicimus enim,aliquid in eo primum mutatu, ante quod no est aliud, in quo res fuerit mutata.
units.tr: Second proposition: the time in which that which is changed was first changed must be taken as indivisible. Understand "indivisible" not of the terminus of the motion itself, but of the time. This proposition is proved thus. For if you posit a time, for example A ⌐———⌝———⌐ B, in which the thing was first changed, as divisible, I ask you: is the thing changed in AC, or in CB, or in the whole AB? Whatever you give, I will prove otherwise. Not in AC, because since it has been posited that it was first changed in AB, and AC exists prior in order, there would be some first prior to the first, which is absurd. For we say that something is first changed in that time before which there is no other time in which the thing had been changed.

units.la: Non item in C B. quia si tantum in his,tum nihil mutationis cœptum esset fieri in A. cum tamen necessario pars aliqua mutationis in A intelligi debeat.Itaq; ne hic quidem potest dici primum mutatu.
units.tr: Nor in CB, because if it were only in these, then nothing of the change would have begun to occur in A, although some part of the change must necessarily be understood in A. So not even here can it be said to be first changed.

units.la: Nec deniq; potest dici primum mutatum in toto A B. quia iterum mutatum esset in A C parte priore, atque ita existeret quoddam primum prius primo . Relinquitur ergo,tempus in quo quid mutatum est primum,indiuisibile existere.
units.tr: Nor finally can it be said to be first changed in the whole AB, because then it would again be changed in the prior part AC, and so there would exist some first prior to the first. It remains, therefore, that the time in which something is first changed is indivisible.

units.la: Ex his autem similiter sequitur,omne quod corruptum est,& omne quod generatum est,esse indi uisibili temporis spacio corruptum & generatum: quia generatio & corruptio sunt termini alteratiónis. Vnde rursus,si quilibet motus terminatur indiuisibili temporis spacio, siue in instanti, sequitur quód generatio & corruptio etiam in instanti fiant.
units.tr: From these things it similarly follows that everything that has been corrupted, and everything that has been generated, is corrupted and generated in an indivisible span of time, because generation and corruption are the termini of alteration. Hence again, if every motion is terminated in an indivisible span of time, or in an instant, it follows that generation and corruption also take place in an instant.

units.la: His ita positis, promptum est directè respondere: si tamen adhuc distinguamus, quomodo intelligi conueniat dici aliquid primum mutatum. Intelligitur autem hìc dupliciter.
units.tr: With these things so laid down, it is easy to answer directly, if we still distinguish how it is fitting to understand that something is said to be first changed. It is understood here in two ways.

units.la: Primum, in quo mutatio est perfecta seu terminata. Tunc enim uerè dicitur aliquid primum mutatum, quando iam mutatio perfecta & consummata est. Atq; hæc uocatur mutatio secundum finem.
units.tr: First, as that in which the change is perfect or terminated. For then something is truly said to be first changed when the change is now perfect and complete. This is called change according to the end.

units.la: Secundum, in quo cœpit primum mutari, in quo quidem nondum uerè dici potuit, quòd iam mutatum esset. Hæc autem uocatur mutatio secundum principium.
units.tr: Second, as that in which something first began to be changed, when indeed it could not yet truly be said that it had already been changed. This is called change according to the beginning.

units.la: Exempla sumi possunt de motu ac tempore, quo pomù uel partus plenè maturuit, quo pulli ab ouo excluduntur, &c.
units.tr: Examples can be taken from motion and time: when a fruit or an offspring has fully ripened, when chicks are hatched from the egg, and so on.

units.la: Si igitur primo modo accipiamus primum mutari, secundum finem uidelicet, dicemus primum in motu monstrari posse, nec non tempus quo quid primum mutatum est, indiuisibile existere.
units.tr: If, therefore, we take "first to be changed" in the first way, namely according to the end, we shall say that the first point in motion can be pointed out, and that the time in which something is first changed is indivisible.

units.la: Sin autem secundo modo accipiatur primum mutari, uidelicet secundum principium, tunc primum non potest monstrari in motu, similiter neq; tempus potest discerni in quo primum aliquid mutetur.
units.tr: But if "first to be changed" is taken in the second way, namely according to the beginning, then the first point cannot be pointed out in motion, and likewise a time cannot be discerned in which something is first changed.

units.la: Liquet ergo, quomodo & quatenus primum in
units.tr: It is clear, therefore, how and in what respect the first in

units.la: motu considerari posit. Aristoteles quædam adhuc hac de re addit. Quinetiam capite sequenti demonstrat, quomodo in ijs quæ inueniuntur in motu seu mutatione, considerari etiá possit quidam ordo corum ad sese inuicem. Sed nos hæc quæ dicta sunt, sattitramur sufficere.
units.tr: motion can be considered. Aristotle adds some further points on this matter. Moreover, in the following chapter he demonstrates how, among the things found in motion or change, a certain order of them to one another can also be considered. But we think that what has been said is sufficient.

units.la: Consideratúrne infinitum in mo- tu: siue, potest' ne dari mo- tus infinitus?
units.tr: Is the infinite to be considered in motion, or can an infinite motion be given?

units.la: Non potest dari, nō magis quàm magnitudo infinita. Si enim constitueretur motus infinitus, oporteret eum pertransire magnitudinē infinitam. Atqui hæc dari nequit: igitur neq; ille. Est autē & magnitudinis & motus par hac in parte ratio.
units.tr: It cannot be given, no more than an infinite magnitude can. For if an infinite motion were posited, it would have to traverse an infinite magnitude. But an infinite magnitude cannot be given; therefore neither can an infinite motion. The reasoning is the same for magnitude and motion in this respect.

units.la: Hucusq; satis diffusè actum est de motus diuisione tam in species, quàm in partes quantas: superest partim explicentur, partim cuertantur quædã con-traria. Nam confutandi etiam sunt quorundam errores, qui de motu perperam senserunt.
units.tr: So far we have treated the division of motion at sufficient length, both into species and into quantitative parts. It remains that some things be explained and some contrary views be refuted, for the errors of certain people who thought wrongly about motion must also be refuted.

units.la: QVAE CONTRARIA?
units.tr: WHAT ARE THE CONTRARY VIEWS?

units.la: An quæ de motu dicta sunt, eadem dici possint de quiete?
units.tr: Can the things said about motion also be said about rest?

units.la: Quid' ni? Et non solùm de quiete, uerumetiam de statione, quæ est quietis generatio, siue ad quietem accessio. Propositiones aliquot cõgeremus, quæ de utraque id manifestum reddent: ac primùm de statione.
units.tr: Why not? And not only about rest, but also about standing still (statio), which is the generation of rest, or the approach to rest. We will set out several propositions that make this clear for both, and first for standing still.

units.la: Prima propositio: Omne quod stat, etiam cum stat mouetur. Probatur: Omne quod natum est moueri, eo tempore, loco & modo, quo natum est moueri, oportet aut moueatur, aut quiescat. Sed quod stat, id est, tendit ad quietem, nondum quiescit: alias enim contingeret aliquid simul & tendere ad quietem, & quiescere: quod est absurdum. Igitur omne quod stat, id est, ad quietem tendit, etiam quando stat mouetur.
units.tr: First proposition: Everything that is standing still is in motion even while it stands still. Proof: Everything that is naturally apt to be moved must, at the time, place and manner in which it is apt to be moved, either be moving or be at rest. But what is standing still, that is, tending toward rest, is not yet at rest; otherwise something would at the same time both tend toward rest and be at rest, which is absurd. Therefore everything that is standing still, that is, tends toward rest, is moving even when it stands still.

units.la: Secunda propositio: Omne quod stat, in tempore stat. Probatur. 1. Omne quod mouetur, in tempore mouetur: sed omne quod stat, etiam mouetur: quod proximè est demonstratum. Igitur omne quod stat, in tempore stat. 2. Velocitas & tarditas spectantur in tempore. Atqui contingit aliquid tardius aut velocius stare, id est, ad quietem tendere. Igitur omne quod stat, in tempore stat.
units.tr: Second proposition: Everything that is standing still does so in time. Proof. (1) Everything that is moved is moved in time; but everything that is standing still is also moved, as was just shown. Therefore everything that is standing still does so in time. (2) Speed and slowness are measured in time. But something can stand still more slowly or more quickly, that is, tend toward rest more slowly or more quickly. Therefore everything that is standing still does so in time.

units.la: Tertia propositio: Primum in quo aliquid stat, dari non potest. Quod prorsus eodem pacto intelligi nō decet, quo pacto ante diximus, primum non dari in motu. Sequuntur nunc propositiones de quiete.
units.tr: Third proposition: A first point in which something stands still cannot be given. This must be understood in exactly the same way as we said before, that no first point can be given in motion. Now follow the propositions about rest.

units.la: Quarta propositio: Sicut uerò neque in motu, neq; in statione, ita neque in quiete potest aliquod primū ostendi. Probatur: Sicut quicquid mouetur, necessariò id in tepore mouetur: ita quicquid quiescit, in tempore quiescit. Atqui illud ipsum tempus, quo quid primum mutatum est, est indiuisibile, neque potest in eo primum ostendi. Igitur & illud tempus, quo quid primum quiescit, indiuisibile est, neq; potest in eo primum aliquid ostendi. Contrariorum eadem prorsus est ratio. Nunc confutentur quorundam errores.
units.tr: Fourth proposition: Just as no first can be shown in motion or in standing still, so neither can any first be shown in rest. Proof: Just as whatever is moved is necessarily moved in time, so whatever is at rest is at rest in time. But that very time in which something is first changed is indivisible, and in it no first can be shown. Therefore that time in which something first comes to rest is also indivisible, and in it nothing first can be shown. The reasoning for the contraries is exactly the same. Now let the errors of certain people be refuted.

units.la: Quis primus error contrarius do- ctrinæ de motu traditæ, con- futandus uenit?
units.tr: What is the first error, contrary to the doctrine of motion handed down, that must be refuted?

units.la: Zenonis. Is namque simpliciter negat motum seu mutationem esse. Argumenta eius quædam referemus ac diluemus.
units.tr: That of Zeno. For he flatly denies that motion or change exists. We will set out and resolve some of his arguments.

units.la: Primum argumentum: Omne quod est in loco sibi æquali, aut mouetur aut quiescit. Sed omne quod fertur in quolibet NVNC, est in aliquo loco sibi æquali. Ergo & in quolibet NVNC aut mouetur, aut quiescit. Atqui non mouetur: igitur quiescit. Porrò si in nullo NVNC mouetur, sequitur quod neq; in toto tempore moueatur, ac proinde toto tempore quiescat. Qua quidem ratione etiam sagitta celerrime & continuè mota quiescere intelligetur. Respondetur, quod ratio posterior non concludit neq; sequitur ex præmissis. Vt enim aliquid moueatur in tempore, opus est moueatur in qualibet eius temporis parte. Cæterum ipsa NVNC non sunt partes temporis: neq; enim tempus coponitur ex ipsis NVNC, quæ sunt indiuisibilia, sicut neq; ulla magnitudo componitur ex indiuisibilibus. Quare non conficitur, aliquid non moueri in tempore, eo quòd in nullo NVNC moueatur.
units.tr: First argument: Whatever is in a place equal to itself is either moving or at rest. But whatever is carried in any NOW is in a place equal to itself. Therefore in any NOW it is either moving or at rest. But it is not moving; therefore it is at rest. Moreover, if it is not moving in any NOW, it follows that it is not moving in the whole time, and so it is at rest for the whole time. By this reasoning even an arrow moved very swiftly and continuously would be understood to be at rest. The answer is that the latter inference does not follow from the premises. For in order for something to be moved in a time, it must be moved in every part of that time. But the NOWS are not parts of time: time is not composed of the NOWS, which are indivisible, just as no magnitude is composed of indivisibles. Hence it does not follow that something is not moving in time because it is not moving in any NOW.

units.la: Secundum argumentum: Si quicquam mouetur per totum aliquod spacium, necessum est pertranseat eius spacij dimidium. Atqui cum hoc ipsum dimidium rursus fit in infinita dimidia diuisibile (sicut magnitudo quoq; in infinitum diuiditur) sequitur, & illud quod mouetur, per infinita trãsire. Sed infinita transire etiã est impossibile. Ergo nihil potest moueri. Respondetur: Sicut infinita dimidia tantum potentia concedimus, nõ actu: ita infinita quoque pertransiri potentia concedemus, actu uero minime. Reliquæ Zenonis obiectiones, earundemq; dilutiones, ex Aristotele peti possunt.
units.tr: Second argument: If anything is moved through a whole space, it must pass over half of that space. But since this very half is again divisible into infinite halves (just as magnitude is divided to infinity), it follows that what is moved must pass over infinite things. But to pass over infinite things is also impossible. Therefore nothing can be moved. Answer: just as we grant infinite halves only in potency, not in act, so we grant that infinite things can be passed over in potency, but by no means in act. The remaining objections of Zeno and their solutions can be drawn from Aristotle.

units.la: Quis est secundus error con- su-tandus?
units.tr: What is the second error to be refuted?

units.la: Democriti, qui dicebat, <bl>ἄτομα</bl> seu indiuisibilia per se moueri. Contra hunc constituendum est, indiuisibilia non moueri nisi per accidens. Intelligimus autem indiuisibile non secundum speciem, quomodo ignis uel aer in plura corpora specie diuersa nõ diuiduntur: sed secundum quantitatem, cuiusmodi est punctum, ut ipse quoq; uult Democritus. Huiusmodi igitur indiuisibile dicimus non posse mutari seu moueri per se, sed tantum per accidens: quemadmodum sedens in naui mouetur ad motum ipsius nauis:
units.tr: That of Democritus, who said that atoms [ἄτομα], or indivisibles, are moved per se. Against this it must be established that indivisibles are not moved except per accidens. We understand by indivisible not what is indivisible according to species (as fire or air is not divided into several bodies of different species), but what is indivisible according to quantity, such as a point, as Democritus himself also holds. Such an indivisible, we say, cannot be changed or moved per se, but only per accidens, just as a man sitting in a ship is moved by the motion of the ship, and when the body of a man is moved, its part and the soul itself are moved too.

units.la: Lib.c. cap.10. nauis:& moto hominis corpore,mouetur eius pars & ipsa anima. Probatur: Si indiuisibile moueretur per se,maxime moueretur quidem secudum locum. Sed hoc non fit. Igitur per se non mouetur. Minor probatur. Nam quicquid in spacio mouetur,prius debet pertransfire spacium minus se, siue æquale sibi,quàm spacium maius. Atqui indiuisibile nihil illorum facit.Igitur indiuisibile non mouetur. Adijciemus & huius minoris probationem: Non transfit spacium minus se. Cum enim ipso indiuisibili nihil sit minus,quomodo intelligetur spacium aliquod minus se transfire ? Quòd item non transfeat æquale spacium,liquet. Transfeat enim indiuisibile per lineam, ibi autem erit punctum puncto coniunctum, & linea prodibit ex indiuisibilibus copofita. Erit namq; ibi indiuisibile sibi æquali continuè coniunctum:sed hoc est absurdum. Erit igitur similiter absurdum,indiuisibile per se moueri.
units.tr: Lib. c. cap. 10. The proof: If an indivisible were moved per se, it would be moved most of all with respect to place. But this does not happen. Therefore it is not moved per se. The minor premise is proved thus: whatever is moved in space must first pass over a space less than itself, or equal to itself, before passing over a larger space. But an indivisible does neither. Therefore an indivisible is not moved. We add also the proof of this minor premise: it does not pass over a space less than itself. For since nothing is less than the indivisible itself, how could one understand it to pass over some space less than itself? That it does not pass over an equal space is likewise clear. For if the indivisible were to pass through a line, there would be a point joined to a point there, and a line would emerge composed of indivisibles. There would be an indivisible continuously joined to an equal indivisible; but this is absurd. Therefore it is similarly absurd for an indivisible to be moved per se.

units.la: Quis est tertius error con- futandus?
units.tr: What is the third error to be refuted?

units.la: Heracliti, qui asseruit, omnia moueri seu mutari semper. Contra hunc definimus,nullum esse motum seu mutationè infinitam. Quod sic probamus: Quod continetur definitis terminis, infinitum non est. Omnis autem mutatio definitis continetur terminis.Igitur nulla mutatio est infinita. Minor declaratur hoc pacto:Generationis & corruptionis termi mini sunt esse & non esse. Augmenti terminus est uniuscuiusq; rei secundum suam naturam perfecta magnitudo. Decremeti terminus similiter certa ex contrario diminutio. Alterationis termini sunt contraria, aut contrario modo se habentia, in quae fit alteratio. Motus secundum locum termini sunt similiter plerunq; contrarij: ut sursum ac deorsum, ad quos cum pervenerint res, debent quiescere. Igitur omnis mutatio definitis continetur terminis. Recte proinde astruemus, nullam esse mutationem, quae non certis contineatur terminis, a quibus speciem habet.
units.tr: The error of Heraclitus, who asserted that all things always move or change. Against him we lay down that there is no motion or change that is infinite. We prove this as follows: what is contained within defined limits is not infinite. But every change is contained within defined limits. Therefore no change is infinite. The minor premise is explained thus. The limits of generation and corruption are being and non-being. The limit of growth is the perfect magnitude of each thing according to its nature. The limit of diminution is likewise a fixed reduction from the opposite. The limits of alteration are contraries, or things related in a contrary way, into which the alteration passes. The limits of motion according to place are likewise for the most part contraries, such as up and down, and when things arrive at these they must come to rest. Therefore every change is contained within defined limits. Rightly, then, we affirm that there is no change which is not contained within certain limits, from which it takes its species.

units.la: Si quis autem istud dicat, dari posse motum infinitum tempore: quandoquidem unus motus sive una mutatio alteram continue sequitur, ut generatio generationem, &c. respondetur, talem motum non posse dici unum & eundem numero, ideoq; neque infinitum.
units.tr: But if someone says that there can be an infinite motion in time, since one motion or change continually follows another, as generation follows generation, and so on, the answer is that such a motion cannot be called one and the same in number, and therefore not infinite either.

units.la: ¶ Percurrimus quae Aristoteles exposuit, primùm de motu per se, ex libro Auscultationis Physicae tertio: deinde motus species, ex lib.5. hinc motus partes, ex lib.6. Reliquum est explicemus quaedam ipsi motui affinia, quae apud eundem traduntur lib. 7. & 8. Quamuis quod ad Aristotelis librum 7 attinet, minime praetercundum est, plerosq;, teste Simplicio, dubitare de eo num sit Aristotelis, maxime quando eadem fere quaestiones iterum tractantur lib.8. Certè Eudemus, quando omnes interpretantur, septimum totum prætermit. Alexander Aristotelis esse simpliciter negat. Themistius nonnulla omittit capita. Simplicius putat, alio tempore & diu ante hos de auscultatione esse scriptum, posse autem haberi ceu introductorium ad librum sequentè, quem vulgò octauum numerant. Quæ cum ita sint, & nos hic breuiores erimus.
units.tr: We have run through what Aristotle set out: first on motion in itself, from the third book of the Physics; then the species of motion, from the fifth book; and then the parts of motion, from the sixth. It remains to explain certain matters akin to motion itself, which are handed down by the same author in books 7 and 8. Yet as regards Aristotle's seventh book, it must not be passed over that many, as Simplicius testifies, doubt whether it is Aristotle's, especially since nearly the same questions are treated again in book 8. Eudemus, when he expounds all the books, certainly omits the seventh entirely. Alexander flatly denies that it is Aristotle's. Themistius omits some chapters. Simplicius thinks that it was written at another time, long before these, as a part of the Physics, but that it may be held as an introduction to the following book, which is commonly numbered the eighth. These things being so, we too shall be briefer here.

units.la: QVAE AFFINIA?
units.tr: WHAT ARE THE KINDRED MATTERS?

units.la: Quæ est motuum inter se comparatio, & quomodo se habent ad inuicem mouentia & mobilia?
units.tr: What is the comparison of motions with one another, and how do movers and movables stand in relation to each other?

units.la: Operæprecium est, prius ostendamus esse primũ aliquê motum & primum motorem. Quod propositionibus aliquot efficere conabimur.
units.tr: It is worth while to show first that there is some first motion and a first mover. We shall try to establish this by several propositions.

units.la: 1. Prima propositio: Omne quod mouetur, necesse est id ab aliquo alio moueatur. Intellige ab alio uel extrinseco & externo & apparente foris, uel interno & latente.
units.tr: 1. First proposition: Everything that is moved must necessarily be moved by something else. Understand "by something else" as either external and outside, visible and apparent, or internal and hidden.

units.la: 2. Secunda propositio: Cum autem quodcunq; motum moueatur ab aliquo mouente, atq; istud ipsum mouens necessariò rursus ab alio quopiam siue externo siue interno moueatur: si non constituatur aliquod primũ mouens, necessum erit procedere ad alia atq; alia mouentia in infinitum. Atqui istud est absurdum. Igitur ponendum est aliquod primum mouens.
units.tr: 2. Second proposition: Since whatever is moved is moved by some mover, and that very mover must necessarily be moved in turn by some other, either external or internal, if some first mover is not posited, it will be necessary to proceed to other and yet other movers to infinity. But this is absurd. Therefore some first mover must be posited.

units.la: Tertia propositio: Movens necessariò simul cum moto esse intelligitur, ita ut inter ea nullum sit medians. Quare oportet in quocunq; motu ad aliquod movens, & tandem ad primum quoddam movens respicere ac pervenire. Movens intellige, unde est principiū ipsius motus, & quod immediatè movet.
units.tr: Third proposition: The mover is necessarily understood to be together with the moved, so that no intermediate lies between them. Therefore in every motion we must look to, and finally arrive at, some mover and at last some first mover. By "mover" understand that whence the beginning of the motion comes, and that which moves immediately.

units.la: Cæterùm movens simul esse cum moto, demonstrari potest eundo per omnes motionis species.
units.tr: Moreover, that the mover is together with the moved can be demonstrated by going through all the species of motion.

units.la: Primò: In motu secundum quantitatem, augens & auctum sunt simul, neque aliquid inter ea medians est, ut fiat augmentatio. Similiter minuens & diminutum sunt simul, neque aliquid inter ea mediat, ut perficiatur diminutio.
units.tr: First: in motion according to quantity, the thing that increases and the thing increased are together, and nothing intervenes between them so that augmentation takes place. Likewise the thing that diminishes and the thing diminished are together, and nothing intervenes between them so that diminution is completed.

units.la: Secundò: In motu secundum qualitatem, cum alteratio fit, alterans & alteratum sunt simul, neque quicquam inter ea mediat. Sic cum alterabilia sint sonus & silentium, albedo & nigredo, dulcedo & amaritudo, calor & frigus, humiditas & siccitas, leuitas & grauitas, mollicies & durities, raritas & densitas: sanè quotiescunq; in his & similibus fit alteratio, agentia sunt simul cum passis, neque quicquā inter ea mediat: sonans namq; simul est cum sonoro, colorans cum colorato, calefaciens cum calefacto, &c.
units.tr: Second: in motion according to quality, when alteration occurs, the thing that alters and the thing altered are together, and nothing intervenes between them. Thus, since sound and silence, whiteness and blackness, sweetness and bitterness, heat and cold, moistness and dryness, lightness and heaviness, softness and hardness, rarity and density are capable of alteration, whenever alteration takes place in these and similar things, the agents are together with the patients, and nothing intervenes between them: for the sounding thing is together with the sounded, the colouring with the coloured, the heating with the heated, and so on.

units.la: Quòd si quis roget, in quota specie qualitatis alteratio consideretur? huic respondemus, quòd cum omnia quae alterantur, maximè alterantur secundum qualitates sensibiles, intelligetur alteratio constitui præcipuè in tertia specie qualitatis. Qua de re plura Aristoteles.
units.tr: But if someone asks in what species of quality alteration is to be considered, we reply that, since all things that are altered are altered chiefly according to sensible qualities, alteration is understood to be placed chiefly in the third species of quality. Aristotle says more about this matter.

units.la: §. Tertiò : In motu secundum locum manifestum est mouens cum motu simul esse. Si namque motus existat à principio externo, certè quilibet intelligit, non esse aliquod motu, nisi quatenus sit & mouens, inter quæ ipsa medium nullum inuenitur. Si autem motus existat à principio interno, tunc omnino necessum est aliqua species ex hisce quatuor prodeat: nēpe aut pulsio, aut tractio, aut vectio, aut rotatio. Atqui in his quoq; pellens est cum pulso, trahens cum tracto, vehens cum vecto, rotans cum rotato. Relinquitur ergo, quòd motus necessariò simul cum moto sit, atq; ita quidem, ut inter ea nihil medict[?]. Pulsio autem, siue ὦσις[?], significat motum, quo quid aliò abijcitur aut detruditur: cuius species sunt impulsio ἔπωσις[?], depulsio ἀπωσις[?], proiectio ῥίψις[?], tractio, ἕλξις[?], est motus quo quippiam adducitur. Vectio, ὄχησις[?], per se non fit, sed per accidens: quocirca in ea spectatur pulsio, tractio & rotatio. Rotatio autem, siue δίνωσις[?], mixta est ex pulsione & tractione. Exhis uero omnibus manifestum euadit, cum agitur de motu, requirendum esse etiam aliquod primum mouens. Hinc autem rectius perspici poterit, quomodo motus cum alijs comparetur.
units.tr: Third: in motion according to place it is evident that the mover is together with the motion. For if the motion arises from an external principle, anyone understands that there is no motion except insofar as there is also a mover, and between these two no intermediate is found. If, however, the motion arises from an internal principle, then it must necessarily proceed in one of these four species: namely, either pushing, or pulling, or carrying, or turning. But in these also the pusher is with the pushed, the puller with the pulled, the carrier with the carried, the turner with the turned. It follows, therefore, that motion is necessarily together with the moved, and in such a way that nothing intervenes between them. Pushing, or ὦσις, signifies the motion by which something is thrown or thrust off elsewhere; its species are impulsion [ἔπωσις], repulsion [ἀπωσις], projection [ῥίψις], and pulling [ἕλξις], which is the motion by which something is drawn towards. Carrying [ὄχησις] does not happen in itself but accidentally; hence in it pushing, pulling and turning are observed. Turning, or δίνωσις, is mixed from pushing and pulling. From all these things it becomes plain that when we are dealing with motion, some first mover must also be sought. From this it can be seen more clearly how motion is compared with other things.

units.la: Explana,qui motus cum quibus com- parari ualeant,& quomodo sese habeant mouentia & mobi- lia ad inuicem.
units.tr: Explanation of which motions can be compared with one another, and how movers and movables stand in relation to each other.

units.la: Non quiuis motus cum quouis uenit comparandus: sed ij tantum comparatur, in quibus spectatur proportio & æqualitas, adeoq; eiusdem sunt naturæ, atq; sub communi quodam genere proximo continentur. Quod quo clarius percipiatur, quatuor subijciemus propositiones, quæ motuum æqualitatem & comparationem ostendunt.
units.tr: Not every motion is to be compared with every other. Only those are compared in which proportion and equality can be observed, and which are of the same nature and fall under some common proximate genus. To understand this more clearly, we will set out four propositions which show the equality and comparison of motions.

units.la: 1. Vt motus aliqui inter se comparentur, atque æquè ueloces dicantur uel tardi, necesse est eos æquali tempore fieri.
units.tr: 1. For some motions to be compared with one another, and to be called equally swift or equally slow, they must necessarily occur in equal time.

units.la: 2. Oportet etiam fieri secundum æqualem magnitudinem, seu æquale spacium.
units.tr: 2. They must also occur over an equal magnitude, or equal space.

units.la: 3. Oportet fieri secundum idem specie indifferes, hoc est, in eadem re.
units.tr: 3. They must occur with respect to the same thing, that is, in the same specifically indifferent subject.

units.la: 4. Oportet ipsos quoq; motus eiusdem esse speciei. Ex quo fit, quòd motus rectus, & motus circularis, non comparantur.
units.tr: 4. The motions themselves must also be of the same species. From this it follows that straight motion and circular motion are not compared.

units.la: Ex his ergo perspicere licet, generationes comparari, atque æquè ueloces uel æquè tardas dici, quæ æquali tempore, æquali magnitudine, & secundum idem specie indifferens fiunt. Ita generatio hominis comparatur cum generatione hominis, non autem cum generatione arboris uel plantæ.
units.tr: From these points it is therefore possible to see that generations are compared, and called equally swift or equally slow, when they occur in equal time, over equal magnitude, and with respect to the same specifically indifferent subject. Thus the generation of a man is compared with the generation of a man, but not with the generation of a tree or a plant.

units.la: Eodem pacto de corruptionibus, praeterea de augmentationibus & diminutionibus est iudicandum. Alterationes item æquè veloces sunt & comparantur, quæ æquali tempore, æquali magnitudine, siue secundum eandem in specie individua passionem (in qua & æqualis sit constitutio) existút. Ita pares sunt alterationes eorum quæ æquali tempore & æqualiter dealbantur seu sanantur. Ex his quoq; loci mutationes æquè veloces facilè intelliguntur. Hæc de comparatione motuum inter se invicem.
units.tr: In the same way we must judge concerning corruptions, and further concerning augmentations and diminutions. Likewise alterations are equally swift and are compared when they occur in equal time, over equal magnitude, or with respect to the same passion in the same individual thing (in which the constitution is also equal). Thus the alterations of things that are whitened or healed equally, in equal time, are equal. From these examples it is also easily understood that changes of place can be equally swift. These are the points concerning the comparison of motions with one another.

units.la: Quòd si jam cognoscere cupis, quomodo in motu perficiendo se habeant moventia atque mobilia: certè ex ijs quæ dicta sunt, non difficulter colligitur, iuxta propositiones consideratas, & secundum rationem temporis, item magnitudinè, & eiusdem speciei cui conveniunt, & sub qua constituuntur, comparationem omnem fieri debere. Sit, exempli causa, A movens, B mobile, idem tempus quo fit motus, spacium siue magnitudo per quam fit motus. hic sanè ubi movens & mobile inter se conveniunt, atq; pari procedút tempore, & quidem in pari magnitudine, intelligentur ipsum movens & mobile inter sese rectè comparari.
units.tr: But if you now wish to know how movers and movables stand in bringing about a motion, then from what has been said it is not difficult to gather that, according to the propositions considered, and with respect to time, likewise magnitude, and the same species to which they belong and under which they are placed, every comparison must be made. Let, for example, A be the mover, B the movable, the same time in which the motion occurs, and the space or magnitude through which the motion occurs. Here, certainly, where the mover and the movable agree with each other and proceed through equal time, and indeed over equal magnitude, the mover and the movable are understood to be rightly compared with one another.

units.la: Si quis consideret vim moventem in generationibus & corruptionibus, in augmentationibus & diminutionibus, in alterationibus rerum naturalium, atq; considerat, quomodo res eiusdem speciei, pari tempore & pari modo generentur, augmententur uel alterentur, poterit de comparatione motuum, item mouentium & mobilium facilius iudicare. Sic poma eiusdem speciei eodem tempore & aequaliter alterantur seu mutantur, inq; ijs proportio motuum cernitur.
units.tr: If someone considers the moving force in generations and corruptions, in augmentations and diminutions, in the alterations of natural things, and considers how things of the same species are generated, augmented or altered in equal time and in the same way, he will be able to judge more easily concerning the comparison of motions, and likewise of movers and movables. Thus apples of the same species are altered or changed in the same time and equally, and in them the proportion of motions is seen.

units.la: Utrum primus motus sit aeternus, id est, aliquando esse coeperit, aut etiam esse desinet?
units.tr: Whether the first motion is eternal, that is, whether it has begun at some time, or will also come to an end?

units.la: Diuersæ de hac quæstione fuerunt opiniones.
units.tr: Opinions on this question have been diverse.

units.la: Prima opinio : Quidam existimarunt infinitos esse mundos, atq; horum quidem alios generari, alios uero corrumpi, necnon perpetua & indefatigabili quadam serie alios alijs succedere. Quocirca ijdem etiam primum motum æternum posuerunt.
units.tr: First opinion: Some thought that there are infinitely many worlds, and that of these some are generated and others corrupted, and that one succeeds another in a perpetual and tireless series. Therefore they also posited an eternal first motion.

units.la: Secunda: Alij posuerunt unum quidem mundum: sed nonnulli eorum statuerunt, sic incœpisse, ut antea nunquam fuerit: in qua sententia fuit Anaxagoras. Quidam uero mundum aliquando incœpisse, sed tamen eundem etiam antea extitisse, adeoq; per interualla modo generatum, modo iterum corruptum: quod arbitratus est Empedocles. Sicut proinde hi de mundo eiusq; origine, ita etiam de motu constituerunt.
units.tr: Second opinion: Others posited one world; but some of them held that it began in such a way that it had never existed before. Anaxagoras held this view. Others held that the world began at some time, but that the same world had existed even before, and so was generated at intervals, now produced and now again corrupted; this was the view of Empedocles. Just as these men thought concerning the world and its origin, so they also settled concerning motion.

units.la: Tertia: Reiectis horum opinionibus tanquam à veritate alienis, sicut mundum æternū, ita primum motum quoq; æternū, hoc est, nunquam incœpisse, ut ante cum alius non fuerit, praeterea nunquam interituru̅m, ut sequi cum alius non posset, statuit Aristoteles. Quia suam sententiam non indiligeter coprobat. Quinetiam confutat eorum rationes, qui probare diuersum, uidelicet[?] primum motum non esse perpetuum, nitebatur. Cæterum nos, qui assecuti sumus certiorem ex libris sacris cognitionem, Aristotelis consentire haud ualemus. Quare duas addemus propositiones, quibus uera atq; indubitata sententia comprehenditur.
units.tr: Third opinion: Rejecting these opinions as alien to the truth, Aristotle established, just as he held the world to be eternal, so also the first motion to be eternal, that is, never to have begun, so that there was never a time when it did not exist, and never to perish, so that there could never be a time when it did not exist. He confirms his view with no little care. He also refutes the arguments of those who strove to prove the contrary, namely that the first motion is not perpetual. But we, who have obtained a more certain knowledge from the holy books, cannot agree with Aristotle. Therefore we will add two propositions, by which the true and indubitable opinion is comprehended.

units.la: 1. Prima propositio: Quoniam nihil fuit ab æterno, præter solum Deum, qui suapte natura est immobilis, & mundus omniaq; creata cœperunt esse in tempore: ideo recte afferimus, motum quoq;, de quo disputatio hic instituitur, in tempore cœpisse. Nam ante mundum conditum, quomodo motum fuisse intelligemus, cum non fuerit in quo esset, aut circa quod versaretur?
units.tr: 1. First proposition: Since nothing was from eternity except God alone, who by his own nature is immovable, and since the world and all created things began to exist in time, we rightly affirm that the motion also, which is the subject of this discussion, began in time. For before the world was made, how shall we understand that there was motion, since there was no thing in which it might be, or about which it might be occupied?

units.la: 2. Secunda propositio: Interea autem eundem motum semper futurum afferimus. Enimuero substantia mundi, licet incœperit, nunquam tamen esse desinet, & semper motus aliqui superer̅ut. Erit namq; etiam post conflagrationem vniuersalem nouum cœlum, & terra noua, testante Petro. Deinde erunt homines in corpore & anima agentes uel feliciter cum æterna gloria in cœlis, uel infeliciter & cum æterna ignominia in inferno. Hæc admonendi causa adiesa adiecimus, ut ne à religionis nostræ dogmatis usquam discedamus. Nunc ad reliqua licebit inoffenso pede progredi.
units.tr: 2. Second proposition: Meanwhile, however, we affirm that the same motion will always be in the future. For the substance of the world, although it began, will nevertheless never cease to exist, and some motions will always remain. For there will also be, after the universal conflagration, a new heaven and a new earth, as Peter testifies. Then there will be men in body and soul, acting either happily with eternal glory in heaven, or unhappily and with eternal disgrace in hell. These things we have added as a reminder, so that we may never depart anywhere from the doctrines of our religion. Now we may proceed to the rest with an unstumbling foot.

units.la: Utrum primum movens semper mo- veatur, an potius sit im- mobile?
units.tr: Whether the first mover is always moved, or rather is immovable?

units.la: Convenit sane, ut statuatur immobile. Quod ita se habere, haud difficulter demonstratur: sed operæprecium est quædam præmittamus, imprimis autem aliquot divisiones. Necessum est dispositionem rerum, quod ad motum & quietem attinet, tripliciter se habere.
units.tr: Indeed it is agreed that it should be established as immovable. That this is so is not difficult to demonstrate, but it is worth while to premise certain things, first of all some divisions. It is necessary that the disposition of things, as regards motion and rest, should be threefold.

units.la: 1. Aut ut omnia semper quiescant, & nihil aliquando moveatur.
units.tr: (1) Either all things always rest, and nothing is ever moved.

units.la: 2. Aut ut omnia semper moveantur, & nihil aliquando quiescat.
units.tr: (2) Or all things are always moved, and nothing ever rests.

units.la: 3. Aut ut quædam moveantur, et quædam quiescant. Rursum autem istud fiet tripliciter.
units.tr: (3) Or some things are moved and some rest. Again, this will happen in three ways.

units.la: 1. Aut ea quæ moventur, semper movebuntur: quæ vero quiescunt, semper quiescent: & nihil erit horum, quod quandoque moveatur, quandoque quiescat.
units.tr: (1) Either the things that are moved will always be moved, and those that rest will always rest, and none of these will be such that it is at one time moved and at another at rest.

units.la: 2. Aut è diverso, omnia nata sint & moveri & quiescere, & nihil sit quod semper moveatur vel semper quiescat.
units.tr: (2) Or conversely, all things are apt by nature both to be moved and to rest, and there is nothing that is always moved or always at rest.

units.la: 3. Aut alia sint semper immobilia, & nunquam moveantur: alia vero semper mobilia, & nunquam quiescant : alia deniq; medio modo sese habeant, ut videlicet quandoq; moueantur, quandoq; quiescant. Ex hoc autem vltimo membro subdiuisionis conficietur necessario, esse quoddam immobile, quod quidem in nullum aliud quàm in primum mouens competit. sed prius excutere conuenit singula totius diuisionis membra.
units.tr: (3) Or some things are always immovable and never moved; others are always movable and never at rest; others finally are disposed in a middle way, so that they are at one time moved and at another at rest. From this last member of the subdivision it will necessarily follow that there is something immovable, which indeed belongs to nothing other than the first mover. But it is fitting first to examine the individual members of the whole division.

units.la: I. Primum igitur membrum diuisionis, quod videlicet omnia semper quiescant, quemadmodum Zeno, Parmenides & Melissus putarunt, non potest consistere. Tolleretur enim eo pacto omnis motus: quod est contrà naturam & sensum communem.
units.tr: I. The first member of the division, namely that all things always rest, as Zeno, Parmenides and Melissus thought, cannot stand. For in that way all motion would be taken away, which is contrary to nature and common sense.

units.la: II. Secundum membrum, omnia videlicet semper moueri, vti volebat Heraclytus, similiter non confistit. Qui enim illud astruere volet, ipsam impugnabit naturam, cùm natura sit principium non solum motus, verum etiam quietis. Quamobrem quietem poni oportet.
units.tr: II. The second member, namely that all things are always moved, as Heraclitus wished, likewise cannot stand. For whoever wishes to assert this will attack nature itself, since nature is the principle not only of motion but also of rest. Wherefore rest must be posited.

units.la: III. Tertium membrum varia cōplectitur: ideoq; singula in subdivisione posita seorsim expendi debet.
units.tr: III. The third member embraces various things; therefore each of the items placed in the subdivision must be weighed separately.

units.la: I. Primum igitur subdivisionis membrum, quod quae mouentur, mouebuntur semper: quae vero quiescunt, quiescet semper: non potest subsistere, id quod patet volenti per singulas motus species progredi. Nam quae generantur, non semper generantur, sed aliquando generationis suae fine capiunt. Quae item corrumpuntur, non semper corrumpuntur, sed necessario constituitur quidam corruptionis eorū terminus. Similiter est iudicandum de augmentatione & diminutione, de alteratione, itemq; de latione.
units.tr: I. The first member of the subdivision, that things which are moved will always be moved, and things which rest will always rest, cannot stand; this is evident to anyone who goes through the individual species of motion. For things that are generated are not always being generated, but at some point reach the end of their generation. Likewise, things that are corrupted are not always corrupted, but a certain term of their corruption is necessarily fixed. The same judgement must be made about increase and decrease, about alteration, and likewise about local motion.

units.la: Secundum subdiuisionis membrum, quòd uidelicet omnia apta nata sint moueri uel quiescere, nihil tamen sit quod semper moueatur, uel semper quiescat: eadem prorsus ratione per contrarium baud subsistere intelligitur. Certè nihil esse quod semper moueatur, quomodo consistet, si consideramus primum motum, quemadmodum supra positum est, esse æternum?
units.tr: The second member of the subdivision, namely that all things are apt by nature to be moved or to rest, yet that there is nothing which is always moved or always at rest, is understood to fail by the same reasoning in reverse. Indeed, if we consider the first motion, as stated above, to be eternal, how can it stand that there is nothing always moved?

units.la: Tertium membrū subdiuisionis magis est præ-senti instituto accommodum, utpote in quo veritas continetur: esse uidelicet quædam semper immobilia, quædam uerò semper mobilia, quædam denique medio quodam modo se habentia.
units.tr: The third member of the subdivision is more suited to our present purpose, since in it the truth is contained: namely, that some things are always immovable, some indeed always movable, and some finally are disposed in a certain middle way.

units.la: Demonstra aliquid esse semper im- mobile, aliquid uerò sem- per mobile.
units.tr: Show that something is always immovable, and something always movable.

units.la: Vt istud præstemus, primò docebimus, necessario omne quod mouetur, ab alio moueri. Secundò, quando omne quod mouetur, ab alio mouetur, necessario peruenien-dū ad aliquod primum & principale mouens. Tertiò, quòd tametsi peruenia-tur ad primum aliquod seipsum mouens, tamen illud ipsum esse immobile. Ordine igitur de his dicamus.
units.tr: To accomplish this, we will first teach that necessarily everything that is moved is moved by another. Second, that when everything that is moved is moved by another, we must necessarily arrive at some first and principal mover. Third, that even if we arrive at some first thing that moves itself, nevertheless that very thing is immovable. Let us speak of these in order.

units.la: k
units.tr: k

units.la: Quomodo probas, omne quod mo- veatur, ab alio moveri?
units.tr: How do you prove that everything that is moved is moved by another?

units.la: Observentur hæ divisiones: Eorū quæ movent vel moventur, quædam movent vel moventur 1. Secundum se: et horum quidem alia A se ipsis: ut animata. Ab alijs: ut inanimata.
units.tr: Let these divisions be observed: Of the things that move or are moved, some move or are moved (1) in themselves; and of these, some by themselves, as animate things, others by others, as inanimate things.

units.la: 2. Secundum partem: ut quando homo dicitur percuti, quia manus percutitur.
units.tr: (2) In part: as when a man is said to be struck because his hand is struck.

units.la: 3. Secundum accidēs: sicut homo movetur, quia est in naui quæ movetur: itē musicus sanat, quia is qui sanat, musices est peritus. Rursus, eorum quæ per se mo{*}uentur, quædā mouentur Natura: ut animata, item gravia & levia. Vi, sive praeter naturam: ut aliquando animata & eorundem partes, tum terra sursum mota.
units.tr: (3) By accident: as a man is moved because he is in a ship that is moved; likewise a musician heals because he who heals is skilled in music. Again, of those things that are moved in themselves, some are moved by nature, as animate things, and likewise heavy and light things; others by force, or contrary to nature, as sometimes animate things and their parts, and earth moved upwards.

units.la: Ex his iam manifestum fiet, quòd quæ mouetur, ab alio moueantur. Primùm ea quæ mouentur secundum partem & secundum accidens, ab alio moueri, nemini est obscurum. Deinde de ijs quæ secundum se mouentur, si moueantur ui seu præter naturam, nulla est dubitatio, ea ab alio moueri: illa autem quæ natura mouentur, demonstrabimus similiter ab alio moueri.
units.tr: From these things it will now become clear that what is moved is moved by another. First, that things which are moved in part and by accident are moved by another, is obvious to no one. Next, concerning those that are moved in themselves: if they are moved by force or contrary to nature, there is no doubt that they are moved by another; but those that are moved by nature we will likewise show to be moved by another.

units.la: Primò, quæ mouet seipsa, suntq; animata, ea mouentur ab alio, nempe ipsa anima, quæ est in illis quoddam internum principium, habens mouendi facultatem, & reuera mouens: sicut nauta solet mouere nauem.
units.tr: First, that which moves itself and is animate is moved by another, namely by the soul itself, which is in them as a certain internal principle, having the faculty of moving and really moving, just as a sailor is accustomed to move a ship.

units.la: Secundò, quæ mouentur secundum naturam, ut grauia & leuia, non mouentur à seipsis, ac proinde ab alio moueri necessum est. Quod autem hæc non mouentur à seipsis, probatur.
units.tr: Second, things that are moved according to nature, such as heavy and light things, are not moved by themselves, and therefore it is necessary that they be moved by another. That these are not moved by themselves is proved as follows.

units.la: Mouere seipsum, est habentium vitam, & proprie animalium. Atqui illa, grauia videlicet & leuia, non habent vitam, neq; etiam animā: igitur non mouentur à seipsis.
units.tr: To move oneself belongs to those having life, and properly to animals. But those things, namely heavy and light things, have neither life nor indeed a soul; therefore they are not moved by themselves.

units.la: Quæ mouent seipsa, possunt etiam sibi esse causa quietis: quod licet obseruare in omnibus animatis. Sed grauia & leuia non possunt sibi esse causa quietis: igitur neq; sunt sibi causa motus.
units.tr: Things that move themselves can also be the cause of their own rest; this can be observed in all animate things. But heavy and light things cannot be the cause of their own rest; therefore neither are they the cause of their own motion.

units.la: Nullum continuum mouet seipsum. Grauia & leuia sunt continua: igitur non mouent seipsa.
units.tr: No continuous thing moves itself. Heavy and light things are continuous; therefore they do not move themselves.

units.la: {a} Quæ mouent seipsa, ea pro nutu moueri diuerso motu possunt. Sed illa non mouentur diuerso motu. Quæ enim grauia sunt, tantum deorsum: quæ leuia, tantum sursum feruntur. Igitur non mouentur à seipsis.
units.tr: Things that move themselves can be moved by different motions at their own will. But those things are not moved by different motions: for heavy things are carried only downwards, and light things only upwards. Therefore they are not moved by themselves.

units.la: Relinquitur ergo antecedens probatum.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is proved.

units.la: Sed dicis, A' quo mouentur grauia & leuia, si non mouentur ab ipsis, sed ab alio?
units.tr: But you say: by what are heavy and light things moved, if they are not moved by themselves but by another?

units.la: Necessum quidem omnino est ab aliquo naturaliter moueri. Scire autem oportet, aliter esse leuia & grauia actu, aliter potentia: & prius debere esse potentia eiusmodi, quam talia fiant actu: sicut aliquis potentia quoq; doctus esse debet, antequam talis fiat actu. porrò ut actu non fit doctus, nisi per aliquod agens, nempe per docentem, &c. ita etiā non fiunt ulla grauia aut leuia actu, nisi per aliquod agens & quasi adiuuans.
units.tr: It is indeed altogether necessary that they be moved naturally by something. But it must be known that light and heavy things are one way actually and another way potentially, and that such a thing must first be potentially so before it becomes actually so; just as someone must also be potentially learned before he becomes actually learned. Moreover, as a person is not made learned actually except through some agent, namely a teacher, and so on, so also no things become heavy or light actually except through some agent and, as it were, helper.

units.la: Cæterum potentia graue aut leue multipliciter aliquid dicitur. Primò quidem, quod adhuc est aqua, est potentia quidem leue, & potest leue fieri. Secundo, cum iam ex aqua facta est exhalatio, adhuc sane potentia est leue, magis tamen quam ante aptu ut fiat actu leue, adeoq; reipsa sursum tendat. Sed quando fit istud actu? Nimirum quādo per aliquod aliud agens, aufertur omne impedimetum, propter quod non poterat illud sursum attolli.
units.tr: But a thing is called heavy or light potentially in many ways. First, what is still water is indeed potentially light, and can become light. Second, when an exhalation has already been made from water, it is still indeed potentially light, but more apt than before to become actually light, and so in fact tends upwards. But when does this become actual? Surely when, through some other agent, every impediment is removed, on account of which it could not be lifted upwards.

units.la: Similiter & graue quippiam potētia graue est, & conatur actu quidem quoque tale fieri, id est, re ipsa deorsum descendere: sed quoniam sorte impositum est excelsæ columnæ, aut simili rei, impeditur, nec potest prius deorsum tendere, quàm columna & omne impedimentum per aliquem remoueatur. Iam ex his licet colligere, quòd leuia sursum, grauia deorsum tendant, duabus id de causis euenire.
units.tr: Similarly, a heavy thing is potentially heavy, and strives indeed also to become such actually, that is, in fact to descend downwards; but since by chance it has been placed on a high column, or some similar thing, it is hindered, and cannot tend downwards before the column and every impediment is removed by some agent. From these things it may be gathered that light things tend upwards and heavy things downwards, this happening for two reasons.

units.la: 1. Quòd à primo generationis suæ tempore accepe-rint formam, secundum quam apta nata sunt, naturaliter sursum uel deorsum ferri.
units.tr: (1) Because from the first time of their generation they have received the form according to which they are naturally apt to be carried upwards or downwards.

units.la: 2. Quòd adiuuentur ab eo quod remouet impedimentum, per quod prohibebantur, ne actu ferent huiusmodi. Prima causa est per se mouens, posterior per accidens. Itaq; mouentur quidem illa sic naturaliter, quandoquidem habent principium motus in seipsis, non tamen habent principium mouendi: hoc est, habent principium passiuum, at non actiuum. Quòd enim moueantur, quò per naturam tendunt, acceptum ferri ei debet, à quo remouetur impedimenta. Ergo grauia & leuia non mouetur à se ipsis, sed præcipuè à remouente impedimentum.
units.tr: 2. Because they are helped by that which removes the impediment through which they were prevented from actually bearing such motion. The first cause moves per se, the latter per accidens. So these things are indeed moved naturally in this way, since they have a principle of motion in themselves, yet they do not have a principle of moving: that is, they have a passive principle but not an active one. For that they are moved toward where they tend by nature must be credited to that which removes the impediments. Therefore heavy and light things are not moved by themselves, but chiefly by that which removes the impediment.

units.la: Probatum igitur abundè est, omne quod mouetur, ab alio moueri.
units.tr: It has therefore been sufficiently proved that everything that is moved is moved by another.

units.la: k s Quo-
units.tr: Quo-

units.la: Quomodo probas necessum esse, ut inter mouentia ueniatur ad quod- dam primum & principa- le mouens?
units.tr: How do you prove that it is necessary for us to arrive, among movers, at something first and principal that moves?

units.la: Duplex est mouens. 1. Per seipsum & citra alterius adminiculum mouens. 2. Ab altero adiutum siue incitatu. Et hoc rursus est duplex. 1. Remotius seu minus principale: ut baculus figuli, mouens rotam. 2. Propinquius: ut manus figuli, baculum ipsum agitans.
units.tr: A mover is twofold. 1. That which moves through itself and without the help of another. 2. That which is aided or spurred on by another. And this again is twofold. 1. More remote or less principal, as the potter's stick moving the wheel. 2. Nearer, as the potter's hand moving the stick itself.

units.la: Ex his uero primum mouens, ueluti manus figuli, uel potius anima figuli mouës ipsam manum, plus agit, quàm quodcunq; mouens secundarium. Vt autem dentur hoc modo plura mouentia simul considerata, atqui oportet tandem peruenire ad quoddam primum mouens, quod ab alio non moueatur. Quod sic probo. Aut enim peruenitur ad huiusmodi aliquod primum mouens, aut proceditur in infinitum ad alia atq; alia mouentia. Atqui istud non est dicendum: illud igitur uerum manebit.
units.tr: Of these, the first mover, like the potter's hand, or rather the potter's soul moving the hand itself, acts more than any secondary mover. But if several movers are considered together in this way, we must in the end arrive at some first mover that is not moved by another. I prove it thus. Either we arrive at some such first mover, or we proceed to infinity through other and other movers. But the latter must not be said; therefore the former will remain true.

units.la: Nec uero dici potest, illud primum ab alio moueri. Si enim co esset aliquod aliud prius, utique primum non esset. Ergo inter mouentia necessum est ad quoddam primum ueniatur, in quo & motus & mouendi infit potestas.
units.tr: Nor can it be said that this first mover is moved by another. For if there were some other prior to it, it would certainly not be first. Therefore among movers we must arrive at some first, in which both motion and the power of moving are present.

units.la: Quomodo demonstrabis, hoc ipsum primum mouens esse immobile, & nihilominus seipsum mouens?
units.tr: How will you demonstrate that this very first mover is immovable, and yet moves itself?

units.la: Si dicas moueri, quaero igitur, nū moueatur per accidens, an per se? Neutrum horū dici potest. Quare est immobile.
units.tr: If you say it is moved, I ask then whether it is moved per accidens or per se? Neither of these can be said. Therefore it is immovable.

units.la: Quòd non moueatur per accidens, patet. Si enim per accidens moueretur, tunc posset motus abeo perinde abesse atq; adesse. Sed abesse ab eo aliquando motum, rationi repugnat. Eo enim pacto motus in omnibus alijs ab eo motis aliquando cessaret. Igitur non mouetur per accidens.
units.tr: That it is not moved per accidens is clear. For if it were moved per accidens, motion could be absent from it just as well as present. But for motion to be absent from it at some time contradicts reason. For in that case motion would at some time cease in all the others moved by it. Therefore it is not moved per accidens.

units.la: Quòd uero non moueatur per se, similiter demonstratur.
units.tr: That it is not moved per se is demonstrated in a similar way.

units.la: 1. Quod per se mouetur, idipsum ab alio quoq; moueri, antea semel dictum est. Atqui quòd primum mouens ab alio moueatur, non potest intelligi. Igitur manet tantum mouens, & non mobile, neq; à se, neq; ab alio. Neq; differentaneum à ratione est, si dicamus, mouere & moueri separata cōsiderari posse, prorsus uti spectantur coniuncta. Nam mouere & moueri spectantur quidem coniuncta in baculo figuli, moueri autem absq; mouere spectatur in rota figuli. Quid' ni igitur contrario modo in primo mouente spectetur mouere absq; moueri?
units.tr: 1. What is moved per se has been said before to be moved also by another. But it cannot be understood that the first mover is moved by another. Therefore it remains only a mover, and not movable, neither by itself nor by another. Nor is it contrary to reason if we say that moving and being moved can be considered separately, although they are observed conjoined. For moving and being moved are indeed seen conjoined in the potter's stick, but being moved without moving is seen in the potter's wheel. Why, then, should moving without being moved not be observed in the first mover, in the opposite way?

units.la: 2. Si primum mouens tam moueretur quàm mouet, uel[?],oporteret aut eodem motu ista in ipso fieri,aut diuerso, ut uidelicet alio moueret, alio moueretur. Atqui neutrum iure potest astrui . Relinquitur ergo,primum mouens plane esse immobile.
units.tr: 2. If the first mover were moved just as it moves, these things would have to happen in it either by the same motion or by different motions, namely that it moves by one and is moved by another. But neither can rightly be maintained. It remains, therefore, that the first mover is plainly immovable.

units.la: Quomodo intelligetur primum mo- uens,si nihil sit in eo mobile, seipsum mouere?
units.tr: How will the first mover be understood to move itself, if nothing in it is movable?

units.la: Vt ad hanc quæstionem principalem, & paulo ante motam,respondeatur,sciendum est,duas debere eius quod ita mouet seipsum , constitui ad minimum partes.Alteram mouentem & immobilem,alteram uero motam & non mouentem. Quod sic probatur.
units.tr: To answer this principal question, raised a little earlier, it must be known that at least two parts must be posited in that which thus moves itself: one moving and immovable, the other moved and not moving. This is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Omne quod mouetur, diuisibile est semper in alia quædam diuisibilia, ut supra in his quæ ex lib. 6.Aristotelis desumpsimus,dictum est. Quare in eo quod seipsum quoq; mouet,quemadmodum totum, ita partes etiam quædam considerabuntur.
units.tr: 1. Everything that is moved is always divisible into other divisible parts, as was said above in those things we drew from the sixth book of Aristotle. Therefore in that which also moves itself, just as the whole, so certain parts too will be considered.

units.la: 2. Totum non potest seipsum mouere ut totum. Necessarium igitur est,in primo mouente, quod seipsum mouet,quasdam partes constituere. Itaq; partes in primo mouete quædam intelligentur,& quidem eæ quas iam diximus.
units.tr: 2. The whole cannot move itself as a whole. It is necessary, therefore, to posit certain parts in the first mover which moves itself. Thus certain parts are understood in the first mover, and indeed those we have already mentioned.

units.la: Quomodo duæ illæ partes coniungentur?
units.tr: How will those two parts be joined?

units.la: Coniungi quidem oportet,ut sint partes alicuius totius. Coniungentur ergo istæ duæ partes,nō quidem per continuationem (quandoquidem movens seipsum, & motum,non possunt cotinuari,) sed per contactum : idq; ut aut ambae partes contingant se invicem,si habeant magnitudinē: aut ut altera tantum pars contingatur ab altera, & non e diuerso: quod etiam fiet, si movens non habeat magnitudinem. Quod enim est incorporeum, potest quidem tangere corpus sua virtute movendo ipsum,non tamen contingitur vicissim a corpore. Duo autem corpora tangunt se invicem ex aequo. Ergo relinquitur demonstratum, quod sit quoddam primum movës, idq; immobile,& tamen seipsum semper movens.
units.tr: They must indeed be joined so as to be parts of some whole. These two parts will therefore be joined not by continuity (since a mover and a moved thing that move themselves cannot be continuous), but by contact: either so that both parts touch each other, if they have magnitude; or so that only one part is touched by the other, and not conversely, which will also happen if the mover has no magnitude. For what is incorporeal can indeed touch a body by moving it through its power, yet it is not in turn touched by the body. But two bodies touch each other equally. Therefore it remains demonstrated that there is a certain first mover, and this immovable, and yet always moving itself.

units.la: Utrum primum movens sit perpetuum & æternum,an non?
units.tr: Is the first mover perpetual and eternal, or not?

units.la: Necesse est constituere illud primum movens immobile perpetuum & æternum. Quod his rationibus probatur:
units.tr: It is necessary to hold that the first mover, which is immobile, is perpetual and eternal. This is proved by these arguments:

units.la: 1. Suprà demonstratum est, motum esse perpetuum. Quare primum quoq; moves tale esse oportet.
units.tr: 1. It was shown above that motion is perpetual. Therefore the first mover must also be such.

units.la: 2. Cum primum movens sit immobile, sanè haud potest id quandoq; esse, & quandoq; nō esse. Quod autem hoc pacto sese habet, est perpetuum. Igitur primum movens est perpetuum.
units.tr: 2. Since the first mover is immobile, it cannot at one time be and at another time not be. What is constituted in this way is perpetual. Therefore the first mover is perpetual.

units.la: 3. Quòd neque per se, neque per accidens movetur, quemadmodum proximè est probatum. Est igitur perpetuum.
units.tr: 3. Because it is moved neither per se nor per accidens, as was just proved. Therefore it is perpetual.

units.la: Est'ne unum tantum primum mo- uens,an plura?
units.tr: Is there only one first mover, or more than one?

units.la: Vnum tantum. Probatur. 1. In his quæ sunt secundū naturam,sicut præstabilius est semper constituere finita quàm infinita,ita & in his quæ finita conceduntur,præstabilius est unū ponere quàm plura,si modò id possit fieri,atq; si unum sufficiat. Sed unum primum mouens sufficit,ut perpetuus motus in natura existat. Igitur tantum unum primum mouens constituetur.
units.tr: Only one. It is proved thus. 1. In things that exist according to nature, just as it is better always to posit finite things than infinite ones, so among those things granted to be finite, it is better to posit one rather than several, provided this can be done and one suffices. But one first mover suffices for perpetual motion to exist in nature. Therefore only one first mover shall be posited.

units.la: 2. Motus est perpetuus & continuus,ut ante dictum. Vt autem motus sit continuus,necessum etiam est idem ut sit unus,hoc est,unius speciei: ut autē sit unus,oportet ab uno mobili & ab uno mouete proficiscatur. Si enim aliud atq; aliud mouès ponatur, non erit totus motus continuus,sed tantū confequen ter se habens. Relinquitur ergo, primum mouens esse,ut perpetuum,ita etiam unum.
units.tr: 2. Motion is perpetual and continuous, as said before. For motion to be continuous, it is also necessary that it be one, that is, of one species; and for it to be one, it must proceed from one mobile and one mover. For if one mover after another were posited, the whole motion would not be continuous but only successive. It follows, therefore, that the first mover is one as well as perpetual.

units.la: Vtrum,sicut est primum mouens perpe- tuum & æternum, ita constitui oportet etiam quoddam mobile perpe- tuum & æternum illi re- spondens?
units.tr: Is it necessary to posit, just as there is a first mover that is perpetual and eternal, also some mobile that is perpetual and eternal corresponding to it?

units.la: Maximè. Nam nisi esset unum aliquod mobile, quod à primo mouete semper agitaretur, nõ posset considerari unus & continuus motus. Etenim si diuersa essent mobilia,tũ oporteret diuersum oriri motũ. Ergo ut conseruetur unius motus ratio, recte sane unum quoq; mobile perpetuum & æternum statuetur.
units.tr: Most certainly. For unless there were some one mobile which was always moved by the first mover, a single continuous motion could not be considered. Indeed, if the mobiles were different, a different motion would have to arise. Therefore, so that the concept of one motion is preserved, rightly one perpetual and eternal mobile too shall be posited.

units.la: Ab hoc autem primo & perpetuo mobili intelligitur motus transfire ad alia quæcunque mobilia, quæ sicut varia sunt, ita varias quoque species motus edunt.
units.tr: Moreover, from this first and perpetual mobile, motion is understood to pass on to all other mobiles, which, being various, likewise produce various species of motion.

units.la: Atq; hinc constare potest veritas postremi membri in diuisione semel posita (ex iis quæ Aristoteles habet lib.8. cap.3.) quo dicebatur, alia semper immobilia & nunquā moueri, alia uero semper mobilia & nunquā quiescere: nimirum sicut primum movens est semper immobile, ita primum mobile est semper mobile & nunquam quiescens. Quare hac ratione abundè probatum est, aliquid semper esse immobile, aliquid uero semper moueri: id quod supra demonstrari petebatur, initio eorum quæ ex Aristotelis cap.4 præsentis libri.
units.tr: And from this the truth of the last member of the division laid down once (from those things which Aristotle has in book 8, chapter 3) can be established, where it was said that some things are always immobile and never moved, and others always mobile and never at rest. Clearly, just as the first mover is always immobile, so the first mobile is always mobile and never at rest. Hence by this reasoning it has been abundantly proved that something is always immobile and something is always moved; which was sought to be demonstrated above, at the beginning of those things from Aristotle's fourth chapter of this book.

units.la: Ad quam speciem motus refertur primus motus, ad qualitatémne, an ad quantitatem, an ad locum?
units.tr: To which species of motion does the first motion belong: to quality, to quantity, or to place?

units.la: Primus motus est motus secundū locum siue localis. Quod probatur quinq; rationibus.
units.tr: The first motion is motion according to place, or local motion. This is proved by five arguments.

units.la: Prima ratio: Motus secundū quantitatē, aut secundum qualitatē, non potest esse primus. Augmentatio nē namq; necessariò præcedit alteratio: alterationē uero præcedit motus localis. Igitur primus motus est motus localis. Quòd augmentatione præcat alte ratio,manifestum est. Augmentatio contrarijs perficitur:illud enim quo aliquid augmetatur, est quodam modo simile,& quodam modo dissimile.Exemplum esto: Alimentum primum est dissimile & contrarium ei quod nutritur,propter diuersitatem nutritionis. Post uero,quando fit augmentatio,efficitur simile, ideoq; transit ad substantiam crescentis. Porro à dissimilitudine non transitur ad similitudinem , nisi per alterationem. Quod uero alterationem præcedat motus localis,similiter fit perspicuum . Vt aliquid alteretur , omnino necessum est prius existat aliquod alterans. Enimuero oportet aliquid fit , per quod illud quod potentia erat calidum,reddatur actu calidum:atq; si huiusmodi alterans non accederet propinquius ad alteratum quàm ante fuerat,profecto non magis etiam quàm ante calefaceret.Ergo ante alterationem necessario est motus aliquis localis.
units.tr: First argument: motion according to quantity or according to quality cannot be first. For augmentation necessarily comes after alteration, and alteration is preceded by local motion. Therefore the first motion is local motion. That alteration precedes augmentation is clear: augmentation is effected by contraries, for that by which something is augmented is in some respects similar and in some respects dissimilar. Take an example: the first food is dissimilar and contrary to what is nourished, on account of the difference of nutrition. Afterwards, when augmentation takes place, it becomes similar, and so passes into the substance of the thing growing. Moreover, one does not pass from dissimilarity to similarity except through alteration. That local motion precedes alteration is likewise plain: for something to be altered, it is absolutely necessary that some altering agent first exists. Indeed something must come about through which what was potentially hot is made actually hot; and if such an altering agent did not approach the thing altered any more closely than before, it would certainly not heat it any more than before. Therefore before alteration there is necessarily some local motion.

units.la: Secunda : Motus localis est prior natura. Illud prius est natura, quod esse potest sine alio, & sine quo alia non existunt.
