Atqui motus localis est huiusmodi.Sine eo enim alij motus non existut,ut iam dictum est: & ipse sine alijs existit,quandoquidem contingit aliquid remoucri loco , nulla interim obveniente secundum qualitatem uel quantitatem alteratione.Igitur motus localis est primus.
units.tr: Second: local motion is prior by nature. That is prior by nature which can exist without another, and without which other things do not exist. But local motion is of this kind. For without it other motions do not exist, as has already been said; and it itself exists without the others, since it happens that something is removed from its place while no alteration according to quality or quantity intervenes. Therefore local motion is first.

units.la: Tertia : Motus localis etiam est prior tempore. Quod enim perpetuum æternumq; est, id prius excellentiusq; existit illo quod est in tempore: Atqui solus motus localis est perpetuus, quod in motu cœli animaduerti potest. Igitur tempore quoq; prior est aliis motibus.
units.tr: Third: local motion is also prior in time. For what is perpetual and eternal is prior to and more excellent than what is in time. But only local motion is perpetual, which can be observed in the motion of the heavens. Therefore it is also prior in time to the other motions.

units.la: Quarta: Motus localis est prior perfectione. Motus localis cernitur in iis quæ secundum naturam maximè sunt perfecta, ut in omnibus animatis quæ sese loco mouent, atq; omnium consensu perfectiora sunt inanimatis. Ergo motus localis reliquis motibus præeminet & perfectior censebitur.
units.tr: Fourth: local motion is prior in perfection. Local motion is seen in those things which are most perfect according to nature, as in all animate beings which move themselves from place, and which, by the consensus of all, are more perfect than inanimate things. Therefore local motion surpasses the other motions and will be judged more perfect.

units.la: Quinta: Confirmatur idem: Ille est perfectior motus, per quem de rerum mobilium natura substantiaq; quàm minimum decedit. Huiusmodi autem est motus localis. Igitur motus localis est perfectior. Minor probatur: Per alias species motus aliquid decedit mobilibus in sua substantia. Nam in alteratione res transmutatur secundum qualitatè, ut calida fiat, quæ ante fuerat frigida: & dura, quæ ante sfuerat mollis. In augmento autem vel decremento fit transmutatio quædam secundum quantitatem, & utrobiq; in substantia subiecti mobilis. Verùm in motu locali nihil decedit de substatia subiecti: manet nàq; prorsus eadem res, quæ antea fuerat, tantùmq; fit mutatio quædam exterius secundum locum. Ergo abundè probatum est, primùm motum esse motum localem, non autè motum secundum qualitatè aut quantitatem.
units.tr: Fifth: the same point is confirmed. That motion is more perfect by which mobiles depart as little as possible from their nature and substance. But local motion is of this kind. Therefore local motion is more perfect. The minor premise is proved thus: through the other species of motion something departs from mobiles in their substance. For in alteration a thing is changed according to quality, so that what was cold becomes hot, and what was soft becomes hard. In augmentation or diminution a certain change occurs according to quantity, and in both cases in the substance of the mobile subject. But in local motion nothing departs from the substance of the subject: for the same thing remains entirely what it was before, and only some external change of place occurs. Therefore it has been abundantly proved that the first motion is local motion, and not motion according to quality or quantity.

units.la: l
units.tr: l

units.la: Cuiusmodi motus localis erit primus motus, rectusne, an circularis, an alius quispiam?
units.tr: What kind of local motion is the first motion: straight, circular, or some other?

units.la: Circularis. Quod sic demonstratur: Oportet imprimis eiusmodi motum esse continuum. Nam si primus erit motus, decet sane eum continuum & perpetuum quoque intelligamus. Qua de re paulo ante dictum est. Eam namque ob causam constitutum est, motum primum esse localem, quia videlicet continuus & perpetuus esse non potest nisi localis. Porro cum motus nullus possit esse continuus praeter circularem, conficitur, primum motum esse motum localem, & quidem circularem.
units.tr: Circular. This is demonstrated as follows. First, such a motion must be continuous. For if it is to be the first motion, we must certainly understand it as continuous and perpetual. We said a little earlier why this is so. For the reason it was established that the first motion is local is that only local motion can be continuous and perpetual. Since no motion can be continuous except circular motion, it follows that the first motion is local motion, and indeed circular.

units.la: Demonstra, quod solus motus circula- ris possit esse continuus?
units.tr: Prove that only circular motion can be continuous.

units.la: Sic demonstratur: Motus localis alius quidem rectus, alius reflexus, alius circularis, alius vero mixtus, nempe ex recto & circulari. Sed ex his motibus neque rectus, neque reflexus, neque mixtus, poterit esse continuus. Relinquitur ergo, quod solus circularis erit continuus.
units.tr: It is demonstrated as follows. Local motion is either straight, or reflected, or circular, or mixed, that is, composed of straight and circular. But of these, neither straight, nor reflected, nor mixed motion can be continuous. It remains, therefore, that only circular motion is continuous.

units.la: Quod rectus non possit esse continuus, probatur. Ut enim talis fieret, oportet dari aliquam lineam rectam actu infinitam, per quam motus deduceretur. Atqui talis linea dari non potest. Igitur neque motus rectus erit continuus.
units.tr: That straight motion cannot be continuous is proved thus. For it to be so, some straight line would have to be actually infinite, along which the motion would be carried. But no such line can be given. Therefore straight motion will not be continuous either.

units.la: Quod item motus reflexus nō possit esse conti-nuus, nuus,probatur. Nam qui ita reflectuntur atq; resiliŭt,ut superne deorsum,vel à dextra sinistrorsum, vel à facie retrorsum reducantur,sunt contrarij sibi inuicem.Quare non potest in eis unus motus continuus considerari. Siquidem ubi unus & cōtinuus erit motus, ibi oportet hæc tria consistere: nempe unū mobile,una forma siue species motus,& unum tempus.
units.tr: That reflected motion likewise cannot be continuous is proved thus. Those motions that are bent back and rebound, so that they are led back from above downwards, or from right to left, or from front to back, are opposed to one another. Hence one continuous motion cannot be recognised in them. For where there is one and continuous motion, three things must be present there: namely one moving body, one form or species of motion, and one time.

units.la: Quod deniq; motus mixtus non possit esse continuus,liquet. Nam in motu mixto nō est unus motus: sed partim est circularis,partim rectus. Quocirca cum nē simplex siue rectus quidem motus ( qui tamen unus est)possit esse continuus, multo minus huiusmodi esse poterit motus mixtus.
units.tr: Finally, that mixed motion cannot be continuous is clear. For in mixed motion there is not one motion; rather it is partly circular and partly straight. Therefore, since not even simple or straight motion (which nevertheless is one) can be continuous, much less can a mixed motion of this kind be so.

units.la: Relinquitur ergo,solum motum circulare posse continuum existere.Atque id quidem ita esse, facile potest demonstrari.
units.tr: It remains, then, that only circular motion can exist as continuous. And that this is so can easily be demonstrated.

units.la: 1. Illud recte dicitur possibile, ad quod nullū sequitur impossibile. Atqui ex eo quod motus circularis continuus statuitur, nullū sequitur impossibile. Igitur motus circularis cōtinuus esse potest. Minor probatur: In motu circulari quod mouetur ex alio, nempe ex puncto A,simul mouetur in idem signū siue puncto,eodem progressu mobilis,& eodē ordine partiū seruato:quod tamen in motu recto,re flexo & mixto nō usuuenit.Neq; enim in his fit motus eodē progressu mobilis, & eode ordine partiū.
units.tr: 1. That is rightly called possible to which no impossibility follows. But from the supposition that circular motion is continuous, no impossibility follows. Therefore continuous circular motion can be. The minor is proved thus: in circular motion, what is moved from another point, namely from point A, is moved at the same time back into the same sign or point, with the same progress of the moving body and the same order of parts preserved. This, however, does not happen in straight, reflected, or mixed motion. For in these there is no motion with the same progress of the moving body and the same order of parts.

units.la: 2. Is motus potest esse continuus, qui & perfectus est, & in quo nulla occurrit oppositio, nulla intercedit quies media. Huiusmodi autem motus est circularis, atq; is solus. Igitur solus motus circularis potest esse continuus.
units.tr: 2. That motion can be continuous which is both perfect and in which no opposition occurs, and no rest intervenes. Now such a motion is circular, and it alone. Therefore circular motion alone can be continuous.

units.la: Vtrum idem motus circularis & continuus sit primus?
units.tr: Is the same motion, circular and continuous, also the first?

units.la: Imo, idq; demonstratur.
units.tr: Indeed, and this is demonstrated.

units.la: 1. Omnis motus localis aut est circularis, aut rectus, aut reflexus, aut mixtus. Atqui ex his circularis & rectus priores sunt reflexo itèq; mixto, praeterea ex illis duobus circularis prior est recto. Igitur motus circularis erit motus primus. Minoris posterius membrum, uidelicet quòd circularis motus sit prior recto, ita probatur: Motus rectus est imperfectus & corruptus. Talis autem non est motus circularis. Igitur motus circularis praestat recto. Maior probatur: Imperfectus est motus rectus: quia cum non possit dari motus rectus infinitus (propterea quòd neq; linea infinita esse potest, per quam talis motus diduceretur,) semper potest illi aliqua accedere additio. Corruptus autem est motus rectus: quia ad terminum magnitudinis cum perucnerit, ibi c ssat. In motum autem circularem nihil horum competere, per se manifestum est.
units.tr: 1. Every local motion is either circular, or straight, or reflected, or mixed. Of these, circular and straight are prior to reflected and likewise to mixed; and of those two, circular is prior to straight. Therefore circular motion will be the first motion. The latter part of the minor, namely that circular motion is prior to straight, is proved thus: straight motion is imperfect and corrupt; circular motion is not. Therefore circular motion is superior to straight. The major is proved thus. Straight motion is imperfect: since an infinite straight motion cannot be given (because an infinite line cannot exist along which such motion would be carried), some addition can always be made to it. Straight motion is also corrupt: when it has reached the end of the magnitude, there it ceases. That none of these things applies to circular motion is evident of itself.

units.la: 2. Motus qui potest esse perpetuus, prior est eo qui non potest esse perpetuus. Motus autem circularis laris potest esse perpetuus, reliqui vero motus non possunt. Igitur motus circularis quocunq; alio motu prior est.
units.tr: 2. Motion that can be perpetual is prior to motion that cannot be perpetual. But circular motion can be perpetual, while the other motions cannot be. Therefore circular motion is prior to every other motion.

units.la: Possunt & aliæ rationes congeri ad demonstrandum, quòd motus circularis sit cōtinuus & primus: sed has arbitramur sufficere.
units.tr: Other arguments might also be gathered to demonstrate that circular motion is continuous and first, but we judge these to be sufficient.

units.la: Consentiúntne cæteri philosophi, motum primum esse mo- tum localem?
units.tr: Do the other philosophers agree that the first motion is local motion?

units.la: Maximè. Primò Empedocles, ponens principia litem & amicitiam, ait hanc congregare, illam segregare. Cæterùm congregatio & segregatio sunt motus locales.
units.tr: Very much so. First, Empedocles, who posits strife and friendship as principles, says that the one gathers things together and the other separates them. But gathering together and separating are local motions.

units.la: Secundò, Democritus, qui principia constituit infinita ἄτομα[?], atq; ex his per segregationem & congregationem fieri omnia.
units.tr: Second, Democritus, who established infinite atoms [ἄτομα] as principles, and from these, by separation and congregation, all things come to be.

units.la: Tertiò, Anaxagoras, ponens intellectum seu mentemtem primam causam moventem, cuius opus sit res quascunq; ex confuso chao segregare.
units.tr: Third, Anaxagoras, who posited intellect or mind as the first moving cause, whose work is to separate all things out of the confused chaos.

units.la: Quartò, Veteres illi, qui unam aliquam causam naturalem rerum constituerunt, nempe aquam vel aerem vel ignem, & ex his res per condensationem & rarefactionem generari atque corrumpi. Ab his namq; condensatione inquam & rarefactione, motus localis abesse non potest.
units.tr: Fourth, those ancients who set up one natural cause of things, namely water or air or fire, and by condensation and rarefaction things are generated and corrupted from these. For local motion cannot be absent from condensation and rarefaction, I say.

units.la: Quintò, Plato asserit animam primam cau-sam esse motus, & primum movens seipsum. Talis autem motus extra locum non potest intelligi.
units.tr: Fifth, Plato asserts that the soul is the first cause of motion, and the first mover, moving itself. Yet such motion cannot be understood apart from place.

units.la: 6. Sexto, Omnes vulgari more loquentes id quasi solum moueri censent, quod loco mouetur.
units.tr: 6. Sixth, all who speak in the common manner think that only that is moved which is moved in place.

units.la: Hæc proinde satis multa ad declarandum, quod omnium consensu motus primus sit motus localis.
units.tr: These many points are enough to show that, by the agreement of all, the first motion is local motion.

units.la: Vtrum primum mouens immobile sit diuisibile, habeatq; magni- tudinem, annon?
units.tr: Whether the first mover, being immobile, is divisible and has magnitude, or not?

units.la: Primum mouens neq; certam habet magnitudinem, neq; diuisibile est. Probatur: Primus motus est, ut constat, continuus, perpetuus & æternus. Ex hoc vero iam sequitur, uim siue potentiam quoque infinitam ei inesse, quando potentia finita non possit moueri infinito tempore. Porrò concessa potentia infinita, non est quòd magnitudo aliqua in primo mouente constituatur. Si enim uelis magnitudinem aliquam constituere, quæro abs te, finitáne illa erit, an infinita? Si dicas infinitam, atqui talis actus non poterit dari: sin dicas finitá, quomodo, inquam, in magnitudine finita consistet potentia infinita? Relinquitur ergo, primum mouens nullam in se habere magnitudinem, ac proinde in nullas quoq; partes posse diuidi.
units.tr: The first mover has neither a determinate magnitude nor is it divisible. This is proved as follows. The first motion is, as is agreed, continuous, perpetual and eternal. From this it follows that it also has infinite power or force, since a finite power could not move something for an infinite time. Granted that its power is infinite, there is no reason to posit any magnitude in the first mover. For if you want to assign it some magnitude, I ask you: will that magnitude be finite or infinite? If you say infinite, such a thing cannot exist. If you say finite, then I ask, how can infinite power consist in a finite magnitude? It follows, therefore, that the first mover has no magnitude in itself, and consequently cannot be divided into any parts.

units.la: Estne unum tantum primum mo- uens ad primum motum, an plura?
units.tr: Is there only one first mover of the first motion, or more?

units.la: Est una tantum prima uis mouës, siue unus pri-mus mus motor. Probatio:Motus primus est continuus, motus continuus est unus. Igitur motus primus est unus. Quod si vero motus primus est unus, sanè oportet sit unius mobilis, & præterea ab uno motore. Enimuero si essent diuersa mobilia, præterea diuersi motores, nequaquam motus unus diceretur, ac proinde nec cōtinuus: sed unus motus necessariò ab alio distinguereturr, prout distincta essent mobilia & mouetia seu motores. Atqui bi[?] plures motus essent motus consequenter se habētes: quomodo & in proiectis licet cernere motus consequeter se habentes, non autem continuos. Siquidē cum proiecta mouentur, ea habent diuersa mouetia, nempe primùm quidem vim ipsam proijcientem, hinc aerem vel simile corpus per quod feruntur, quod sanè à proijciente aliquid accipit, ut moueat, vel etiam moueatur: denique aliquid etiam accedit à natura ipsius rei proiectæ: præterea non est unus motus secundū formam, cum initiò sit vehementior, prope finem vero remissior. Quæ omnia efficiunt, quo minus in proiectis unus atq; continuus motus agnoscatur.
units.tr: There is only one first moving force, or one first mover. Proof: the first motion is continuous, and a continuous motion is one. Therefore the first motion is one. But if the first motion is one, it must certainly belong to one moveable and also come from one mover. For if there were different moveables, and also different movers, the motion would not be called one, and so not continuous either; rather, one motion would necessarily be distinguished from another according as the moveables and the movers or motors were distinct. Yet there would then be several motions following one another in succession, not continuous ones. We can see this even in projectiles: when projectiles are moved, they have different movers. First there is the force that throws them; then the air or similar body through which they are carried, which receives something from the thrower so that it may move or be moved; and finally something also comes from the nature of the projected thing itself. Moreover, the motion is not one in form, since at the beginning it is more vehement and near the end more feeble. All these things prevent us from recognising one and continuous motion in projectiles.

units.la: Cum primus motus fit circularis, ubi nam intelligetur prima uis mouendi existere, in centrone circuli, an in peripheria?
units.tr: Since the first motion is circular, where shall we understand the first moving force to exist: at the centre of the circle, or at the periphery?

units.la: Sunt quidem centrum & circumferentia principia magnitudinis circularis: sed cum in primo mouente non respiciatur magnitudo corporea, nequaquam promptum est eas partes crasso more in illo constituere. Si quid tamen ex ratione ipsius motus posset colligi, videtur uis mouens potius collocata in peripheria, quàm in centro. Ratio hæc est: Quanto motus propinquior est primo moueti, tantò est uelocior, magisq; à mouente circumagitur. Sed motus firmamenti, ut circumagitur à primo mouente immobili, est uelocissimus. Quare uis mouendi uidetur potius in primi mouentis extimo & peripheria, quàm in medio siue centro sedem habere.
units.tr: Indeed the centre and the circumference are the principles of a circular magnitude; but since in the first mover no corporeal magnitude is considered, it is by no means easy to locate these parts in it in a crude manner. Yet if anything can be gathered from the very reasoning about the motion, the moving force seems to be placed rather at the periphery than at the centre. The reason is this: the nearer a motion is to the first mover, the swifter it is, and the more it is driven around by the mover. But the motion of the firmament, as it is turned around by the first immovable mover, is the swiftest. Therefore the power of moving seems to have its seat rather in the outermost part and periphery of the first mover than in the middle or centre.

units.la: Finis octo librorum Aristotelis φυσικῆς ἀκροά-σεως, ἢ περὶ φυσικῶν ἀρχῶν.
units.tr: End of the eight books of Aristotle's Physics [φυσικῆς ἀκροάσεως], or On the Principles of Nature [περὶ φυσικῶν ἀρχῶν].

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS.
units.tr: Book Two.

units.la: Quænam post disputationes de mo- tu ueniunt tractanda?
units.tr: What topics come next to be treated after the disputations on motion?

units.la: CVm naturalis scientiæ subiectum sit corpus, quatenus mobile est: consentaneum est, post disputationes de motu etiā de corpore differere. Et quia decet ante de uniuerso corpore differi, quàm de partibus: deinde prius de simplicibus corporibus, quàm de mixtis: adhæc inter simplicia prius de cœlesti corpore, quàm de alijs quatuor, igne, inquâ, aqua, aere, terra: ideo de his primarijs corporibus ordine dicemus, quo etiam ordine animaduertimus Aristotelem post 8 libros de Auscultatione physica seu de motu inscriptos, mox ad disputandum de corpore descendere: vbi primum de vniuerso, lib.1. de Coelo: hinc de simplici corpore coelesti, eiusdem operis lib.2. postremò de aliis quoque quatuor corporibus simplicibus, libris 3 & 4.
units.tr: Since the subject of natural science is body, insofar as it is mobile, it is fitting that after the disputations on motion we should also discourse about body. And because it is proper to treat the whole body before its parts, and simple bodies before mixed ones, and among the simple bodies the heavenly body before the other four, namely fire, air, water and earth, therefore we shall speak of these primary bodies in that order. We observe that Aristotle, in the same order, after the eight books of the Physics, or the books on motion, descended at once to dispute about body: first about the whole universe, in the first book of On the Heavens; then about the simple heavenly body, in the second book of the same work; and finally about the other four simple bodies, in the third and fourth books.

units.la: DE CORPORE vniuerso.
units.tr: DE CORPORE vniuerso.

units.la: Quid est corpus?
units.tr: What is a body?

units.la: EST continuum omni ex parte diuisibile. Continuum vero est, quod diuidi potest in alia plura diuisibilia. Definitionem autem illam corporis aptam esse, hunc in modum probatur: Id omni ex parte potest diuidi, quod secundum tres dimensiones mensuratur. Atqui corpus mensuratur secundum tres dimensiones, longitudinem, inquam, latitudinem & profunditate. Igitur corpus potest omni ex parte diuidi. Caeterum linea non potest diuidi, nisi secundum longitudinem: superficies vero secundum longitudinem & latitudinem.
units.tr: It is that which is continuous and divisible in every respect. Now a continuum is that which can be divided into several other divisible parts. That this definition of body is apt may be proved in this way: that which can be divided in every respect is that which is measured in three dimensions. But a body is measured in three dimensions, namely length, breadth and depth. Therefore a body can be divided in every respect. Moreover, a line can be divided only in its length, but a surface in its length and breadth.

units.la: Est'ne corpus magnitudo per- fectissima?
units.tr: Is body the most perfect magnitude?

units.la: Est: quod probatur duabus rationibus.
units.tr: It is; and this is proved by two arguments.

units.la: Prima: Nulla magnitudo pluribus dimensionibus mensuratur quàm corpus. Igitur corpus est magnitudo perfectißima. Antecedens manifestum est: siquidem linea diuiditur tantùm secundum unam dimensionem, nempe longitudinem: superficies secundum duas, longitudinem uidelicet & latitudinem: at corpus mensuratur tribus dimensionibus, longitudine, latitudine & profunditate.
units.tr: The first: No magnitude is measured by more dimensions than a body. Therefore a body is the most perfect magnitude. The antecedent is plain: a line is divided only in one dimension, namely length; a surface in two, namely length and breadth; but a body is measured by three dimensions, length, breadth and depth.

units.la: 2. Secunda: Numerus ternarius est perfectissimus: quare corpus quoq;, quoniam tribus dimensionibus mensuratur, erit magnitudo perfectissima. Antecedens probatur tum authoritate Pythagoricorum, tum quòd idem numerus diuino cultui est cõsecratus. Nam tribus olim rebus sacra peragebantur, thure, igne, & precatione.
units.tr: 2. The second: The number three is the most perfect number; therefore a body also, since it is measured by three dimensions, will be the most perfect magnitude. The antecedent is proved both by the authority of the Pythagoreans and because the same number has been consecrated to divine worship. For formerly sacred rites were performed with three things: incense, fire, and prayer.

units.la: Est ne uniuersum ipsum per- fectissimum?
units.tr: Is the universe itself most perfect?

units.la: Maximè, idq; duabus de causis.
units.tr: Most certainly, and for two reasons.

units.la: 1. Prima: Quia corporeum est. Enimuero corpus est magnitudo perfectissima.
units.tr: 1. The first: because it is corporeal. Indeed, a body is the most perfect magnitude.

units.la: 2. Secunda: Quia est uniuersum. Nasiue fiat comparatio uniuersi ad partes, siue spectetur ipsum nomen uniuersi, inuenietur sanè multò perfectissimum. Vniuersum lògè praestat suis partibus: atq; ipsum nomen maiestatem quandā & plenitudinē significat.
units.tr: 2. The second: because it is the universe. Whether the universe is compared with its parts, or the very name of the universe is considered, it will certainly be found to be far the most perfect. The universe surpasses its parts by far, and the name itself signifies a certain majesty and fullness.

units.la: Quibus constat partibus uniuersum?
units.tr: Of what parts does the universe consist?

units.la: Quinq; simplicibus corporibus: cœlo inquam, & quatuor simplicibus elementis.
units.tr: Of five simple bodies: I mean the heaven and the four simple elements.

units.la: DE QUINTO CORPORE simplici, videlicet cœlo.
units.tr: ON THE FIFTH SIMPLE BODY, namely heaven.

units.la: AN SIT?
units.tr: WHETHER THERE IS ONE?

units.la: Est'ne præter quatuor elementa simplicia quoddam corpus simplex quintum?
units.tr: Is there, besides the four simple elements, some fifth simple body?

units.la: MAXIME. Prius tamen quàm istud declaremus, quædam sunt annotanda.
units.tr: Most certainly. Before we explain this, some things must be noted.

units.la: 1. Omnia corpora naturalia sunt per se mobilia secundum locum. Probatur: Corpora naturalia sunt, quæ habent naturam. Atqui natura est principium motus in eis in quibus est. Igitur corpora naturalia habent principium motus in seipsis.
units.tr: 1. All natural bodies are of themselves mobile with respect to place. Proof: natural bodies are those which have a nature. But nature is a principle of motion in those things in which it is. Therefore natural bodies have a principle of motion in themselves.

units.la: 2. Distinguere oportet motum localem.
units.tr: 2. One must distinguish local motion.

units.la: 3. Distinguere oportet ipsa corpora mobilia. Corpora mo-bilia alia Simplicia. Composita. Pro ratione autem horum corporum est etiam mo-tus aut Simplex. Mixtus seu compositum. Omnis motus localis aut est Restus, quo nidi-licet sursum itur è medio, aut de-orsum ad medium. Circularis, qui fit circum medium. Mixtus. Sunt autem hi superiores duo motus simplices, qua-re simplex latio triplex quoq; est: 1. è medio. 2. ad medium. 3. circum medium. Quæ diuisio perfectissi-ma est.
units.tr: 3. One must distinguish the mobile bodies themselves. Some mobile bodies are simple, others composite. Corresponding to these bodies there is also motion, either simple or mixed (composite). Every local motion is either straight, namely upward from the middle, or downward to the middle; or circular, which takes place around the middle; or mixed. The two former motions are simple, so simple local motion is threefold: (1) from the middle, (2) to the middle, (3) around the middle. This division is the most perfect.

units.la: His ita expositis, procliue est ad quaestione respondere. Praeter quatuor corpora simplicia, uocata elementa, quae natura feruntur motu recto, est quoddam quintum corpus simplex, idque circulari motu circumactum. Quod probatur tribus rationibus.
units.tr: With these things thus set out, it is easy to answer the question. Besides the four simple bodies called elements, which by nature are carried with straight motion, there is a fifth simple body, which is carried round in circular motion. This is proved by three arguments.

units.la: 1. Motus simplex conuenit corpori simplici. Atqui motus circularis est motus simplex, qui nō spectatur in aliquo è quatuor elementis corporibus simplicibus. Igitur necessum est, aliud quoddā quintum corpus existat, cui simplex iste motus circularis conueniat. Maior est manifesta ex antecedentibus, similiter prior pars minoris: posterior uero pars eiusdem hinc perspicua euadit, quòd quatuor illa corpora simplicia, uocata elementa, feruntur omnia simplici motu recto. Nam ignis & aer, secundum naturam, motu recto feruntur sursum, aqua & terra motu recto feruntur deorsum. Si quando hæc aliter ferri contingat, id sanè non secundum naturam, sed praeter naturam.
units.tr: 1. Simple motion belongs to a simple body. But circular motion is a simple motion, which is not observed in any of the four simple bodies, the elements. Therefore it is necessary that some other fifth body exist, to which this simple circular motion belongs. The major is clear from what has gone before, and the first part of the minor likewise; the latter part of the minor is evident from this, that those four simple bodies called elements are all carried with simple straight motion. For fire and air, according to nature, are carried upward with straight motion, while water and earth are carried downward with straight motion. If these are ever carried otherwise, this is certainly not according to nature but contrary to nature.

units.la: 2. Par est, motum natura priore inueniri in corpore simplici, quod itidem sit natura prius. Sed motus circularis est natura prior, quàm motus rectus. Igitur constitui debet quoddam corpus simplex, cui circularis motus conueniat, idque etiam prius & excellentius ijs corporibus quibus conuenit motus rectus. Maior nota est ex obseruatione proportionū. Minor probatur:Sicut inter figuras circulus est per fectior recta linea (nam ille ubiq; est sui similis, nihilq; addi ei potest)ita inter motus,circularis persectior est recto. Atqui perfectiora sunt natura priora. Igitur & circularis motus prior.
units.tr: 2. It is fitting that a motion which is prior in nature is found in a simple body which is likewise prior in nature. But circular motion is prior in nature to straight motion. Therefore a simple body must be posited to which circular motion belongs, and which is also prior to and more excellent than those bodies to which straight motion belongs. The major is known from the observation of proportions. The minor is proved: just as among figures the circle is more perfect than the straight line (for it is everywhere like itself, and nothing can be added to it), so among motions the circular is more perfect than the straight. But more perfect things are prior in nature. Therefore circular motion is also prior.

units.la: 3. Omnis motus simplex conuenit corpori aut secundum naturam,aut præter naturam:& qui uni præter naturam conuenit,ueluti si ignis feratur deorsum,is alteri conuenit secundum naturā,quemadmodo terra secundum naturam fertur deorsum. Atqui motus circularis non conuenit ulli ex quatuor simplicibus corporibus secundum naturam:sed si in aliquo horum spectetur, id certe præter naturam contingit. Ergo necessum[?] est, præter illa quatuor elementa corpora simplicia constituere aliud corpus quintū simplex, cui simplex motus circularis secundum naturam conuenit. Relinquitur ergo,præter quatuor elementa corpora simplicia superesse quoddam quintum corpus simplex.
units.tr: 3. Every simple motion belongs to a body either according to nature or contrary to nature; and what belongs to one body contrary to nature, as when fire is carried downward, belongs to another according to nature, just as earth is carried downward according to nature. But circular motion belongs to none of the four simple bodies according to nature; if it is observed in any of these, it certainly happens contrary to nature. Therefore it is necessary to posit, besides those four elements, another fifth simple body, to which simple circular motion belongs according to nature. It remains, therefore, that besides the four simple elements there is some fifth simple body.

units.la: Quomodo differt quintum cor- pus simplex à quatuor elementis?
units.tr: How does the fifth simple body differ from the four elements?

units.la: I. Primo. Ratione motus localis.Elementa enim mouentur motu recto: atq; alia quidem à medio sursum, ut ignis et aer: alia ad medium deorsum, ut terra & aqua. Quintū autem illud corpus simplex mouetur motu circulari. Sunt autem elementa alia grauia, alia leuia,atq; inde cōtingit illis talis motus rectus.Quintum autem corpus simplex neq; graue neque leue est,quamobrem nec potest motu recto ferri.
units.tr: I. First, by reason of local motion. For the elements are moved with straight motion: some indeed from the middle upward, as fire and air, others to the middle downward, as earth and water. But that fifth simple body is moved with circular motion. Moreover, some elements are heavy and others light, and from this such straight motion arises for them. But the fifth simple body is neither heavy nor light, wherefore it cannot be carried with straight motion.

units.la: Secundò:Ratione aliorum motuum. Nam quintum corpus simplex non est obnoxium generationi aut corruptioni, augmetationi uel diminutioni,deniq; nulli alterationi.Reliqua uero corpora simplicia sunt mutationi obnoxia.
units.tr: Secondly, by reason of the other motions. For the fifth simple body is not subject to generation or corruption, increase or diminution, and finally to no alteration. The other simple bodies, however, are subject to change.

units.la: Quòd neq; generetur neq; corrumpatur quintum corpus,sic patefit:Generatio & corruptio habent rationē contrariorum.Omne quod generatur, fit ex contrario & subiecto quodam. Omne item quod corrumpitur, in contrariū corrumpitur,existente etiā aliquo subiecto. Sed quinto corpori non inest aliquid contrariū : Ergo nec generationi nec corruptioni est obnoxiū.Minor probatur:Contrariorum sunt contrarij motus . Sed motui circulari, qui naturalis & proprius est quinto corpori,nullus motus est contrarius (qua de re fusius paulo post.) Igitur neq; ipsi quinto corpori est aliquid contrarium,itaq; ingenitū & incorruptibile censebitur.
units.tr: That the fifth body is neither generated nor corrupted is shown thus. Generation and corruption have the character of contraries. Everything that is generated comes from a contrary and some subject. Likewise everything that is corrupted is corrupted into a contrary, there also being some subject. But no contrary is present in the fifth body. Therefore it is subject neither to generation nor to corruption. The minor is proved: contraries have contrary motions. But to circular motion, which is natural and proper to the fifth body, no motion is contrary (on which more fully a little later). Therefore there is nothing contrary to the fifth body itself either, and so it will be judged ungenerated and incorruptible.

units.la: Quòd uero non fit obnoxium augmentationi uel diminutioni [?], hinc accipe : Augmentatio fit accessione alicuius materiæ connaturalis, quæ cum prius fuisset dissimilis, fit per resolutionē similis. Diminutio aut fit decessione alicuius materiæ cōnaturalis. Atqui quinto corpori neq; inuenitur cōnaturalis ulla materia,neq; in eo locum habet talis refolutio, utpote quam fieri ex contrario oportet. Igitur nullo modo est augmentationi uel diminutioni obnoxium. Nec potest augmenti fpeciari ratio,ubi generationi & corruptioni locus non est.
units.tr: That it is not subject to increase or diminution, take this: increase happens by the addition of some connatural matter, which, having previously been unlike, becomes like through resolution. Diminution happens by the loss of some connatural matter. But no connatural matter is found in the fifth body, nor does such resolution take place in it, since it would have to come about from a contrary. Therefore it is in no way subject to increase or diminution. Nor can the nature of increase be considered where there is no place for generation and corruption.

units.la: 3. Quod autem quintum corpus non subiacet alte rationi,ita probatur: Quod nō potest generari aut corrumpi,nec augeri nec minui, fieri non potest ut id alteretur.Nam alteratio omnis ad generationem aut corruptionem, uel ad augmentationem aut diminutionem tendit: quod animaduertere licet in elementis,animalibus,plantis, & reliquis sensibilibus, in quibus diuersæ hæ species motus cernuntur.
units.tr: 3. That the fifth body is not subject to alteration is proved thus: what cannot be generated or corrupted, nor increased or diminished, cannot be altered. For all alteration tends towards generation or corruption, or towards increase or diminution; which can be seen in the elements, animals, plants and the other sensible things, in which these different kinds of motion are discerned.

units.la: Manifestum igitur est, quintum corpus non esse his motibus subiectum ,sed plane ingenitum atque incorruptibile existere. Confirmatur uero idem fignis tribus.
units.tr: It is therefore manifest that the fifth body is not subject to these motions, but clearly exists as ungenerated and incorruptible. The same is confirmed by three signs.

units.la: 1. Omnes homines cœlum statuerunt propriam sedem summi Dei ingeniti & immortalis:quo haud dubie declararunt,fe quoq; iudicare,quintum cor-pus simplex,cœlum inquam, esse ingenitum & incorruptibile, & sic digna & conuenicns [?] Deo sedes attribuatur.
units.tr: 1. All men have regarded heaven as the proper seat of the unbegotten and immortal supreme God; by which they undoubtedly declared that they also judge the fifth simple body, heaven I say, to be unbegotten and incorruptible, and that a fitting and worthy seat is thus assigned to God.

units.la: 2. Nunquam post hominum memoriam obseruatum est ab ullis astrologis, uel alijs eruditis, aliquid in cœlo esse transmutatum, fiue fecundum totum, fiue fecundum aliquam eius partem. Igitur non est generatione uel corruptioni, uel ulli omnino motui obnoxium.
units.tr: 2. Never since the memory of man has it been observed by any astrologers, or other learned men, that anything in heaven has been changed, whether in the whole or in any part of it. Therefore it is not subject to generation or corruption, or to any motion at all.

units.la: §. A' plurimis uocatum est cœlum ἀιθὴρ, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀεὶ θέεῖν, quòd semper currat et circumeat. Si autem semper currit moueturq;, recte sane intelligitur ingenitum, incorruptibile, nulliq; mutationi expositum.
units.tr: §. By many heaven is called aether [αἰθήρ], from "always running" [ἀπὸ τῆς ἀεὶ θεῖν], because it always runs and goes round. If indeed it always runs and is moved, it is rightly understood to be unbegotten, incorruptible, and exposed to no change.

units.la: Ex his igitur perspicuum euadit, quintum corpus simplex, cœlum uidelicet, multum distare à reliquis corporibus quatuor simplicibus, uocatis elementis.
units.tr: From these things it is therefore clear that the fifth simple body, namely heaven, differs greatly from the other four simple bodies, called elements.

units.la: Vtrum uerum sit, motui circulari nullum motum esse con- trarium?
units.tr: Whether it is true that no motion is contrary to circular motion?

units.la: Nullus motus est circulari motui cōtrarius. Probatur: Si motui circulari ullus esset contrarius, aut is esset motus rectus, aut aliquis motus separatus in partibus ipsius motus circularis, aut omnino aliquis alius integer motus circularis. Atqui horum nullum dici potest. Igitur motui circulari nullus motus est contrarius.
units.tr: No motion is contrary to circular motion. This is proved thus: if some motion were contrary to circular motion, it would be either a straight motion, or some separate motion in the parts of the circular motion itself, or altogether some other whole circular motion. But none of these can be said. Therefore no motion is contrary to circular motion.

units.la: 1. Quòd autem motus rectus nō fit ei contrarius, manifestum fit. Motui recto, ut ei qui sursum tendit, opponitur alius motus rectus tendēs deorsum: sunt enim sursum ac deorsum contrariæ motuum differentiæ. Non potest autem uni motui nisi unus motus poni contrarius. Igitur motus rectus nullo modo contrarius existit motui circulari.
units.tr: 1. That straight motion is not contrary to it is clear. To straight motion, as to that which tends upward, there is opposed another straight motion tending downward, for up and down are contrary directions of motion. But to one motion only one contrary can be assigned. Therefore straight motion is in no way contrary to circular motion.

units.la: 2. Quod
units.tr: 2. That

units.la: 2. Quòd uero motui circulari nò aduersetur motus aliquis separatus in partibus, hoc pacto cuincitur: Cum in circulo partes sint infinitæ,possent etiã infiniti motus diuersi ijs aptari. Sed uni motui non debet opponi nisi unus. Igitur circulari motui non potest motus aliquis contrarius in eius partibus constitui. Quamuis neq; sufficeret sanè contrarietas in parte aliqua ad constituendum motum contrarium toti motui circulari.
units.tr: 2. That some separate motion in its parts is not opposed to circular motion is proved in this way: since in a circle the parts are infinite, infinitely many different motions could be fitted to them. But only one motion ought to be opposed to one motion. Therefore no contrary motion can be set up in its parts against circular motion. Although contrariety in some part would certainly not suffice to constitute a motion contrary to the whole circular motion.

units.la: 3. Quòd non aliquis alius motus circularis sit ei cõtrarius, hoc pacto demõstratur. Aut enim is alius motus circularis in eodem ipso circulo constituetur, aut in alio. Neutrũ uero dici potest. Igitur neq; talis contrarius constituetur. Quòd non in alio, mã nifestũ est. Nam si infiniti essent tales circuli, oportet motum hunc circularem infinitis illorum motibus esse contrarium: quod quidem est absurdum. Quòd autem non in eodem, hinc patet. Nam quamcunq; in partem motus ille ducatur, fiet tamen per easdem partes eademq; puncta, & redibit ad eade. Vt exempli causa, circulus esto A, B, C. in quo motus alter circularis incipiat ab A, & tendat uersus B, deinde per C redeat ad A. Rursus uero alter motus circularis incipiat ab A, & tendat uersus C, deinde redeat per B ad A. Hi certè duo motus nõ sunt contrarij. Nam uterq; ab eodem puncto incipit, & in eodem terminatur, uidelicet A. Vt autem motus locales intelligantur contrarii, oportet eos à contrario ferri in contrariū, necnon tum incipere à contrario, tum terminari ad contrarium.
units.tr: 3. That some other circular motion is not contrary to it is demonstrated thus. For that other circular motion would be set up either in the same circle or in another. Neither can be said. Therefore neither would such a contrary be set up. That it is not in another is clear. For if there were infinitely many such circles, this circular motion would have to be contrary to infinitely many of their motions, which is absurd. That it is not in the same follows from this: whatever direction that motion is led in, it will nevertheless pass through the same parts and the same points, and return to the same places. For example, let there be a circle A, B, C, in which another circular motion begins at A and tends towards B, then returns through C to A. Again, another circular motion begins at A and tends towards C, then returns through B to A. Certainly these two motions are not contrary. For each begins from the same point and ends at the same point, namely A. But in order that local motions be understood as contrary, they must be carried from a contrary towards a contrary, and likewise begin from a contrary and end at a contrary.

units.la: Sed idem insuper manifestum fit, accommodando motum circularem corporibus naturalibus. In eodem circulo simul existere contrarii motus non possunt. Nam si simul adessent, aut agitarentur illi motus æquè validè, aut non. Si æquè validè, tum alter alterū impediret, iustusq; motus inverteretur: si non æquè validè, sed alter altero potentius, tum quidem ab altero semper moucbitur mobile, ab altero vero nunquam, atq; ita posterior is superuacaneus crit & frustra positus. Atqui absurdum est, dicere, motum aliquè poni, cuius nullus sit usus: Deus namq; & natura nihil faciunt frustra. Ergo non potest constitui in eodem circulo motus circularis, motui circulari contrarius.
units.tr: But the same is further made clear by applying circular motion to natural bodies. Contrary motions cannot exist together in the same circle. For if they were present together, either those motions would be driven with equal force or not. If with equal force, then one would hinder the other, and the uniform motion would be reversed. If not with equal force, but one more powerful than the other, then the moved body would indeed always be moved by one and never by the other, and so the latter would be superfluous and placed in vain. But it is absurd to say that some motion is posited whose use is nil, for God and nature do nothing in vain. Therefore a motion circular and contrary to circular motion cannot be set up in the same circle.

units.la: Sùntne plura corpora quàm quinque simplicia ad perfectionem uni- versi necessaria?
units.tr: Are there more simple bodies than five necessary for the perfection of the universe?

units.la: Nō sunt. Probatur: Cuiuslibet simplicis corporis necesse est motus quoq; simplex existat. Sed nō sunt alij motus simplices, præter duos illos, circulare, inquā, qui convenit quinto corpori cœlo, & rectum, qui bifariā divisus spectatur in quatuor elementis. Igitur non est aliud corpus simplex, quod sit pars universi, præter illa quinq; enumerata.
units.tr: They are not. This is proved: for every simple body there must also exist a simple motion. But there are no simple motions other than those two: circular, namely, which belongs to the fifth body, the heaven, and straight, which is seen divided into two in the four elements. Therefore there is no other simple body that is a part of the universe, besides those five enumerated.

units.la: Hactenus de partibus quibus uniuersum constat, & e quibus perfectio eius cognoscitur. Restat ut, quoniam quod perfectum est, nonnulli id dixerunt infinitu, num uniuersum fit infinitum, disquiramus.
units.tr: So far concerning the parts of which the universe consists, and from which its perfection is known. It remains that, since some have said that what is perfect is infinite, we inquire whether the universe is infinite.

units.la: AN VNIVERSVM SIT infinitum. Quot modis dicitur Infinitum?
units.tr: WHETHER THE UNIVERSE IS INFINITE. In how many ways is "infinite" said?

units.la: Tribus. Aliud namq; infinitum est magnitudine, aliud numero, aliud duratione. Itaq; secundum hos tres modos par est de Vniuerso quaestiones institui.
units.tr: In three. For one thing is infinite in magnitude, another in number, another in duration. Therefore, according to these three modes, questions about the universe must be raised.

units.la: Vtrum uniuersum fit infinitum magnitudine?
units.tr: Whether the universe is infinite in magnitude?

units.la: Non. Probatur: Si corpus aliquod effet infinitum, id aut simplex effet, aut copofitum. Atqui nullum horum dari infinitum potest. Igitur nullum est infinitum: quamobrem nec uniuersum fiue mundus erit infinitus.
units.tr: No. This is proved: if some body were infinite, it would be either simple or composite. But none of these can be infinite. Therefore nothing is infinite; wherefore neither will the universe or world be infinite.

units.la: Quod uero nullum compositum corpus infinitum esse queat, hinc manifestum fit: Vt compositum aliquod corpus infinitum existeret, oporteret simplicia, ex quibus illud constaret, esse infinita. Sed nullum simplex existit infinitum: igitur neque ullum compositum.
units.tr: That no composite body can be infinite is clear from this: for some composite body to be infinite, the simple bodies from which it is made would have to be infinite. But no simple body exists infinite; therefore neither does any composite.

units.la: Quod autem nullum simplex corpus existat nisi finitum, restat demonstremus.
units.tr: That no simple body exists except as finite remains to be demonstrated.

units.la: 1. Nullum corpus circulariter motum potest esse infinitum. Probatio: Corpus quod infinitum est, non potest circulariter moueri. Atqui quintum corpus simplex mouetur circulariter. Igitur nō potest cōstitui infinitum. Maior probatur: Si corpus quod circulariter mouetur, esset infinitum, tum necessarió etiam lineæ à centro ductæ essent infinitæ, & inter earundem extremitates, infinita quoq; foret distantia. Sed infinita magnitudo & infinita distantia non potest pertransiri. Igitur corpus tale infinitum non posset circulariter moueri. Relinquitur ergo, primum corpus simplex, quoniam circulariter mouetur, necessariò finitum existere. Confirmatur: Vbi linea finita est et terminata, ibi superficies quoque atq; corpus necessariò finitum intelligitur. Sed quinti corporis linea per medium trásiens (seu diameter & axis) est finita. Igitur totum quoque illud corpus finitum erit.
units.tr: 1. No circularly moved body can be infinite. Proof: a body that is infinite, cannot be moved circularly. But the fifth simple body is moved circularly. Therefore it cannot be constituted infinite. The major is proved: if a body that is moved circularly were infinite, then necessarily the lines drawn from the centre would also be infinite, and between their extremities the distance would also be infinite. But an infinite magnitude and an infinite distance cannot be traversed. Therefore such an infinite body could not be moved circularly. It remains, then, that the first simple body, since it is moved circularly, must necessarily exist as finite. Confirmed: where a line is finite and terminated, there a surface and a body too must necessarily be understood as finite. But the line of the fifth body passing through the middle (that is, the diameter and axis) is finite. Therefore that whole body too will be finite.

units.la: 2. Nullum corpus quod mouetur motu recto, est infinitum. Probatio: Corpora simplicia, quæ feruntur motu recto, mouentur ad loca contraria: alia namq; à medio sursum, alia uero ad medium deorsum. Atqui loca ista contraria sunt terminata ac finita. Igitur & corpora ipsa, quæ per loca illa feruntur, finita existere, necesse est. Maior est nota. Minor probatur: Locus quo ad medium tenditur deorsum, ad centrum uidelicet terræ, est finitus: siquidem ultra medium illud non licet descēdendo progredi. Atqui ubi unum contrariorum est finitum, necessario etiam finitum est & alterum. Igitur loca illa cōtraria, per quæ prima illa corpora simplicia, quibus motus recti conuenit, moventur, sunt finita. Hæc autè loca si sint finita, sanè & corpora quæ per ea feruntur, finita erunt. Quomodo enim intelligentur corpora esse infinita, quæ moventur locis finitis? Ex his porrò manifestum fit, nullum corpus simplex, siue motu circulari, siue motu recto agatur, esse infinitum magnitudine. Si autem nullum horum est infinitum magnitudine, sanè neq; ipsum universum, id est, ipse mundus, magnitudine infinitus existet. Aristoteles ulterius progreditur, ac docet, nullum omnino corpus naturale infinitum existere: quod rationibus tum physicis, nempe & ob motum localem, & ob actionem atq; passionem, tum logicis, id est, sumptis ex communioribus principijs & probabilibus, euincit[?].
units.tr: 2. No body that is moved with straight motion is infinite. Proof: simple bodies that are carried by straight motion are moved to contrary places, for some from the middle upward, others downward to the middle. But these contrary places are bounded and finite. Therefore the bodies themselves that are carried through those places must necessarily be finite. The major is known. The minor is proved: the place to which a thing tends downward, namely the centre of the earth, is finite, since beyond that middle one cannot go on descending. But where one of two contraries is finite, the other is necessarily finite too. Therefore those contrary places through which the first simple bodies, to which straight motion belongs, are moved, are finite. But if these places are finite, surely the bodies carried through them will be finite. For how can bodies be understood to be infinite which are moved through finite places? From these things it is further clear that no simple body, whether driven by circular or by straight motion, is infinite in magnitude. And if none of these is infinite in magnitude, surely neither will the universe itself, that is, the world itself, be infinite in magnitude. Aristotle goes further and teaches that no natural body at all exists as infinite, which he proves by physical reasons, namely from local motion and from action and passion, and by logical reasons, that is, drawn from more common principles and probabilities.

units.la: Vtrum uniuersum fit infinitum numero?
units.tr: Whether the universe is infinite in number?

units.la: Nequaquam[?]. Quæstio enim hæc tantundem sibi vult, atque si rogaret quispiam, Utrum sint infiniti mundi? Itaq; respōdetur, unum tantum esse mundum. Probatur: Si essent duo mundi, oporteret in utroq; esse terram, item ignem, &c. sicut in isto terram & ignem, &c. esse scimus. Quo ita posito, terra unius mundi necessario moveretur ad terram alterius mundi, & ignis ad ignem. Atqui istud ita fie-ri,est ri,est absurdum. Igitur peræquè absurdū foret,duos aut plures mundos ponere.
units.tr: By no means. For this question amounts to the same thing as if someone asked, "Are there infinitely many worlds?" The answer, therefore, is that there is only one world. It is proved thus: if there were two worlds, each would have to contain earth, likewise fire, and so on, just as we know that this world contains earth and fire, and so on. Given this, the earth of one world would necessarily move towards the earth of the other world, and the fire towards the fire. But this happening is absurd. Therefore it would be equally absurd to posit two or more worlds.

units.la: Maior probatur: Oporteret quidem corpora simplicia in utroque mundo eiusdem esse naturæ & speciei. Corpus autem simplex unius eiusdemq; speciei et naturæ ad eundē locū, in quo possit quiescere, natura aspirat atque contendit. Omne enim graue tendit ad unum locum deorsum, in quo quiescat: similiter omne leue contendit sursum, quietis locum quærens. Igitur alterius mundi terra ad nostram terram ferri desideraret, ignis ad ignem.
units.tr: The major premise is proved thus: the simple bodies in each world would certainly have to be of the same nature and kind. But a simple body of one and the same kind and nature strives and tends by nature towards one and the same place, in which it can rest. For every heavy body tends downwards to one place, in which it may rest; similarly every light body tends upwards, seeking the place of its rest. Therefore the earth of the other world would desire to be carried towards our earth, and the fire towards fire.

units.la: Minor similiter probatur. Nam terra ab uno mundo ad alterum transire uolens, deberet sui orbis ignem pertrāsire, atq; ita ferretur sursum: quod naturæ eius repugnat, estque impossibile. Similiter ignis per medium unius orbis deuolaret ad ignem alterius: quo quidem pacto necessum foret igne ferri deorsum, quod itidem impossibile est. Igitur nullo modo sunt plures mundi.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved in a similar way. For earth wishing to pass from one world to the other would have to cross the fire of its own sphere, and so would be carried upwards, which is contrary to its nature and impossible. Likewise fire would have to fall downwards through the middle of one sphere to the fire of the other, which in that manner would necessarily be carried downwards, and this too is impossible. Therefore there are in no way several worlds.

units.la: Possibile'ne esset plures mun- dos fieri?
units.tr: Whether it could be possible for several worlds to come into being?

units.la: Non modò non sunt plures mundi, sed imposbile quoq; est plures mundos fieri. Quod quo clarius percipiatur, notandum est, cœli triplicem esse significationem.
units.tr: Not only are there not several worlds, but it is impossible for several worlds to come into being. So that this may be perceived more clearly, it must be noted that the word "heaven" has three meanings.

units.la: Primum significat solam supremam & extimam sphæram, quæ circulariter mouetur, atq; aliàs uocatur primum mobile: quo pacto loquuntur homines de motu cœli, deq; stellis in cœlo fixis.
units.tr: First, it signifies only the highest and outermost sphere, which moves circularly and is otherwise called the first mover; in this sense men speak of the motion of the heavens and of the stars fixed in the heavens.

units.la: Secundò : Nomine cœli comprehenduntur cum extima illa sphæra etiam orbes inferiores reliqui: quo pacto distinguimus cœlum Saturni, Iouis, &c.
units.tr: Second, under the name of heaven are comprehended, together with that outermost sphere, the remaining lower spheres; in this sense we distinguish the heaven of Saturn, of Jupiter, and so on.

units.la: Tertiò : Cœlum significat totam machinam supremæ & extremæ circumferentiæ inclusam, quod quidem definitur constare omni naturali & sensibili corpore, atq; tota sua materia. Accipiendo igitur cœlum hoc tertio modo, respondetur ad quæstionem, non posse plures cœlos siue mundos constituì. Probatur: Extra cœlum tertio modo dictum nō est aliud corpus sensibile. Igitur neq; alius mundus esse potest. Antecedens probatur: Si extra illud cœlum esset aliquod corpus sensibile, oporteret id esse aut simplex, aut compositum: item, esset ibi secundum naturam, aut præter naturam. Atqui nullum tale dari potest. Igitur nullum est extra cœlum corpus sensibile. Quòd ibi nullum fit corpus simplex, patet. Corporum simplicium aliud mouetur circulariter, aliud rectà à medio, aliud rectà ad medium, quod & in medio ipso subsistit. Atqui nullum horum potest esse extra supremam circumferentiam. Igitur nullum simplex corpus ibi existit. Ac corpus quidem circulariter motum non posse ullum extra cœlum esse, ita demonstratur: Si aliquod corpus circulariter motum extra supremam circumserentiam esset, tanquam in loco naturali, oporteret id aut esse translatum ex eo loco, in quo huiusmodi corpus circulariter motu consistit, aut ex illius mundi loco transferri ad corpus circulariter motum in hoc mundo. Utrumq; vero horum est absurdum. Igitur & illud ex quo sequitur. Maior probatur: Nam quod circulariter movetur, cupit semper ad illum locum adiungere, in quo per naturam quiescat: ac talis quidem est locus proprius quinto corpori simplici, quod circulariter movetur. Minor probatur: Corpus quod circulariter fertur, non potest totum mutare locum proprium: quamobrè non est possibile, ut ad alium locum, quam in quo est, transferatur. Atq; hinc quoq; constat, quod nullo modo extra caelum possit esse aliud corpus circulariter motum per naturam. Neq; etiam potest ibi esse praeter naturam: nam si ei ibi esset locus praeter naturam, necessum foret, alicui alteri rei ibi locum esse secundum naturam, quod sane falsum est.
units.tr: Third, heaven signifies the whole machine enclosed by the supreme and outermost circumference, which is defined as consisting of every natural and sensible body together with its whole matter. Taking heaven in this third sense, we answer the question that several heavens or worlds cannot be constituted. It is proved thus: outside the heaven taken in the third sense there is no other sensible body. Therefore no other world can exist either. The antecedent is proved thus: if there were some sensible body outside that heaven, it would have to be either simple or compound; again, it would be there either according to nature or contrary to nature. But no such thing can be given. Therefore there is no sensible body outside the heaven. That there is no simple body there is plain. Of simple bodies, one moves circularly, another moves straight from the centre, another moves straight towards the centre, and it also rests in the centre itself. But none of these can be outside the supreme circumference. Therefore no simple body exists there. That a body moved circularly cannot be outside the heaven at all is demonstrated thus: if some circularly moved body were outside the supreme circumference, as in its natural place, it would have to have been transferred either from that place in which such a body is circularly moved in this world, or from the place of that other world to a circularly moved body in this world. But both of these alternatives are absurd. Therefore the premise from which this follows is also absurd. The major premise is proved thus: what is moved circularly always desires to attach itself to that place in which it may rest by nature; and such indeed is the proper place of the fifth simple body, which is moved circularly. The minor premise is proved thus: a body that is carried circularly cannot change its whole proper place; therefore it is not possible for it to be transferred to any place other than that in which it is. From this too it is clear that there can in no way be any other body moved circularly by nature outside the heaven. Nor can it be there contrary to nature: for if there were a place there contrary to nature, it would necessarily follow that there would be a place there according to nature for some other thing, which is certainly false.

units.la: Deinde vero, nullum corpus quod motu recto fertur, ibi esse potest, ac primo quidem non per naturam: nam quae motu recto feruntur, atque grauia sunt vel leuia, ea alibi suum locum secundum naturam habent. Repugnat autem, aliqua corpora in diversis locis secundum naturam existere: nam grauibus itemq; leuibus omnibus non conuenit nisi unus locus numero. Igitur nullum corpus quod motu resto fertur, ibi per naturam esse potest.
units.tr: Next, however, no body that is carried by straight motion can be there; and first of all not by nature: for those bodies which are carried by straight motion, and which are heavy or light, have their natural place elsewhere. But it is contradictory for some bodies to exist by nature in different places; for to all heavy and light bodies alike belongs only one place in number. Therefore no body that is carried by straight motion can be there by nature.

units.la: Quoditem nullum corpus simplex recta motum ibi existat præter naturā, manifestum est. Quo enim loco aliquid existet præter naturā, in eo oportet aliquid etiam posse existere per naturā. Sed iam demonstratum est, nullum ibi esse corpus per naturam, quare neq; ullum erit præter naturam.
units.tr: That likewise no simple body moved in a straight line exists there contrary to nature is manifest. For in whatever place something exists contrary to nature, in that place something must also be able to exist according to nature. But it has already been demonstrated that no body exists there by nature; therefore neither will there be any body contrary to nature.

units.la: Abundè igitur probatū est, nullum omnino corpus simplex extra cœlum esse posse, neque per naturā, neq; præter naturam. Reliquū est demonstremus, nullum etiam corpus cōpositum ibi esse posse.
units.tr: It has therefore been sufficiently proved that no simple body at all can be outside the heaven, neither by nature nor contrary to nature. It remains for us to demonstrate that no compound body can be there either.

units.la: Ubi non est aliquod corpus simplex, ibi etiā non potest esse aliquod corpus cōpositum. Corpus namque compositum semper præsupponit corpus simplex, ex quo conficiatur:quinetiam corpus compositum locum sibi aptum quærit pro natura corporis simplicis quod in ipso dominatur. Adhæc, ex his sequitur, si nullum ibi est corpus, neq; secundum naturam, neq; præter naturā, nihil etiam ibi posse fieri, neq; secundum naturam, neq; præter naturam. Ex nihilo nihil fit. Postremò, si nullum corpus extra cœlum est, consequitur, neq; locum, neq; vacuū, neq; tempus (quæ solent corpora sensibilia comitari) ibi esse.
units.tr: Where there is no simple body, there also cannot be any compound body. For a compound body always presupposes the simple body out of which it is made; moreover a compound body seeks a place suited to it according to the nature of the simple body which rules in it. Besides, it follows from these things that if there is no body there, neither according to nature nor contrary to nature, then nothing can come to be there either, neither according to nature nor contrary to nature. Nothing comes from nothing. Lastly, if there is no body outside the heaven, it follows that there is neither place, nor void, nor time (which are wont to accompany sensible bodies) there.

units.la: Ex his igitur omnib. manifestū euadit, possibile non esse, ut extra hunc mundū plures mundi fiant.
units.tr: From all these things, therefore, it becomes manifest that it is not possible that several worlds should come to be outside this world.

units.la: Vtrum uniuersum sit infinitum duratione?
units.tr: Whether the universe is infinite in duration?

units.la: De hac quæstione variæ fuerunt veterum opiniones.
units.tr: Opinions on this question among the ancients have been varied.

units.la: Prima: Quidam statuerunt, mundum quidem esse in tempore genitum, cæterum nunquam corrumpendum, semperq; mansuru. Sic Orpheus,Hesiodus,Plato,&c.
units.tr: The first view: some held that the world indeed was generated in time, but that it will never be corrupted and will remain forever. So Orpheus, Hesiod, Plato, etc.

units.la: Secunda: Democritus,& qui eum secuti sunt, senserunt esse genitum, itemq; interiturum, nunquam vero postea instaurandum.
units.tr: The second view: Democritus and those who followed him judged that it was generated, and likewise that it will perish, but that it will never afterwards be restored.

units.la: Tertia: Empedocli, Heraclito, Ephesio placuit, mundum frequenter genitum,& frequenter corruptum esse, easdemq; vicissitudines adhuc crebras futuras.
units.tr: The third view: it pleased Empedocles and Heraclitus of Ephesus that the world has been generated and corrupted many times over, and that the same alternations will recur frequently in the future.

units.la: Sed hæ opiniones non sunt retinendæ. Prima evertitur hac ratione: Omnia quæ generantur, videmus corruptioi[?] quoq; esse obnoxia. Ergo repugnat, dicere mundum esse genitum,& cunde[?] non corrumpi.
units.tr: But these opinions are not to be retained. The first is overturned by this reasoning: we see that all things which are generated are also subject to corruption. Therefore it is contradictory to say that the world has been generated and yet is not corrupted.

units.la: Secunda opinio sic confutatur: Qui mundum posuerunt genitum, idem constituerunt haud dubiè substantiam aliquam præexistétem, ex qua mundus est genitus. Iam autem quæro, utrum substantia illa fuerit obnoxia transmutationi & generationi, an non? Si non potuerat in ea fieri transmutatio, tum nec potuisset ex ea mundus gigni. Si autem potuerat fieri transmutatio, sane qua ratione semel hæc facta est, cum mundus ex ea fieret, eadem poterit aliàs quoque transmutatio fieri, ut iterum novus mundus ex ea producatur. Ergo absurdum est dicere, mundum aliquando esse genitum, itemq; interiturum, nec posse denuò instaurari.
units.tr: The second opinion is refuted as follows: those who posited that the world was generated undoubtedly also posited some pre-existing substance from which the world was generated. Now I ask: was that substance subject to change and generation, or not? If no change could take place in it, then neither could the world have been generated from it. But if change could take place in it, then, by the same reasoning by which it once happened when the world was made from it, the same change could also happen at other times, so that a new world would be produced from it again. Therefore it is absurd to say that the world was at some time generated, and will likewise perish, and cannot be restored again.

units.la: Tertia opinio sic confutatur: Afferere mundum frequenter genitum, & frequeter corruptum, perinde est atq; si dicas, mundum quidem semper eundem manere substantia, verùm forma tantùm & qualitatibus mutari, prorsus quemadmodum si homo unus idemq; numero & substantia ex iuvene fieret senex, & rursus ex sene iuvenis, atque ita saepius mutarentur in eo qualitates. Sed istud est absurdum: igitur & illud peræque absurdum habebitur. Ergo opiniones illæ explodi debent.
units.tr: The third opinion is refuted as follows: to assert that the world is generated frequently and corrupted frequently is just the same as if you said that the world indeed remains the same in substance, but is changed only in form and qualities, exactly as if one and the same man, identical in number and substance, were to become old from young, and then young again from old, and so his qualities were changed over and over. But that is absurd; therefore that too must be held equally absurd. Therefore those opinions ought to be rejected.

units.la: Ut autem certa habeatur de propositâ quæstione sententia, primùm quarundam vocum, videlicet Ingeniti & Geniti, item Incorruptibilis & Corruptibilis, varia acceptio explicanda est, postea quid sentire deceat definiemus.
units.tr: But so that a certain judgment may be reached on the question proposed, first the various senses of certain terms, namely 'unbegotten' and 'begotten', and likewise 'incorruptible' and 'corruptible', must be explained; afterwards we will define what it is proper to think.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur ingenitum?
units.tr: In how many ways is the unbegotten spoken of?

units.la: Tribus. Primò ingenitum dicitur, quod cum prius non existeret, nunc est, sed sine generatione ac transmutatione: ut contactus, motus, &c.
units.tr: In three ways. First, the unbegotten is that which, though it did not exist before, now exists, but without generation or change: as contact, motion, etc.

units.la: Secundò, quod contingit quidem fieri per generationem, vel non fieri, sed tamen nondum factum est. quo pacto homo, qui cras quidè gignetur, hodie uero nondum est,dicitur hodie adhuc ingenitus.
units.tr: Secondly, that which may indeed come to be through generation, or may not come to be, but has not yet come into being. In this way a man, who will indeed be born tomorrow but today is not yet, is said today to be still unbegotten.

units.la: Tertiò,quod omnino impossibile est fieri,& neque per generationem, neq; alio pacto potest quam doq; esse,aut quandoq; non esse.
units.tr: Thirdly, that which is wholly impossible to come to be, and which, neither through generation nor in any other way, can be at one time and at another time not be.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur genitum?
units.tr: In how many ways is the begotten spoken of?

units.la: Tribus. Primò,quod prius non fuit,& iam esse coepit, atq; per generationem seu transmutationem productum est.
units.tr: In three ways. First, that which did not exist before and has now begun to be, and has been produced through generation or change.

units.la: Secundò,quod est,non autem esse contingit.
units.tr: Secondly, that which is, but which may also not be.

units.la: Tertiò, quod aliquo modo esse aut fieri contingit,siue faciliter id fiat,siue difficulter.
units.tr: Thirdly, that which can in some way be or come to be, whether this happens easily or with difficulty.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur incorru- ptibile?
units.tr: In how many ways is the corruptible spoken of?

units.la: Tribus. Primò corruptibile dicitur, quod cum prius sit, paulo post non est, vel contingit non esse, idq; siue per corruptionem & transmutationem, qua ratione homo est corruptibilis: siue citra corruptionem & transmutationem, quomodo tactus & motus sunt corruptibiles.
units.tr: In three ways. First, the corruptible is that which, though it exists now, a little later is not, or may not be; and this whether through corruption and change, in which way a man is corruptible, or without corruption and change, as contact and motion are corruptible.

units.la: Secundò,quod cōtingit non esse,atq; certa quadam ratione corrumpitur : quemadmodum plures res naturaliter quotidie corrumpi cernimus.
units.tr: Secondly, that which may not be, and is corrupted by a certain fixed cause, just as we see many things naturally corrupted every day.

units.la: Tertiò,quod facilè & citò corrumpitur.
units.tr: Thirdly, that which is corrupted easily and quickly.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur incorru- ptibile?
units.tr: In how many ways is the incorruptible spoken of?

units.la: Tribus. Primò, quod cum sit, tamen aliquando esse desistit,sed citra transmutationem:ut contactus & & motus esse desinunt, uerum non facta ulla transmutatione aut naturali corruptione.
units.tr: In three ways. First, that which, though it is, nevertheless at some time ceases to be, but without change: as contact and & motion cease to be, yet without any change or natural corruption taking place.

units.la: Secundò, quod nunc est, & impossibile est ut postea non sit, uel quandoque non sit futurum. Quod recte dixerimus incorruptibile simpliciter.
units.tr: Secondly, that which now is, and it is impossible that it should afterwards not be, or that at some time it will not be. This we rightly call incorruptible simply.

units.la: Tertiò dicitur incorruptibile, quod non facilè corrumpitur: sicut res quæ diu ad usum asseruatur, dicuntur sine corruptione retineri.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is called incorruptible that which is not easily corrupted: just as things that are kept for a long time for use are said to be preserved without corruption.

units.la: Vt autem hæ ipsæ distinctiones, tum nonnulla quæ sequuntur, facilius intelligantur, operæprecium est exponere, quid dicatur possibile & impossibile.
units.tr: But in order that these very distinctions, and some of those that follow, may be more easily understood, it is worth while to explain what is called possible and impossible.

units.la: Quid dicitur possibile?
units.tr: What is called possible?

units.la: Possibile vocatur, quod quis in re quapiam certa, cum æstimantur præcipuæ eius vires & summa facultas præstare potest. Si enim, quantum quis possit, quæritur, statim intelligimus de arduis & magnis rebus quæstione fieri, ideoq; proferimus quod maximum in eo putamus. Sic Archias dicitur plurimos & optimos uersus etiam ex tempore effundere, robustus Milo dicitur posse gestare bovem, & dies aliquis posse persoluere tria millia aureorum.
units.tr: That is called possible which someone can accomplish in some particular thing, when his principal powers and greatest ability are taken into account. For if we ask how much someone is able to do, we at once understand the question to concern difficult and great matters, and so we state what we think is greatest in him. Thus Archias is said to pour out very many and excellent verses even extempore; the strong Milo is said to be able to carry an ox; and a certain man is said to be able to pay three thousand gold pieces.

units.la: Quid est impossibile?
units.tr: What is impossible?

units.la: Quod quis, cum æstimatur summa eius facultas, præstare nullo modo queat. Ac dicitur quidem impossibile duobus modis. Primò simpliciter seu absolutè, quod neq; est, neq; fieri ulla ratione potest.
units.tr: That which, when a person's greatest capacity is assessed, can by no means be achieved. Now, the impossible is indeed spoken of in two ways. First, simply or absolutely: that which neither is nor can come about by any means.

units.la: Secundò, quod difficulter admodum fit. Eadem ratione licet iudicare & de possibili.
units.tr: Second, that which comes about with great difficulty. By the same reasoning one may also judge what is possible.

units.la: His ita expositis, observabimus, praesenti loco spectari has voces: Genitum, Ingenitum, Corruptibile, Incorruptibile, item Possibile & Impossibile, simpliciter et absolute acceptas: atq; ita promptum est ad quaestione principalem, utrum videlicet universum sit infinitum duratione, respondere.
units.tr: Having set out these things, we shall observe that in the present place the following terms are to be considered: begotten, unbegotten, corruptible, incorruptible, likewise possible and impossible, taken simply and absolutely. And so it is ready to answer the principal question, namely whether the universe is infinite in duration.

units.la: Est'ne igitur universum infini- tum duratione?
units.tr: Is the universe therefore infinite in duration?

units.la: Mundus est semper existens, sive sempiternus, idcoq; neq; generationi neq; corruptioni obnoxius. Declaratur haec conclusio aliquot propositionibus.
units.tr: The world is always existing, that is, everlasting, and therefore subject neither to generation nor to corruption. This conclusion is demonstrated by several propositions.

units.la: Prima: Omne sempiternum est incorruptibile.
units.tr: First: Everything everlasting is incorruptible.

units.la: Probatio: Constituatur sempiternum A. Quando igitur A est sempiternum & semper existens, si dicas id corruptioni obnoxium, tum aliquando non erit. Atqui impossibile est, id quod semper existit, aliquando non esse. Igitur falsum est, imo impossibile, sempiternum esse corruptibile.
units.tr: Proof: Let A be something everlasting. Since, then, A is everlasting and always existing, if you say it is subject to corruption, then at some time it will not be. But what always exists is impossible to not exist at some time. Therefore it is false, indeed impossible, that the everlasting is corruptible.

units.la: Secunda: Omne sempiternum est ingenitum.
units.tr: Second: Everything everlasting is unbegotten.

units.la: Probatio: Omne sempiternū semper existit. Quod autem genitum est, id aliquando existit, aliquando vero non fuit. Igitur repugnat, idem sempiternum esse & genitum. Etenim, si quod potest omni tempore esse, aliquando posset non esse, eidem convenirent contraria seu contradictoria, nempe esse & non esse. Quod est impossibile & absurdum.
units.tr: Proof: Everything everlasting always exists. But what has been begotten exists at some time, and at some time did not exist. Therefore it is contradictory for the same thing to be everlasting and begotten. For if what can be at every time could at some time not be, then contraries, or contradictories, namely to be and not to be, would belong to the same thing. This is impossible and absurd.

units.la: 3. Tertia:Sempiternum & corruptibile, item sempiternum & genitum, simul esse non possunt. Probatio:Cum enim esse sempiternum & esse genitum, similiter esse sempiternum & esse corruptibile,pugnent inter sese,sintq; contraria,ut paulo ante commonstratum,facile intelligimus, ea simul esse haud posse.
units.tr: 3. Third: The everlasting and the corruptible, and likewise the everlasting and the begotten, cannot be together.
