Proof: Since to be everlasting and to be begotten, and likewise to be everlasting and to be corruptible, are opposed to one another and are contraries, as was shown a little earlier, we readily understand that they cannot be together.

units.la: 4. Quarta: Ingenitum & incorruptibile sese mutuo consequuntur.
units.tr: 4. Fourth: The unbegotten and the incorruptible follow one another mutually.

units.la: 5. Quinta: Genitum & corruptibile sese mutuo consequuntur.
units.tr: 5. Fifth: The begotten and the corruptible follow one another mutually.

units.la: Satis possunt intelligi hæ propositiones ex eo quod Incorruptibile & Ingenitum,item Corruptibile & Genitum habent in se naturam relativorum vel causarum & effectuum, ut in quo unum ponitur, necessario & alterum ei oppositum ponatur. Itaq; quam rem constat esse genitam,eandem concedi oportet & corruptibile esse:ac vice versa,quam rem constat esse corruptibilem,eadē necessario conceditur genita. Item, quæcunq; res fuerit ingenita, eandem necesse est incorruptibilem concedere: & vice versa , quæ fuerit incorruptibilis, erit eadem quoq; ingenita.
units.tr: These propositions can be sufficiently understood from the fact that the incorruptible and the unbegotten, and likewise the corruptible and the begotten, have the nature of relatives or of causes and effects, so that when one is posited, the opposite of it is necessarily posited too. Thus whatever thing is agreed to be begotten, the same must be conceded to be corruptible; and conversely, whatever thing is agreed to be corruptible, the same is necessarily conceded to be begotten. Likewise, whatever thing is unbegotten, the same must necessarily be conceded to be incorruptible; and conversely, whatever is incorruptible will be the same also unbegotten.

units.la: 6. Sexta: Quod ingenitum est, itemq; incorruptibile,idem semper existens & sempiternum est.Manifesta est hæc propositio ex iis quæ dicta sunt.
units.tr: 6. Sixth: What is unbegotten, and likewise incorruptible, is always existing and everlasting. This proposition is manifest from what has been said.

units.la: Ex his ergo omnibus ( maximè si etiam in memoriam reuocetur quæ suprà exposita sunt, de uno & æterno primo mouente) constat, mundum, siue uniuersum, sempiternum existere, ac proinde etiam ingenitum & incorruptibile. Quo circa cadit corum opinio, qui posuerunt, mundum quidem esse genitum, sed tamen incorruptibilem: item eorum qui dixerunt, frequenter genitū & frequenter corruptum, at interim secundum substantiam semper manere: deniq; eorum qui dixerūt, genitum & interiturum, nunquam uerò postea instaurandum. pugnantia enim inter sese loquuntur. Quæ res mouit Aristotelem ad colligendam eam sententiam, quam iam exposuimus.
units.tr: From all these things therefore (especially if one also recalls what was set out above concerning the one and eternal first mover), it is established that the world, or the universe, exists everlasting, and consequently also unbegotten and incorruptible. Hence the opinion of those falls, who held that the world is indeed begotten but nevertheless incorruptible; likewise of those who said that it is begotten and corrupted frequently, yet meanwhile remains the same in substance; and finally of those who said that it is begotten and will perish, but never afterwards to be restored. For they speak things that are inconsistent with one another. This consideration moved Aristotle to adopt that opinion which we have now set out.

units.la: Cæterùm est hoc loco adnotandum, ne Aristotelis quidem sententiam à nobis Christianam religionem profitentibus probari posse. Etenim ex arcanis nostris literis edocti sumus, mundum in tempore esse cœpisse, nec uerò per generationem quasi ex materia præiacente (philosophicè enim ac physicè loquendo, ex nihilo nihil fit) sicut producuntur quæcunq; aliæ res naturales, sed ex nihilo, solo Dei uerbo imperante creatum & conditū, subitò emersisse, partibus deinde ipsius uniuersi pulchrè distinctis: Genef.1.
units.tr: Moreover, it must be noted here that Aristotle's opinion cannot be approved even by us who profess the Christian religion. For we have been taught from our sacred writings that the world began to be in time, and was not produced by generation, as from a pre-existing matter (for speaking philosophically and physically, nothing comes from nothing), as all other natural things are produced; but was created and made from nothing, by the word of God alone commanding, and suddenly emerged, its parts then beautifully distinguished within the universe itself: Genesis 1.

units.la: Has quæstiones de uniuerso discussisse sufficiat. Superest, ut de corporibus simplicibus, quæ sunt uniuersi partes, differamus, ac primùm quidem de quinto corpore simplici, id est cælo, ante omnia vero de cæli substantia ac duratione.
units.tr: It is enough to have discussed these questions about the universe. It remains that we treat of the simple bodies, which are the parts of the universe, and first of the fifth simple body, that is, the heaven, and above all of the substance and duration of the heaven.

units.la: QVID COELVM.
units.tr: What heaven is.

units.la: Estne cælum substantia quædam sempiterna?
units.tr: Is heaven an everlasting substance?

units.la: Cælum neque genitum, neque corruptibile est, sed sempiternum, principio ac fine carens. Comprobatur hæc propositio aliquot rationibus.
units.tr: Heaven is neither generated nor corruptible, but everlasting, without beginning or end. This proposition is supported by several arguments.

units.la: Prima: Si ipsum universum est ingenitum & incorruptibile & sempiternū, necesse est cælū quoq;, quod est nobilissima & amplissima universi pars, ingenitū, incorruptibile ac sempiternum existere. Partes naturam totius induunt.
units.tr: First: if the universe itself is unbegotten, incorruptible and everlasting, then heaven, which is the noblest and largest part of the universe, must also be unbegotten, incorruptible and everlasting. The parts take on the nature of the whole.

units.la: Secunda: Eadem quoq; fuit maiorum nostrorum sententia, quam non licet temere aspernari.
units.tr: Second: this was also the opinion of our ancestors, which we may not rashly despise.

units.la: Tertia: Decet proportionem quandam esse cæli ad suum motum. Atqui motus cæli, qui est circularis, multò est perfectissimus, neq; principium unde moueri incipiat, neq; finem in quo moueri desinat, habens, sed infinito tempore, ac sine ulla intermissione circumactus. Ergo cælum quoq; ipsum persectissimum, principio & fine carens, semperq; existens, merito censebitur. Corpus cuius motus est infinitus, ipsum quoq; infinitum sit necesse est. Huc faciunt quæ de primo motu æterno supra sunt exposita.
units.tr: Third: heaven ought to bear some proportion to its motion. But the motion of heaven, which is circular, is by far the most perfect. It has neither a starting point from which it begins to move nor an end at which it ceases, but it is carried round for infinite time and without any interruption. Therefore heaven too, most perfect, without beginning or end and always existing, will rightly be judged to be so. A body whose motion is infinite must itself necessarily be infinite. To this point belongs what was set out above concerning the eternal first motion.

units.la: Quarta: Antiquitas constituit cælum Deorum Immortalium sedem: non posset autem esse immortalium sedes, nisi ipsum quoq; immortale, ingenitum incorruptibilecq; existeret.
units.tr: Fourth: antiquity made heaven the seat of the immortal gods. But heaven could not be the seat of the immortals unless it were itself immortal, unbegotten and incorruptible.

units.la: Est'ne coeli substantia grauis?
units.tr: Is the substance of heaven heavy?

units.la: Non. Cum enim motus eius sit perpetuus semperq; in se rediens, perspicuum fit ex hac motus ratione, cœlum nullo modo graue esse. Si namq; graue esset aut in toto, aut in parte, motus eius aliquo modo extra ordinem deorsum aliquando ferretur. Inane igitur est commentum de Atlante cœlum humeris sustinente, ne pondere suo delabatur. Vana quoq; est opinio Empedoclis aliorumq;, existimantium cœlum quidem esse graue sua natura, verùm celeritate motus prohiberi ne dimoueatur: quemadmodum aqua quoq; celeriter cum vase mota, ne decidat, impeditur.
units.tr: No. For since its motion is perpetual and always returns into itself, it is plain from this very nature of its motion that heaven is in no way heavy. For if it were heavy, either as a whole or in part, its motion would at some time be carried downward in some way out of its order. It is therefore an empty fiction that Atlas supports heaven on his shoulders, lest it fall by its own weight. Likewise the opinion of Empedocles and others is vain, who think that heaven is indeed heavy by its own nature, but is kept from falling by the speed of its motion, just as water too, when swiftly moved in a vessel, is prevented from spilling.

units.la: Est'ne cœlum animal seu substan- tia animata?
units.tr: Is heaven an animal, or an animated substance?

units.la: Plato in Timæo sensit cœlum esse animatum, atque ab anima ratione prædita suo in loco atq; motu perpetuo contineri, prorsus quemadmodum corpora nostra ab animis nostris movetur. Verùm hæc sententia retineri nullo modo potest. Probatur.
units.tr: Plato in the Timaeus held that heaven is animated, and is held in its place and in its perpetual motion by a rational soul, just as our bodies are moved by our souls. But this opinion cannot be maintained in any way. It is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Si vi animæ cœlum suo in loco ac motu continetur, nō posset ita perpetuo subsistere. Nam retentio illa cœli violenta quodammodo esset. Nihil autem quod ut fiat, diuturnum, multò minus sempiternum esse potest.
units.tr: 1. If heaven is held in its place and motion by the power of a soul, it could not continue thus perpetually. For that restraint of heaven would in some sense be violent. Nothing that is brought about by force can be lasting, much less everlasting.

units.la: 2. Anima illa grauata perpetuo mouendi labore impedirctur à contemplatione. Quamobrem beata nullo modo esse posset, cū nemo nesciat, animæ beatitudinem omnem in contemplatione esse positam. Sedenim absurdum foret, cœlo tribuere animā quæ à beatitudine excluderetur.
units.tr: 2. That soul, burdened with the labour of perpetual motion, would be hindered from contemplation. Wherefore it could in no way be blessed, since no one doubts that all the blessedness of a soul lies in contemplation. Indeed it would be absurd to attribute to heaven a soul that would be excluded from blessedness.

units.la: QVOT PARTES COELI. Tribuuntúrne rectè cœlo duæ tan- tùm partes, dextera videli- cet & sinistra?
units.tr: HOW MANY PARTS OF HEAVEN. Are two parts only rightly attributed to heaven, namely the right and the left?

units.la: Minimè, quantùuis Pythagorici id sint arbitrati. Hi enim volentes omnia reducere ad duo principia, bonum videlicet & malum, atq; in supputandis iis quæ sub his principijs collocantur, numerum binarium non excedentes, sub bono constituerunt dextrum, sub malo sinistrum. Itaq; hac ratione nō nisi duas situs formas recensuerunt, atq; in cœlo quidem tantùm duas partes distinxerunt, dextram videlicet & sinistram. Cæterùm non rectè eos id fecisse, rationibus aliquot probatur.
units.tr: By no means, although the Pythagoreans thought so. For they, wishing to reduce all things to two principles, namely good and evil, and in counting those things which are placed under these principles, not exceeding the number two, placed the right under good and the left under evil. Thus by this reasoning they reckoned only two forms of position, and in heaven they distinguished only two parts, namely the right and the left. But that they did not do this rightly is proved by several arguments.

units.la: 1. Cū sint sex positus formæ, videlicet dextrorsum & sinistrorsum, sursum ac deorsum, ante & retrò, nulla adserri probabilis potest ratio, cur tantùm duæ illæ formæ in cœlo constituantur, reliquæ autem quatuor prætermittantur.
units.tr: 1. Since there are six forms of position, namely right and left, up and down, before and behind, no probable reason can be given why only those two forms should be set up in heaven while the remaining four are passed over.

units.la: Si quæ formæ prætermitti possunt, maximè eæ quæ minoris sunt dignitatis. Atqui quatuor illæ prætermissæ non sunt minoris dignitatis. Igitur prætereriri haudquaquà debuerant. Minor probatur: Sursum ac deorsum sunt maioris dignitatis, quàm reliquæ positionum formæ. Nam ubi dextrum & sinistrum differùt tantùm virtute, sursum ac deorsum, sicut ante & retrò, differunt tum virtute, tum figura. Deinde sursum ac deorsum spectatur in omnibus corporibus animatis, id est, tam in animalibus quàm plantis: dextrum verò & sinistrum non spectantur in plantis, sed tantùm in animalibus perfectis.
units.tr: If any forms may be passed over, those most of all may be which are of lesser dignity. But those four that were passed over are not of lesser dignity. Therefore they ought by no means to have been passed over. The minor premise is proved thus: up and down are of greater dignity than the other forms of position. For where right and left differ only in power, up and down differ both in power and in shape, as do before and behind. Next, up and down are observed in all animated bodies, that is, in animals as well as in plants; but right and left are not observed in plants, only in perfect animals.

units.la: Postremò, cum longitudo sit prior & amplior latitudine, ac sursum ac deorsum commensurent longitudinem, dextrum verò & sinistrum latitudinem, hinc quoq; sursum ac deorsum excellunt.
units.tr: Finally, since length is prior to and greater than breadth, and up and down measure length, while right and left measure breadth, up and down are therefore also superior in this respect.

units.la: Tribus igitur rationibus comprobatur, sursum ac deorsum maioris esse dignitatis. Relinquitur ergo, Pythagoricos reprehensionem incurrere, quòd duas tantùm partes ac situs differentias, dextram videlicet & sinistram, cœlo attribuerint.
units.tr: Therefore by three arguments it is proved that up and down are of greater dignity. It remains, then, that the Pythagoreans incur blame, because they attributed to heaven only two parts and differences of position, namely the right and the left.

units.la: Tribuenturne cœlo sex posi- tus formæ?
units.tr: Can the heaven be assigned the six forms of position?

units.la: Quid'ni? Probatio. Nam omnes has formas, dextrum videlicet & sinistrum, sursum ac deorsum, ante ac retrò, constat observari in corporibus animatis. Atqui cœlum cum habeat principium motus in se, est veluti corpus quoddam animatum. Igitur uel hac ratione omnes hæ situs formæ in cælo recte distinguentur.
units.tr: Why not? Proof: all these forms, namely right and left, up and down, before and behind, are plainly observed in animate bodies. But the heaven, since it has the principle of its motion within itself, is like some animate body. Therefore, on this ground alone, all these forms of position are rightly distinguished in the heaven.

units.la: Neque obest, quod cælum sit figura circulari, quæ quidem figura partes omnes sibi undique sunt similes. Non enim distinguuntur diuersæ formæ situs in cælo propter cæli figuram, sed propter diversitatem virtutis agendi, quæ in illius figuræ partibus alia atque alia hinc inde deprehenditur. Etenim circum duos polos, quoniam hi loco non movențur, animaducertimus distinctionem fieri duorum hemisphæriorum: deinde ab oriente in occidentem animaducertimus alia ratione perpetuum quendam motum fieri. Vtrumque stellæ fixæ non obscure declarant.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that the heaven is circular in shape, a figure in which all its parts are alike on every side. For the diverse forms of position in the heaven are not distinguished because of the shape of the heaven, but because of the diversity of its power of acting, which is found to differ from part to part of that figure on this side and that. For around the two poles, since these do not move from their place, we observe a distinction between the two hemispheres; then, from east to west, we observe a perpetual motion of another kind. The fixed stars clearly show both.

units.la: Vbi distinguuntur in cælo sex situum formæ?
units.tr: Where in the heaven are the six forms of position distinguished?

units.la: Constituatur homo capite ipso ac vultu conversus ad septentrionem seu polum arcticum, pedibus vero ad meridiem seu polum ἀντάρκτικον, ac tum quidem manus eius dextra exporrigetur ad orientem, sinistra vero ad occidentem. Hinc autem promptum erit iudicare, sursum sive supremam partem mundi spectari ante polum antarcticum nobis semper occultum, deorsum autem sive infernam partem spectari apud polum arcticum nobis semper apparentem: deinde dextram partem habere in oriente, sinistram uero in occasu. Ex quibus non difficile est colligere, quænam pars cœli anterior, quæue posterior. Ac dextram quidem partem recte in cœlo constitui ad orientem, uel ex eo constare potest, quòd dextrum merito appellatur, unde localis motus cœli fit initium. Nam & animalia dextra parte semper plus ualent uiribus, dextra item pars in animalibus plus caloris obtinet, quo nimirum ad motum atque ad agitationem fit paratior. Fit autem motus cœlestis initium ab oriente: quandoquidem uidemus stellas quotidie ab oriente in occidentem rapi. Igitur in oriente dextra cœli pars appositè notatur. Porrò perspecta ratione unius partis, procliue est iudicare de omnibus partibus reliquis.
units.tr: Let a man be set up with his head and face turned toward the north or the arctic pole, but his feet toward the south or the antarctic pole [ἀντάρκτικον], and then his right hand will be stretched out toward the east and his left toward the west. From this it will be easy to judge that the upper or highest part of the world is looked at in front of the antarctic pole, which is always hidden from us, and the lower or inferior part is looked at near the arctic pole, which is always visible to us; then that the right part lies in the east and the left part in the west. From these it is not difficult to gather which part of the heaven is anterior and which posterior. That the right part of the heaven is rightly placed in the east can be established from this, that it is properly called right, since the local motion of the heaven begins from it. For animals always have more strength in the right part, and the right part in animals also has more heat, which makes it more ready for motion and agitation. But the heavenly motion begins from the east, since we see the stars swept every day from east to west. Therefore the right part of the heaven is appropriately located in the east. Moreover, once the reasoning for one part is understood, it is easy to judge concerning all the remaining parts.

units.la: Utrum cœlum dividatur in plura corpora seu sphæras mo- biles?
units.tr: Whether the heaven is divided into several moving bodies or spheres?

units.la: Cœlum dividitur in plures partes, plura corpora siue sphæras, easdemq; circulariter circumactas: quod probatur μεθόδῳ συνθετικῇ [?], id est, compositiua, in qua à primo proceditur ad ultimum id de quo est quæstio.
units.tr: The heaven is divided into several parts, several bodies or spheres, each carried around in a circle. This is proved by the synthetic method [μεθόδῳ συνθετικῇ], that is, the compositive method, in which one proceeds from the first thing to the last thing that is in question.

units.la: Si cœlum est quoddam corpus diuinum perfeƈtissimum, necessum est motum quoq; eius sempiternum & circularem, ac plane perfectissimum existere. qua de re nonnulla ante dicta sunt.
units.tr: If the heaven is a certain most perfect divine body, its motion must also be eternal, circular, and altogether most perfect. Several things have been said about this matter before.

units.la: Si motus cœli est sempiternus & circularis, necesse est aliquid quoq; poni, quod semper quiescat: id uero terra est.
units.tr: If the motion of the heaven is eternal and circular, something must also be posited that always remains at rest; and that is the earth.

units.la: Si terra est, necessario erit etiam ignis. Vno enim contrariorum posito, alterum etiam poni necesse erit: & posito posteriori, oportet ponatur quod prius est. Iam uero terra & ignis se habent ut contraria, ac terra quidem posterius quiddam est ignobiliusq;: ignis uero prius ac nobilius. Siquidem ignis calidus est & leuis, & per se mobilis semperq; agitari gaudet: terra e contrario frigida, grauis, immobilis, ab agitatione abhorrens.
units.tr: If there is earth, there must necessarily be fire too. For when one of two contraries is posited, the other must also be posited, and when the latter is posited, what is prior must be posited as well. Now earth and fire stand to each other as contraries: earth is something posterior and baser, while fire is prior and nobler. For fire is hot and light, and by its own nature is mobile and delights to be always in motion; earth, on the contrary, is cold, heavy, immobile, and shrinks from agitation.

units.la: Si & terra & ignis est, necessario quoq; erunt alia quaedam corpora media, aer nempe, & aqua. Nam haec ipsa sunt terrae & igni contraria: igni quidem aqua, terrae uero aer. Ex omnibus elementis semper alterum alteri contrarium est, ratione pugnantium qualitatum. Positis ergo illis prioribus corporibus contrarijs, necessum est ponantur & ista corpora media eorundem contraria.
units.tr: If there is both earth and fire, there must necessarily also be certain intermediate bodies, namely air and water. For these very things are contrary to earth and fire: water to fire, and air to earth. Among all the elements, one is always contrary to another, by reason of their opposing qualities. Therefore, since those former bodies are contraries, these intermediate bodies too must be posited as their contraries.

units.la: Si autem sint corpora quaedam media, necessario exsistit generatio corruptioq;. Constitutis enim elementis, ex quibus omnia fiunt, decet generationem quoq; & corruptionem constitui. Neq; enim otiosa aut frustra posita illa sunt, atq; necesse est illa semper inter se agere aut pati.
units.tr: If there are certain intermediate bodies, generation and corruption necessarily exist. For once the elements, from which all things are made, have been established, generation and corruption ought to be established as well. Those elements are not posited idly or in vain, and they must always act upon or undergo one another.

units.la: Si generatio & corruptio est, necesse est dissimiles motus in cœlo existere. Nam si unus tantum esset in cœlo motus,nulla esset in corporibus inferioribus diuersitas: atq; tam elementa ipsa,quam reliqua corpora naturalia simili modo se haberent. Id uero si daretur, tum neq; generatio esset, neq; corruptio. Ergo si cœlum est, corpus quoddam diuinum atq; sempiternum fieri haud potest, quin plures quoq; motus in cœlo existant,ac proinde & corpora mobilia, siue sphæræ, quib.motus illi aptetur.
units.tr: If there is generation and corruption, dissimilar motions must necessarily exist in the heaven. For if there were only one motion in the heaven, there would be no diversity in the lower bodies, and the elements themselves, as well as the other natural bodies, would all be in the same condition. But if that were so, there would be neither generation nor corruption. Therefore, if there is a heaven, a certain divine and eternal body, it cannot be that several motions do not also exist in the heaven, and consequently also movable bodies, or spheres, to which those motions are fitted.

units.la: Ex his manifestum fit, cœlum in diuersos orbes siue sphæras, quæ singulæ proprio suo motu gaudeant,rectè distingui.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the heaven is rightly distinguished into diverse orbs or spheres, each of which enjoys its own proper motion.

units.la: QUALE SIT COELUM?
units.tr: WHAT SORT OF THING THE HEAVEN IS?

units.la: Qua figura est cœlum?
units.tr: What shape is the heaven?

units.la: Sphærica siue rotunda. Probatur tribus rationibus.
units.tr: It is spherical or round. This is proved by three arguments.

units.la: Prima à dignitate sphæricæ figuræ. Primo & præstantissimo corpori, quod est cœlum, conuenit etiam præstantissima figura. Atqui sphærica figura est omnium præstantissima: igitur eadem cœlo conuenit. Maior nullam habet obscuritatē. Minor probatur: Inter figuras (quæ omnes sunt aut rectæ lineæ, aut circulares) ea excellit, quæ paucioribus lineis absoluitur. Atqui circularis figura una tantum linea contenta est, recta linea uero requirit plures & ad minimū tres. Igitur circularis figura reliquas omnes excellit. In unoquoq; genere unitas prior est multitudinē,et quo qd plurib.eget,eo est impfectiõ[?].
units.tr: The first is from the dignity of the spherical figure. To the first and most excellent body, which is the heaven, there belongs also the most excellent figure. But the spherical figure is the most excellent of all: therefore the same belongs to the heaven. The major premise has no obscurity. The minor is proved thus: among figures (which are all either straight lines or circular), that one excels which is bounded by fewer lines. But a circular figure is contained by one line only, whereas a straight-lined figure requires several, at least three. Therefore the circular figure surpasses all the others. In every kind, the unit is prior to the multitude, and whatever needs more things is the less perfect.

units.la: Secunda,à dignitate ipsius cœli: Si cœlum nō est figura sphærica & circulari,tū oportet sit prædituʼ figura aliqua recta linea, nēpe aut figura triangulari,aut quadrangulari,&c. Si autem sit cœlum aliqua huiusmodi figura, conficietur sanè, extra cœlum esse uacuum, & proinde aliquem etiam locum et aliquod corpus.Sed ista omnia sunt absurda,cum cœlum omnia in se comprehendat, nihilq; extra id positum queat intelligi. Ergo ad dignitatem cœli pertinet,ut figura sphærica ornatum sit.
units.tr: Second, from the dignity of the heaven itself: if the heaven is not a spherical and circular figure, then it must have some rectilinear figure, namely either triangular or quadrangular, and so on. But if the heaven were of some such figure, it would surely follow that there is empty space outside the heaven, and therefore also some place and some body there. But all these things are absurd, since the heaven comprehends all things within itself, and nothing can be conceived as placed outside it. Therefore it belongs to the dignity of the heaven to be adorned with a spherical figure.

units.la: Tertia,ex qualitate corporū inferiorum:Corpora inferiora, terra, aqua, ignis, cæteraq; sub cœlo coprehensa, sunt sphæricæ figuræ.Igitur & cœlum ipsum, illa omnia in se sine interpositione ullarum rerū comprehendens,erit figuræ sphæricæ.Antecedens probatur: Terra in primis est rotunda: quod aliquato post plenius demonstrabitur.Aqua deinde terrā ambit,& ipsa in orbem circumducta,quàuis non omni ex parte terram contegat: quod ita fieri necesse est propter rerum naturaliū generationem & conseruationem,in primis animaliū atq; plantarum. Aer rursus circumdat aquam,ignis deniq; aerem. Eodem deinde ordine reliqua corpora superiora disposita sunt,& tanquam orbes inclusi orbibus. Igitur cœlum ipsum, quod est tanquam theca cui hæc omnia includuntur,rotundum est, & multò sanè rotundius, quàm ullum corpus aptè posset ad rotunditatem deduci.
units.tr: Third, from the quality of the lower bodies: the lower bodies, earth, water, fire, and the other things contained under the heaven, are of spherical figure. Therefore the heaven itself, which comprehends all those things within itself without the interposition of any other things, will be of spherical figure. The antecedent is proved: the earth is first of all round, which will be demonstrated more fully a little later. Next, water surrounds the earth, and being itself drawn round in a circle, although it does not cover the earth on every side; this must necessarily happen for the generation and preservation of natural things, above all of animals and plants. Air in turn surrounds the water, and finally fire surrounds the air. In the same order the remaining higher bodies are arranged, and are like spheres enclosed within spheres. Therefore the heaven itself, which is like a casing in which all these things are enclosed, is round, and far more round than any body could aptly be brought to roundness.

units.la: Cur cœlum mouetur perpetuò ab oriente in occidentem?
units.tr: Why does the heaven move continually from east to west?

units.la: Cum cœlum fit sempiternum, non est quòd suspicemur, aliquid in eo cõtingenter aut casu fieri. Debet igitur iusta ac necessaria esse causa, ob quam cœlum ab oriente in occidentem moueatur. Est autem hæc: Natura semper id facit ac sequitur, quo nihil melius fieri posset. Atqui non posset cœlum rectius, vel pro sua dignitate commodius moueri, quàm à dextra ad sinistrâ. Ergo cœlum, in quo quàm optimè omnia fieri necessum est, iustè à dextra parte, id est ab oriente, moueri incipit, atq; ad sinistram, id est occidetem, rapitur. Minor probatur: Dextra pars nobilior est ac dignior quàm sinistra, sicut anterior dignior est quàm posterior, et superior quàm inferior: quod in animantibus, & præcipuè in hominibus animaduerti potest. Nam dextra parte omnes plus uirium habent, expeditioresq; sunt ad alï[?] quid efficiendũ, quàm in sinistra: & superiore parte caput ac sensus, cæteraq; dignissima membra, inferiore autem membra uiliora: & anterior pars hominis uarijs decoratur ornamentis, & in actionibus præcipuè occupatur, at posterior non item. Hæc igitur idonea est ratio, cur cœlum moueri incipiat potiũs à parte dextra, quàm à sinistra.
units.tr: Since the heaven is everlasting, we should not suspect that anything in it happens by chance or accident. There must therefore be a just and necessary cause why the heaven moves from east to west. This cause is: nature always does that and follows that which nothing better could be done. But the heaven could not be moved more rightly, or more suitably to its dignity, than from right to left. Therefore the heaven, in which everything must be done in the best possible way, rightly begins to move from the right part, that is from the east, and is carried to the left, that is to the west. The minor is proved thus: the right part is nobler and worthier than the left, just as the front is worthier than the back, and the upper than the lower; this can be observed in animals, and especially in human beings. For on the right side all have more strength and are more ready to accomplish something than on the left; and in the upper part are the head and the senses and the other most worthy members, while in the lower part are the meaner members; and the front part of a human being is adorned with various ornaments and is chiefly occupied in actions, but the back part is not so. This, therefore, is a suitable reason why the heaven begins to move rather from the right part than from the left.

units.la: Est'ne motus cœli ab oriente in occi- dentem ubique uniformis & sui similis?
units.tr: Is the motion of the heaven from east to west everywhere uniform and like itself?

units.la: Est. Nam in cœlo non potest motus irregularis, ut videlicet modò celerius, modò tardius circūagatur, locum habere. In planetarum quidem orbibus potest spectari motus irregularis, circulis nimirum excentricis id efficietibus, præterea etiam ipsorum planetarum retrogressione, progressione, statione: at vero in primo mobili, seu cœlo stellarũ fixarum, nullo modo. quod quidem hac ratione coprobatur
units.tr: It is. For in the heaven an irregular motion, namely one that goes round now more quickly, now more slowly, cannot take place. In the orbs of the planets indeed an irregular motion can be observed, certainly brought about by eccentric circles, and besides also by the retrogression, progression and stationing of the planets themselves; but in the first mover, or the heaven of the fixed stars, in no way. This is proved by the following reasoning.

units.la: Si primi cœli motus esset irregularis, oporteret in eo considerari hæc tria, quæ plerunq; in motu irregulari concurrunt: nempe suprema virtus, seu vigor motus, incrementum & decrementum motus. Enimvero in motu irregulari secundum naturam virtûs seu vigor motus in principio est imbeccillior, in motu non naturali & violento in fine, in animalibus interdum in medio. Atqui in primo cœlo non possunt hæc considerari. Igitur neque motu irregulari illud fertur.
units.tr: If the motion of the first heaven were irregular, there would have to be considered in it these three things, which commonly concur in irregular motion: namely the highest power, or vigour, of the motion, and the increase and decrease of the motion. Indeed, in irregular motion, according to its nature, the power or vigour of the motion is weakest at the beginning, in a non-natural and violent motion at the end, and in animals sometimes in the middle. But in the first heaven these cannot be considered. Therefore it is not carried with an irregular motion either.

units.la: Maior est nota. Minor probatur. Quo enim loco possis demonstrare virtutem atq; vigorem motus in cœlo, quando cœlum est sempiternum, immortale, incorruptibile, in nullas partes secabile, et neq; principium, neq; medium, neq; finem habens?
units.tr: The major is well known. The minor is proved: for at what place could you demonstrate the power and vigour of motion in the heaven, since the heaven is everlasting, immortal, incorruptible, divisible into no parts, and has neither beginning, nor middle, nor end?

units.la: Aristoteles addit tres alias rationes idem coprobantes, uerum nos breuitatis causa eas prætermittimus. Quando autē hactenus satis dictum est de cœlo, par est nonnulla etiam de stellis adijciamus.
units.tr: Aristotle adds three other arguments proving the same thing, but for the sake of brevity we pass them over. Since enough has been said so far about the heaven, it is fitting that we add something also about the stars.

units.la: QUID SINT STELLAE. Quænam est substantia stellarum?
units.tr: WHAT THE STARS ARE. What is the substance of the stars?

units.la: Eadem quam & cœli esse suprà diximus. Pro-batur.
units.tr: The same as that of the heaven, as we said above. It is proved.

units.la: 1. Consentaneum est, corpora quævis sortiri eius loci, in quo posita sunt, indolem ac naturam. Cum igitur stellæ & moueantur pariter cum cœlo, & plurima cum cœlo ipso habeant communia, æquum est, eiusdem quoque substantiæ cum cœlo esse eas dicamus.
units.tr: 1. It is fitting that any bodies take on the nature and character of the place in which they are situated. Since, then, the stars both move together with the heaven and have very much in common with it, it is right to say that they are of the same substance as the heaven.

units.la: 2. Confirmatur hæc ratio illorum quoque sententia, qui existimarunt stellas esse igneas, propterea quòd opinabantur ipsum cœlum esse igneum. Itaque eadem ratione stellas merito dicimus eiusdem esse substantiæ, cuius est cœlum. Interea autem cœlum esse ignem non concedemus: nam antè demonstratum est, cœlum neque graue, neque leue dici posse, ideoque alterius omnino & plane purioris esse substantiæ, quàm quæcunque elementa.
units.tr: 2. This argument is confirmed for those also who held that the stars are fiery, because they thought the heaven itself was fiery. By the same reasoning we rightly say that the stars are of the same substance as the heaven. Meanwhile, however, we shall not concede that the heaven is fire, for it was demonstrated before that the heaven can be called neither heavy nor light, and therefore is of an altogether different and plainly purer substance than any of the elements.

units.la: Unde habent stellæ vim calefacien- di, si non sunt igneæ?
units.tr: Whence do the stars have the power of heating, if they are not fiery?

units.la: Calor à cœlo ad nos usq; deriuatus, non à stellis inducitur, sed à cœli orbiumq; cœlestium vehementi, celeri ac perpetuo motu: quo efficitur, ut aer quoque nobis uicinus rapido cursu circumagatur, atq; ita etiam magis magisq; incalescat. Enimuero motus uehemens calefacit etiam ferrum, ligna & lapides, quanto magis aerem? Comprobatur id experimento de sagittis, quæ cum per aera uolant, calefiunt, atq; adeò quidem, ut uel plumbum ipsum ijs affixum liquetur.Si uero sic calefiunt sagittæ, oportet multò magis caleat ipse aer, per quem feruntur. Ergo motus ille cœlestium orbium, itemq; aeris, qui impetu orbium simul circumagitur, calorem, quem à cœlo uenire sentimus, inducit, non stellæ ipsæ: nam ne hæ quidem ipsæ calefiunt, idq; partim quia procul dissitæ sunt ab aere, per quem calor dispargitur, partim quòd est ea stellis natura siue substantia, quæ accidentia eius generis, ueluti calorem & frigus, nō admittat: & stellæ sunt lucidæ quidem, non tamen ignitæ, atq; suo lumine aliquid momenti ad calorem adferunt, ut multis placet.
units.tr: The heat that comes down to us from the heaven is not induced by the stars, but by the vehement, swift and perpetual motion of the heaven and the heavenly orbs, by which it comes about that the air nearest us is also whirled round in rapid course and so grows warmer and warmer. Indeed, violent motion heats even iron, wood and stones; how much more the air? This is proved by the experiment with arrows, which become hot as they fly through the air, and so much so that even the lead fixed to them melts. If arrows become so hot, the air itself through which they are carried must be much hotter. Therefore that motion of the heavenly orbs, and likewise of the air which is carried round together with the orbs by their impetus, produces the heat which we feel comes from the heaven, not the stars themselves. For the stars themselves are not heated either, partly because they are far distant from the air through which the heat is spread, and partly because their nature or substance is such that it does not admit accidents of that kind, such as heat and cold. The stars are indeed luminous, but not fiery, and their light contributes something of moment to the heat, as many think.

units.la: QVALES SINT STELLAE. Mouentúrne stellæ per sese,an potius cum orbibus quibus sunt adfixæ?
units.tr: OF WHAT KIND THE STARS ARE. Do the stars move of themselves, or rather together with the spheres to which they are fixed?

units.la: Non mouentur per sese, sed cum orbibus quibus affixæ sunt. Probatur.Nam stellas quidem moueri aut circumferri, sensu compertum habemus. Iam quòd moueantur, ita oportet fieri, ut aut stellæ & orbes quibus inhærent pariter quiescant: aut utrinque, hinc uidelicet stellæ, inde orbes, pariter mouentur: aut denique, ut alteris quiescentibus, alteri tantum mouentur. Atqui duo ista priora dici nequeunt. Relinquitur ergo, tertium esse uerum. Minor probatur.
units.tr: They do not move of themselves, but together with the spheres to which they are fixed. This is proved. For we have it established by the senses that the stars are carried round and moved. Now, for them to move, it must happen in one of three ways: either the stars and the spheres in which they inhere rest together; or both move together, the stars on one side and the spheres on the other; or finally, one remains at rest while the other alone moves. But the first two cannot be asserted. It remains, therefore, that the third is true. The minor premise is proved.

units.la: Primò: Cum Stellas aperte sentiamus loco dimoveri, atq; ab occidente in orientem rapi, si ponas & orbes cœlestes et stellas quiescere, necessum erit concedas quoq;, quòd terra ipsa circumagatur: atq; cum terra circuagitur, nos opinari, quòd stellæ circumvoluantur. Atqui absurdū est dicere, quòd terra moveatur (plenius id loco suo probabitur.) Igitur satius est dicere, quòd motus omnis conueniat orbibus aut stellis, nulloq; modo pariter quiescant.
units.tr: First: since we clearly perceive the stars to be displaced in place and carried from west to east, if you posit that both the heavenly spheres and the stars are at rest, you will necessarily have to concede also that the earth itself is turned round; and when the earth is turned round, we would suppose that the stars revolve. But it is absurd to say that the earth moves (this will be proved more fully in its own place). Therefore it is better to say that all motion belongs to the spheres or to the stars, and that in no way do they rest together.

units.la: Secundò: Quòd autem stellæ & orbes non moveantur utriq; pariter, ita manifestum est. Si enim pariter moverentur, tum necessario æque velociter moveretur ipsa stella, atq; orbis eam deferens. Sed istud est absurdum: igitur & illud ex quo sequitur. Minor probatur. Oporteret nãq; circulos maiores velocius moveri, quam minores: similiterq; stellas in maiorib. circulis oporteret velocius circuagi, quàm stellas circulorum minorum. Quod enim æquali tempore mouebitur per spacium maius, id velocius moveri necesse est, quàm id quod eodem tempore mouebitur per spacium minus. Sed illud ipsum quoq; absurdum est,quemadmodum perspicuè licet obserVare in stellis planetarijs. Igitur non potest fieri,ut hinc stellæ, inde orbes pariter utrique moueantur. Iam quod ad tertium membrum attinet, id ita comprobatur:Operæprecium est,aut orbes moueri,aut stellas moueri. Non est autem uerisimile,quòd stellæ tantùm moueantur. Necessum enim foret,eas suo ingressu quasi discindere aliquam circuli partem, adcoq; sulcum inducere, itemq; in omnibus circulis tam magnis quàm paruis æque celerem spectari motum. Conficitur ergo, quòd moueantur ipsi orbes. Igitur tenenda est sententia, quòd stellæ per se non moueantur, sed cum orbibus quibus sunt infixæ, sicut clauus ferreus infixus rotæ circumagitur cum ipsa rota.
units.tr: Second: that the stars and the spheres do not move together in the same way is clear enough. For if they moved together, the star itself would necessarily move as swiftly as the sphere that carries it. But this is absurd, and so is that from which it follows. The minor premise is proved. For larger circles would have to move more swiftly than smaller ones, and likewise stars in larger circles would have to revolve more swiftly than stars in smaller circles. For what moves through a greater space in the same time must necessarily move more swiftly than what moves through a smaller space in the same time. But this very thing is also absurd, as can plainly be observed in the planetary stars. Therefore it cannot happen that the stars and the spheres both move together. As for the third member, it is proved thus: either the spheres move or the stars move. But it is not likely that only the stars move. For it would be necessary for them to cut, as it were, some part of the circle by their passage, and so to induce a furrow; and in all circles, great as well as small, the motion would be seen to be equally swift. It follows, therefore, that the spheres themselves move. Therefore the opinion must be held that the stars do not move of themselves, but together with the spheres to which they are fixed, just as an iron nail fixed in a wheel is turned round together with the wheel itself.

units.la: Si quis plenius istud explicari desiderat,duas adhuc probationes apud Aristotelem inueniet.
units.tr: If anyone desires this explained more fully, he will find two further proofs in Aristotle.

units.la: Utrum cœlestium orbium motus concentum aliquem mu- sicum edat?
units.tr: Do the motions of the heavenly spheres produce some musical harmony?

units.la: Non.Pythagorici quidem omnia ad numeros & sonos referentes,imaginati sunt sonos in cœlo è motu orbium gigni. Et sicut orbes ipsi ordine ac magnitudine sunt distincti, ita sonos quoq; illos distinguì,atq; harmoniam quandam reddere. Sed hæc opinio iustis rationibus euertitur.
units.tr: No. The Pythagoreans, who referred all things to numbers and sounds, imagined that sounds arise in the heavens from the motion of the spheres. And just as the spheres are distinguished by their order and size, so those sounds are distinguished too and produce a certain harmony. But this opinion is overturned by sound reasons.

units.la: Si tanta, tam multa ac celeriter mota corpora sonum ederent, non possret fieri, quin is exaudiretur,deinde suo fragore noceret his inferioribus corporibus. Compertum namque est,ualidis sonis, veluti tonitruis & similibus,aliquando grauiter læsos sensus animalium,item lapides aliaq; solida corpora esse fracta & dissecta. Atqui nihil horum sic evenire animadvertitur. Igitur sonum nullum orbes cœlestes edunt.
units.tr: If bodies so great, so many and so swiftly moved produced a sound, it could not fail to be heard, and by its crash it would harm these lower bodies. For it is known that the senses of animals have sometimes been gravely injured by loud sounds, such as thunder and the like, and that stones and other solid bodies have been broken and split. Yet nothing of this sort is observed to happen. Therefore the heavenly spheres produce no sound.

units.la: 2. Si sonus aliquis fieret in cœlo,oporteret ipsum gigni ex stellarum sive orbium inter se collisione: quemadmodum solent corpora dura,si quando violenter colliduntur,sonum edere. Atqui neq; stellæ,neq; orbes ipsi eius sunt materiæ sive substantiæ, quæ collisionem eiusmodi admittit . Igitur nequaquam suo motu sonum ullum procreant.
units.tr: 2. If some sound were made in the heavens, it would have to arise from a collision of the stars or spheres with one another, just as hard bodies give off a sound when they strike each other violently. But neither the stars nor the spheres themselves are of a substance that admits such a collision. Therefore by their motion they produce no sound at all.

units.la: •Quo ordine collocati sunt orbes cœlestes,& utrum alij alijs circumaguntur celerius?
units.tr: In what order are the heavenly spheres arranged, and do some revolve more quickly than others?

units.la: Quosdam orbes esse superiores, & extimo cœlo primoq; mobili viciniores, præterquam quód ratio ipsa satis declarat, tum astronomi in Elementis suæ artis perspicuè docét.Porrò ex ipso ordine atq; situ eorundem intelligere licet,alios citius, alios tardius circumagi.Enimuero motus primi & suprcmi cœli fertur quotidie rapidissimè ab oriente in occidentem: reliqui autem orbes planetarum, motu feruntur contrario,nimirũ ab occidente in orientem.
units.tr: That some spheres are higher, and nearer to the outermost heaven and the first mover, is clear from reason itself, and the astronomers teach it plainly in the elements of their art. Moreover, from their very order and position it can be understood that some revolve more swiftly and others more slowly. Indeed the motion of the first and highest heaven is carried round very rapidly every day from east to west, while the remaining spheres of the planets move in the opposite direction, namely from west to east.

units.la: Quare ob hanc motuum uicinorum contrarietate efficitur, ut quo orbes cœlo supremo sunt propinquiores, eo quoq; tardius motum & circuitum suum absoluant.
units.tr: Therefore, because of this contrariety of the neighbouring motions, it follows that the spheres nearer to the highest heaven also complete their motion and circuit more slowly.

units.la: Hinc igitur factum, quòd Mathematici tempora & interualla motuum singulis orbibus conuenientiû accuratè distinxerint. Saturnum aiunt cursum suum perficere spacio annorum 30. Iouem 12. Martem 2. Solem unius, Venerem & Mercurium spacio minore, Lunam mense.
units.tr: Hence the mathematicians have carefully distinguished the times and intervals of the motions appropriate to each sphere. They say that Saturn completes its course in a period of 30 years, Jupiter in 12, Mars in 2, the Sun in one; Venus and Mercury in a shorter period, and the Moon in a month.

units.la: Qua figura sunt stellæ? Rotunda seu orbiculari. Probatur.
units.tr: What shape are the stars? Round, or spherical. It is proved.

units.la: 1. Cum stellæ non moueatur per se, sed cū ipsis orbibus, quibus sunt infixæ, natura quæ nihil agit frustra, eam haud dubiè figuram stellis tribuit, quæ minimè apta est ad progressionem faciendam. Atqui talis est figura rotunda, utpote quæ nullum habet adiunctum instrumentum ad progressionem faciendam accōmodum, sed tantum apta est ad motum circularem. Igitur rectè constituitur, stellas esse figura rotunda.
units.tr: 1. Since a star does not move of itself, but together with the spheres in which it is fixed, nature, which does nothing in vain, has undoubtedly given stars that shape which is least suited to making progress. Now such is the round shape, since it has no attached instrument suited to making progress, but is fitted only for circular motion. Therefore it is rightly established that the stars are round.

units.la: 2. Rectæ rationi consentaneum est, stellas omnes iudicemus eiusdem esse figuræ, cuius unam aliquam earum esse manifestè deprehendimus. Atqui lunam, siue crescat, siue decrescat, semper rotunditate præ se ferre animaduertimus. Igitur omnes quoq; stellæ rotundæ sunt.
units.tr: 2. It accords with sound reason that we should judge all the stars to be of the same shape as the one we clearly perceive any of them to be. Now we observe that the Moon, whether it is waxing or waning, always presents a round surface to us. Therefore all the stars are round too.

units.la: Qui fit, quòd orbes cœlestes nō mouen- tur eo pluribus motibus, quo lon- gius distant à cœlo su- premo?
units.tr: Why do the heavenly spheres not have more motions the further they are from the highest heaven?

units.la: Hæc quæstio hinc nata est: Supremi orbis, in quo sunt stellæ fixæ, cum unus tantùm sit motus, quo nimirum quotidie circumagitur ab oriente in occidentem: aliorum tamen orbium, qui sunt planetarum, deprehenduntur plures motus. Deinde in his ipsis alij paucioribus contenti sunt, alij pluribus, neque id quidem certo ordine. Nam Sol & Luna, quos duos ætas Aristotelis, ut apparet, collocauit infimos, paucioribus feruntur motibus, quàm planetæ reliqui superiores. Ex sententia enim Eudoxi Sol & Luna, tantùm triplici motu ferebantur, reliqui planetæ quadruplici. Nunc autē æquius videbatur, ut juxta situm orbium, etiam motus in illis variarentur & multiplicarentur: ita nimirum, ut cùm suprema sphæra voluatur uno motu, secundus orbis, Saturni videlicet, volucretur duobus motibus, tertius tribus, quartus quatuor, atq; ita deinceps. Cur igitur istud hoc pacto non fiat? Aristoteles inquit, atque rationem reddere conatur. Respondet autem ad quæstionem adhibita similitudine de diuersis gradibus, qui spectantur in habitudine & constitutione corporum.
units.tr: This question arises from the following. The highest sphere, in which the fixed stars are, has only one motion, namely that by which it is carried round every day from east to west; yet in the other spheres, those of the planets, several motions are observed. Moreover, among these themselves some are content with fewer motions and others with more, and this not in any fixed order. For the Sun and the Moon, whom Aristotle's age evidently placed lowest, are carried by fewer motions than the other, higher planets. For according to the opinion of Eudoxus, the Sun and Moon were carried by only three motions, and the remaining planets by four. Now it seemed more fitting that, according to the position of the spheres, their motions too should vary and multiply: so that, while the highest sphere turns with one motion, the second sphere, namely that of Saturn, should turn with two motions, the third with three, the fourth with four, and so on in order. Why then is this not done in this way? Aristotle says so, and tries to give a reason. He answers the question by means of a comparison with the different degrees observed in the condition and constitution of bodies.

units.la: Primus gradus est: Corpora quædam optima sunt[?] habitudine,nec egent illa omnino exercitatione.
units.tr: The first degree: some bodies are in the best condition [?] and need no exercise at all.

units.la: Secundus gradus:Corpora quædam ut bene habeant,egent saltem una exercitatione:veluti deambulatione.
units.tr: The second degree: some bodies, in order to be in good condition, need at least one exercise, such as walking.

units.la: Tertius gradus: Quædam ut bene habeant,eget pluribus exercitijs:ut cursu,pugna,lucta,&c.
units.tr: The third degree: some, in order to be in good condition, need several exercises, such as running, boxing, wrestling, etc.

units.la: Quartus gradus: Quædam corpora nullis prorsus exercitijs possunt ad bonam habitudinem persectam peruenire,sed tamen modicè illis adiuuantur.
units.tr: The fourth degree: some bodies can by no exercise at all attain to perfect good condition, yet they are moderately helped by them.

units.la: Quintus gradus:Quædam corpora neq; perueniunt ad bonam habitudinem ullis exercitijs, neq; etiam his ullo modo adiuuatur. Perfectio autem maior, prætereà actio facilior in ijs omnibus esse iudicatur,quæ quam minimo negotio bene habent.
units.tr: The fifth degree: some bodies neither attain good condition by any exercises, nor are they helped in any way by them. Moreover, it is judged that in all those bodies which are in good condition with the least effort, there is greater perfection and, besides, easier activity.

units.la: Ad eundem igitur modum iudicandum est de rebus cœlestibus atq; ipsis orbibus.
units.tr: Therefore one must judge in the same way about the heavenly bodies and the spheres themselves.

units.la: Ipsum primum mouens, quod per se optimum est, nulliusq; prorsus indiget, quin potius omnibus aliis aliquid impartit & communicat, se habet ut corpora illa primi gradus.
units.tr: The first mover, which is in itself the best and needs nothing at all, but rather imparts and communicates something to all the others, stands in the place of those bodies of the first degree.

units.la: Suprema sphæra eidem primo enti & optimo proxima est,ideoq; perfectior, atq; se habet ut corpora secundi gradus: quamobrem uno etiam motu contenta est.
units.tr: The highest sphere, being nearest to that first and best being, is more perfect, and stands in the place of bodies of the second degree; for this reason it is content with one motion alone.

units.la: Superiores planetæ sub hac constituti plusculum distant à primo atq; optimo ente, ideoq; minus perfectionis in ijs spectatur: quocirca se habent ut corpora tertij gradus: hinc vero pluribus etiam motibus circumvoluuntur.
units.tr: The higher planets, placed beneath it, are somewhat further from the first and best being, and so less perfection is seen in them; therefore they stand in the place of bodies of the third degree, and for this reason they are carried round by several motions.

units.la: 4. Planetæ inferiores, Sol & Luna, quoniam longius distant à primo atq; optimo ente, non possunt ab eo tantam perfectionem accipere, quantam planetæ superiores: tamen aliquid ab eo participât, unde se habent ut corpora quarti gradus. Itaq; paucioribus etiâ motibus quàm superiores circumagūtur.
units.tr: 4. The lower planets, the Sun and Moon, since they are further from the first and best being, cannot receive from it as much perfection as the higher planets; yet they share something of it, and so they stand in the place of bodies of the fourth degree. Therefore they are also carried round by fewer motions than the higher planets.

units.la: 5. Longissimè à primo illo ente abest terra, eaq; se habet ut corpora quinti gradus: quamobrem omni motu destituta cernitur.
units.tr: 5. The earth is furthest away from that first being, and it stands in the place of bodies of the fifth degree; for this reason it is seen to be devoid of all motion.

units.la: Itaq; ex hac cōparatione intelligere promptum est, quî fiat, quòd orbium cœlestium alij pluribus, alij paucioribus motibus circumagantur.
units.tr: From this comparison, therefore, it is easy to understand why some of the heavenly spheres are carried round by more motions and others by fewer.

units.la: Quare in sphæra suprema stellæ sunt innumerabiles, in singulis autem inferioribus tantùm singulæ?
units.tr: Why are the stars in the highest sphere innumerable, but in each of the lower spheres only single stars?

units.la: Rationes duæ reddi possunt. Prior, à dignitate supremæ sphæræ: Quo sphæra est dignior, eo pluribus stellis ornari eam æquum est. Atqui suprema sphæra omnium dignissima est: igitur merito infinitis stellis ornatur. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur: In prima sphæra est plus vitæ quam in reliquis, imò ipsa est quasi vita omnium reliquarum, cum ab ea vitis quasi influat in reliquas, cum item ipsa cōtineat secumq; volvat omnes sphæras inferiores: deinde ipsa est ucluti principium respectu aliarum, utpote quae primo moventi sit proxima, necnon simplicissimo velocissimoq; gaudeat motu.
units.tr: Two reasons can be given. The first comes from the dignity of the highest sphere: the more worthy a sphere is, the more fitting it is that it be adorned with many stars. But the highest sphere is the most worthy of all, so it is rightly adorned with infinite stars. The major premise is obvious. The minor is proved thus: there is more life in the first sphere than in the rest; indeed it is in a way the life of all the others, since life flows from it into the others, and it also contains and carries round all the lower spheres. Then it is as it were the principle with respect to the others, since it is nearest to the first mover and rejoices in the simplest and swiftest motion.

units.la: Posterior, ex proportione: Orbes inferiores pluribus circumaguntur motibus, orbis autem supremus tantum uno. Quare ut sit quaedam proportio dignitatis orbium inter se, recte natura ordinavit, ut quantum aliis orbibus superadditum est in motu, tantum addatur primo orbi in ornatu & frequentia stellarum.
units.tr: The second reason comes from proportion: the lower orbs are carried round by several motions, but the highest orb by only one. Therefore, so that there may be a certain proportion of dignity among the orbs, nature has rightly ordained that as much as is added to the other orbs in motion, so much is added to the first orb in adornment and number of stars.

units.la: Hucusq; satis multa de coelo atq; stellis: restat nonnulla disquiramus de terra, non quidem ut elemento, sed ut centro, circum quod coelum in orbem voluitur. Ac primum quidem differemus de terrae situ, hinc de eius quiete, postremo de figura.
units.tr: Thus far enough has been said about the heavens and the stars. It remains to inquire into some things concerning the earth, not indeed as an element but as the centre around which the heavens revolve in a circle. First we shall discuss the position of the earth, then its rest, and last its shape.

units.la: DE TERRA MVNDI centro.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE EARTH, THE centre OF THE WORLD

units.la: Utrum terra sit in mundi medio, sitq; mundi ipsius centrum?
units.tr: Whether the earth is in the middle of the world, and is the very centre of the world?

units.la: Variae fuerunt veterum philosophorum de hac quaestione opiniones.
units.tr: The opinions of the ancient philosophers on this question have been various.

units.la: I. Prima: Plurimorum, & fere omnium qui dixerunt mundum esse finitum, consensus est, terram sitam esse in mundi medio. Qui autem infinitum esse mundum arbitrati sunt, non potuerunt aliquid definire. Ubi enim designent medium in infinito?
units.tr: I. The first: most, and almost all, of those who have said that the world is finite agree that the earth is situated in the middle of the world. Those, however, who thought the world infinite could define nothing, for where would they mark the middle in the infinite?

units.la: II. Secunda: Pythagoricis placuit, in mundi medio esse ignem: terram autem ueluti stellam quandam circū illum moueri, suoq; motu diem ac noctem efficere: diem quidem, in parte ad ignem conuersa: no Iidemq; aliam adhuc terram posuerunt, huic nostræ oppositam, quam <bl>ἀντίχθονα</bl> terram appellarunt.
units.tr: II. The second: it pleased the Pythagoreans that fire is in the middle of the world, and that the earth, like a certain star, moves around it and by its motion produces day and night: day in the part turned toward the fire, and night in the part turned away. They also posited another earth, opposite to this one of ours, which they called the counter-earth [ἀντίχθονα].

units.la: Ignem aut in medio debere constitui, probarūt. Quo dignius est corpus, eo digniore occupare locū meretur. Ignis autem tum ob claritatem, tum ob subtilitatem, deniq; et ob uim agendi dignior est terra. Quare & digniore locū, mediū uidelicet (nam is quocunq; extremo loco est honoratior) obtinebit.
units.tr: They proved that fire ought to be placed in the middle. The more worthy a body is, the more it deserves to occupy a worthier place. Fire, however, is more worthy than earth, both on account of its brightness, its subtlety, and finally its power of acting. Therefore it will also obtain the more worthy place, namely the middle, for that is more honourable than any extreme place.

units.la: Quo quid preciosius et nobilius est, eo debet diligetius conseruari. Ignis autem inter elementa praestat: igitur diligentissime debet conseruari. Commodius aut conseruari non posset, quam in ipso mundi medio, ubi terra aliisq; circumpositis tanquam muris includeretur. Quare ignis in mundi medio situs est.
units.tr: The more precious and noble a thing is, the more carefully it ought to be preserved. Fire, however, excels among the elements, so it must be preserved most carefully. It could not be preserved more conveniently than in the very middle of the world, where it would be enclosed as if by walls by the earth and the other bodies surrounding it. Therefore fire is situated in the middle of the world.

units.la: Sed diluuntur hæ rationes, si animaduertamus, alia ratione ignem posse dici mundi medium, alia ratione terram. Dupliciter namq; medium dicitur. uno modo, ut refertur ad magnitudinem tantum: ueluti cum umbilicus appellatur medium corporis humani, quòd quando tota hominis spectatur magnitudo, ipse in medio positus inuenitur. Alio modo medium refertur ad uirtutē & naturam: quo quidem pacto corporis humani medium erit thorax siue pectus, utpote in quo cor, membrum uirtute nobilissimum, sedem habet. Ergo si medium spectemus secundum uirtutem ac naturā, sane hoc pacto ignis in medio positus, non male dicetur: sin autem medium mundi spectemus secundum magnitudinem, tum quidem terra proprie erit mundi medium. Ita aute debet praesens quaestio accipi, ut intelligamus inquiri, num terra medium locum obtineat in uniuersa mundi magnitudine.Recepta aute est sententia,Terram in mūdi medio sitam esse.quam sententiam esse ueram, in sequetibus clarius perspicietur.
units.tr: But these arguments are refuted if we notice that fire can be called the middle of the world in one way, and earth in another. For "middle" is said in two ways. In one way it refers to magnitude only: thus the navel is called the middle of the human body, because when the whole magnitude of a man is considered, it is found to be placed in the middle. In another way the middle refers to power and nature: in this way the middle of the human body will be the thorax or chest, since the heart, the member most noble in power, has its seat there. If, then, we consider the middle according to power and nature, fire placed in the middle is certainly not wrongly said to be so; but if we consider the middle of the world according to magnitude, then the earth will properly be the middle of the world. The present question ought to be understood in this way, that we see what is being inquired: whether the earth holds the middle place in the whole magnitude of the world. The accepted opinion, however, is that the earth is situated in the middle of the world, which opinion will be seen more clearly to be true in what follows.

units.la: Terra mouetūrne, an quiescit?
units.tr: Does the earth move, or does it rest?

units.la: De hac quoq; quaestione opiniones philosophorum diuersae fuerunt.
units.tr: On this question too the opinions of the philosophers have differed.

units.la: I. Prima: Pythagorici, & quibuscunque uisum est terram non esse sitam in medio, arbitrati sunt eam moueri.
units.tr: I. The first: the Pythagoreans, and whoever thought that the earth is not situated in the middle, judged that it moves.

units.la: II. Secunda: Eorum qui terram dixerunt sitam in medio, nonnulli etiam asseruerunt eam moueri, idq; circum mundi axem: quod in Platonis Timæo relatum est.
units.tr: II. The second: of those who said that the earth is situated in the middle, some also asserted that it moves, and that around the axis of the world; this is reported in Plato's Timaeus.

units.la: III. Tertia: Caeteris fere omnibus placet terra quiescere, quamuis nō omnes adducunt pares & æquē ualidas rationes.
units.tr: III. The third: almost all the others hold that the earth rests, although not all of them bring equal and equally strong reasons.

units.la: 1.[?] Xenophanes Colophonius existimauit terram quiescere, quòd inferior eius pars infinitae existat magnitudinis: uastam enim molem omnem motum prohibere. Quam rationem ut vanam irrisit Empedocles, dicēs, posita infinita terra, debere etiam infinitam constituì aquam, atq; ita deinceps.
units.tr: 1. Xenophanes of Colophon thought the earth rests because its lower part is of infinite extent, for a vast mass prevents every motion. Empedocles mocked this reason as vain, saying that if the earth is posited infinite, water must also be posited infinite, and so on in turn.

units.la: 2.[?] Thales Milesius dixit terram quiescere, quòd ligni instar innatet aquæ, neq; aqua patiatur illam deorsum, aut ullam in partem ferri. Sed eadem ratione quæri potest, cui rei incumbat aqua terram sustinens? Deinde sicut aer non impedit casum seu motum aquæ: ita verisimile non est, ab aqua impediri motum terræ, maximè cum quantum aqua pondere superat aerem, tantum etiam terra pondere superat aquam. Postremò, palàm uidemus, exiguam terræ portionem, si in aquam proijciatur, statim moueri, & ima petere: quid ni igitur eodem modo moueretur atq; descenderet in aquas ingens terræ moles?
units.tr: 2. Thales of Miletus said the earth rests because it floats on water like wood, and the water does not allow it to be carried downward or in any direction. But by the same reasoning one may ask: on what does the water rest, supporting the earth? Further, just as air does not impede the fall or motion of water, so it is not likely that the motion of the earth is impeded by water, especially since as much as water surpasses air in weight, so much does earth surpass water in weight. Lastly, we plainly see that a small portion of earth, if thrown into water, immediately moves and seeks the bottom; why, then, would not an immense mass of earth move in the same way and sink into the waters?

units.la: 3.[?] Anaximanes, Anaxagoras & Democritus terræ motu prohiberi opinabantur, propter amplam eius latitudinem æquatamq; superficiem: hanc enim tantam esse, ut aerem circumpositum diuidere nullo modo possit. Aere autem nulla ex parte diuiso, quo moueatur terra? Sed neque aer potest loco cedere, utpote non habens quo se recipiat: quare nec terra aliquem aeris locum subire valet. Eadem autem ratione uidemus, in vasculū, cui unum tantum sit exiguum foramen, non ingredi aquam, quòd nimirum aer inclusus, qui nusquam potest egredi, obsistat. Quòd si autè superne foramen aliud fiat, per quod erumpat aer, tum aqua facilè ingredietur. Sed non potest hæc ratio subsistere. Primò, quia imaginantur, terram tantùm esse latam, & æquabili superficie extentam. quod falsum esse, ubi de figura terræ dicetur, apparebit. Secundò: Eodem modo posset dici, ipsam magnitudinem (quamuis sphæricæ figuræ) obstare, quo minus terra moueatur. Tertiò: Quies terræ debet omnino esse aut naturalis, aut uiolen-ta. Si autem quiescit tantùm propter obsistentem aquam uel aerem, tum erit quies terræ uiolenta. Hoc autem si detur, multas hinc absurditates sequi necesse est.
units.tr: 3. Anaximenes, Anaxagoras and Democritus thought the earth was prevented from moving by its broad extent and level surface, for this is so great that it can in no way divide the air around it. But if the air is divided nowhere, where is the earth to be moved? Nor can the air give way to a place, since it has nowhere to withdraw; therefore neither can the earth enter any place of air. By the same reasoning we see that water does not enter a little vessel which has only one tiny hole, because, of course, the enclosed air, which can escape nowhere, resists. But if another hole is made above, through which the air may burst out, then the water will enter easily. But this reasoning cannot stand. First, because they imagine the earth to be only broad and extended with an even surface; that this is false will appear when the shape of the earth is discussed. Second, in the same way it could be said that its very magnitude (although it is of spherical shape) hinders the earth from moving. Third, the rest of the earth must be either natural or violent. If, however, it rests only because of the water or air resisting, then the rest of the earth will be violent. But if this is granted, many absurdities must necessarily follow from it.

units.la: 4. Empedocles arbitratus est terram quiescere ob celerrimâ & rapidissimam ipsius cœli circumactionem. quemadmodum namque, si uasculum celeriter in orbem rotetur, aqua ei imposita nequaquam effluit, sed ob celerrimam circumactionem inclusa manet: ita etiam, cum cœlum ocyssimè circumagatur, terra in medio fixa immobilisque hæret. Atqui infirma est et hæc ratio Empedoclis. Quæri enim potest ex Empedocle, qui litem & amicitiam constituit omnium rerum naturalium principia: Qua de causa quievit terra, quo tempore per litem nondum erant cœlum & elementa ab invicem separata, atque cœlum non circumvoluebatur? Item, vis circumactionis cœli non derivatur ad terram usque: etenim si quæ paulò grauiora ferantur per aerem, ea non rapiuntur cum aere à motu cœli, sed rectà descendunt ad terram. Adhæc, sicut non est dicendum, quòd ignis moueatur & feratur sursum propter cœli circumactionem, cum tamen cœlo sit admodum propinquus: ita non est dicendum, quòd terra quiescat feratúrque deorsum propter cœli circumactionem, præsertim cum à cœlo absit longius. Breuiter, Circumactione fieri, ut leuia ascendant sursum, grauia descendant deorsum, nullo modo dici potest.
units.tr: 4. Empedocles thought the earth rests because of the very swift and rapid circular motion of the heaven. For just as, if a little vessel is whirled round quickly, water placed in it by no means flows out but remains enclosed by the very rapid rotation, so also, since the heaven is turned round most swiftly, the earth, fixed in the middle, remains immovable. Yet this reasoning of Empedocles is weak. For it may be asked of Empedocles, who made strife and friendship the principles of all natural things: for what reason did the earth rest at the time when, through strife, heaven and the elements were not yet separated from one another, and heaven was not revolving? Likewise, the force of the heaven's rotation does not extend down as far as the earth; for if somewhat heavier things are carried through the air, they are not swept along with the air by the motion of heaven, but fall straight down to the earth. Besides, just as it must not be said that fire moves and is carried upward because of the rotation of heaven, although it is very near to heaven, so it must not be said that the earth rests and is carried downward because of the rotation of heaven, especially since it is much farther from heaven. In short, it cannot in any way be said that light things ascend and heavy things descend by rotation.

units.la: 5. Anaximandro placuit, terram ideo quiescere, quòd cum sit in medio collocata, atq; omni ex parte æqualiter distans ab extremis, ubiq; etiam sui similis, nihil esse potest ob quod uel in hanc, uel il-lam partem moueretur. Verùm hæc sententia si certa esset, tum necessum foret quiescere quicquid usquam in medio ponitur, quasi uero in medio poni causa esset quietis. Deinde, ne id quidem quietis causa esse potest, quòd sit ubique sui similis: sed debet potius spectari aliquid positū in natura eius, quod causam monstret, non modò cur quiescat, uerumetiam cur deorsum feratur. Peraquè absurdum est quærere, cur terra ponatur & quiescat in medio: atque quærere, cur ignis constitutus sit inter elementa loco supremo. Rationes peti debent ex naturali grauitate & leuitate.
units.tr: 5. Anaximander held that the earth rests because, being placed in the middle and equally distant on every side from the extremities, and being alike everywhere, there can be nothing for which it should move towards this part or that. But if this opinion were sound, then whatever is placed anywhere in the middle would have to be at rest, as though being in the middle were the cause of rest. Again, not even its being alike in every part can be the cause of rest. Rather, we should look for something in its nature that shows the cause, not only why it rests but also why it is carried downwards. It is just as absurd to ask why the earth is placed and rests in the middle as to ask why fire is set in the highest place among the elements. The reasons must be drawn from natural heaviness and lightness.

units.la: Hactenus satis persecuti sumus rationes aliorum philosophorum, quibus docere conantur, cur terra quiescat. Cum autem ea infirmae sint, uti comprobatum abunde est, operaepretium est, alias magis firmas certioresq; proferri. Tales igitur iam ex ipsius Aristotelis sententia subijciemus.
units.tr: So far we have sufficiently pursued the reasons of other philosophers, by which they try to teach why the earth rests. Since these are weak, as has been amply shown, it is worth while to put forward others that are firmer and more certain. Such we shall now set out from the very opinion of Aristotle himself.

units.la: Prima ratio, cuincens[?] quod terra non possit moveri circulariter, sicut Pythagorici existimabant: Si terra moveretur circulariter, sive in medio mundi, sive extra medium mundi, tum motus in ea esset violentus: si autem violentus esset, & praeter naturam, tum non posset esse perpetuus & sempiternus. Nullum enim violentum perpetuum. Atqui absurdum est dicere, terra agitari eo motu qui non sit ei perpetuus & sempiternus. Igitur falsum est, terram moveri circulariter. Maior probatur: Si motus circularis esset terrae naturalis, & non violentus, necessario procul dubio spectaretur idem motus etiam in singulis terrae partibus. Idem namque motus naturalis convenit & toti, & partibus. Atqui nullae partes terrae natura moventur circulariter: igitur neque tota terra. Quare si motus circularis terrae adsit, eum violentum esse oportet iudicemus.
units.tr: The first reason, that the earth cannot be moved circularly, as the Pythagoreans thought: If the earth were moved circularly, whether in the middle of the world or outside the middle of the world, then its motion would be violent. But if its motion were violent and contrary to nature, it could not be perpetual and everlasting, for no violent motion is perpetual. Yet it is absurd to say that the earth is moved by a motion that is not perpetual and everlasting for it. Therefore it is false that the earth moves circularly. The major premise is proved thus: If circular motion were natural to the earth and not violent, the same motion would certainly be found in each single part of the earth, without doubt. For the same natural motion belongs both to the whole and to the parts. But no parts of the earth are naturally moved circularly; therefore neither is the whole earth. Hence, if a circular motion of the earth were present, we must judge it to be violent.

units.la: Secunda ratio idem probans: Omnia corpora quae circulariter circumaguntur, ea pluribus quoq; motibus quam uno (excepta sphaera prima & suprema) feruntur. Atqui terra non fertur pluribus motibus. Igitur neq; circulariter mouetur. Maior probatur: Præterquam enim quòd corpora mouentur motu circulari sibi proprio, etiam circumaguntur motu sphærae primæ circum axem & polos zodiaci. Minor similiter probatur: Si alio motu adhuc moueretur terra, tum stellæ fixæ non semper cernentur ad easdem terræ partes oriri & occidere, quemadmodum planetas id uidemus in diuersis facere partibus.
units.tr: The second reason proving the same: All bodies that are turned round circularly are also carried by more motions than one (except the first and highest sphere). But the earth is not carried by more motions. Therefore it is not moved circularly. The major premise is proved thus: For apart from the fact that bodies are moved by their own circular motion, they are also turned round by the motion of the first sphere about the axis and the poles of the zodiac. The minor premise is proved similarly: If the earth were moved by yet another motion, then the fixed stars would not always be seen to rise and set at the same parts of the earth, as we see the planets do in different parts.

units.la: Tertia ratio: Eundem oportet esse motum terræ totius, qui est partium. Atqui partes natura feruntur ad medium, nec mouentur circulariter. Igitur tota quoq; terra ad medium fertur, & non mouetur circulariter. Maior est manifesta. Minor probatur tum experientia, tum eo quòd omne graue natura tendit deorsum: quamobrem terram, cum sit omnium grauissima, oportet recta linea deorsum tendere. Ex his igitur manifestum euadit, terram nullo modo moueri circulariter, sed ad medium ferri. Porrò si terra fertur ad medium, necessum est etiam in medio quiescat. Quod ita demonstratur: Nulla res naturalis in loco ad quem naturaliter fertur, mouetur, sed ibi gaudet quiescere. Atqui terra naturaliter ad medium mundi fertur. Ergo cùm ipsa in medio mundi sit posita (quod suprà probatum est) necessario ibi quiescit. Enimuero sicut ignis semper contendit ad locum superiorem, neq; cum eo peruenerit, ibi quiescit: ita etiam terra semper ad medium contendit, quò cum peruenerit, quiescit.
units.tr: The third reason: The motion of the whole earth must be the same as that of its parts. But by nature the parts are carried towards the middle and are not moved circularly. Therefore the whole earth too is carried towards the middle and is not moved circularly. The major premise is plain. The minor is proved both by experience and by the fact that every heavy thing naturally tends downwards; wherefore the earth, since it is the heaviest of all, must tend downwards in a straight line. From these things it becomes evident that the earth is in no way moved circularly, but is carried towards the middle. Moreover, if the earth is carried towards the middle, it must also rest in the middle. This is shown thus: No natural thing moves in the place to which it is naturally carried, but there it rejoices to rest. But the earth is naturally carried to the middle of the world. Therefore, since it is placed in the middle of the world (as was proved above), it necessarily rests there. Indeed, just as fire always strives towards the higher place and, once it has arrived there, rests, so the earth also always strives towards the middle, and when it has arrived there, it rests.

units.la: Confirmatur conclusio hæc suffragijs Astrologorum,qui,postquam deprehenderūt,quamuis terræ partem æquis spacijs ab utroq; polo semper distare, item stellas fixas ad eadem loca semper oriri & occidere : definiuerunt omnes,terram in medio mundi esse positam atq; quiescere.
