units.tr: This conclusion is confirmed by the testimony of the astrologers, who, having observed that a part of the earth is always equally distant from each pole, and likewise that the fixed stars always rise and set at the same places, have all determined that the earth is placed in the middle of the world and rests.

units.la: Quænam est figura terræ?
units.tr: What is the shape of the earth?

units.la: Iterum diuersæ de terræ figura opiniones extiterunt. 1. Quamplurimi dixerunt,eam esse rotundam. 2. Alij senserunt, habere figuram tympani: quod duobus argumentis nisi sunt comprobare.
units.tr: Again, different opinions have arisen about the shape of the earth. 1. Very many have said that it is round. 2. Others have thought it has the figure of a drum, which they tried to prove by two arguments.

units.la: Primum argumentum: Cum Solis pars supra terram, pars verò infra terram consistit, seu cum oritur, seu cum occidit, tunc Sol fertur recta linea, & non circulari. Si autem terra esset rotunda, deberet sectio illa fieri linea circulari siue arcu. Atqui intelligere debebant, circulorum, præsertim magnorum, partes si procul conspiciantur, plane rectas lineas apparere: quando constat, etiam paruorum circulorum lineas, si longo interuallo sint dissitæ, rectas uideri.
units.tr: The first argument: Since part of the sun stands above the earth and part below it, whether it is rising or setting, then the sun moves in a straight line and not in a circle. But if the earth were round, that section would have to be made by a circular line or arc. Yet they ought to have understood that the parts of circles, especially great circles, when seen from afar, appear to be plainly straight lines, since it is established that even the lines of small circles appear straight if they are viewed from a long distance.

units.la: Secundum: Si terra quiescit, necessum est figura habeat quieti maximè accōmodā. Atqui figura tympani,quoniam latitudinem habet, magis accommoda est ad quietem quàm sphærica, quæ corpus reddit admodum uolubile. Ergo terra tympani figurā habet. Sed cum quietis aut motus causæ non à figurā, sed ex rerum ipsarum natura, ueluti ex gravitate aut leuitate, peti debeant: intelligit quiuis, infirmum esse & hoc argumentum.
units.tr: The second: If the earth rests, it must have a shape very well suited to rest. But the shape of a drum, since it has breadth, is better suited to rest than a spherical shape, which renders the body very easily rolled. Therefore the earth has the shape of a drum. But since the causes of rest or motion ought to be sought not from the shape but from the nature of the things themselves, such as from heaviness or lightness, anyone can see that this argument is also weak.

units.la: Retinenda igitur sententia est, Terram esse rotundam. Conclusio hæc probatur.
units.tr: The opinion that the earth is round must therefore be retained. This conclusion is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. A' motu ipsius terræ: Necesse est terra esse figurae rotundae, quoniam quælibet eius pars natura ad medium siue centrum quoddam commune contendit. Vbi autem quælibet pars ad medium fertur, una non vult longius abesse quàm alia, sed simul in orbem omnes conglomerantur.
units.tr: 1. From the motion of the earth itself: It is necessary that the earth be of a round shape, since each of its parts naturally tends towards the middle or some common centre. Where each part is carried towards the middle, no part wishes to be farther away than another, but all are gathered together into a sphere.

units.la: 2. Omnia corpora grauia in cœlo descendentia feruntur recta linea ad medium, siue ad unum idemq; commune centrum, prorsus uti in circuli peripheria ducuntur ad unum centrum rectæ lineæ. Talis igitur grauium corporum descensus argumento est, quòd terra sit rotunda, in medio sui centrum habens. Sumptum est argumetum à natura corporum grauium. Confirmatur idem nonnullis experimentis Mathematicorum.
units.tr: 2. All heavy bodies descending in the heavens are carried in a straight line to the middle, or to one and the same common centre, just as straight lines drawn from the circumference of a circle lead to one centre. Such a descent of heavy bodies is therefore evidence that the earth is round, having its centre in the middle of itself. The argument is taken from the nature of heavy bodies. The same is confirmed by some experiments of the mathematicians.

units.la: 3. Ex eclipsi Lunæ: Eclipsis Lunæ euenit interpositione terræ inter Solem & Lunam, adeoq; terra umbrā procreante in corpore Lunæ. Atqui quotiescunq; contingit Lunam pati eclipsin, pars obscurata rescinditur ab alia per lineam curuam seu circularem . Igitur terrā,quæ talem umbram procreat,rotundam esse oportet.
units.tr: 3. From the eclipse of the moon: An eclipse of the moon happens by the interposition of the earth between the sun and the moon, and so the earth, casting its shadow upon the body of the moon. But whenever the moon suffers an eclipse, the darkened part is cut off from the rest by a curved or circular line. Therefore the earth, which casts such a shadow, must be round.

units.la: 4. Ex mutatione horizontis: Si ab arctico seu meridie progrediamur septentrionem versus, semper quo longius progredimur, in eo magis diversos horizontes incidimus, & stellæ quæ prope meridiem lucebant, incipiunt occultari: contrà ad septentrionalem plagam incipiunt novæ stellæ, quæ antea occultæ fuerant, apparere. Hoc autem non fieret, si terra esset alia figura quàm rotunda. Ergo planum hinc fit, terram rotundam existere.
units.tr: 4. From the change of the horizon: If we advance from the arctic, or from the south, towards the north, the farther we go, the more different horizons we encounter, and the stars that shone near the south begin to be hidden, while on the northern side new stars, which had been hidden before, begin to appear. But this would not happen if the earth were of any shape other than round. Therefore it is plain from this that the earth exists as a round body.

units.la: 5. Mathematici volentes metiri terræ magnitudinem, observarunt, omni gradui in cœlo respondere 56 milliaria Gallica & duas tertias milliaris, ex sententia Alfragani. Quamobrem ad 360 gradus cœli respicientes, & unicuiq; gradui opponentes 56 milliaria cum duabus tertijs, collegerunt absolutam terræ amplitudinem. Hinc vero conficitur, sicut cœlum ipsum est rotundum, ita terram quoque rotundam existere. Hæc de terra, ut centrum mundi est, satis multa.
units.tr: 5. The mathematicians, wishing to measure the size of the earth, observed that each degree in the heavens corresponds to 56 and two-thirds Gallic miles, according to the opinion of Alfraganus. Wherefore, looking to the 360 degrees of the heavens and assigning 56 and two-thirds miles to each degree, they gathered the whole extent of the earth. From this, moreover, it follows that, just as the heaven itself is round, so the earth too is round. So much, then, about the earth as the centre of the world.

units.la: Cæterum posteaquam hucusque disseruimus, primum de universo, deinde de cœlo, quod est primum è quinque corporibus simplicibus, præterea etiam de terra, quæ mundi medium est: restat de reliquis corporibus simplicibus, præcipuè aut de generatione & corruptione, de grauitate & leuitate, quæ sunt eorundem corporum affectiones, dicamus. Cum enim ex corporibus simplicibus, id est elementis, omnia fiant, & eorum aliud propter leuitatem à medio, aliud propter grauitatem ad medium feratur: sane qui has eorum affectiones norit, is de natura elementorum uidebitur recte iudicare posse.
units.tr: But since we have so far discussed, first the universe, then the heavens, which is the first of the five simple bodies, and besides this also the earth, which is the middle of the world, there remains to speak of the other simple bodies, chiefly concerning generation and corruption, and concerning heaviness and lightness, which are affections of these same bodies. For since all things are made from simple bodies, that is, the elements, and of these one is carried away from the middle on account of its lightness, another is carried to the middle on account of its heaviness, surely whoever knows these affections will seem able to judge rightly about the nature of the elements.

units.la: DE GENERATIONE & motu corporum na- turalium. An sit generatio & corruptio?
units.tr: On the generation and motion of natural bodies. Is there generation and corruption?

units.la: CErtum est, Generatio debet esse ex elementis, & in his quae ex elementis constant: aut generatio prorsus non est. Itaq; variae fuerunt veterum philosophorum de hac quaestione, An uidelicet sit generatio, opiniones.
units.tr: It is certain that generation must take place out of the elements and in those things which are composed of the elements; otherwise generation does not occur at all. Therefore the opinions of the ancient philosophers on this question, namely whether there is generation, have been various.

units.la: 1. Parmenides & Melissus generationem & corruptionem simpliciter negarunt: nihil enim quicquam generari aut corrumpi, sed tantum nobis uideri. Qui quidem non omnino male statuerunt, sententes nimirum, quaedam esse ingenerabilia & incorruptibilia sempiternaq;: sed in hoc aberrarunt, quod arbitrati sunt, idem dici posse de rebus naturalibus uniuersis: deinde non satis physicè locuti sunt, cum de ingenerabilibus & incorruptibilibus non differat physicus, sed metaphysicus.
units.tr: 1. Parmenides and Melissus denied generation and corruption outright: nothing is generated or corrupted, but it only seems so to us. They were not entirely wrong in holding that some things are ungenerable, incorruptible and everlasting. But they erred in thinking the same could be said of all natural things. Moreover, they did not speak sufficiently as physicists, since the ungenerable and incorruptible is the concern not of the physicist but of the metaphysician.

units.la: 2. Alij generationem & corruptione constituerunt, quamuis non omnes prorsus eodē modo. Quibusdam namque placuit, omnia quidem generari: caeterum ex his quae generata sunt, quaedam corrumpi, quaedam autem permanere. Ascribitur haec sententia Hesiodo.
units.tr: 2. Others posited generation and corruption, though not all in exactly the same way. For some held that all things are indeed generated, but that of the things generated, some are corrupted and others remain. This view is ascribed to Hesiod.

units.la: 3. Nonnulli putarunt, omnia generari & corrumpi, unum tamen principium materiale existere, quod tam generationis quam corruptionis fit prorsus expers. Profecta est haec opinio à Thalete, Anaximone, caeterisq; qui unum tantum principiū posuerunt.
units.tr: 3. Some thought that all things are generated and corrupted, yet that there exists one material principle which is wholly free from both generation and corruption. This opinion came from Thales, Anaximenes and the others who posited only one principle.

units.la: 4. Visum est Platoni, uniuersa generari & corrumpi: ac generari quidē ex superficiebus, corrumpi uerò & resolui iterum in superficies.
units.tr: 4. Plato thought that all things are generated and corrupted: generated out of surfaces, and corrupted and resolved again into surfaces.

units.la: Caeterum tres illas opiniones priores Aristoteles praesenti loco plenius non impugnat (enimuero prima in lib. 1. Physicae auscultationis discussa est, de secunda disseritur in lib. de generatione, de tertia agitur paulo post in libro praesenti.) At quartam longa oratione refellit, docens ex ea sequi plura incommoda, tum in disciplinis mathematicis, tum in ordine rerum naturalium: quae argumenta nos brevitatis causa praetermittimus. Satis igitur sit, ad quaestionem propositam simpliciter respondere affirmatiuè, nempe quod generatio & corruptio fit: neque opus est probationes attexere, quando praeter communem omnium eruditorum consensum, praeter suum experimēta, plura sequentur idē declarantia.
units.tr: Aristotle, however, does not refute those three earlier opinions more fully in the present place. (The first was discussed in Book 1 of the Physics; the second is treated in the book On Generation; the third is taken up shortly after, in the present book.) But the fourth he refutes at length, showing that many difficulties follow from it, both in the mathematical disciplines and in the order of natural things. We omit these arguments for the sake of brevity. It is enough, then, to answer the question posed simply in the affirmative, namely that generation and corruption take place. Nor is there any need to add proofs, since, apart from the common agreement of all the learned, many further experiences, which he himself has, confirm the same thing.

units.la: Utrum corpora naturalia habeant motus naturales?
units.tr: Whether natural bodies have natural motions?

units.la: Omnibus corporibus simplicibus inest aliquis motus naturalis. Corpora vero mixta sequuntur motum corporis simplicis quod in eis dominatur. Probatur primo ratione ipsius motus. Etenim cum sensu deprehendamus res ipsas moveri, necessum est eas aut motu proprio, aut motu violento ita ferri. Si prius dixeris, iam causam obtinemus: sin dixeris motu violento, tum sic argumentor: Violentus motus, est motus praeter naturam. Atqui ubicunque est motus praeter naturam, ibi oportet alium quoque esse secundum naturam. Ergo unaquaeque res naturalis aliquo naturali motu fertur. Minor probatur: Omnis privatio praesupponit habitum. Sicut aegritudo est praeter naturam, ita sanitas est secundum naturam: neque dicitur aegritudo, nisi respectu sanitatis: quare neque motus dicitur praeter naturam, nisi respectu alterius secundum naturam. Et motus praeter naturam posterior est, pluresque simul esse possunt: motus autem secundum naturam prior est atque unus tantum.
units.tr: Every simple body has some natural motion, and mixed bodies follow the motion of the simple body that dominates in them. This is proved first by the reasoning concerning motion itself. For since we perceive by the senses that things are moved, they must be moved either by their own motion or by violent motion carried along. If you say the former, we already have the cause. But if you say violent motion, I argue thus: violent motion is motion contrary to nature. But wherever there is motion contrary to nature, there must also be another motion according to nature. Therefore every natural thing is borne by some natural motion. The minor premise is proved as follows: every privation presupposes a habit. Just as sickness is contrary to nature, so health is according to nature; and sickness is not called sickness except in relation to health. So too motion is not called contrary to nature except in relation to another motion that is according to nature. Moreover, motion contrary to nature is posterior, and several such motions can exist at once; but motion according to nature is prior and is only one.

units.la: Secundo ratione quietis: Sensu deprehendimus, corpus aliquod quiescere in medio: veluti terra aut lapidem. Iam vero corpus illud quiescit ibi secundum naturam, vel praeter naturam et violente. Si dixeris quod quiescat ibi secundum naturam: sequitur, quod etiam aliquis sit motus eius ad eum locum secundum naturam. Si autem quiescit praeter naturam, oportet aliquid sit violenter id impellens et prohibens eo moveri, quo secundum naturam tendere desiderat. Ubicunq; autem ponitur aliquid violenter impediens, atque a motu naturali prohibens, ibi necesse est per contrarium aliquid constitui, et quidem naturale, quod remoto impedimento iterum motum induceret. Quemadmodum si lapis in sublimi detineatur, et violenter prohibeatur, quo minus cadat deorsum: certum est, si impedimentum illud removeatur, ipse statim deorsum feretur. Ergo posita quiete violenta, necessario sequitur, ut remoto impedimento quod quietem violentam induxit, motus naturalis succedat. Neque vero possent tam multae poni causae motus vel quietis praeter naturam, quin tandem pervenire oporteret ad aliquam causam motus vel quietis secundum naturam. Relinquitur ergo probata conclusio, quod omnia corpora naturalia naturalem habent motum. Errarunt ergo Leucippus et Democritus, dicentes corpora ἄτομα, quae ipsi existimarunt esse naturalia rerum principia, semper in spatio infinito et in vacuo moveri. Cum enim motum illis concederet, tamen neglexerunt explicare quo genere motus, id est, violentone, an naturali, illa moverentur: tum quis motus, id est, circularis ne, an recus, illis secundum naturam conueniret. Errauit item Plato in Timaeo, asserens, elementa, antequam mundus conderetur, confuse & sine ordine inter se fuisse mota. Quem quidem errorem Aristoteles refellit quatuor validis argumentis, deinde aliorum philosophorum, qui rectius sentire visi sunt, authoritate.
units.tr: Secondly, from the reasoning about rest: we perceive by the senses that some body rests in a place, as earth or a stone does. Now that body rests there either according to nature or contrary to nature and by violence. If you say it rests there according to nature, it follows that there is also some motion of it to that place according to nature. But if it rests contrary to nature, something must be forcibly impelling it and preventing it from moving to where it desires by nature to tend. Wherever something is placed that violently hinders and restrains a body from its natural motion, there must necessarily be set up, by contrast, something natural which, once the hindrance is removed, would again induce motion. Just as if a stone is held aloft and forcibly prevented from falling downward, it is certain that, if that hindrance is removed, it will at once be carried downward. Therefore, once violent rest is posited, it necessarily follows that when the hindrance which induced the violent rest is removed, natural motion takes its place. Nor could so many causes of motion or rest contrary to nature be posited without our eventually arriving at some cause of motion or rest according to nature. Therefore the conclusion is proved: all natural bodies have a natural motion. Leucippus and Democritus therefore erred, saying that the atoms [ἄτομα], which they thought to be the natural principles of things, are always moving in infinite space and in the void. For although they granted motion to them, they neglected to explain by what kind of motion they were moved, that is, whether violent or natural, and which motion, circular or straight, belonged to them according to nature. Plato also erred in the Timaeus, asserting that the elements were moved confusedly and without order among themselves before the world was framed. Aristotle refutes this error with four strong arguments, and then by the authority of other philosophers who seemed to judge more rightly.

units.la: Vtrum in corporibus, quae motu recto feruntur, causa motus existat le- uitas aut grauitas?
units.tr: Whether, in bodies that are carried by straight motion, the cause of the motion is levity or gravity?

units.la: Maxime. Probatur: Necessum omnino est corpora naturalia moueri, adeoque principium quoddam motus in se habere. Sed non potest in corporibus naturalibus insita uis naturalis, per quam ad certum locum feruntur, commodior demonstrari, quam grauitas uel leuitas: illa quidem, qua feruntur deorsum: haec vero, qua feruntur sursum. Igitur necesse est, corpora quae mouentur motu recto, initium sui motus ab ingenita grauitate aut leuitate accipere.
units.tr: Most certainly. It is proved thus: bodies in nature must necessarily be moved, and so must have in themselves some principle of motion. But no more suitable explanation can be given for the natural force inborn in natural bodies, by which they are carried to a certain place, than gravity or levity: gravity, by which they are carried downwards, and levity, by which they are carried upwards. Therefore, bodies that are moved by straight motion must receive the beginning of their motion from their innate gravity or levity.

units.la: Quomodo distinguitur motus secun- dum naturam, seu naturalis, a motu praeter naturam seu uiolento?
units.tr: How is motion according to nature, or natural, distinguished from motion beyond nature, or violent?

units.la: Distinguuntur ratione principiorum. Motus secundum naturam principium est ipsa natura, quae definitur principium eius motus in quo est: veluti cum lapis cadit deorsum, id a natura sua accipit, nimirum ab ingenita grauitate. Motus uiolenti principium est uirtus seu potentia mouens, ab alio proueniens corpore: ut cum lapis sursum propellitur manu cuiuspiam, aut instrumento aliquo. Aliquando uero hi duo motus commiscentur, atq; in eodem corpore simul existunt: ueluti quando lapis, qui natura fertur deorsum, etiam ui quadam eodem abigitur. Quod cum fit, ipse motus uiolentus in causa est, ut motus naturalis multo celerius perficiatur. Quinetiam aer ad utrumq; motum uehemēter adiuuat. Cum enim aer fit partim grauis, partim leuis (nam simpliciter grauis sola est terra, simpliciter leuis solus ignis: aer uero & aqua utriusque qualitatis sunt participes:) sua leuitate adiuuat motū uiolentū qui sursum dirigitur, sua uero grauitate adiuat motum uiolentum qui deorsum tendit. Deinde iisdem de causis aer adiuuat & permouet motū naturalem, siue sursum, siue deorsum agitetur.
units.tr: They are distinguished by their principles. The principle of motion according to nature is nature itself, which is defined as the principle of the motion in which a thing is. For example, when a stone falls downwards, it receives this from its nature, namely from its innate gravity. The principle of violent motion is a power or force that moves, coming from another body, as when a stone is pushed upwards by someone's hand or by some instrument. Sometimes, however, these two motions are mingled and exist together in the same body, as when a stone, which by nature is carried downwards, is also driven down by some force. When this happens, the violent motion itself is the cause that the natural motion is completed much more quickly. Moreover, the air greatly assists both motions. For since air is partly heavy and partly light (for earth alone is simply heavy, and fire alone simply light, while air and water partake of both qualities), by its lightness it assists the violent motion that is directed upwards, and by its heaviness it assists the violent motion that tends downwards. Then, for the same reasons, the air assists and furthers the natural motion, whether it is driven upwards or downwards.

units.la: Quorum corporum est generatio, siue quae corpora sunt causa gene- rationis?
units.tr: Of what bodies is generation, or which bodies are the cause of generation?

units.la: Manifestum est, quod elementa sunt quarumlibet rerum prima principia inter ea quae rebus ipsis insunt. Quare priusquam de generatione corporum plenius differatur, necessaria omnino est elementorum cognitio.
units.tr: It is clear that the elements are the first principles of all things, among those things that are inherent in the things themselves. Therefore, before generation of bodies is treated more fully, a knowledge of the elements is absolutely necessary.

units.la: QVID SIT? Quid est elementum?
units.tr: WHAT IS IT? What is an element?

units.la: EST corpus, in quod caetera corpora, quibus inest potentia aut actu, resoluuntur, ipsum vero nequaquam in alia corpora specie diuersa resoluitur. Qua definitione plerique omnes contenti sunt. Accommodam vero esse eam, sic declaratur. Inueniuntur namque corpora, in quibus elementorum, ex quibus illa constant, vis manifestè deprehendi potest. In carne, ligno, & similibus, ignis, terra, aqua insunt potentia: quoniam ex illis ipsis illa per alterationem quandam sunt procreata, deinde vero in eadem iterum resoluuntur. Etenim corpus animalis resoluitur in pulverem, humorem & vaporem, in quibus trium elementorum, quae enumerauimus, vis elucet. Interea autem ipsa elementa non resoluuntur in talia corpora: siquidem in igne carnem aut lignum actu seu potentia inesse, nullo modo dici potest. Neque enim generatur ex igne caro aut lignum per resolutionem ipsius ignis, sed per adiunctionem aliorum corporum simplicium, quae commixtione quadam alterantur.
units.tr: It is a body into which other bodies, which have the power or actuality of it, are resolved, while it itself is never resolved into other bodies of a different kind. Most people are content with this definition. That it is an appropriate one is shown as follows. There are bodies in which the power of the elements from which they are composed can clearly be detected. Fire, earth and water are present potentially in flesh, wood and similar things, since these were produced from them by a certain alteration, and afterwards are resolved again into them. For the body of an animal is resolved into dust, moisture and vapour, in which the power of the three elements we have listed is evident. Meanwhile, however, the elements themselves are not resolved into such bodies: for it cannot in any way be said that flesh or wood is present, actually or potentially, in fire. Indeed, flesh or wood is not generated from fire by the resolution of the fire itself, but by the addition of other simple bodies, which are altered by a certain mixture.

units.la: QVOT SINT ELEMENTA? Quot sunt elementa?
units.tr: HOW MANY ARE THE ELEMENTS? How many elements are there?

units.la: Diuersae fuerunt de hac quaestione philosophorum sententiae.
units.tr: The opinions of philosophers on this question have been diverse.

units.la: I. Quidam existimarunt elementa esse infinita, in quibus Anaxagoras censuit infinita esse elementa, eademq; corpora ὁμοιόμερα, id est, habentia similes partes. Sed reprobatur hæc opinio.
units.tr: I. Some have thought that the elements are infinite. Anaxagoras held that the elements are infinite, and that the bodies are homoeomerous [ὁμοιόμερα], that is, having like parts. But this opinion is rejected.

units.la: Primo : Palàm aduertimus, multa corpora esse ὁμοιόμερα, necnon in partes similes resoluì: cuius generis sunt caro, os, lignum. Hæc uero ipsa non sunt elementa.
units.tr: First: we plainly observe that many bodies are homoeomerous and can be resolved into like parts; of this kind are flesh, bone and wood. Yet these themselves are not elements.

units.la: Secundo : Etiamsi elementa essent eiusmodi, tamen ne propterea quidem opus foret infinita constituere. Etenim uniuersa elementorum natura rectius explicari potest, si ponantur finita, quàm si ponantur infinita. Siquidem infinitorum non potest haberi certa cognitio. Estq; communis omnium philosophorum sententia, Principia debere esse finita aut quantitate, aut specie.
units.tr: Second: even if the elements were of this kind, there would still be no need to posit them as infinite. For the whole nature of the elements can be explained more correctly if they are posited as finite than if they are posited as infinite, since no certain knowledge of the infinite can be had. And it is the common opinion of all philosophers that principles must be finite, either in quantity or in kind.

units.la: Tertio : Vnuquodq; corpus distinguitur ab alio secundum proprias eius differentias. Atqui elementorum differentiæ, quæ sunt primæ qualitates sensibiles, sunt finitæ. Ergo oportet ipsa quoque elementa finita existere.
units.tr: Third: each body is distinguished from another by its own differences. But the differences of the elements, which are the primary sensible qualities, are finite. Therefore the elements themselves must also be finite.

units.la: II. Democritus & Leucippus definierunt, magnitudines esse prima corporum elementa, atq; illas quidem multitudine infinitas, magnitudine uero indiuisibiles: ideoq; ex uno non fieri multa, neque ex multis fieri unum: sed omnium magnitudinum mutua inter se complectione produci omnia, eademq; protinus figura, ordine ac positione distingui. Verum ne hæc quidem sententia potest subsistere.
units.tr: II. Democritus and Leucippus defined magnitudes as the first elements of bodies, and these indeed infinite in multitude but indivisible in magnitude. Therefore, they held, many things do not arise from one, nor one from many; rather, all things are produced by the mutual interconnection of all magnitudes, and are distinguished at once by shape, order and position. But even this opinion cannot stand.

units.la: Primò: Nihil opus est elementa ponere infinita, ut co pacto res producantur: possunt enim etiam ex finitis produci.
units.tr: First: there is no need to posit the elements as infinite in order that things may be produced in this way, for they can also be produced from finite elements.

units.la: Secundò: Primæ qualitates, quibus distinguuntur elementa, sunt finitæ: quare ipsa quoque elementa finita esse oportet.
units.tr: Second: the primary qualities by which the elements are distinguished are finite; therefore the elements themselves must also be finite.

units.la: Tertiò: Quando constituunt magnitudines indivisibiles, euertunt [?] principia quædam artium Mathematicarum, quale hoc est: Omne continuum est divisibile in infinitum. item: Indivisibile non est continuum divisibili.
units.tr: Third: when they set up indivisible magnitudes, they overthrow certain principles of the mathematical arts, such as this: every continuum is divisible to infinity; likewise, what is indivisible is not a continuum divisible in parts.

units.la: Quartò: Pugnantia dicunt. aiunt enim, elementa esse magnitudine indiuisibilia: & interim statuunt, ignem, aerem, aquam, terram, sola differre magnitudine. Denique multa alia incommoda sequuntur ex illorum assertione, quæ enumerare longum foret. Relinquitur ergo, elementa nullo modo esse infinita. Confirmatur hæc conclusio hoc argumento: Vnicuiq; elemento & corpori simplici conuenit unus simplexq; motus. Sed motus simplices sunt finiti. Igitur ipsa quoq; corpora simplicia atq; elementa debent esse finita.
units.tr: Fourth: they say contradictory things. For they say that the elements are indivisible in magnitude, and yet at the same time they maintain that fire, air, water and earth differ only in magnitude. Finally, many other absurdities follow from their assertion, which would be too long to list. It remains, then, that the elements are by no means infinite. This conclusion is confirmed by this argument: to each element and simple body belongs one simple motion. But simple motions are finite. Therefore the simple bodies and the elements themselves must also be finite.

units.la: III. Cum duæ præcedentes opiniones non possint subsistere, quamplurimi philosophi definierunt elementa esse finita, quamuis de numero inter eos non conuenit. Primo:Quidam tantum unum esse affirmarunt: quorum alijs id esse placuit aerem, alijs ignem, alijs aquam, alijs nescio quid aqua subtilius, aere uero densius. Caeterum haud magno negotio singulorum singulae sententiae confutari possent (quod & Aristotelem uidemus erudite facere) uerum nobis satis erit una ratione generali omnes pariter refellere, quicunq; unum tantum elementum constituere sunt conati. Si enim unum tantum foret elementum, sane cum unius elementi seu corporis simplicis non posset nisi unus simplexq; motus existere, necesse esset ponere unum tantum motum simplicem. Atqui istud est absurdum: igitur & illud ex quo sequitur. Maior manifesta est ex ijs quae supra sunt tradita. Minor probatur. Nam si res naturales omnes ex uno tantum producerentur elemento, non conueniret ijs nisi unus modus eidem elemento proprius: ueluti si omnia generata essent ex igne, necessario etiam omnia tenderent sursum, atque ita de caeteris iudicandum. Atqui sensu deprehendimus, res naturales diuersis ferri motibus, atq; alias quidem semper sursum, alias uero semper deorsum, idq; secundum elemetorū, ex quibus constant, naturam. Igitur necesse est propter hac diuersitate motuum, plura quam unum elementum constituamus. Relinquitur ergo, non unum esse elementum, sed plura. Verum de certo numero paulo post.
units.tr: III. Since the two preceding opinions cannot stand, very many philosophers have defined the elements as finite, although they do not agree on their number. First, some have affirmed that there is only one: some have preferred this to be air, others fire, others water, and others something I know not what, more subtle than water and denser than air. Indeed, each of these individual opinions could be refuted with no great difficulty (as we see Aristotle doing learnedly), but for us it will be enough to refute all of them equally by one general argument, all who have tried to set up only one element. For if there were only one element, then, since one element or simple body can have only one simple motion, it would necessarily follow that only one simple motion exists. But this is absurd; therefore the premise from which it follows is also absurd. The major premise is evident from what has been delivered above. The minor is proved thus: if all natural things were produced from only one element, only one mode of motion proper to that element would belong to them; for example, if all things were generated from fire, all of them would necessarily tend upwards, and similarly for the others. But we perceive by the senses that natural things are carried by diverse motions, some always upwards and others always downwards, and this according to the nature of the elements of which they consist. Therefore, because of this diversity of motions, we must posit more than one element. It follows, then, that there is not one element but several. But concerning the definite number, we shall speak shortly.

units.la: QVALIA SINT? Sunt'ne elementa sempiterna, an potius generabilia & cor- ruptibilia?
units.tr: WHAT SORTS OF THINGS ARE THEY? Are the elements eternal, or rather generable and corruptible?

units.la: Nullo modo sempiterna dici possunt.Probatur: Quotidie experimur terram & aquam, caeteraq; corpora simplicia resolui atque corrumpi. Necessarium autem est, huiusmodi resolutionem aut infinitam esse, & nunquam terminari: aut finitam, & aliquando terminari.Non est autem dicendum prius, igitur posterius.
units.tr: They cannot be called eternal in any way. This is proved as follows: every day we experience earth, water and the other simple bodies being dissolved and corrupted. Now this dissolution must either be infinite and never come to an end, or finite and at some point come to an end. But the first cannot be said; therefore the second holds.

units.la: Quomodo elementa sunt generabilia?
units.tr: How are the elements generable?

units.la: Generantur ex se invicem. Probatur: Si sunt generabilia, oportet ea generari aut ex incorporeo, aut ex corporeo: deinde si ex corporeo, aut ex alio corpore, aut ex sese invicem. Non autem generantur ex incorporeo. Qui enim incorporeum constituit, idem constituit & vacuum separatum. Nam si ex incorporeo debeat corpus aliquod novum fieri, necessum est, ubi novum illud corpus generabitur, vacuum prius extitisse. Hoc aut absurdum esse, quis non intelligit? Conficitur ergo, quòd ex aliquo corporeo elementa generetur. Porrò si ex corporeo generatur, non tamē ex alio corpore. Si enim dicas ex alio corpore, sequitur aliquod corpus separatum ante elementa extitisse. Quod quidem absurdum est. Deinde corpus illud aut habet grauitatem, aut leuitatem, aut omnino neutrũ ex his habet. Si dicas habere, erit igitur illud ipsum quoddã elementũ: si dicas non habere, quomodo inquam motus in eo aliquis spectabitur? Certè si nullus ei motus conuenit, tum erit corpus immobile, Mathematicum, adeoq; nusquam in rerum natura subsistens, ac proinde generationi prorsus ineptum. Ex his ergo rectè concluditur, elementa generari ex sese mutuò.
units.tr: They are generated from one another. This is proved as follows. If they are generable, they must be generated either from the incorporeal or from the corporeal; and if from the corporeal, then either from another body or from one another. But they are not generated from the incorporeal. For whoever posits the incorporeal also posits separate void. For if some new body is to come into being from the incorporeal, then when that new body is to be generated, void must have existed beforehand. Who does not see that this is absurd? It follows, therefore, that the elements are generated from something corporeal. Moreover, if they are generated from the corporeal, they are not generated from another body. For if you say from another body, it follows that some separate body existed before the elements, which is indeed absurd. Further, that body either has heaviness, or lightness, or neither of these. If you say it has them, then that body will itself be some element; if you say it does not, then how, I ask, will any motion be observed in it? Certainly, if no motion belongs to it, it will be an immobile body, a mathematical one, subsisting nowhere in nature and therefore wholly unfit for generation. From these considerations, then, it is rightly concluded that the elements are generated from one another mutually.

units.la: Quomodo generantur elementa ex sese inuicem?
units.tr: How are the elements generated from one another?

units.la: Variè de hac quæstione opiniones extiterunt.
units.tr: Opinions on this question have varied.

units.la: 1. Empedocles & Democritus arbitrati sunt, elementa generari ex se inuicem per segregationem. Sed errasse hos, manifestum est. Generatio namque significat aliquid transfire à non esse ad esse. Segregatio autem tantùm significat separationem ex loco in quo quid fuerat, in locum alium: veluti cum è vase aliquid educitur in conspectum, quod antea in eodem erat abditum & inconspicuum. Itaq; quando isti imaginantur, omnia confusa permixtaq; iacere tanquam in vasto quodam chao, postea autem exeri producíq;, sane non constituunt isti veram generationem, sed tantùm apparentem. Subijcit Aristoteles adhuc tres alias rationes confutatorias, quas nos breuitatis ergò praeterimus.
units.tr: 1. Empedocles and Democritus held that the elements are generated from one another by segregation. But that these men erred is plain. For generation signifies something passing from non-being to being. Segregation, however, signifies only separation from one place, where something was, into another place, as when something is brought out of a vessel into view which had previously been hidden and unseen inside it. So when they imagine that everything lies confused and mixed together as in some vast chaos, and afterwards is brought forth and produced, they certainly do not establish true generation, but only apparent generation. Aristotle adds three further refutations, which for the sake of brevity we pass over.

units.la: 2. Aliis visum est, elementa generari ex se inui-cem, sem,facta in eis quadam commutatione seu figurarum nouatione:qucmadmodum uidemus ex eadem cera inducta modica transformatione formari modo pilam,modo tessarâ,modo aliud quippiam. Atqui à vero aliena est hæc sententia. Si namq; ita esset,necessarium foret ponere elementa corpora quædam indiuisibilia & ἄτομα : quod absurdum est. Probatur consequentiæ ratio hoc pacto.Nâ si econtrario ponantur diuisibilia,atque distinguenda veniant ratione transfigurationis: sequetur,quod pars ignis non erit ignis,& pars terræ non erit terra: ut neq; pars pyramidis est pyramis, neq; pars tessera est tessera. Sicut namq; se habet pars figurae ad figuram,ita se habet pars corporis ad corpus. Sed absurdum est dicere,quod pars ignis nō sit ignis, &c. Igitur æquè absurdum erit astruere,quod elementa sint diuisibilia atque per figuras distincta. Si autem absurdum est ponere diuisibilia, erit profecto necessarium constituere indiuisibilia: quod itidem admittendum non est.
units.tr: 2. Others have thought that the elements are generated from one another by a certain change made in them, or a renewal of figures, just as we see that from the same wax, with a slight reshaping, now a ball, now a die, now something else is formed. Yet this opinion is alien to the truth. For if it were so, it would be necessary to posit certain indivisible bodies, atoms, which is absurd. The proof of this consequence runs thus. For if, on the contrary, divisible bodies are posited, and they are to be distinguished by transfiguration, it will follow that a part of fire is not fire, and a part of earth is not earth, just as a part of a pyramid is not a pyramid, nor a part of a die a die. For as the part of a figure stands to the figure, so the part of a body stands to the body. But it is absurd to say that a part of fire is not fire, and so on. Therefore it will be equally absurd to assert that the elements are divisible and distinguished by figures. And if it is absurd to posit divisibles, it will certainly be necessary to posit indivisibles, which likewise must not be admitted.

units.la: 3. Quidam opinati sunt, elementa ex se invicem gigni,per resolutionem unius corporis corrumpendum in superficies primas, & generationem alterius ex iisdem superficiebus. Verùm multa ex hac opinione sequuntur incommoda: atq; ut cætera omittamus,uel hoc uno ipsa refellitur, quòd constituta generatione & superficiebus quæ non sunt corpora, simul constituuntur res generari ex non corpore: quod sane nullus physicis rationibus assuefactus concedet.
units.tr: 3. Some have thought that the elements are generated from one another by the resolution of one body, when it is corrupted, into first surfaces, and the generation of another from those same surfaces. But many inconveniences follow from this opinion; and, to omit the rest, it is refuted by this one point alone: once generation and surfaces, which are not bodies, are posited, it is at the same time posited that things are generated from what is not body. No one trained in physical reasoning will concede this.

units.la: Ergo tres hæ opiniones, de modo quo elementa generantur ex se invicem, reijciendæ sunt. Quæ autem vera retinendaq; [?]sit sententia, Aristoteles lib. 1. de Generatione abundè explicat.
units.tr: Therefore these three opinions about the manner in which the elements are generated from one another must be rejected. Which opinion is true and to be retained, Aristotle explains fully in the first book of On Generation.

units.la: An elementis aptè tribuantur di- versæ figuræ?
units.tr: Are various figures rightly attributed to the elements?

units.la: Philosophi nonnulli, in primis autem qui dixerunt Elementa ex se invicem generari per transfigurationem, certa figurâ unicuique corpori simplici elementoq; attribuerunt, atq; cœlo quidem sphæricam, igni pyramidalem, aeri octohedrâ, aquæ εἰκο-σαέδρῳ[?], terræ verò cubicâ: hisq; ita figuratis mundum universum constare arbitrati sunt. Sed has figuras nullo pacto elementis tribui posse, haud difficile est demonstrare.
units.tr: Some philosophers, especially those who said that the elements are generated from one another by transfiguration, assigned a definite figure to each simple body and element: to the heaven a spherical figure, to fire a pyramidal, to air an octahedral, to water an icosahedral [εἰκοσαέδρῳ], and to earth a cubic. They thought the whole universe consists of bodies so shaped. But that these figures can in no way be assigned to the elements is not difficult to demonstrate.

units.la: 1. Si ea astruantur primorum & simplicium corporum figuræ, necessarium erit concedere aliquid actu vacuum: quod cum natura pugnat. Probatur consequentia. Tam variæ enim figuræ non replebunt omne spacium, præsertim cum non possint undequaque mutuo sese contingere atq; angulos coniungere.
units.tr: 1. If the figures of the first and simple bodies are asserted, it will be necessary to concede something actually void, which is contrary to nature. The consequence is proved. Such various figures will not fill every space, especially since they cannot touch one another on every side and join their angles.

units.la: 2. Corpora simplicia figuram accipiunt pro ratione corporis contmentis[?]: quoniam gaudent undiq; attingere implereq; ipsum continens. Animadverti id perspicuè potest in aere & aqua. Quomodo igitur illis tribuentur figuræ ante nominatæ?
units.tr: 2. Simple bodies take on a figure according to the shape of the body that contains them, since they delight to touch and fill on every side the thing that contains them. This can clearly be observed in air and water. How, then, can the aforesaid figures be assigned to them?

units.la: 3. Denique non conueniunt illæ figuræ ipsorum elementorum motui locali, quem natura habent, quoq; alia propter grauitatem deorsum, alia propter leuitatem (non propter ullas figuras) sursum tendunt: neque conueniunt elementorum qualitatibus sensibilibus, quæ sunt calor, frigus, humiditas, siccitas: neque conueniunt elementorum actionibus, hoc est, facultatibus calefaciendi, humectandi, &c. Quid multa? concurrunt sanè plurima, ex quibus procliue est cuincere, quòd eæ figuræ nullo modo elementis aptari queant. Apud Aristotelem promptum est plures rationes colligere. Rectissimè autem omnia cum ipso uniuerso atque cœlo, cui inclusa sunt elementa, in orbem coacta intelliguntur. Reliquum est, de elementorum motu sermonem faciamus.
units.tr: 3. Finally, those figures do not agree with the local motion which the elements have by nature: some tend downward on account of heaviness, others upward on account of lightness (not on account of any figures). Nor do they agree with the sensible qualities of the elements, which are heat, cold, moisture and dryness, nor with the actions of the elements, that is, their powers of heating, moistening, and so on. Why say more? Very many considerations converge, from which it is easy to conclude that those figures can in no way be fitted to the elements. In Aristotle it is easy to gather several reasons. But it is rightly understood that all things are gathered into a sphere together with the universe itself and the heaven, in which the elements are enclosed. It remains that we speak of the motion of the elements.

units.la: Unde elementis inest natura- lis motus?
units.tr: Whence does natural motion arise in the elements?

units.la: Ab insita in illis grauitate & leuitate. Itaq; ad iudicandum de elementorum motu, cognosci grauitatis & leuitatis proprietas in primis debet.
units.tr: From the heaviness and lightness implanted in them. Therefore, in order to judge the motion of the elements, the property of heaviness and lightness must first be understood.

units.la: Quid est graue, quid item leue?
units.tr: What is heavy, and likewise what is light?

units.la: Graue est, quod ad medium ferri natum est. Leue est, quod à medio extremum uersus ferri natũ est. Duplicitèr autè tàm graue,quàm leue dicitur. Grauè simpliciter & absolutè est,quod deorsum & ad medium tendit:graue ad aliud est,cùm datis duobus grauibus corporibus, quæ sunt æquali mole ,alterû quidem uelociùs , alterum uerò tardius fertur deorsum.ex his autem duobus,quòd celerius fertur deorsum,id appellatur grauius:quod uerò tardius, id minus graue , & graue ad aliud appellatur. Leue simpliciter est,quod sursum & à medio fertur.Leue ad aliud est , cùm datis duobus leuibus corporibus, quæ sunt æquali mole, alterum quidem uelocius,alterum uerò tardius sursum contendit. Ex his autem duobus, quod citius fertur sursum, appellatur leuius : quod tardius eò fertur,id minus leue,& leue ad aliud appellatur. Quia uerò nonnulli arbitrati sunt , in uniuerso non posse discerni, quænam pars supra sit aut infrà,cum uniuersum sit undique sibi simile, & partes undiq; habeat æquales : sciendum est , superam quidem partem uniuersi omne spacium appellari,quo uersus extremum undequaque discedit: inferam uerò,quod ad medium siue centrum directum est. Errarunt igitur philosophi, qui graue & leue aliter definierunt.
units.tr: That is heavy which is naturally carried towards the middle, and that is light which is naturally carried from the middle towards the extremity. Both heavy and light are said in two ways. Heavy simply and absolutely is that which tends downwards and towards the middle. Heavy relative to something else is said when, of two heavy bodies of equal bulk, one is carried downwards more quickly and the other more slowly. Of these two, the one carried downwards more quickly is called heavier, and the one carried more slowly is less heavy, and is called heavy relative to the other. Light simply is that which is carried upwards and away from the middle. Light relative to something else is said when, of two light bodies of equal bulk, one strives upwards more quickly and the other more slowly. Of these two, the one carried upwards more quickly is called lighter, and the one carried more slowly is less light, and is called light relative to the other. But since some have thought that in the universe it cannot be discerned which part is above or below, because the universe is everywhere like itself and has its parts equal on every side, it must be understood that the upper part of the universe is called the whole space towards which the extremity recedes on every side, while the lower part is that which is directed towards the middle or centre. The philosophers therefore erred who defined heavy and light otherwise.

units.la: I. Error est in Timæo Platonis,ubi definitur illud efle grauius,quod ex pluribus et æqualibus partibus,ueluti superficiebus aut triangulis,constat:leuius uerò,quod ex æqualibus paucioribus. Atq; ita ignem, cui formam tribuerunt pyramidalem, propter pauciores superficies esse leuiorem, quàm est terra, cui octohædram, id est, pluribus superficiebus distinctam figurâ assignarunt. Quo pacto & plumbum habes plures superficies, dicitur grauius plumbo cui adsunt pauciores superficies. Atqui uel hinc error iste deprehenditur, quòd hac ratione non definitur graue simpliciter dictum, sed tantùm graue ad aliud: cum hic nihil aliud quàm graue cum graui comparatur, & alterum altero definitur grauius.
units.tr: I. There is an error in Plato's Timaeus, where that is defined as heavier which consists of more numerous equal parts, such as surfaces or triangles, and lighter that which consists of fewer equal parts. And so they say that fire, to which they assigned a pyramidal form, is lighter than earth, to which they assigned an octahedral figure, that is, a figure divided into more surfaces, because it has fewer surfaces. By this reasoning lead, which has more surfaces, is said to be heavier than gold, which has fewer surfaces. Yet this very error is detected from the fact that by this reasoning heavy is not defined simply, but only heavy relative to something else, since here one heavy thing is merely compared with another heavy thing, and one is defined as heavier than the other.

units.la: Deinde sequitur ex illa sententia, quòd quo maiori mole corpus aliquod existit, eò id fore grauius: & quo minori mole, eò leuius: quod sane falsum est. Nā modicū æris grauiꝰ[?] est magna mole lanæ, et magnus ignis celerius subinde sursum tendit quàm modicus.
units.tr: Further, it follows from that opinion that the larger in bulk a body is, the heavier it will be, and the smaller in bulk, the lighter; which is certainly false. For a small amount of bronze is heavier than a large mass of wool, and a large fire at times tends upwards more quickly than a small one.

units.la: II. Errauerunt etiam Leucippus & Democritus, qui nolentes spectare superficies vel magnitudines rerum, definiuerunt corpora illa esse graviora, in quibus minus inest uacui: atqz è diuerso leuiora, in quibus plus inest uacui. Sed non satis caute hos loqui, manifestum est.
units.tr: II. Leucippus and Democritus also erred, who, not wishing to consider the surfaces or magnitudes of things, defined those bodies as heavier in which there is less void, and conversely lighter those in which there is more void. But that these men did not speak with sufficient caution is manifest.

units.la: 1. Non satis est dicere, leuia esse, quibus inest plus uacui: sed addèdum insuper, quæ minus sunt solida. Deinde, grauia esse non tantum quòd minus insit illis uacui: sed præterea, quòd magis sunt solida meliusqz compacta. Ita namqz ex duobus lapidibus æqualis magnitudinis alter grauior erit, nimirum in quo minus erit vacui, quiq; melius est compactus.
units.tr: 1. It is not enough to say that those things are light in which there is more void; it must be added besides that they are less solid. Again, things are heavy not merely because less void is in them, but moreover because they are more solid and better compacted. Thus of two stones of equal size, one will be heavier, namely that in which there is less void and which is better compacted.

units.la: 2. Eadem incommoda sequuntur ex hac opinione, quæ ex præcedenti in Timæo relata, imò et alia plura, quæ omnia recensere minime opus est.
units.tr: 2. The same inconveniences follow from this opinion as from the preceding one related in the Timaeus, and indeed many others besides, all of which it is by no means necessary to recount.

units.la: 3. Errarunt postremo & illi, qui leuitate & grauitatem æstimari voluerunt, primùm quidè ex magnitudine & paruitate, deinde vero etiam ex materia, siue omnia essent composita ex una materia, siue ex materijs contrarijs. Facile autem est hanc opinionem euertere. Primùm ex ijs quæ dicta sunt, manifestum est, imò & experientia comprobat, non statim, quorum magna est moles, ea grauiora his esse quæ sunt parua mole. Magnus ignis non est grauior modica terra. Deinde si una constituatur omnium materia, nihil erit simpliciter leue, nihil item simpliciter graue: sed tantùm dicetur aliquid leue vel graue ad aliud: quinetiam una tantùm erit motus species, qua nimirum omnia necessariò feruntur aut sursum, aut deorsum: atq; ita tolletur aut omnis grauitas, aut omnis leuitas. Quòd si contrariæ ponuntur materiæ, tum non erunt graue aut leue nisi simpliciter: atque omnia medio modo se habentia negabuntur.
units.tr: 3. Finally, those also erred who wished heaviness and lightness to be measured, first indeed by size and smallness, and then also by matter, whether all things were composed of one matter or of contrary matters. But this opinion is easily overthrown. First, from what has been said it is manifest, and indeed experience confirms it, that things of great bulk are not at once heavier than those of small bulk. A large fire is not heavier than a small amount of earth. Next, if the matter of all things is one, nothing will be simply light and nothing simply heavy, but something will be called light or heavy only relative to something else; moreover there will be only one kind of motion, by which all things would of necessity be carried either upwards or downwards, and so either all heaviness or all lightness would be taken away. But if contrary matters are posited, then things will be heavy or light only simply, and all things standing in an intermediate condition will be denied.

units.la: Cæterùm ut plenius natura grauitatis ac leuitatis, præterea quomodo in elementis hæc considerentur, perspectum fiat, paulo accuratius sunt quædam exploranda.
units.tr: However, in order that the nature of heaviness and lightness may be made more fully clear, and also how these are considered in the elements, certain things must be investigated a little more carefully.

units.la: Quid est ferri in locum naturalem, siue qui fit quòd unumquodque cor- pus natura ad suum lo- cum fertur?
units.tr: What is it to be carried to the natural place, or how does it come about that every body is carried by nature to its own place?

units.la: Tres sunt motus species:alia secundum quantitatem, alia secundum qualitatem, alia secundum locum. In unaquaq; autè specie motus fit mutatio è contrariis in cōtraria, aut certè in media quædam, neq; citra discrimē quiduis mutatur in quoduis.Hac autem ratione aliqua res augetur vel diminuitur in eam speciem, in quam augeri diminuiue apta est, & non in aliam: item aliqua res alteratur in eam speciem, in quam alterari apta est, & non in aliam.Ad eundem igitur modum res quævis naturalis mutatur loco, atque ad eum[?] locum fertur, ad quem ferri apta est. Atqui ut res aliqua sursum feratur, haud dubiè in causa est leuitas: ut vero feratur deorsum, in causa est grauitas. Quocirca catenus omnino aliquid loco mouetur, atq; ad locum naturalem tendit, quatenus potentia graue aut leue est.
units.tr: There are three species of motion: one according to quantity, another according to quality, and another according to place. In each species, change goes from contraries to contraries, or else to some intermediates, and nothing is changed into just anything without distinction. In this way a thing is increased or diminished only in the species into which it is apt to be increased or diminished, and not into another. Likewise a thing is altered only in the species into which it is apt to be altered, and not into another. In the same way, then, any natural thing is changed in place and is carried to that place to which it is apt to be carried. But surely, for a thing to be carried upward, lightness is undoubtedly the cause, and for it to be carried downward, heaviness is the cause. Hence a thing is moved in place at all, and tends to its natural place, only so far as it is heavy or light by its potential.

units.la: Unde dicitur principium motus in grauibus & leuibus?
units.tr: Whence is the principle of motion said to lie in heavy and light things?

units.la: Poterit id clarius intelligi,si ea quæ mouetur secundum locum,his quæ mouentur secundum quantitatem vel qualitatem, comparentur. Quod igitur ad mutationis modum attinet, eodem se prorsus pacto habent, ita ut pari modo aliquid sursum feratur uel deorsum, quo augmentabile augmentatur, & alterabile alteratur. Caeterum si spectatur causa efficiens motus, differentia quaedam existit.
units.tr: This can be understood more clearly if what is moved according to place is compared with what is moved according to quantity or quality. As far as the manner of change goes, they stand in exactly the same relation: something is carried upward or downward in the same way as what can be augmented is augmented, and what can be altered is altered. However, if one considers the efficient cause of the motion, some difference exists.

units.la: 1. Mobilia secundum locum, leue uidelicet & graue, habent principium motus à sese & in sese: mobilia uero secundum quantitatem uel qualitatem habent principium motus aliunde, quamuis aliquando etiam à sese.
units.tr: 1. Things movable according to place, namely light and heavy, have the principle of their motion from themselves and in themselves; but things movable according to quantity or quality have the principle of their motion from elsewhere, although sometimes also from themselves.

units.la: 2. Mobilia secundum locum habet sua principia substantiæ propinqua, alia uero remota. Argumento est, quòd tum dicuntur res perfectæ secundum substantiam, quando loco mouentur. Augmentatio autem uel alteratio seperatim à substantijs considerantur, neq; ex augmentatione uel alteratione iudicium de perfectione substantiæ petitur. Ex his autem animaduerti potest, grauia & leuia principiū sui motus in sese habere.
units.tr: 2. Things movable according to place have their principles close to their substance, but others remote. The proof is that things are then said to be perfect according to substance when they are moved in place. Augmentation or alteration, however, are considered apart from substances, and a judgement of the perfection of a substance is not drawn from augmentation or alteration. From these points it can be noticed that heavy and light things have the principle of their motion in themselves.

units.la: Quomodo describuntur graue & leue ratione motus ad locum?
units.tr: How are heavy and light things described in respect of motion to a place?

units.la: Graue simpliciter est, quod omnibus substat: ut terra. Leue simpliciter est, quod omnibus supereminet: ut ignis. Graue secundum quid est, cui conuenit partim ut substet, partim ut superemineat: quo in genere sunt aer & aqua. Nam aer substat igni, superemi-net uero aquæ: & aqua substat aeri, supereminet autem terræ. Leue secundum quid est, quod partim substat,partim supereminet:ut aer,itemq; aqua, quæ respectu diuerso supereminent & substant.Sed alijs quoq; exemplis hæc illustriora reddemus.Corpora simpliciter leuia aut grauia sunt ignis & terra:quorū ille semper,ubi non occurrit impedimentum,eluctatur sursum : hæc uero, cum non inuenit obstaculum,semper tendit deorsum uersus medium.
units.tr: That which is heavy without qualification is what underlies all things, as earth. That which is light without qualification is what rises above all things, as fire. That which is heavy in a relative sense is what partly underlies and partly rises above; to this kind belong air and water. For air underlies fire but rises above water, and water underlies air but rises above earth. That which is light in a relative sense is what partly underlies and partly rises above, as air and likewise water, which rise above and underlie in different respects. But we shall make these things clearer by other examples as well. Bodies that are simply light or heavy are fire and earth. Of these, fire always struggles upward wherever no hindrance occurs, while earth, when it finds no obstacle, always tends downward toward the middle.

units.la: Corpora autem composita sunt grauia & leuia secundum quid, nimirum pro ratione elementorum, ex quibus ipsa componuntur. Facit autē diuersitas corporum simplicium,ex quibus conflata sunt corpora composita , ut unum idemq; corpus in diuersis locis aliter atq; aliter leuitatem aut grauitatem suam ostendat, atq; in uno quidem loco animaduertatur grauius,in altero uero leuius.Si namque hinc lignum 100 librarum, inde plumbum 1. librę pariter costituantur in aere, animaduertetur sanè illud multò esse grauius: at uero si eadem simul ponatur in aqua, deprehendetur plumbum statim ferri ad fundum, lignum uero supernatabit. Vnde autē hæc diuersitas?nimirum in ligno præter naturā terream etiam abundat aer, ob quem aquis supereminet : in plumbo uero,quod ualde cōpactum est,non est aer ita permixtus , sed terra dominatur, qua de causa sub aquas labitur. Enimuero omnia præter ignem habent aliquam grauitatem, rursumq; omnia præter terram habēt aliquam leuitatem. Atq; aeri quidem inesse aliquid grauitatis, uel ex eo cognoscitur, quòd uter inflatus ponderosior sit utre uacuo: ut nō dicam, quòd aer sit suapte natura calidus & humidus, ideoq; etiam igni substans & in latus fluens. Quæ cum ita sint, corpus in quo plus aeris fuerit quàm terræ aut aquæ, id in aqua sentietur leuius, in aere autem potest esse grauius. En igitur, quæ corpora leuia, quæ grauia simpliciter, quæ item eiusmodi secundum quid. Tantum de grauibus & leuibus secundum quid.
units.tr: Composite bodies, however, are heavy and light in a relative sense, namely according to the proportion of the elements of which they are composed. The diversity of the simple bodies from which composite bodies are compounded causes one and the same body to show its lightness or heaviness differently in different places, so that in one place it is noticed as heavier and in another as lighter. For if a 100-pound piece of wood is set on one side and a pound of lead on the other, equally in air, the wood will certainly be found to be much heavier. But if the same two are placed together in water, the lead will be seen to sink straight to the bottom, while the wood floats. Whence this difference? Clearly, in wood there is abundant air besides its earthy nature, on account of which it floats above water. But in lead, which is very dense, air is not mixed in to the same degree; earth prevails, and for this reason it slides under the water. Indeed, all things except fire have some heaviness, and again all things except earth have some lightness. That air has some heaviness is known from the fact that a bladder that is inflated is heavier than an empty one, not to mention that air is by nature warm and moist, and therefore also underlies fire and flows sideways. These things being so, a body in which there is more air than earth or water will be felt lighter in water, but may be heavier in air. Behold, then, which bodies are light, which heavy, simply, and likewise which are such in a relative sense. So much on heavy and light things in a relative sense.

units.la: Estne certum medium, quò feruntur omnia grauia: & certum extremum, quò feruntur omnia leuia?
units.tr: Is there a certain middle place to which all heavy things are carried, and a certain extremity to which all light things are carried?

units.la: Maxime. Quod probatur hisce rationibus.
units.tr: Most certainly. This is proved by the following arguments.

units.la: 1. Non contingit graue aut leue in infinitum ferri, sed certis finitisq; locis quiescere ea necessum est. Est igitur & medium certum, ad quod omne graue: & extremum certum, ad quod omne leue tendit.
units.tr: 1. A heavy or light thing cannot be carried to infinity, but it must of necessity rest in certain and finite places. There is therefore both a certain middle, to which every heavy thing tends, and a certain extremity, to which every light thing tends.

units.la: 2. Tam ignis tendens sursum versus cœli concauum, quàm terra tendens deorsum versus mundi centrum, rectis lineis & ad angulos pares feruntur. Sed ubi rectæ lineæ pares angulos creant, ibi certum spacium, adeoq; finis quidam constituitur. Ergo certum medium ad quod graue, & certum extremum ad quod leue fertur, constitui necessariò debet.
units.tr: 2. Fire, tending upwards towards the concave surface of the heavens, and earth, tending downwards towards the centre of the world, are carried along straight lines and at equal angles. But where straight lines make equal angles, there a certain space is marked out, and so a certain limit is fixed. Therefore a certain middle, to which the heavy thing is carried, and a certain extremity, to which the light thing is carried, must necessarily be established.

units.la: 3. Simpliciter graue omnibus substat, simpliciter leue omnibus supereminet: quamobrem graue & leue sunt contraria. Contrariorum autem sunt contraria loca. Atqui contraria oportet esse certa & finita. Igitur tum medium ad quod graue, tum extremum ad quod leue omne tendit, certa finitaq; sunt. Contraria autem esse graue & leue, etiam aliis rationibus declarari potest. Quae sursum feruntur, perfectiora sunt, quoniam continent: quae deorsum feruntur, imperfectiora sunt, quoniam continentur. Et quod continet, se habet ut forma: quod continetur, se habet ut materia.
units.tr: 3. The heavy is simply beneath all things, and the light simply rises above all things; wherefore heavy and light are contraries. But contraries have contrary places. Yet contraries must be certain and finite. Therefore both the middle to which the heavy thing goes and the extremity to which the light thing goes are certain and finite. That heavy and light are contraries can also be shown by other arguments. Things that are carried upwards are more perfect, since they contain; things that are carried downwards are less perfect, since they are contained. And what contains stands in the relation of form; what is contained stands in the relation of matter.

units.la: Quot sunt elementa?
units.tr: How many elements are there?

units.la: Quatuor: quod ex iis quae hactenus exposita sunt, demonstrari hunc in modum potest. Unum est elementum simpliciter leue, quod semper fertur sursum ad certum extremum, nempe ignis. Deinde aliud est elementum simpliciter graue, quod semper fertur deorsum ad certum medium, nempe terra. Praeterea necesse est duo alia esse leuia & grauia secundum quid, quaeq; aliis quodammodo substant, aliis quodammodo supereminet: haec autem sunt aer & aqua. Igitur quatuor numero sunt elementa. Sicut autem elementa quae habent grauitatem & leuitatem, aer, inquam, & aqua, plus habent ponderis suo in loco constituta, atque ideo contingit, si quae infra ipsa posita sunt, loco cedunt, statim in eorundem locum se recipere: aer namq; descendit in locum recedentis aquæ, & aqua in locum recedentis terræ. ita ipsa terra non ascedit sursum in locum recedentis aquæ: & ignis, quoniā[?] leuissimus est, non descendit deorsum in locum recedentis aeris. Unde profecto tum leuitas & grauitas, tum etiam ordo atque numerus elementorum animadverti rectius potest.
units.tr: Four. This can be demonstrated in the following manner from what has been set out so far. One element is simply light, which is always carried upwards to a certain extremity, namely fire. Next, another element is simply heavy, which is always carried downwards to a certain middle, namely earth. Besides, it is necessary that two other things are light and heavy in a relative sense, and that they in some way stand beneath some things and in some way rise above others: these are air and water. Therefore there are four elements in number. Moreover, the elements which have heaviness and lightness, air and water I mean, have more weight when they are placed in their own place; and so it happens that if the things placed below them yield their place, they at once withdraw into the place of those things: for air descends into the place of water that gives way, and water into the place of earth that gives way. Thus earth itself does not rise upwards into the place of the water that gives way, and fire, since it is the lightest, does not descend downwards into the place of the air that gives way. Whence indeed both the lightness and heaviness, and also the order and number of the elements, can more correctly be observed.

units.la: Porrò quando quatuor esse constat elementa, inter se grauitate & leuitate distincta, sequitur hinc necessario, quatuor quoq; esse particulares materias, ex quibus res omnes corporeæ conficiuntur. Enimvero si una eademq; poneretur omnium elementorum materia, tum necessario quoque omnia eodem modo grauia & leuia existerent. Qua ratione evertuntur illorum sententiæ, qui omnia ex una materia, nempe aut vacuo, aut solido, aut superficiebus, constare sunt arbitrati.
units.tr: Furthermore, since it is established that there are four elements, distinguished from one another by heaviness and lightness, it necessarily follows from this that there are also four particular matters, out of which all corporeal things are made. Indeed, if one and the same matter were posited for all the elements, then of necessity all things would also exist heavy and light in the same way. By this reasoning the opinions of those are overthrown who have judged that all things consist of one matter, namely either the void, or the solid, or surfaces.

units.la: Efficit'ne figura quoq;, ut elementa sursum deorsumue mo- ueantur?
units.tr: Does figure also cause the elements to be moved upwards or downwards?

units.la: Figura non facit ut res ullæ sursum vel deorsum moveatur, sed tantum adjuvat ut celerius tardiusve ad suum locum perveniant. Etenim ubi corpora, dum moventur, dividunt medium, non habet figura ipsa potestatem movendi: verum anguli eius tales esse possunt, ut ad dividendum medium plus minusve cooperentur.
units.tr: Figure does not make any things move upwards or downwards, but only helps them to reach their place more quickly or more slowly. For when bodies, while they are moving, divide the medium, figure itself has no power of moving; but its angles may be such that they contribute more or less to dividing the medium.

units.la: Obiectio: Videmus ferrum & plumbū, quae per se grauia sunt, si latam figurā habeant, super aquas natare: contrà si rotunda vel longa sit figura, statim descendere. Igitur figura ipsa causa motus existit.
units.tr: Objection: We see that iron and lead, which are heavy in themselves, float upon water if they have a broad shape; on the contrary, if the shape is round or long, they sink at once. Therefore figure itself is the cause of motion.

units.la: Item minuta corpuscula, etiam terrea & grauioris substantiæ, ut metalli, in aere suspensa manent, ibiq; circumferuntur, nec statim decidunt. Igitur figura videtur in causa esse, ut aliquae res moueantur. Responsio: Corpora continua quaedam facile diuidi possunt, quaedam difficulter. Sic aer facile diuidi potest, at difficilius aqua, omnium vero difficilime terra.
units.tr: Likewise, tiny particles, even earthy ones and of heavier substance, such as metal, remain suspended in the air and are carried about there, and do not fall at once. Therefore figure seems to be the cause that some things are moved. Answer: Some continuous bodies can be divided easily, some with difficulty. Thus air can be divided easily, but water with more difficulty, and earth most difficultly of all.

units.la: Praeterea corpora quaedam facilius diuiduntur, ut acuta, cuspidata, angulosa: quaedam difficulter, ut obtusa, lata, &c. Itaq; tametsi figura aliquo modo adiuuet ad diuisionem perficiendam, tamen praecipue oportet intueri in naturam ipsorum corporum subiectorum. Quod si igitur corpora subiecta difficulter diuiduntur, tum necessum est ea quae imponuntur superfluitare: si vero subiecta corpora sunt facile diuisibilia, tum ea quae imponuntur cito descendunt. Vnde quaecunq; figura corporibus superimpositis adsit, saepe tamen ipsa eorundem corporum grauitas in subiecta corpora praevalet, necnon efficit, ut haec corpora subiecta facile diuidantur. Democ-ritus quidem existimauit, ideò aliqua in aere vel in aquis suspensa detineri, quòd perpetuò calidi quidam vapores tum in aere, tum in aquis attollantur, qui corpora imposita sustineant. Sed ratio hæc infirma est. Tutius est considerare ingenitam naturam ipsorum corporum.
units.tr: Moreover, some bodies are divided more easily, such as sharp, pointed, and angular ones; some with difficulty, such as blunt, broad ones, etc. And so, although figure in some way assists in bringing about division, nevertheless one must chiefly look to the nature of the underlying bodies themselves. If therefore the underlying bodies are divided with difficulty, then it is necessary that the things laid upon them float; but if the underlying bodies are easily divisible, then the things laid upon them quickly sink. Whence, whatever figure is present in the superimposed bodies, often the very heaviness of those bodies prevails over the underlying bodies, and brings it about that these underlying bodies are easily divided. Democritus indeed thought that some things are held suspended in air or in water because certain warm vapours are perpetually raised up both in air and in water, and these sustain the bodies laid upon them. But this reasoning is weak. It is safer to consider the innate nature of the bodies themselves.

units.la: Cæterùm quando hactenus disputatum est de mundo uniuerso, eiusdemq; partibus, cœlo, inquâ, & elementis: reliquum est de generatione, id est, quomodo res omnes ex illis ipsis elementis generentur, sermonem prosequamur.Ergo primùm de generatione, quid uidelicet ea sit, quomodo perficiatur, quo differat ab aliis motus speciebus, alteratione, inquâ, & augmentatione, quid deniq; actio & passio, quæ ad generationem omnesq; species motus concurrunt: deinde uerò de elementis, de eorundem qualitatibus, de modo productionis rerum ex ijsdem, déque aliis eorundem accidentibus ordine est dicendum.
units.tr: Moreover, since hitherto we have disputed about the whole world and its parts, the heavens, I mean, and the elements, it remains to pursue our discourse on generation, that is, how all things are generated from those very elements. Therefore we must speak first of generation: what it is, namely, how it is brought about, how it differs from the other species of motion, alteration and augmentation, and finally what action and passion are, which concur in generation and all species of motion; then indeed, in order, we must speak of the elements, of their qualities, of the mode of the production of things from them, and of their other accidents.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS. De generatione rerum naturalium.
units.tr: BOOK III. On the generation of natural things.

units.la: QVID SIT? Quid est generatio?
units.tr: WHAT IS IT? What is generation?

units.la: DVæ de hac quæstione fuerunt ueterum philosophorum opiniones.
units.tr: There were two opinions of the ancient philosophers on this question.

units.la: I. Quidam existimarunt, res omnes naturales gigni ex una tantum materia: atque hanc[?] generationem definiuerunt simpliciter esse quandam alterationem. Quod & necessariò debebant statuere: posito enim omnium rerum uno communi principio, atq; subiecto materiali, sola alteratio ad rerum productionem sufficit.
units.tr: I. Some thought that all natural things are generated from one matter only, and they defined this generation simply as a certain alteration. They were bound to hold this, since, once a single common principle and material subject of all things is posited, alteration alone is enough for the production of things.

units.la: II. Alij statuerunt plura principia materialia: atque horum nonnulli quatuor elementa: ut Empedocles, qui tantùm addit duo principia efficientia, litem uidelicet & amicitiam. Nonnulli infinita corpora similaria, ueluti os, carnem, medullam, &c. ut Anaxagoras. Nonnulli infinita corpuscula ἄτομα, id est, insecabilia: ut Democritus & Leucippus. Hi autem omnes plures materias constituentes, negarunt esse alterationem. Quamuis quomodo & quibus de causis generatio ab alteratione differat, non potuerunt, positis talibus principijs, satis demonstrare. Quod Aristoteles rationibus aliquot demonstrat, quas nos breuitatis causa praetermittimus. Multa ijdem philosophi de generatione & corruptione absurdè commenti sunt. Ipse Plato neque de quauis generatione, neque de alteratione uel augmentatione quicquam est complexus. Caeteri plurima praeterierunt, quae maximè decuerat in hoc negotio considerare.
units.tr: II. Others posited several material principles: some of them four elements, as Empedocles, who added only two efficient principles, namely strife and friendship; some infinite similar bodies, such as bone, flesh, marrow, and so on, as Anaxagoras; some infinite small bodies that cannot be cut, called atoms [ἄτομα], as Democritus and Leucippus. All of these, however, who posit several constituent matters, denied that there is alteration. Yet, with such principles posited, they could not sufficiently demonstrate how and for what causes generation differs from alteration. Aristotle demonstrates this by several arguments, which for the sake of brevity we pass over. The same philosophers also devised many absurd things about generation and corruption. Plato himself did not treat of generation in general, nor of alteration or augmentation at all. The others passed over very many things which it was most fitting to consider in this matter.

units.la: Democritus & Leucippus generationem arbitrati sunt quandam corporum ἀτόμων cōcretionem seu congregationem: corruptionem uerò, eorundem corporum secretionem: porrò alteratione fieri tantum ordine atq; situ. Qua ratione testati sunt, generationem ab alteratione distingui. Sed interim ex illis assertionibus necessariò multæ absurditates sequerentur. Adhæc, si libet conferre opiniones inter se, probabilior videbitur sententia Democriti, ponentis generationem fieri ex corporibus ἀτόμοις [?]: quàm Platonis, cui placuit eandem fieri ex superficiebus, in quas iterum res omnes corrumpantur ac resoluantur.
units.tr: Democritus and Leucippus thought that generation is a certain concretion or gathering together of atomic bodies, and corruption is their separation; and that alteration happens only by order and position. By this reasoning they showed that generation is distinguished from alteration. But meanwhile many absurdities would necessarily follow from those assertions.
