Moreover, if one wishes to compare the opinions with one another, the view of Democritus, who holds that generation comes about from bodies atoms [ἀτόμοις], will seem more probable than that of Plato, who held that it comes about from surfaces, into which in turn all things are corrupted and dissolved.

units.la: III. Sed omissis omnibus disceptationibus, aliorumq; opinionibus, definitio generationis talis colligi potest, qualem Aristoteles quoq; obiter subijcit: Generatio perfecta est mutatio huius totius in hoc totum, nullo sensibili subiecto permanente eodem: hoc est, ut crassius loquamur, generatio substantialis est motus, per quem ex una substantia producitur alia, ita ut nulla substantia, quæ prius erat in ipso producto, maneat. Enimuero in ipsa generatione non manet eadem substantia ante & post, cum in cæteris speciebus mutationis, alteratione inquâ & augmentatione, eadem prorsus substantia maneat, tantumq; varietur qualitas aut quantitas. Hinc verò etiam patet, quòd mutatio hæc, quam dicimus generationem, nullo modo fit alteratio: quod breviter duabus rationibus declaratur.
units.tr: III. But, setting aside all disputations and the opinions of others, a definition of generation can be gathered such as Aristotle also adds in passing: generation, taken absolutely, is a change of this whole into that whole, with no sensible subject remaining the same. That is, to speak more plainly, substantial generation is a motion by which one substance is produced from another, in such a way that no substance which was previously in the product itself remains. Indeed, in generation the same substance does not remain before and after, whereas in the other species of change, alteration and augmentation, the very same substance remains and only its quality or quantity varies. Hence it is also clear that this change, which we call generation, is in no way alteration; and this is shown briefly by two reasons.

units.la: ¶ Generationis subiectum est materia præiacès: alterationis uero, corpus iam formatum actuq; existens.
units.tr: ¶ The subject of generation is matter lying beneath, whereas the subject of alteration is a body already formed and existing in actuality.

units.la: 2. Generatio omnis secundum substantiam intelligitur: alteratio uero secundum qualitatem atque accidentarias adfectiones. Atq; haec quidem de quaestione, Quid sit generatio. quo autem propius generationis naturam exploremus, atq; etiam qualis sit generatio percipiamus, restant alia quaedam inuestiganda.
units.tr: 2. Every generation is understood with respect to substance, whereas alteration is with respect to quality and accidental affections. These things concern the question, What is generation? But in order to examine more closely the nature of generation, and also to grasp what sort of thing generation is, certain other matters remain to be investigated.

units.la: QVALIS SIT? Vtrum contingat aliquid generari uel corrumpi simpliciter?
units.tr: WHAT KIND OF THING IS IT? Whether anything is generated or corrupted absolutely?

units.la: Videtur sane quod non, quod rationibus aliquot probatur.
units.tr: It certainly seems not, which is proved by several arguments.

units.la: 1. Quicquid usquam mutatione aliqua fit, id ex aliquo fiat necesse est: quemadmodum ex aegroto fit sanus, uicissimq; ex sano aegrotus: & ex magno fit pusillum, iterumq; ex pusillo magnum. Igitur nihil generatur simpliciter.
units.tr: (1) Whatever comes about by any change must come from something; just as the sick becomes well, and conversely the well becomes sick, and the large becomes small, and again the small becomes large. Therefore nothing is generated absolutely.

units.la: 2. Si quicquā generabitur simpliciter, tum id ex non ente generabitur. Si autem aliquid generatur ex non ente, tum non ens erit aliquid. Hoc autem longe est absurdissimum. Igitur nihil simpliciter generatur.
units.tr: (2) If anything is generated absolutely, then it will be generated from non-being. But if something is generated from non-being, then non-being will be something. This, however, is most absurd. Therefore nothing is absolutely generated.

units.la: 3. Si quid generabitur secundum quid, generabitur id ex non ente secundum quid: veluti ex non albo generabitur album, & ex non bono bonum. Igitur per contrarium, si quid generabitur simpliciter, necessario id ex non ente simpliciter generabitur. Est autem & hoc impossibile. Igitur etiam impossibile est, ut aliquid simpliciter generetur.
units.tr: (3) If something is generated in a certain respect, it will be generated from non-being in a certain respect: for example, the white is generated from the non-white, and the good from the non-good. Therefore, conversely, if something is generated absolutely, it must necessarily be generated from non-being absolutely. But this too is impossible. Therefore it is also impossible for anything to be generated absolutely.

units.la: Sed ut ad quæstionem propositam respondeamus, necnon allatæ rationes in partem negatiuam possint excuti, sciendum duplicitér[?] aliquid dici simpliciter generari.
units.tr: But in order to answer the question proposed, and so that the arguments brought forward on the negative side can be examined, it must be known that something is said to be generated absolutely in two ways.

units.la: 1. Generatur aliquid simpliciter ex non ente simpliciter, non quod omnino non sit ens, sed quod non sit ens actu.
units.tr: (1) Something is generated absolutely from non-being absolutely, not because it is altogether not a being, but because it is not a being in actuality.

units.la: 2. Generatur aliquid simpliciter ex semper ente, quod videlicet potestate quidem semper sit, non autem actu. Hinc igitur intelligi potest, recte dici posse, quod aliquid simpliciter generetur, nempe ex ente quod semper existit potestate, licet non actu. Atque ens illud potestate non est simpliciter & plene substantia, sed potius substantia quaedam incompleta, utpote quam non possis ad certam substantiae speciem reducere, nata interim est formis subijci. Cum autem non sit substantia completa, consentaneum est, non esse substantiam actu, ac proinde neque quantam vel qualem actu. Atque hac ratione perspicuum fit, non generari aliquid ex nihilo: quod argumentis illis antecedentibus concludi videbatur.
units.tr: (2) Something is generated absolutely from a being that always exists, namely a being that is always in potentiality but not in actuality. From this it can therefore be understood that it can rightly be said that something is generated absolutely, namely from a being that always exists in potentiality, though not in actuality. And that being in potentiality is not simply and fully a substance, but rather an incomplete substance, inasmuch as it cannot be reduced to a certain species of substance, yet is meanwhile apt to be subjected to forms. Since it is not a complete substance, it follows that it is not a substance in actuality, and consequently neither a quantity nor a quality in actuality. And by this reasoning it becomes clear that nothing is generated from nothing, which seemed to be concluded from those preceding arguments.

units.la: Qui fit, quòd rerum generationes per- petua quadam successione semper durant?
units.tr: How is it that the generations of things last forever through a certain continuous succession?

units.la: Duæ huc concurrunt causæ: altera materia subiecta perpetuò manens, altera primum principium immobile semper movens & agens. Quamdiu istud invenit paratam materiam, tamdiu operatur, atque res natura-les producit, omniumq; motuum naturalium causa est. Deinde, quando aliquid corrumpitur, id statim in non ens, non quidem actu, sed potentia, corrumpitur, ex quo rursus aliud quidpiam generari potest. Itaq; ex corruptione sequitur generatio perpetua quadam serie.
units.tr: Two causes come together here: one is the underlying matter, which remains constantly, and the other is the first principle, immovable yet always moving and acting. As long as this principle finds matter prepared, it keeps working and produces natural things, and it is the cause of all natural motions. Then, whenever something is corrupted, it immediately passes into non-being, not indeed actually but potentially, and from this something else can again be generated. Thus corruption is followed by generation in a perpetual series.

units.la: Falluntur interea, qui putant ideo generationes esse perpetuas, quòd existat infinita quædam materia. Nam infinitum actu esse non posse, alibi demonstravimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile those are mistaken who think that generations are perpetual because some infinite matter exists. For we have shown elsewhere that an actually infinite cannot exist.

units.la: Cur aliquid simpliciter, aliquid vero secundum quid generari aut corrumpi dicitur?
units.tr: Why is something said to be generated or corrupted simply, but something else only in a certain respect?

units.la: Dicitur aliquid generari simpliciter, quādo materia ex qua quid generatur, est ens simpliciter sive substantia: cuius generis est, si ignis aut terra, quæ sunt entia simpliciter, generetur. Enimvero ea tantum simpliciter generari intelligitur, quæ substantiæ significatione habet. Dicitur aliquid generari secūdū qd, quādo quod generatur, est ens secūdū qd, id est, accidens ipsi substantiæ circumdatum: veluti cum substantiæ accedit quantitas, vel qualitas, aut ubi, aut omnino alterius cuiuspiam prædicamenti adfectio. Itaq; ubi aliquid fit magnum aut parvum, peritum aut imperitum, tunc fit generatio secundum quid. Ex his autem perfacile est iudicare, quomodo vice versa aliquid simpliciter, aliquid vero secundum quid corrumpatur.
units.tr: Something is said to be generated simply when the matter from which it is generated is a being simply, that is, a substance. This is the case when fire or earth, which are beings simply, is generated. Indeed, only those things are understood to be generated simply which have the meaning of substance. Something is said to be generated in a certain respect when what is generated is a being in a certain respect, that is, an accident surrounding the substance itself: for example, when quantity or quality, or place, or in general an affection of some other category, attaches to a substance. So when something becomes large or small, skilled or unskilled, then generation occurs in a certain respect. From these points it is quite easy to judge how, conversely, something is corrupted simply and something else only in a certain respect.

units.la: Cur corruptio rei unius, causa est ge- nerationis rei alterius?
units.tr: Why is the corruption of one thing the cause of the generation of another?

units.la: Corruptio fit in non ens: generatio autem fit, quemadmodum paulo ante demonstratum est, ex nō ente, quod videlicet est ens potestate. Ergo quandocunque virtute corruptionis adest non ens, & quidem potestate (quod sane est incompleta quaedam substantia) ibi adest novae generationis materia. Ex quo fit, ut generationis & corruptionis vicissitudines nunquam intermittantur: quoniam tam ipsa generatio rerum, quàm corruptio in non ente consideratur, atq; utraq; ex non ente dependet.
units.tr: Corruption passes into non-being, and generation, as was shown a little earlier, arises from non-being, which is, of course, being in potency. Therefore, whenever non-being is present by virtue of corruption, and indeed potentially (which is certainly an incomplete substance), there is present the matter of a new generation. From this it follows that the alternations of generation and corruption are never interrupted, since both generation and corruption of things are considered in relation to non-being, and both depend upon non-being.

units.la: Illud non ens, in quod fit corruptio, & ex quo iterum fit generatio, est ne alicui contrarium?
units.tr: Is that non-being, into which corruption passes and from which generation again arises, contrary to anything?

units.la: Non est alicui contrarium. Ratio:Illud non e ns est materia atque substantia quaedam incompleta. Temporis tamen progressu posset contrarietas in eo spectari.
units.tr: It is not contrary to anything. The reason: that non-being is matter and a certain incomplete substance. Yet, as time goes on, a contrariety could be observed in it.

units.la: Est ne eadem tam eius quod gignitur, quàm quod corrumpitur, materia?
units.tr: Is the matter of what is generated the same as the matter of what is corrupted?

units.la: Est eadem, subiecto inquam. Nam ibi subiectum est id quod aliquando est ens. Ratione autem non est eadem: veluti quando aqua corrumpitur, fit sane non ens: at paulo post ex eo non ente generatur aer. Sunt autem aqua & aer ratione quidem admodum diuersa.
units.tr: It is the same in the subject, I mean. For the subject there is that which at some time is a being. But it is not the same in notion: for example, when water is corrupted it certainly becomes non-being, but shortly afterwards air is generated from that non-being. Yet water and air are, in notion, quite different.

units.la: Tantum de generatione, quid sit, qualis sit: superest de reliquis speciebus motus, alteratione inquam & augmentatione, differamus.
units.tr: So much concerning generation: what it is and what sort it is. There remain the other species of motion, I mean alteration and augmentation, which we shall now discuss.

units.la: DE ALTERATIONE.
units.tr: ON ALTERATION.

units.la: Quid est alteratio, & quomodo differt à generatione?
units.tr: What is alteration, and how does it differ from generation?

units.la: ALteratio est, cùm substantia siue subiectum sen sile manet, in eo autem fit quædam mutatio per contrarias uel medias passiones, subiecto illi inesse natas. Ita hominis corpus subiectum est, quod quidem manet: at fit in eo mutatio, quādo quod sanum fuerat, efficitur ægrum: & rursus, quando quod ægrum fuerat, fit sanum.
units.tr: Alteration is when the substance or sensible subject remains, and in it some change occurs through contrary or intermediate affections, which are natural to be in that subject. Thus the body of a man is a subject which indeed remains; but change takes place in it when what was healthy becomes sick, and again when what was sick becomes healthy.

units.la: Generatio autem, est mutatio totius in totum, non manente eodem subiecto sensili: veluti cum ex tota aqua fit aer, & ex aliquo aere fit aqua. Vbi quidem aquae & aeris fit corruptio, postea autem aeris & r ris & aquæ noua succedit generatio. Ac tunc sane generatio consummata intelligitur, quando totum quod transmutatur, integrè plenéq; absolutum, ut sensibus discerni queat, existit.
units.tr: Generation, however, is the change of the whole into the whole, the same sensible subject not remaining: for example, when the whole of the water becomes air, and some air becomes water. Where indeed the corruption of water and air takes place, but afterwards a new generation of air and water succeeds. And then generation is rightly understood to be complete when the whole thing that is changed exists wholly and fully finished, so that it can be distinguished by the senses.

units.la: Utrum, ubi in generato manet aliqua adfectio seu passio quæ fuit in corru- pto, fit dicenda generatio, uel tantùm alteratio?
units.tr: Whether, when some affection or passion that was in the corrupted thing remains in the generated thing, it should be called generation or only alteration?

units.la: Potest quidem fieri, ut ubi ex aere fit aqua, frigiditas, quæ fuerat in aere, hæreat adhuc in aqua, ita ut aeris perspicuitas (est enim aer, si ullum aliud corpus, maximè διαφανὴς[?]) maneat in aqua. Verum hic quidem non spectatur simpliciter alteratio: quoniam facta est mutatio totius in totum, quæ quidem locum nō habet in alteratione. Deinde non etiam potest hic dici simpliciter generatio, quando animadvertitur transitio quædam facta etiā passionis seu accidetis (nimirum frigiditatis & perspicuitatis) quæ transitio seu transmutatio à generatione aliena est. Quid ergo? Separatim iudicium peti debet de mutatione quæ fit in ipsa materia, & rursus separatim de mutatione quæ fit in passionibus. Ubi igitur mutatio deprehenditur in materia ipsa, ibi generationem esse pronunciabis: ubi uero mutatio facta deprehenditur in passionibus, si ea facta fit secundum quantitatem, tum necesse est euadat augmentatio uel diminutio: si uero secundum qualitatem, tum spectatur alteratio : si uero secundum locum, tum spectatur loci mutatio.
units.tr: It can indeed happen that when air becomes water, the coldness that was in the air still clings to the water, and the transparency of the air (for air is, if any other body is, most transparent [διαφανὴς]) remains in the water. But here alteration is not simply observed, since a change of the whole into the whole has taken place, which does not occur in alteration. Next, it cannot here be called simply generation either, since a certain transition of the passion or accident (namely the coldness and transparency) is observed, and this transition or transmutation is foreign to generation. What then? Judgment must be sought separately about the change that takes place in the matter itself, and again separately about the change that takes place in the passions. Where change is perceived in the matter itself, there you will pronounce it to be generation; but where change is perceived in the passions, if it takes place according to quantity, then it must turn out to be augmentation or diminution; if indeed according to quality, then alteration is observed; if according to place, then change of place is observed.

units.la: DE AUGMENTATIONE. Quomodo differt augmentatio à cæteris speciebus motus?
units.tr: On augmentation. How does augmentation differ from the other species of motion?

units.la: 1. Differt ratione prædicameti. Generatio et corruptio proprie fit in ipsa substantia, augmentatio uero et reliquæ species motus in substantiæ passionibus siue accidentibus. Atq; ex reliquis speciebus, alteratio fit secundum qualitatem, motus localis secundum ubi: at augmentatio diminutioq; secundum quantitatem.
units.tr: 1. It differs in the category of predicament. Generation and corruption take place in the substance itself, whereas augmentation and the other species of motion take place in the affections or accidents of a substance. Among the remaining species, alteration takes place with respect to quality, local motion with respect to place, but augmentation and diminution with respect to quantity.

units.la: 2. Ratione diuersitatis in motu locali. Quod generatur aut corrumpitur, non necessario mutat locum. Quod item alteratur, non necessario mutat locum. Quod fertur motu locali circulari, id semper eundem locum seruat. Quod fertur motu locali recto, id semper locum mutat. Quod autem augetur, neq; omnino locum mutat, neq; omnino eundem seruat: sed cum quem primum occupat angustiorem, postea occupat ampliorem: atque e diuerso, quod minuitur, primum habet locum ampliorem, postea angustiorem. Igitur augmetatio ab aliis motus speciebus hoc pacto distinguitur.
units.tr: 2. It differs in the kind of local motion involved. What is generated or corrupted does not necessarily change place. Likewise, what is altered does not necessarily change place. What is carried by circular local motion always keeps the same place. What is carried by straight local motion always changes place. But what is augmented neither wholly changes place nor wholly keeps the same place: rather, it occupies a narrower place at first and afterwards a wider one. Conversely, what is diminished first occupies a wider place and afterwards a narrower one. So augmentation is distinguished from the other species of motion in this way.

units.la: Cæterum hoc nomine augmentationi conuenit cum reliquis motus speciebus, quod sicut in his omnibus, ita in augmentatione quoq;, ex eo quod erat potentia, aliquid fit mutatur q; actu.
units.tr: Yet in this respect augmentation agrees with the other species of motion: just as in all of these, so in augmentation too, something is changed from what was potential into what is actual.

units.la: Utrum augmentatio fiat ex ali- quo corporeo?
units.tr: Whether augmentation takes place through something corporeal.

units.la: Augmentatio fit ex aliquo corporeo.Enimvero & id quod augetur,corporeum est: & quod eidem advenit, corporeum sit necesse est. Nam incorporeum si corpori advenirét, nequaquam maius corpus efficeret:atq; è diverso,si corpori detraheretur aliquod incorporeum,nequaquam ob id corpus efficeretur minus.
units.tr: Augmentation takes place through something corporeal. For indeed that which is augmented is corporeal, and what comes to it must be corporeal. For if something incorporeal were to come to a body, it would by no means make the body larger; and conversely, if something incorporeal were taken away from a body, the body would by no means for that reason become smaller.

units.la: Utrum illud corporeum,ex quo fit au- gmentatio,fit adiunctum ipsi ma- teriæ,an ab eadem se- paratum?
units.tr: Whether that corporeal thing through which augmentation takes place is joined to the matter itself, or is separate from it.

units.la: Corporeum illud ex quo, sive per quod fit augmentatio,nullo modo est à materia separatu.Nam in qua & ex qua materia fit generatio,in eadem et ex eadem par est intelligamus fieri etiam augmentationem. Atqui generatio fit ex aliquo ente actu, sive ὁμογενίῳ, sive ἑτερογενίῳ[?] : veluti cum ignis fit ex igne,planta ex planta.Nec potest quidem materia substantiæ corporeæ reipsa atq; actu à generatione sive re genita separari,quamuis id fortassis ratione atq; intellectu possit fieri:ergo neq; augmentatio potest à materia substantiæ corporeæ separari.Deinde augmentatio est quātitatis prius exi-stentis in materia generationis accessio:diminutio vero est quantitatis prius exi-stentis decessio. Si autē sunt quantitatis in materia præexistetis(neq; enim quantitas sine materiali subiecto existit,) igitur non potest augmentatio à materia separari.
units.tr: That corporeal thing from which, or through which, augmentation takes place is in no way separate from the matter. For we should understand that augmentation takes place in and from the same matter in which and from which generation takes place. But generation takes place from some being that is actual, whether of the same kind [ὁμογενίῳ] or of a different kind [ἑτερογενίῳ]: for example, when fire comes from fire, or a plant from a plant. Nor indeed can the matter of a corporeal substance be separated in reality and in act from what is generated, though perhaps this can be done in reason and in thought. Therefore augmentation also cannot be separated from the matter of the corporeal substance. Next, augmentation is the addition of a quantity that already existed in the matter of generation, and diminution is the departure of a quantity that already existed. But if quantities exist in the matter beforehand (for quantity does not exist without a material subject), then augmentation cannot be separated from matter.

units.la: In quo proprie spectatur augmentatio, in eóne cui aliquid accedit,an in eo quod accedit,an potius in utroq; simul?
units.tr: In what does augmentation properly consist: in that to which something is added, or in that which is added, or rather in both together?

units.la: In eo spectatur augmētatio, cui aliquid accedit: veluti quando animato corpori additur cibus, non quidem cibus,sed ipsum corpus augmentatur. quod rationibus aliquot manifestum fit.
units.tr: Augmentation is considered in that to which something is added: for example, when food is added to an animate body, it is not the food but the body itself that is augmented. This is made clear by several arguments.

units.la: 1. Id proprie augetur, quod ante & post manet idem substantia . Atqui cum fit augmentatio , idem manens substantia, est ipsum corpus, non autem cibus. Igitur in corpore augmentatio proprie consideratur.
units.tr: 1. That is properly augmented which remains the same substance before and after. But when augmentation takes place, what remains the same substance is the body itself, not the food. Therefore augmentation is properly considered in the body.

units.la: 2. Si carni adueniat passio,fiatq; in carne semper eadem manente alteratio, tum ipsa caro dicitur alterari,& non ipsa passio.Ergo eodem pacto,si corpori adueniat accessio, dicitur ipsum corpus augeri,non autem accessio.
units.tr: 2. If an affection comes to flesh, and alteration takes place while the flesh always remains the same, then the flesh itself is said to be altered, and not the affection. Therefore, in the same way, if an addition comes to a body, the body itself is said to be augmented, and not the addition.

units.la: 3. Id proprie augetur, in quo est præcipuum movens ad augmentationem cooperans.Sed in corpore animato est præcipuum movens, cum cibus qui accedit potius corrūpatur, quàm aliquid assumat. Ergo augmentatio in ipso corpore, cui aliquid accedit, cernitur. Sed quo hæ rationes clarius percipiantur, prodesse adijcere aliquot augmentationis proprietates.
units.tr: 3. That is properly augmented in which the chief agent of augmentation works together. But in an animate body the chief agent is such that the food which is added is rather corrupted than assimilates anything. Therefore augmentation is seen in the very body to which something is added. But in order that these arguments may be grasped more clearly, it will be useful to add some properties of augmentation.

units.la: Quot sunt augmentationis proprietates?
units.tr: How many properties of augmentation are there?

units.la: Sex. 1. Manet eadem substantia & ante augmentationem, & post.
units.tr: Six. 1. The same substance remains both before augmentation and after it.

units.la: 2. Quod augetur, aliqua accessione augetur: quod vero minuitur, aliqua decessione minuitur.
units.tr: 2. What is augmented is increased by some addition; what is diminished is lessened by some subtraction.

units.la: 3. Eius quod augetur, quaelibet pars augetur: eius vero quod minuitur, quaelibet pars minuitur.
units.tr: 3. Every part of what is augmented is increased; every part of what is diminished is lessened.

units.la: 4. Vt aliquid augeatur, non necesse est constituere vacuum, in quod id quod augetur, se recipiat.
units.tr: 4. In order for something to be augmented, it is not necessary to posit a void into which what is augmented receives itself.

units.la: 5. Neque necesse est ut augmentatio fiat, corpora se in eodem loco occupare: sed quodammodo locum, ut supra diximus, mutant.
units.tr: 5. Nor is it necessary, for augmentation to occur, that bodies occupy the same place; rather, as we said above, they change place in a certain way.

units.la: 6. Augmentatio non fit adveniente incorporeo, sed corporeo.
units.tr: 6. Augmentation does not occur when something incorporeal arrives, but when something corporeal does.

units.la: Vtrum, ut augmentatio fiat, necesse sit non solum secundum materiam, ve- rumetiam secundum speciem aliquid accedere?
units.tr: Whether, for augmentation to occur, it is necessary that something be added not only in respect of matter but also in respect of species.

units.la: Ei quod augmentabitur, accedere aliquid debet non tantum secundum materiam, sed etiam secundum speciem. Nam tametsi materia aliqua rei cuipiam accedat, non tamen propterea haec maior efficietur: veluti si aquae accedat non aqua, ossi non os, nequaquam sane propter hanc accessionem aqua vel os augeaugebũtur. At uero si ijsdem accedat quod eiusdem est speciei, nempe aqua ad aquam, os ad os, tunc augmentatio sequetur. Quocirca necessarium quoq; est, ut id per quod augmentatio fiet, similitudinem atq; συμπαθείαν[?] quandam cum eo habeat quod augebitur, nec non saltem potentia tale sit, quale id quod augetur, actu est. Itaq; cibus potentia esse debet eius speciei, cuius est ipsum corpus actu, quod incrementum suscipiet. Etenim si augenda est caro, necesse est cibo inesse aliquam cum carne συμπαθείαν[?] siue similitudine, ut paulatim in speciem carnis transfire possit. Et si ossa augeri debent, oportet id per quod fiet augmentatio, ossis speciem temporis progressu inducere.
units.tr: Something must be added to that which is to be augmented not only in respect of matter but also in respect of species. For although some matter may be added to a certain thing, that thing will not for that reason become greater: for example, if water is added to something that is not water, or bone to something that is not bone, then surely neither water nor bone will be augmented on account of such an addition. But if something of the same species is added, namely water to water or bone to bone, then augmentation follows. Hence it is also necessary that that through which augmentation takes place have some likeness and some sympathy [συμπαθείαν] with that which is to be augmented, and that it be at least potentially such as the thing augmented is actually. Thus food must be potentially of the species of which the body that is to receive the increase is actually. For if flesh is to be augmented, it is necessary that there be in the food some sympathy or likeness with flesh, so that it can gradually pass over into the species of flesh. And if bones are to be increased, that through which the augmentation will take place must, as time goes on, introduce the species of bone.

units.la: Sed hæc de generatione, alteratione & augmentatione, quæ sunt distinctæ species motus secundum substantiam, qualitatem & quantitatem, in præsenti sufficiant. Porrò quia generatio nō fit sine actione & passione (siquidem in generatione semper est aliquid quod agit, & aliquid quod patitur:) deinde non contingit agere & pati aliqua, nisi mutuo sese attingant: adhæc, neque generatio, neque alteratio, neq; augmentatio, perficitur sine rerum mutua inter sese commixtione: ideo de his tribus, attactu, inquam, actione & passione, mixtione, nonnulla sunt dicenda.
units.tr: But these points about generation, alteration and augmentation, which are distinct species of motion with respect to substance, quality and quantity, are enough for the present. Moreover, since generation does not take place without action and passion (for in generation there is always something that acts and something that is acted upon), and since some things cannot act and be acted upon unless they touch one another mutually, and since neither generation, nor alteration, nor augmentation is accomplished without the mutual commingling of things, therefore some things must be said about these three: touch, I mean, action and passion, and mixture.

units.la: Quot modis dicitur attactus?
units.tr: How many ways is contact spoken of?

units.la: Quatuor. 1. Cum eorum corporū, quibus certa est magnitudo, atque positus, extremitates coniunguntur. Quo quidem in genere attactus tria hæc, extremitates, locus, positus, simul ut sint necesse est. Certarum magnitudinum certus esse locus debet, & ut illæ sese attingat, certus quoq; positus earundem requiritur. Ita namq; poni possent, ut neque quaquam sese attingerent.
units.tr: In four ways. (1) When the extremities of those bodies which have a definite size and position are joined together. In this kind of contact these three things must necessarily exist together: extremities, place, and position. Bodies of definite size must have a definite place, and for them to touch one another their definite position is also required. For they could be placed in such a way that they did not touch at all.

units.la: 2. Sese attingunt, quæ diuersas habentia magnitudines atq; positus coniunguntur suis extremitatibus, præterea ad inuicem agunt ac patiuntur. Itaq; ad hoc genus attactus quatuor concurrunt: nimirum inæqualium magnitudinum locus, positus, extremitates coniunctæ, & vis agendi patiendique[?]. Quamobrem hic attactus in motibus naturalibus proprie atq; præcipuè consideratur. Unde quādo corpora grauia & leuia diuersas habent magnitudines atq; positus: deinde diuersa loca, quandoquidem leue sursum, graue autem tendit deorsum: præterea extremitates eorundem corporum sibi coniunguntur: postremò illa ipsa corpora inter se & agunt & patiuntur: in his sanè physicus iste attactus deprehendi potest, deq; hoc attactu præcipuè nobis sermo est, utpote qui in speciebus motus locum habet.
units.tr: (2) Those things touch which, having different sizes and positions, are joined by their extremities, and besides act upon and are acted upon by one another. Thus four things concur in this kind of contact: namely, the place of unequal magnitudes, their position, their joined extremities, and the power of acting and being acted upon. Hence this contact is considered properly and chiefly in natural motions. Whenever heavy and light bodies have different sizes and positions, and different places (since the light tends upwards and the heavy downwards), and moreover their extremities are joined together, and finally those same bodies both act and are acted upon by one another, then indeed this physical contact can be detected, and it is of this contact that our discussion is chiefly concerned, since it has a place among the species of motion.

units.la: 3. Sese attingunt, quæ diuersas habentia magnitudines coniunguntur suis extremitatibus, atq; alterum quidem movet (quod ipsum interea manet immobile) alterum vero movetur: & hæc forma in speciebus motus naturalis cernitur, cum quod movet se habeat ut agens, quod movetur ut patiens.
units.tr: (3) Those things touch which, having different sizes, are joined by their extremities, and one of them indeed moves (while it itself remains immobile) and the other is moved. This form is seen in the species of natural motion, when that which moves stands as the agent, and that which is moved as the patient.

units.la: 4. Sese attingunt, quando unius alicuius rei vis transfit in alteram, quæ tamen rei illi nequaquam coniungitur vicissim: quo pacto molestia atq; dolor hominem aliquem dicitur tangere, ipse autem homo molestiam seu dolorem non tangit vicissim, neq; ei coniungitur. Huius autem formæ non est usus in præsentia.
units.tr: (4) Things touch when the power of one thing passes over into another, which nevertheless is not joined to that thing in return. In this way pain and grief are said to touch a man, while the man himself does not touch the pain or grief in return, nor is he joined to it. The use of this form is not relevant at present.

units.la: DE ACTIONE ET passione. Quæ inter se agunt & patiuntur, si- milia'ne sunt, an dissi- milia?
units.tr: ON ACTION AND passion. Do things that act upon and are acted upon by one another resemble each other, or do they differ?

units.la: DE hac quæstione alij aliter opinati sunt.
units.tr: Concerning this question, different people have held different opinions.

units.la: 1. Quidam definiuerunt, simile non posse pati à simili. Nulla enim ratio reddi potest, cur è duobus prorsus similibus unum potius agat quàm alterum. Itaq; ut aliqua inter se agant & patiantur, ea dissimilia esse oportet. Atque hoc quidem pacto magnus ignis aget, parvus vero ab eodem patictur, &c.
units.tr: (1) Some have defined that a like thing cannot be acted upon by a like thing. For no reason can be given why, of two perfectly alike things, one should act rather than the other. Therefore, for things to act upon and be acted upon one another, they must be unlike. In this way a large fire will act, and a small one will be acted upon by it, and so on.

units.la: 2. Democritus arbitratus est, contrario modo simile agere in simile, & simile itidem pati à simili. Quæ enim dissimilia sunt ac contraria, non sic posse inter se consentire, ut alterum agat, alterum patiatur.
units.tr: (2) Democritus thought that like acts on like in a contrary manner, and likewise that like is acted upon by like. For things that are unlike and contrary cannot so agree with one another that one acts and the other is acted upon.

units.la: 3. Certa opinio, quam retinere liceat, quamque Aristoteles ex duabus præcedentibus conflauit, & quasi mediam constituit, hæc est: Quæcunque inter se agent & patientur, ea aliquo modo similia, & aliquo modo dissimilia esse debent.
units.tr: (3) The certain opinion, which may be held, and which Aristotle compounded out of the two preceding ones and set up as a kind of middle course, is this: whatever things act upon and are acted upon by one another must be in some respect alike and in some respect unlike.

units.la: Etenim quæcunque nata sunt inter se agere aut pati, aut sunt contraria, aut contrarietatem aliquam habentia. Si autem sunt contraria, tum necesse est eiusdem esse generis. Ponuntur namque contraria sub eodem genere: ut virtus & vitium, calidum & frigidum. Interea autem illa ipsa distinguuntur specie inter se. Ergo quatenus quæ agunt & patiuntur, sub eodem genere sunt posita, aliquomodo sunt similia: quatenus vero distinguuntur specie, sunt dissimilia. Hoc autem facto videmus corpus pati a corpore, colorem a colore, saporem a sapore. Hinc vero fit, ut omne agens paulatim patiens reddat sibi simile. Sic calefaciens paulatim id quod calefit, anteaq; frigidum erat, reddit calidum: item frigefaciens reddit id quod frigefit, calidumq; fuerat, frigidum. Ac sunt quidem agens ac patiens sibi contraria, nimirum sub eodem posita genere, ideoq; similia, attamen specie dissimilia. Deinde agens in id laborat, ut transmutet. Omnis autem transmutatio è contrario fit in contrarium. Quare agens, dum contrarium suum, patiens uidelicet, transmutat, prorsus transmutat in contrarium, atque diuersum reddit ab eo quod antea fuerat: ueluti agens calidum facit, ut contrarium eius patiens frigidum contrariam naturam induat, id est, ut ex frigido fiat etiam calidum. Ergo hinc manifestum fit, quòd omne agens paulatim reddit contrarium suum patiens sibi simile.
units.tr: For whatever things are by nature apt to act or be acted upon by one another are either contraries or have some contrariety. If they are contraries, then they must necessarily be of the same genus. For contraries are placed under the same genus, as virtue and vice, hot and cold. Yet at the same time these same things are distinguished from one another in species. Therefore, insofar as things that act and are acted upon are placed under the same genus, they are in some way alike; insofar as they are distinguished in species, they are unlike. Now we see that this is so: a body is acted upon by a body, a colour by a colour, a flavour by a flavour. Hence it comes about that every agent gradually makes the patient like itself. Thus that which heats gradually makes what is being heated, which before was cold, hot; likewise that which cools makes what is being cooled, which had been hot, cold. And indeed the agent and the patient are contrary to each other, namely placed under the same genus, and therefore alike, yet different in species. Next, the agent labours to change the patient. But every change takes place from a contrary into a contrary. Therefore the agent, while it changes its contrary, namely the patient, changes it wholly into the contrary, and makes it different from what it was before: as when the agent makes something hot, so that its contrary, the patient, which is cold, takes on the contrary nature, that is, so that from cold it becomes hot too. Hence it is made manifest that every agent gradually makes its contrary, the patient, like itself.

units.la: Quomodo fit actio & passio in re- bus naturalibus?
units.tr: How do action and passion take place in natural things?

units.la: Variae de hac quaestione extiterunt opiniones. Vt enim plerique varia constituerunt rerum naturalium principia, ita variis quoque modis actionem & passionem fieri existimarunt.
units.tr: Various opinions have arisen concerning this question. For just as many have set up various principles of natural things, so they have also thought that action and passion come about in various ways.

units.la: 1. Empedocles arbitratus est, fieri actionem & passionem, quando agens & patiens principale subit, ueluti poros rerum naturalium, qui patiuntur: deinde, fieri comixtionem rerum, ubi pari quadam proportione sibi iunguntur.
units.tr: (1) Empedocles thought that action and passion take place when the agent and the patient enter the principal pores of natural things, which are what is acted upon; then a mixture of things takes place where they are joined together in a certain equal proportion.

units.la: 2. Democritus & Leucippus putarunt, fieri actionem & passionem motu quodam atque concursu corpusculorum atomorum, quae ipsi posuerunt rerum principia.
units.tr: (2) Democritus and Leucippus held that action and passion come about through a certain motion and collision of atomic corpuscles, which they posited as the principles of things.

units.la: 3. Melissus constituit rerum principium unum, ens immobile, idemque infinitum, atque ab hoc ipso fieri omnem actionem & passionem voluit.
units.tr: (3) Melissus set up one principle of things, an immobile being, which is also infinite, and he wished that all action and passion arise from this very being.

units.la: 4. Plato actionem & passione acceptas ferebat superficiebus, ex quibus omnia, ut ipse putat, fiunt, & in quas rursus omnia oportet resolui.
units.tr: (4) Plato attributed action and passion to surfaces, from which all things, as he himself thinks, are made, and into which again all things must be resolved.

units.la: Quæ opiniones si inter se conferantur, omnium invenictur absurdissima tertia, utpote quæ contra omnes recte philosophantes ponit principium infinitum, deinde idipsum omni motu spoliat. Nulla autem est opinio hic recitata, quam non sit facile ei refellere, qui rationes illorum philosophorum, præterea quæ supra sæpius sunt exposita, paulo accuratius intuetur.
units.tr: If these opinions are compared with one another, the third is found to be the most absurd of all, since it, contrary to all who philosophise rightly, posits an infinite principle, and then strips that very principle of all motion. Yet there is no opinion recited here which it is not easy to refute for anyone who looks a little more carefully at the arguments of those philosophers, and also at those that have been set out more than once above.

units.la: Cæterum ut ad quæstionem propositam respondeatur, operæprecium est quinq; proprietates actionis & passionis explicare.
units.tr: But, to answer the question proposed, it is worth while to explain five properties of action and passion.

units.la: 1. Quale est ipsum agens actu, tale debet omne patiens esse potentia. Nisi enim istud fiat, actio impeditur.
units.tr: (1) Whatever the agent is in act, every patient must be in potency of that kind. For unless this happens, action is hindered.

units.la: 2. Patiens aptum natum est, non tantum secundum unam aliquam partem pati, verum secundum quamlibet & totum, quantumcunq; id fuerit: nisi enim totum pati possit, actio non perficitur.
units.tr: (2) A patient is fitted and born to be acted upon not only in one part but in any part and in the whole, however large it may be; for unless the whole can be acted upon, the action is not completed.

units.la: 3. Quod magis idoneum dispositumq; est ad patiendum, id citius & perfectius patietur: quod vero minus idoneum dispositumq; est, id difficilius minusq;[?] patitur.
units.tr: (3) That which is more suitable and disposed to be acted upon will be acted upon more quickly and more completely; that which is less suitable and disposed is acted upon with more difficulty and less.

units.la: 4. Omne patiens continuum est, & nullo modo actu divisum separatumque: quod ex secunda proprietate intelligi melius potest.
units.tr: (4) Every patient is continuous, and in no way divided or separated in act; this can be understood better from the second property.

units.la: §. Agens propinquum fieri debet ipsi patienti, ut illud attingat, atque ita vim suam exerat. Calefacit quidem ignis corpora paulo longius distita: sed id fit, quod prius calefaciat aerem propinquum, a quo aere sive per quem aerem calor deinde transit ad remota corpora.
units.tr: §. The agent must be near the patient itself, so that it touches it and so exerts its power. Fire indeed heats bodies somewhat further apart, but this happens because it first heats the neighbouring air, and from that air, or through that air, the heat then passes on to the distant bodies.

units.la: Ex his igitur manifestum est, in iis & per ea actionem atq; passionem fieri, in quibus proprietates hae, quas diximus, conspiciuntur: non autem ratione principiorum materialium, sicut veteres quidam philosophi suspicati sunt, ipsa rerum dispositi-o, & non simpliciter materia actionis & passionis causa existunt.
units.tr: From these things, therefore, it is manifest that action and passion take place in and through those things in which these properties which we have mentioned are seen; not by reason of material principles, as certain ancient philosophers suspected, but the very arrangement of things and not simply matter are the cause of action and passion.

units.la: DE MIXTIONE.
units.tr: CONCERNING MIXTURE.

units.la: An sit mixtio?
units.tr: Is there such a thing as mixture?

units.la: Quidam voluerunt negare mixtionem esse, sed revincuntur manifestis in rebus naturalibus experimentis. Sic autem illi sunt ratiocinati: Si est mixtio, tum oportet ea quae miscentur, aut manere integra, aut corrumpi. Atqui neutrum horum est dicendum. Igitur nulla est mixtio. Si dicas, quod manet integra: tu certe non magis manet mixta, quam antea fuerant, sed tantum erunt prope posita. Si dicas, quod corrumpantur: tum sequitur, mixta ea esse quae non existunt, sed esse desierunt: quod absurdum est. Si dicas, partem quidem manere, partem vero corrumpi: corrupi: tum adhuc sequentur ea quæ iam diximus incomoda, uidelicet aliqua esse tantum prope posita, & aliqua mixta esse quæ non sunt entia. Sed & hæ rationes ex sequentibus facilè diluentur.
units.tr: Some have wished to deny that mixture exists, but they are refuted by the plain evidence of experience in natural things. They reasoned thus: If there is mixture, then the things that are mixed must either remain intact or be corrupted. But neither of these can be said. Therefore there is no mixture. If you say that they remain intact, then they are certainly not more mixed than they were before, but will merely be placed close together. If you say that they are corrupted, then it follows that the things which are mixed are those which do not exist but have ceased to be, which is absurd. If you say that part remains and part is corrupted, then the inconveniences we have already mentioned still follow: namely, that some things are merely placed close together, and some things are mixed though they are not existing beings. But these arguments will easily be dissolved from what follows.

units.la: QVID ET QVALIS MIXTIO.
units.tr: WHAT MIXTURE IS, AND OF WHAT KIND

units.la: Quomodo differt mixtio à gene- ratione, alteratione & au- gmentatione?
units.tr: How does mixture differ from generation, alteration and augmentation?

units.la: 1. Differt à generatione, quia in generatione forma quæ potentia increvit, accedit quidè ad materiam, veruntamè materiæ nequaquam miscetur. Ita ignis generatur, quando lignum accenditur: non autem ignis dicitur ligno misceri. Nam ignis quidem generatur, lignum verò corrumpitur.
units.tr: 1. It differs from generation, because in generation the form, having grown in potency, indeed attaches itself to the matter, but is by no means mixed with the matter. Thus fire is generated when wood is set alight, but fire is not said to be mixed with the wood. For fire is generated, while the wood is corrupted.

units.la: 2. Differt ab alteratione, quia per passionem miscetur suo subiecto: ut albedo corpori, figura cerae, tumor vel rotunditas figurae, disciplina animae. Enimuero passiones & habitus adiungi vel induci subiectis possunt, ijsque inhærent, verùm admisceri impossibile est.
units.tr: 2. It differs from alteration, because in mixture one thing is mixed with its subject by way of a passion: as whiteness with a body, shape with wax, a swelling or roundness with a figure, learning with the soul. Indeed passions and habits can be added to or induced in subjects, and they inhere in them, but it is impossible for them to be mixed in.

units.la: 3. Differt ab augmentatione. Nam in hac id per quod augmentatio fiet, oportet corrumpi, necnon simile ei fieri quod augetur. Cibus namque corrumpitur, & similis fit corpori animali aucto. At verò in mixtione non oportet id per quod fiet mixtio, corrumpi. Igitur mixtio neque generatio est, neque alteratio, neque augmentatio.
units.tr: 3. It differs from augmentation. For in augmentation, that by which the augmentation is made must be corrupted, and must become like the thing that is increased. Food, for instance, is corrupted and becomes like the body of the animal that is grown. In mixture, however, that by which the mixture is made need not be corrupted. Therefore mixture is neither generation, nor alteration, nor augmentation.

units.la: Quid est mixtio,& quomodo ea fit?
units.tr: What is mixture, and how is it brought about?

units.la: Mixtio est, in qua una pars altera quadam proportione ita contemperatur, ut eiusdem fiant generis, necnon commune sortiantur nomen. Atq; hac quidem de causa mixtio non fit, ubi alterum iuxta alterum ponitur, caq; inter se non contemperantur. Vbi enim alterum iuxta alterum tantùm ponitur, ibi omnia actu manent uti fuerant antea. Similiter mixtio non fit ex iis quorum non est eadem materia. Etenim quaecunq; mixtione contemperabuntur, eorum oportet quaedam sint actiua, quaedam uero passiua ad invicem. Atqui quae ad invicem sunt actiua & passiua, eadem necesse est communi constare materia. Igitur & quae miscebuntur, eiusdem esse materiae necesse est. Intellige autem eiusdem esse materiae, quae inter se misceri & contemperari apta nata sunt. Sic liquida inter sese commiscentur. Adhaec mixtio non est, ubi ea coniunguntur, quorum nulla est in quantitate proportio: veluti si paucula opponantur valde multis, & parua valde magnis. Siquidem paucula illa in valde multis consumuntur protinus & evanescunt, neq; percipiuntur per partes late diffusa. Idem iudicium, cum parua adiiciuntur valde magnis. Videre aut id licet, ubi guttula uini apponitur magno vasi pleno aquae, hic certe nihil reliqui manet ex uini materia, neq; aqua eius sensu ullo deprehenditur.
units.tr: Mixture is that in which one part is so tempered with another in a certain proportion that they become of the same kind and acquire a common name. For this reason mixture does not take place where one thing is merely placed beside another and they are not tempered with each other. For where one thing is only placed beside another, there everything remains actually as it was before. Likewise, mixture does not take place from things that do not have the same matter. For whatever things are going to be tempered by mixture, some of them must be active and others passive towards each other. But things that are active and passive towards one another must necessarily share a common matter. Therefore the things that are to be mixed must also be of the same matter. Now by "of the same matter" understand those things which are naturally fit to be mixed and tempered with one another; thus liquids mix with one another. Moreover, there is no mixture where things are joined between which there is no proportion in quantity, as when very few things are set against very many, or very small things against very large. For the few are at once used up and vanish among the many, and are not perceived as they are spread widely through the parts. The same judgment holds when small things are added to very large ones. One can see this where a drop of wine is put into a large vessel full of water: here certainly nothing of the wine's matter remains, and the water is not detected by any sense as wine.

units.la: Quænam sunt miscibilia?
units.tr: What things are capable of being mixed?

units.la: Quæ proportione quadam sibi æquantur, & contrarietatem aliquam in se habent, necnon facile dividuntur contemperanturq;. Ex definitione antecedenti possunt hæc membra utcunque intelligi:nos tamen maioris lucis causa breuiter explicabimus.
units.tr: Those things which are equal to one another in a certain proportion, which have some contrariety within themselves, and which are easily divided and tempered. From the preceding definition these points can be understood in some way; nevertheless, for greater clarity, we will briefly explain them.

units.la: 1. Oportet res miscibiles proportione quadam sibi æquari. Nam si non esset aliqua inter eas proportio, difficulter contemperarentur, atq; tertium quiddam, in quo utrarumque rerum natura aliquo modo eluceret, nunquam constitueretur.
units.tr: 1. Things capable of being mixed must be equal to one another in a certain proportion. For if there were no proportion between them, they would be tempered with difficulty, and some third thing, in which the nature of both substances would somehow shine forth, would never be formed.

units.la: 2. Oportet ite res miscibiles esse contrarias, quando alias actioni & passioni non potest in eis esse locus.
units.tr: 2. Things capable of being mixed must also be contrary, since otherwise there is no room for action and passion between them.

units.la: 3. Oportet res miscibiles facile diuidi, dispergi & contemperari. Nisi enim sint huiusmodi, ipsa mixtio impeditur. Vnde fit, quod quæ diuersorum sunt generum, ut liquida & solida, non facile commiscentur. sed liquida inter se, ueluti aqua & uinū: item sicca, ut arena & terra, miscentur, &c. Item modica modicis facilius miscentur, quàm multa multis.
units.tr: 3. Things capable of being mixed must be easily divided, dispersed and tempered. For unless they are of this kind, the mixture itself is hindered. Hence it comes about that things of different kinds, such as liquids and solids, do not mix easily; but liquids mix with one another, as water and wine, and likewise dry things, as sand and earth, mix, and so on. Also, small quantities mix more easily with small quantities than large with large.

units.la: Atq; ut in aliquibus rebus magis, in quibusdam uerò minus proprietates illæ sese exerunt: ita quasdam res magis, quasdam uerò minus miscibiles decet intelligamus.
units.tr: And just as those properties show themselves more in some things and less in others, so we should understand that some things are more and some less capable of being mixed.

units.la: Porrò ubi hoc pacto, quid & qualis sit genera-tio, tio,tum quæ ipsius affinia,alteratio,inquâ, augmentatio,deinde actio & passio,deinde mixtio,satis superq; est expositum:superest de materia generationis, hoc est, de elementis, ex quibus generationem omnem fieri necessum est,quædam dicamus.
units.tr: Moreover, since in this way what generation is and of what kind, together with alteration, augmentation (which are akin to it), then action and passion, and then mixture, has been set out sufficiently and more than sufficiently, there remains to say something concerning the matter of generation, that is, concerning the elements, out of which all generation must necessarily come about.

units.la: DE MATERIA GENERA- tionis,seu de elementis.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE MATTER OF GENERATION, OR CONCERNING THE ELEMENTS.

units.la: Quæ nam sunt principia materia- lia,ex quibus res naturales generantur?
units.tr: What are the material principles from which natural things are generated?

units.la: Variæ de hac quæstione fuerunt opiniones. I. Quidam unum dixerunt principium materiale omnium rerum, & ex his alij ignem. II. Alij aerem. III. Alij aquam. IIII. Alij medium quiddam inter ignem & aerem. V. Quidam posuerunt duo principia, ignem videlicet & terram. VI. Quidam tria: ac nonnulli quidem ignem, terram, aquam. VII. Nonnulli ignem, terram, aerem. VIII. Quidam quatuor constituerunt: ut Empedocles quatuor elementa, ignem, aerem, aquam, terram, dicens ex his per congregationem & segregationem generari & corrumpi omnia. IX. Plato in Timæo quatuor illis elementis addidit quandam materiam augustissimam, quæ omnia illa in se comprehendit, vocatque eam communem omnium receptaculum. Cæterum quàm aberret à vero illarum septem
units.tr: Various opinions have been held on this question. I. Some said that there is one material principle of all things, and of these some said fire. II. Others said air. III. Others said water. IV. Others said something intermediate between fire and air. V. Some posited two principles, namely fire and earth. VI. Some posited three: some indeed fire, earth and water. VII. Some fire, earth and air. VIII. Some set up four: as Empedocles did, four elements, fire, air, water and earth, saying that all things are generated and corrupted from these by union and separation. IX. Plato in the Timaeus added to those four elements a certain most excellent matter, which comprehends all those within itself, and he calls it the common receptacle of all. How far the authors of those seven opinions stray from the truth, and Plato himself too (for we set aside Empedocles, who did not speak altogether wrongly about matter itself), in positing a certain sensible body separate from the four elements, can be judged without difficulty. If anyone wants a refutation of the Platonic view, let him seek it from Aristotle.

units.la: opinionum authores, deinde ipse etiam Plato (nam Empedoclem, qui non omnino male locutus est de ipsa materia, excludimus) ponens quoddam corpus sensibile a quatuor elementis separatum, nullo negotio iudicari potest.Confutationem Platonicae sententiae si quis desiderat,ex Aristotele petat. X. Post omnes Aristoteles principium materiale omnium rerum sensibilium definit esse materiam siue substantiam a forma minime separabilem,atq; ita contrarietatis capacem, ut actio passioq; locu in ea habere queant, tum ciusmodi, ut ex ea quae uocantur elementa gignantur.
units.tr: After all of them, Aristotle defines the material principle of all sensible things as matter or substance that can by no means be separated from form, and is thus capable of contrariety, so that action and passion can take place in it, and from which the so-called elements are then generated.

units.la: 1. Substantia aliqua seu materia ad rei naturalis generationem existere oportet, cum ex nihilo nihil possit fieri.Atq; eidem inseparabiliter adiuncta esse debet forma, non quidem haec uel illa, sed talis quae hanc uel illam possit interueniente generatione suscipere: nam materia sensibilem ponere, quae omni simpliciter forma sit destituta,absurdum est.
units.tr: 1. Some substance or matter must exist for the generation of a natural thing, since nothing can come from nothing. And a form must be inseparably joined to it, not indeed this or that form, but such a form as can admit this or that form when generation intervenes; for to posit a sensible matter altogether destitute of any form is absurd.

units.la: 2. Requiritur in illa materia cōtrarietas, ac talis quidem accipitur in pugnantibus qualitatibus, calido uidelicet & frigido, humido & sicco: quae nisi adessent materiae generationis, nulla scqueretur actio & passio,ac proinde neq; generatio.
units.tr: 2. In that matter there is required contrariety, and this is found in opposing qualities, namely hot and cold, moist and dry. Unless these were present in the matter of generation, no action and passion would follow, and consequently no generation either.

units.la: 3. Ex illa materia necessum est constent elementa, quae quidem antedictis qualitatibus praecipue discernuntur, & per easdem qualitates inter se mutanmutantur, itemque & agunt & patiuntur.
units.tr: 3. The elements, which are chiefly distinguished by the aforesaid qualities, and which change into one another through the same qualities, and likewise both act and are acted upon, must necessarily be made from that matter.

units.la: En igitur, quae sit generationis materia, & quae in ea spectari debeant, ut generatio procedat.
units.tr: Here, then, is what the matter of generation is, and what must be observed in it for generation to proceed.

units.la: Quot sunt principia seu differentiae, quibus elementa distinguuntur, & ex quibus eorundem rectus colligitur numerus?
units.tr: How many are the principles, or differences, by which the elements are distinguished, and from which the correct number of them is gathered?

units.la: Quatuor sunt elementorum principia, ex quibus illa & oriuntur & distinguuntur: videlicet calidum, frigidum, siccum & humidum. Quae qualitates sunt tangibiles, atque tactu potissimum deprehenduntur. Possunt quidem aliae quoque qualitates in elementis animadverti, veluti gravitas & levitas, quae illis diversorum motuum causa existunt. Sunt insuper in illis adhuc aliae qualitates, de quibus sensus tactus iudicat: ut duritiei [?] & mollities, asperitas, leuitas, subtilitas, crassities, &c. Sed tamen ex illis quatuor ante nominatis origo atque differentia elementorum colligi debet: idque his de causis.
units.tr: There are four principles of the elements, from which they both arise and are distinguished: namely hot, cold, dry and moist. These qualities are tangible, and are grasped chiefly by touch. Indeed other qualities also can be noticed in the elements, such as heaviness and lightness, which exist in them as the causes of their different motions. Moreover, there are still other qualities in them, which the sense of touch judges: such as hardness [?] and softness, roughness, smoothness, fineness, coarseness, and so on. But nevertheless the origin and difference of the elements ought to be gathered from those four named above, and this for the following reasons.

units.la: 1. Elementa secundum has potissimum quatuor qualitates tangibiles inter se agunt & patiuntur. Etenim ob gravitatem & levitatem ea non agere aut pati, facile est intelligere. Levia enim, si ad altissimum locum: & gravia, si ad infimum possent pervenire, tum statim quiescerent. Ergo aliae sunt quaedam qualitates, a quibus actio & passio in elementis provenit.Itaq; calidum,ut ignis,coniungit ὁμογενῆ[?], quæq; sunt eiusdem ordinis seu naturæ: & separat ἑτερογενῆ[?], quæq; sunt diversæ. Frigidu homogenia & heterogenia iungit & congregat.Humidum facile separatur à termino proprio,ac bene coniungitur alieno:siccum è diverso bene coniungitur termino proprio,ac male alieno. Itaq; omnes æqualitates vim habent agendi & patiendi: quamuis calidum & frigidum maximè agunt, humidum verò & siccum maximè patiuntur.
units.tr: 1. The elements act upon and are acted upon by one another chiefly according to these four tangible qualities. For that the elements do not act or suffer through heaviness and lightness is easy to understand. For light things, if they could reach the highest place, and heavy things, if they could reach the lowest, would at once come to rest. Therefore there are certain qualities from which action and passion arise in the elements. Thus the hot, like fire, joins together the like [ὁμογενῆ], that is, things of the same order or nature, and separates the unlike [ἑτερογενῆ], that is, things that are different. The cold joins and gathers together both the like and the unlike. The moist is easily separated from its proper boundary and joins well with an alien one; the dry, on the other hand, joins well with its proper boundary and badly with an alien one. So all the qualities have the power of acting and being acted upon, although the hot and the cold act most, and the moist and the dry are most acted upon.

units.la: 2. Hæ quatuor qualitates sunt primariæ, utpote ad quas reliquæ omnes,ut subtile & crassum,lubricum & aridum,molle & durum,asperum & læve, &c. reducuntur. Nam subtile,lubricum,molle,reducuntur ad humidum: sed crassum,aridum,durum, ad siccum ; atq; ita deinceps.
units.tr: 2. These four qualities are the primary ones, since all the others, such as subtle and thick, slippery and dry, soft and hard, rough and smooth, etc., are reduced to them. For subtle, slippery and soft are reduced to moist, but thick, dry and hard are reduced to dry; and so on.

units.la: Cum igitur quatuor illæ qualitates sint primariæ, reliquæ verò tantùm secundariæ,merito ex illis sumentur elementorum differentiæ.
units.tr: Since these four qualities are primary, and the rest are only secondary, the differences of the elements are rightly taken from them.

units.la: Quomodo ex illis qualitatibus com- probabitur elementorum numerus?
units.tr: How will the number of the elements be proved from those qualities?

units.la: Duabus rationibus. 1. Ex eo quòd qualitates illæ constituunt inter se quatuor συζυγίας[?], seu coniugationes,hoc pacto: Calidum & ficum. Calidum & humidu. Frigidum & siccum. Frigidu & humidu. Hoc modo qualitates hæ in ali quo elemeto con iunguntur: ut in Igne. Aere. Terra. Aqua.
units.tr: In two ways. 1. From the fact that these qualities form among themselves four pairings, or conjugations, as follows: hot and dry; hot and moist; cold and dry; cold and moist. In this way these qualities are joined together in a certain element: as in Fire, Air, Earth, Water.

units.la: Calidum & frigidum, humidum & siccū, quum sint qualitates maximè pugnantes, συζυγίαν[?] nullam admittunt, neq; in uno aliquo elemento coniunguntur. Igitur cū ex qualitatibus illis rectè constituantur quatuor coniugationes, eædemq; singulæ singulis accomodentur elementis, merito etiam quatuor elementa numerantur.
units.tr: Hot and cold, moist and dry, since they are the most opposed qualities, admit no pairing and are not joined together in any one element. Therefore, since four pairings are rightly constituted from those qualities, and each of these is fitted to a single element, the four elements are rightly counted as well.

units.la: 2. Ex ueterum authoritate, quorum tametsi aliqui pauciora posuerunt elementa quàm quatuor, tamè nulli ausi sunt ultra quaternarium numerum progredi, & quidem permoti quadruplici illa συζυγία[?] qua diximus. Atq; illi ipsi qui pauciora quàm quatuor posuerunt, semper in assignandis cuiq; elemento primis qualitatibus aberrarunt. Ergo ratione illarum quatuor qualitatum, quatuor συζυγίας[?] constituentium, quaternarius elementorum numerus rectè asstruetur.
units.tr: 2. From the authority of the ancients, of whom, although some posited fewer than four elements, none dared to go beyond the number four, and indeed they were moved by that fourfold pairing of which we have spoken. And those very men who posited fewer than four always went wrong in assigning the primary qualities to each element. Therefore, by reason of those four qualities constituting four pairings, the number of four elements is rightly asserted.

units.la: Quot sunt proprietates ele- mentorum?
units.tr: What are the properties of the elements?

units.la: Sex. 1. Vnicuiq; elemento inuenitur aliquid agnatum & simile, quod non est purum uel simplex, ut ipsum elementum. Itaq; quod simile agnatumq; est igni, non est ignis, sed potius igneum: & quod simile est aeri, non est aer, sed aereum: eadem ratione quod aquæ,aqueum: quod terræ, terreum.
units.tr: Six. 1. In each element there is found something akin and similar, which is not pure or simple, as the element itself is. So what is similar and akin to fire is not fire but fiery; what is similar to air is not air but airy; by the same reasoning what belongs to water is watery, and what belongs to earth is earthy.

units.la: 2. Quamdiu elementa perfistunt in ea qualitate quæ in ipsis excellit, tamdiu nihil ex illis efficitur seu generatur. Porrò in igne excellit calidum, in aqua frigidum, in aere humidum, in terra siccum. Vt igitur ex iis elementis aliquid fiat, necessum est hæ qualitates aliquantum remittantur. Vt ex igne fiat aer, opus est aliquousque remitti uim caloris, & assumi aliquantam humiditatem, atque ita de cæteris.
units.tr: 2. As long as the elements persist in the quality that excels in them, nothing is made or generated from them. But in fire heat excels, in water cold, in air moisture, in earth dryness. Therefore, in order that something be made from these elements, these qualities must be somewhat relaxed. For fire to become air, it is necessary that the force of heat be relaxed to some extent and a certain amount of moisture be taken up, and so on for the rest.

units.la: 3. Ignis & aer semper tendunt sursum, atq; supero gaudet loco. Terra & aqua ex aduerso semper tendunt deorsum, atq; infero loco gaudent.
units.tr: 3. Fire and air always tend upward, and rejoice in the higher place. Earth and water, on the contrary, always tend downward, and rejoice in the lower place.

units.la: 4. Ex elementis, quæ medio loco posita sunt, ut aer & aqua, citius permiscentur, atque etiam uiciantur, quàm quæ extremum locum occupant, nempe ignis & terra. Ipsa situs propinquitas in illis duobus, rursusq; situs magna distantia in his duobus causam eius rei uidetur adferre. Quæ propè posita sunt, ea ad inuicem agunt & patiuntur facilius.
units.tr: 4. Of the elements placed in the middle position, such as air and water, those mix together and even change into one another more quickly than those that occupy the extreme place, namely fire and earth. The nearness of position in the first two, and again the great distance of position in the latter two, seems to be the cause of this. Things placed close together act and are acted upon more readily with one another.

units.la: 5. Cum in omnibus elementis inueniatur contrarietas ob unam saltem qualitatem, in quibusdam tamen inuenitur contrarietas & ob duas qualitates. Atque hoc quidem pacto aduersantur sibi ignis & aqua, aer & terra. Etenim ignis calidus est & siccus: aqua uero frigida & humida. Item aer calidus est & humidus: terra vero frigida & sicca.
units.tr: 5. Although in all the elements contrariety is found on account of at least one quality, in some it is found on account of two qualities. In this way fire and water, air and earth, are opposed to one another. For fire is hot and dry, but water is cold and moist. Likewise air is hot and moist, but earth is cold and dry.

units.la: 6. Etsi vero in unoquoque elemento reperiatur coiugatio duarum qualitatum, ut supra dictum est: semper tamen una qualitas intelligitur dominari, magisq; proprie ipsi elemento conuenire. Itaque in igne, qui est calidus & siccus, dominatur calor: in aere, qui est calidus & humidus, dominatur humiditas: in aqua, quae est frigida & humida, dominatur frigus: in terra, quae est frigida & sicca, dominatur siccitas. Ex his igitur proclive est de proprietatibus tam omnium elementorum, quam singulorum, iudicare. Ignis calidus & siccus, aer calidus & humidus, aqua frigida & humida, terra frigida & sicca.
units.tr: 6. Although indeed in each element a pairing of two qualities is found, as has been said above, nevertheless one quality is always understood to predominate and to belong more properly to the element itself. Thus in fire, which is hot and dry, heat predominates; in air, which is hot and moist, moisture predominates; in water, which is cold and moist, cold predominates; in earth, which is cold and dry, dryness predominates. From these things, therefore, it is easy to judge the properties both of all the elements and of each one. Fire is hot and dry, air hot and moist, water cold and moist, earth cold and dry.

units.la: Quomodo ex principiis materialibus, quae vocantur elementa, fit generatio?
units.tr: How does generation take place from the material principles, which are called elements?

units.la: Aliquot propositionibus id declaratur.
units.tr: This is explained in several propositions.

units.la: 1. Elementa gignuntur ex sese mutuo. Probatur. Nam agunt & patiuntur inter se invicem, mutuaq; est inter ea alteratio: ex quo cōsequitur, quod etiam ex se mutuo generentur.
units.tr: 1. The elements are generated from one another mutually. This is proved. For they act and are acted upon among one another, and there is a mutual alteration among them; from which it follows that they are also generated from one another.

units.la: 2. Ex quolibet elemēto quodlibet etiam elementum gigni potest. Probatur. Nã omnia sunt sibi invicem cōtraria, idq; aut duabus differentijs seu qualitatibus, aut saltē una, quemadmodū ex ante dictis cognosci potest. Si autem sunt sibi invicē cōtraria, conficitur, quòd cum agere, tum pati inter se inuicem queant, ac proinde[?] quodlibet quoque ex quolibet generari.
units.tr: 2. From any element any element whatever can be generated. This is proved. For all are mutually contrary, and this either by two differences or qualities, or at least by one, as can be known from what was said before. But if they are mutually contrary, it follows that they can both act and be acted upon among one another, and consequently any one can be generated from any other.

units.la: 3. Ea elementa in se mutuò transmutantur facilius, quæ quandam habent inter se coniunctionem ac συμφωνίαν: utpote in quibus unius tantum differentia transmutatio requiritur. Transmutantur uero difficilius, quæ nullam inter se coniunctionem habet. Habentia autem συμφωνίαν sunt, ignis & aer, terra & aqua: non habentia συμφωνίαν, ignis & aqua, aer & terra.
units.tr: 3. Those elements are changed into one another more easily which have a certain conjunction and symphonia [συμφωνία] among themselves, inasmuch as in them only the change of one difference is required. But those that have no conjunction among themselves are changed with more difficulty. Those having symphonia [συμφωνία] are fire and air, earth and water; those not having symphonia [συμφωνία] are fire and water, air and earth.

units.la: 4. Ex duobus elementis συμφωνίαν non habentibus possunt gigni elementa reliqua. Ex igne & aqua possunt generari aer & terra: ex aere uero & terra possunt generari ignis & aqua. Etenim si ex duabus qualitatibus ignis corrumpatur caliditas, tum remanet siccitas: deinde si ex duabus qualitatibus aquæ corrumpatur humiditas, tum remanet frigiditas. Quod igitur reliquum est, id siccum & frigidum est: hoc autem ipsum terra est. Propriæ namq; terræ qualitates sunt frigidu & siccum. Item ex igne et aqua fit aer, corrupta uidelicet ignis siccitate, atq; aquæ frigiditate. Tunc enim restant duæ qualitates, calidum uidelicet & humidum, quæ aeris propriæ existunt. Ad eundem uero modum iudicabis, ex aere & terra procreari ignem, itemq; aquam, &c.
units.tr: 4. From two elements not having symphonia [συμφωνία] the remaining elements can be generated. From fire and water air and earth can be generated; and from air and earth fire and water can be generated. For if from the two qualities of fire its heat is corrupted, then its dryness remains; then if from the two qualities of water its moisture is corrupted, then its coldness remains. What is left over, therefore, is dry and cold: and this very thing is earth. For the proper qualities of earth are cold and dry. Likewise from fire and water air is made, namely when the dryness of fire and the coldness of water are corrupted. For then two qualities remain, namely hot and moist, which are the proper qualities of air. In the same way you will judge that fire, and likewise water, etc., are produced from air and earth.

units.la: §. Ex duobus elementis συμφωνίαν habentibus unum quidem eorum ex altero gigni potest: non autem gignuntur ex eis reliqua elementa. Cuius propositionis prius membrum ex praecedentibus manifestum est. Quum enim unam tantum alterari in elementis illis qualitatem oporteat, perfacile transmutatio perficitur. Posterius autem membrum hoc pacto declaratur: Accipiamus, uerbi causa, ignem & aerem: ex his autem si aliquod diuersum elementum procrearetur, necessum foret, aut manere solam caliditatem, in qua conueniunt, atq; corrumpi hinc ignis siccitatem, inde aeris humiditatem: aut manere tum siccitatem, tum humiditatem, atq; corrumpi caliditatem. Atqui si remaneat sola caliditas, nullum certe ex ea elementum potest constitui: sin remaneant siccitas & humiditas, nec hae quidem qualitates uni alicui elemento congruunt, quamobrem nullum elementum producet. Igitur ex igne & aere nullum aliud elementum gigni potest. Idem uero iudicium est accipiendum de aqua & terra.
units.tr: §. From two elements having symphonia [συμφωνία], one of them can indeed be generated from the other, but the remaining elements are not generated from them. The first part of this proposition is clear from what has gone before. For since only one quality in those elements needs to be altered, the change is effected very easily. The second part is explained as follows. Let us take, for example, fire and air. If some different element were produced from these, it would be necessary either that only heat remain, in which they agree, and that the dryness of fire and the moisture of air be corrupted on either side; or that dryness and moisture both remain, and heat be corrupted. But if only heat remains, certainly no element can be constituted from it; but if dryness and moisture remain, these qualities do not belong together in any one element, and therefore they will produce no element. Therefore no other element can be generated from fire and air. The same judgement is to be taken concerning water and earth.

units.la: Obiectio. Vtrum unum elementum posit dici principium uel materia ele- menti alterius?
units.tr: Objection. Whether one element can be called the principle or matter of another element?

units.la: Dilutio. 1. Diximus quidem, Elementa ex elementis produci, & quadam uicissitudine alterum alterius induere natura. Atqui haec omnia ita accipi debent, ut potius intelligamus alterationem ac transmutationē in toto hoc negotio fieri, quàm generationem. Quod cum ita sit, elementum elementi principium vel materia dici nequit.
units.tr: Answer. 1. We have indeed said that elements are produced from elements, and that by a certain alternation one takes on the nature of another. But all these things must be understood in such a way that we recognise that in this whole matter what takes place is alteration and transmutation rather than generation. Since this is so, one element cannot be called the principle or matter of another element.

units.la: 2. Et quomodo posset fieri, ut elementum ex elemento generaretur? Aut enim ex uno aliquo essent omnia, aut ex pluribus procrearentur cætera. At verò non posse istud fieri, illæ qualitatum differentiæ, de quibus sæpius dictum, abundè declarant.
units.tr: 2. And how could it come about that one element is generated from another? For either all things would come from some one thing, or the rest would be produced from several. But that this cannot happen, those differences of qualities, of which we have often spoken, make abundantly clear.

units.la: 3. Si bene aducertimus, elementa ne aliarum quidem rerum naturalium atq; mixtorum corporum possunt dici materia siue principium simpliciter: quando manifestum est, res naturales nullas producì, nisi facta multiplici transmutatione: veluti cum ex terra fit os vel caro. Atque in ipsis corporibus compositis potius licet cernere aliquid aereum, quàm ipsum aerem: aliquid igneum, quàm ipsum ignem.
units.tr: 3. If we pay careful attention, elements cannot be called the matter or principle, simply speaking, even of other natural things and of mixed bodies. For it is evident that no natural things are produced except after many transmutations, as when bone or flesh comes from earth. And in the compound bodies themselves we may perceive something airy rather than air itself, and something fiery rather than fire itself.

units.la: Obiectio.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Empedocles negat, elementa in sese mutuò transfmutari. Ex ijs quæ dicta sunt, deprehendi potest, Empedoclem hac in parte errasse.
