Deceptus namq; est in eo, quòd elementa cuncta inter se æqualia esse existimauit, ut comparari quidem & alterari nullo modo possent. Huius tamen contrariam partem, id est, posse elementa in sese mutuò transmutari, satis ostendimus[?]. Hinc autem factum est, ut una absurditate posita. Empedocles ad alias quoq; absurdas sententias deductus fit. Itaq; ineptè idem statuit pleraque de ipsa generationis forma siue modo, dum omnia generari ac perfici uult per litem & amicitiam, tanquam primarias causas efficientes. Supra dictum est, ad generationem, sicut ad reliquas motus species, requiri quidem actionem & passionem: uerùm amicitia & lite nihil opus est. Deniq; & hoc absurdum est, quòd astruit res uniuersas ex elementis constitui. Nam animi adfectiones, itemq; habitus, ut memoria, obliuio, dolor, scientia, &c. non possunt dici ex elementis prouenire. Cauillus autem subesse huic rationi uidetur. Etsi enim hæ res non sunt immediatè ex elementis, sunt tamen affectiones siue assectus earum quæ ex elementis conflatæ cognoscuntur. Atque hæc quidem hactenus de elementis, quæ sunt corpora simplicia non generata ex alijs, quâuis ipsa inter se mutuò transmutentur. Superest, ut dicamus de generatione corporum compositorum seu mixtorum.
units.tr: Empedocles denies that the elements are transmuted into one another. From what has been said, it can be seen that Empedocles erred in this point. For he was deceived in this, that he thought all the elements to be equal to one another, so that they could in no way be compared or altered. We have, however, sufficiently shown the opposite part of this, namely that the elements can be transmuted into one another. Moreover, from this it came about that, one absurdity having been posited, Empedocles was also led to other absurd opinions. Thus he foolishly held many things also about the very form or manner of generation, while he wishes all things to be generated and perfected through strife and friendship as the primary efficient causes. It has been said above that generation, like the other species of motion, requires indeed action and passion, but there is no need of friendship and strife. Finally, this too is absurd, that he asserts all things to be constituted from the elements. For affections of the mind, and likewise habits, such as memory, forgetfulness, grief, knowledge, and so on, cannot be said to arise from the elements. A quibble, however, seems to lie behind this argument. For although these things are not immediately from the elements, they are nevertheless affections or attributes of those things which are known to be compounded from the elements. And so far, indeed, concerning the elements, which are simple bodies not generated from others, although they may be transmuted into one another. It remains that we speak of the generation of compound or mixed bodies.

units.la: DE GENERATIONE corporum mixtorum.
units.tr: ON THE GENERATION OF MIXED BODIES.

units.la: Quomodo ex elementis fit aliquod corpus mixtum: ut caro?
units.tr: How is a mixed body, such as flesh, formed from the elements?

units.la: IN generatione corporis mixti elementa simul concurrunt, atq; suarum qualitatum uim remittunt, ut eousque contemperari possint, dum apta fiant, ut corpus aliquod mixtum ex illis prodeat: veluti caro, os, nervus, &c. prorsus quemadmodum aquæ nimium calidæ contemperantur frigida affusa, donec apta fiat, ut quis in ea lavet. Quo quidem pacto neque elementa, neque eorundem extrema contraria, sunt simpliciter ipsius corporis mixti materia: sed ipsorum elementorum commune temperamentum, ad corporis mixti naturam ita accedens, ut certa species proveniat, a quo & nomen rei inditur. Hoc inquam commune elementorum temperamentum corporis mixti materia existit.
units.tr: In the generation of a mixed body, the elements come together and temper their qualities, so that they can be blended until they become suitable for some mixed body to arise from them, such as flesh, bone, sinew, and so on. This is just as very hot water is tempered when cold water is poured into it, until it is fit for someone to bathe in. In this way, neither the elements nor their contrary extremes are strictly the matter of the mixed body itself. Rather, the common temperament of the elements, approaching the nature of the mixed body so as to produce a definite species, is the matter, and the thing takes its name from it. I say that this common temperament of the elements is the matter of the mixed body.

units.la: Unde fit, quod corporum mixtorum adeo variæ generentur species?
units.tr: Whence come so many different species of mixed bodies?

units.la: Ex eo quod elementa non contemperentur semper cadè inter se proportione. Itaque, si ab igne domi netur calor, prodit aliqua species, in qua uis ignea eminet. Si ite dominetur in cotemperatione elementorum frigiditas, prodit aliqua species, in qua domi natur aqua: veluti glacies, &c. Sic & caro generatur ex terra & aqua, unde siccitas & frigiditas in ea deprehenditur.
units.tr: From the fact that the elements are not always blended in exactly the same proportion. So if heat prevails from fire in the blend, some species arises in which the fiery power stands out. If coldness prevails in the blend of the elements, some species arises in which water predominates, such as ice. In the same way, flesh is generated from earth and water, so that dryness and coldness are found in it.

units.la: Vtrum ad generatione corporum com- positorum necessario concurrat aliquid de singulis ele- mentis?
units.tr: Does something from each of the elements necessarily concur in the generation of composite bodies?

units.la: Maximè. Probatur duabus rationibus.
units.tr: Certainly. This is proved by two arguments.

units.la: I. Participant corpora mixta primùm aliquid de terra, quoniâ generatur in terra: ac necessum quidem est, unaquamq; rem de natura eius loci aliquid accipere, in quo nascitur: ac terrea quidem materia causa est, ut contrectari sensibusq; percipi corpora mixta possint. 2. Participant aliquid de aqua, cum hæc necessaria sit ad res naturales compingendas conglutinandasq;. Siquidem aqua optimè & coniungit rerum terminos, & coniungitur. 3. Si autem participat de aqua & terra, necessum sanè est, partem etiam habeant ab elementis contrarijs, videlicet igne, qui aduersatur aquæ: & aere, qui oppositus est terræ. Etenim ad productionem corporum mixtorum, necessarium est elementorum contrariorum temperamentum. Igitur ad productionem corporum mixtorum elementa simul omnia cocurrunt.
units.tr: I. Mixed bodies first partake of earth, since they are generated on the earth. It is indeed necessary that everything receive something of the nature of the place in which it arises, and earthy matter is the reason why mixed bodies can be handled and perceived by the senses. Second, they partake of water, since this is needed to bind and glue natural things together; for water joins the boundaries of things very well and is itself joined to them. Third, if they partake of water and earth, they must surely also have a share of the contrary elements, namely fire, which opposes water, and air, which is set against earth. For the production of mixed bodies requires a blend of contrary elements. Therefore all the elements concur together in the production of mixed bodies.

units.la: II. Quibus rebus corpora mixta nutriuntur & conseruantur, ex iisdem oportet illa quoque esse generata. Atqui corpora mixta nutriuntur atq; conseruantur quatuor elementis. Igitur ex his quoque sunt generata. Maiori nulla est obscuritas. Minor probatur. Accipiamus verbi causa plantas: hæ nutriuntur terra & aqua, quod omnibus notum est: deinde etiam calore, qui ab igne provenit: denique & aere, cui sunt expositæ, & quo undiq; cinguntur. Nam si vel hæc omnia, vel ex his unum aliquod eis ademeris, marcescere, emori, et statim corrumpi eas necessum est. Atque hactenus quidem de principijs materialibus generationis & corruptionis rerum naturalium. Restat dicamus de earundem causis. Post principiorum namq; cognitionem, eundum est ad inueftigandas causas.
units.tr: II. Mixed bodies must be generated from those things by which they are nourished and preserved. But mixed bodies are nourished and preserved by the four elements. Therefore they are also generated from these. The major premise is not obscure. The minor is proved thus: let us take plants as an example. These are nourished by earth and water, which is known to all; then also by heat, which comes from fire; and finally by air, to which they are exposed and by which they are surrounded on every side. For if you take away all of these, or any one of them, they must wither, die, and at once decay. So much for the material principles of the generation and corruption of natural things. It remains to speak of their causes. For after knowing the principles, one must proceed to investigate the causes.

units.la: Quot causae concurrunt ad genera- tionem & corruptionem re- rum naturalium?
units.tr: How many causes concur in the generation and corruption of natural things?

units.la: Tres: Materia, Forma, & efficiens. Probatur: In coelo ipso, quod est ex sententia Ariftotelis fempiternum, ingenerabile & incorruptibile, spectantur hae tres causae quodammodo: multo igitur magis in rebus temporaneis, generabilibus & corruptibilibus. Antecedens probatur: Vt materia quidem fe habet in coelo potetia illa fubftantiaq;, quae dimensionum atq; motuum eius subiectum est: ut forma fe habet uis omnium tranfmutationu effectrix, quae substantiae coeli inhaeret, quaq; rotundum est. ac ut causa efficiens fe habet alia uis, qua coelum perpetuo & ordinata circumlatione agitatur. Igitur in coelo tres illae causae considerantur. Probatur etiam consequens, seu declaratur: Quaedam entia necessario semper sunt (Ariftotelice loquendo:) ut coelum. Quaedam entia nunquam sunt: nempe quae tantum potentia existunt, nunquam vero actu. Quaedam modo sunt, modo non sunt: cuius generis sunt generabilia omnia & corruptibilia. Atqui cum materia sit principium ut reliquæ res sint, uel non sint: cōsequitur sane, ad rerum omnium generationem & corruptione debere materiam aliquam præexistere. Vbi autem est materia, ibi oportet etiam adesse & causam, cuius gratia materia existit. Existit autem materia propter formam, & naturaliter materia forma expetit, utpote per quam absoluitur & perficitur substantiæ cuiusq; ratio. Ergo ad generationem et corruptionem etiam forma concurrit. Porro quoniam ad generationem res duæ simpliciter non sufficiunt, siquidem materia per se nihil efficit seu producit, forma etiam nō accidit sponte, nisi adsit aliquid efficiens & quasi impellens: ideo necessarium est, ad generationem & corruptionem adiungere & tertiam causam, uidelicet efficientem. Quicunq; igitur aliter statuerunt, à uero aberrarunt.
units.tr: Three: matter, form, and the efficient cause. This is proved as follows. In the heavens themselves, which according to Aristotle's opinion are everlasting, ungenerated and incorruptible, these three causes are in some way observed; much more, then, in temporal things that are generable and corruptible. The antecedent is proved thus: in the heavens, matter is that power and substance which is the subject of its dimensions and motions; form is the power effecting all changes, which inheres in the substance of the heaven and by which it is round; and the efficient cause is another power by which the heaven is driven in a perpetual and orderly revolution. Therefore those three causes are considered in the heaven. The consequent is also proved, or made clear: some beings necessarily always exist (speaking in Aristotle's manner), such as the heaven. Some beings never exist, namely those which exist only potentially and never actually. Some beings now exist and now do not; of this kind are all things that are generable and corruptible. Now since matter is the principle by which things are or are not, it certainly follows that some matter must pre-exist for the generation and corruption of all things. Where matter is, there must also be present the cause for whose sake the matter exists. Matter exists for the sake of form, and matter by nature longs for form, since through form the essence of each substance is completed and perfected. Therefore form also concurs in generation and corruption. Moreover, since two things do not suffice for generation, matter by itself effecting or producing nothing, and form not arising of its own accord unless something efficient and, as it were, impelling is present, it is necessary to add a third cause to generation and corruption, namely the efficient. Whoever has thought otherwise has strayed from the truth.

units.la: 1. Errauit igitur Socrates in Phædone, opinatus ad generationem sufficere formas, id est, species quasdam uocatas ἰδέας[?], omni causa efficiente interim exclusa. Quid uero illæ formæ, si sint otiosæ, atque ad producendas res non impellantur aliunde? Et si in omnibus aliis motibus naturalibus spectatur causa quædam efficiens, quid' ni etiam in generatione?
units.tr: 1. Socrates therefore erred in the Phaedo, supposing that forms, that is, certain species called ideas [ἰδέας], suffice for generation, with every efficient cause meanwhile excluded. But what are those forms if they are idle, and are not driven to produce things from elsewhere? And if in all other natural motions some efficient cause is observed, why not also in generation?

units.la: 2. Errarunt qui arbitrati sunt, sola posita materia perfici generationem posse. Materia namq; non potest in se pati et moueri: atqui necesse est aliquid insuper adesse, quod agat moueatq;, quādo in omnib. quæ natura uel arte fiunt, tale quippiā uelut causa præcipua requiritur. Exèpli causa, ex aqua uel terra nihil producitur, nisi adsit aliquid operâs: ex ligno non fit lectica, nisi adsit aliquis arte fabricans. Eandem etiam ob causam omni corpori generanti, certa tribuuntur organa, quæ se ut causæ efficientes habent. Si corpus seu materia ad generationem sufficeret, superuacanea essent addita organa.
units.tr: 2. Those erred who judged that generation can be accomplished by matter alone. For matter cannot of itself be acted upon and moved; yet something must be present besides, which acts and moves, since in all things that are made by nature or by art such a principal cause is required. For example, nothing is produced from water or earth unless some worker is present; a litter is not made from wood unless someone skilled in the craft fashions it. For this same reason, certain organs are assigned to every generating body, which stand as efficient causes. If the body or matter sufficed for generation, the added organs would be superfluous.

units.la: 3. Errarunt qui censuerunt qualitates elementorum, calidum uidelicet & frigidum, humidum & siccū, esse causas efficientes generationis præcipuas. Si namq; ita esset, tum elementorum illud semper & ubiq; ageret efficacius, cui ualidior inest agendi uis: uelut ignis. Hoc autem si daretur, tum necessum foret, res omnes naturales [?] obtinere à natura ignis, quàm ab aliis elementis: quod falsum est. Igitur seorsim ab ipsa elementorum materia & qualitatibus disiuncta debet causa efficiens in rebus naturalibus considerari. Quemadmodum quoq; in rebus artificialibus seorsim spectari debet artifex operans, qui est causa efficiens principalis: & seorsim serra, quæ est tantum efficiens instrumentaria. Itaq; qualitates elementorum intelligentur quodammodo instrumentariæ tantum esse causæ efficientes generationis.
units.tr: 3. Those erred who thought that the qualities of the elements, namely hot and cold, moist and dry, are the chief efficient causes of generation. For if this were so, then whichever element has the stronger power of acting would always and everywhere act more effectively, as fire does. But if this were granted, it would follow that all natural things would obtain their nature from fire rather than from the other elements, which is false. Therefore the efficient cause in natural things must be considered apart from the matter of the elements themselves and their qualities. Just as in artificial things the craftsman working must be considered separately, as the principal efficient cause, and the saw separately, which is only an instrumental efficient cause. Thus the qualities of the elements are to be understood as, in some way, merely instrumental efficient causes of generation.

units.la: Est'ne generationum & corruptionum series perpetua æternaq;?
units.tr: Is there a perpetual and eternal series of generations and corruptions?

units.la: Est. Quod rationibus duabus ostenditur, loquendo,ininquam, ex sententia Aristotelis, constituentis mundum esse sempiternum.
units.tr: It is. This is shown by two arguments, which I set out, as Aristotle does, holding that the world is everlasting.

units.la: 1. Tum supremi cœli, tum inferiorum orbium motus, qui contrarij sunt & multiplices, perpetui atq; æterni existunt. Atqui hi ipsi sunt causa efficiens atque operans generationum atq; corruptionum, quæ similiter contrariæ sunt ac multiplices. Igitur posita perpetua æternaq; causa efficiente & operante, merito etiam ponentur perpetui æterniq; effectus, generationes inquā et corruptiones. Etenim quemadmodum motus cœli extimi & orbium inferiorum sunt diuersi atq; contrarij, ita causæ sunt contrariorum effectuum, generationis videlicet & corruptionis, necnon diuersarum specierum in rebus naturalibus. Iidem etiam motus sunt in causa, videlicet tempus corruptionis, cuiusq; rei plurimum respondeat tempori generationis eiusdem. Quod cito fit, cito corrumpitur: & quod tardius fit, tardius corrumpitur. Verbi causa: Sole paulatim accedente, paulatim etiam generantur & excrescunt plantæ: rursusq; sole sensim discedente, sensim etiam corrumpuntur plantæ. Eodem pacto de reliquis est iudicandum.
units.tr: (1) Both the motion of the highest heaven and the motions of the lower spheres are contrary and manifold, and they are perpetual and eternal. These motions are themselves the efficient and operative cause of generations and corruptions, which are likewise contrary and manifold. Therefore, since the efficient and operative cause is posited as perpetual and eternal, the effects, namely generations and corruptions, will rightly be posited as perpetual and eternal as well. For just as the motions of the outermost heaven and of the lower spheres are diverse and contrary, so they are the causes of contrary effects, namely generation and corruption, and of the diverse species of natural things. The same motions are also the cause of the time of each thing's corruption, which for the most part corresponds to the time of its generation. What comes about quickly is corrupted quickly, and what comes about more slowly is corrupted more slowly. For instance, as the sun gradually draws near, plants are gradually generated and grow; and again, as the sun gradually withdraws, plants are gradually corrupted. The same judgement is to be made of the rest.

units.la: 2. Non possunt res semel generatæ semper existere, sed necessario tandem corrumpuntur: quod per se manifestum est. Cæterum natura semper expetit, quod melius præstantiusq; est. Atqui melius præstantiusq; est esse, quàm non esse. Igitur quandocunq; ali quid corruptu est,& non amplius est,totics natura laborat, ut rursus noua aliqua res generetur,atque ex unius corruptione sequatur generatio alterius.
units.tr: (2) Things once generated cannot always exist, but must in the end necessarily be corrupted; this is manifest in itself. Moreover, nature always seeks what is better and more excellent. But to be is better and more excellent than not to be. Therefore whenever something is corrupted and no longer exists, nature labours continually that some new thing may be generated again, so that from the corruption of one thing the generation of another follows.

units.la: Ergo manifestu est, naturæ maximè esse confentaneum, ut perpetua æternaq; generationum series statuatur.
units.tr: Therefore it is manifest that a perpetual and eternal series of generations is most consonant with nature.

units.la: Cum perpetua sit generationum & cor- ruptionum series,utrum omnia sint necessitate,an potius omnia sint contingenter?
units.tr: Since the series of generations and corruptions is perpetual, are all things by necessity, or rather are all things contingent?

units.la: Aliqua sunt necessitate, aliqua cōtingeter.Quemadmodū namq; potest fieri, ut qui ambulare habet in animo, aliquādo post ambulet vel nō ambulet: ita potest fieri, ut quod generari est idoneū, paulo post generetur vel non generetur. Necessitate autē illa sunt præcipuè, quorum posteriora iam existunt: si namque posteriora sunt necessitate, sunt etiam priora. Sicut existente effectu, non potest fieri quin existat etiam causa. Ubi fumus [?] vel calor, necessariò ibi aliquid igneum est. At posteriora sunt plerunque omnia contingenter: sicut posita causa, non semper necessariò sequitur effectus.
units.tr: Some things are by necessity, and some contingently. For just as it can happen that one who intends to walk afterwards walks or does not walk, so it can happen that what is apt to be generated is generated a little later or is not generated. But those things are especially by necessity whose later members already exist: for if the later things are necessary, the earlier things are too. Just as, when the effect exists, it cannot be that the cause does not also exist: where there is smoke or heat, necessarily something fiery is there. But later things are for the most part all contingent, just as, when the cause is posited, the effect does not always necessarily follow.

units.la: Vtrum generationum & corruptionum perpetua series fiat circulo atque ambitu quodam,an pro- gressu recto?
units.tr: Does the perpetual series of generations and corruptions proceed by a certain circle and cycle, or by straight progression?

units.la: Magis circulo & circuitu,quàm progressu re-cto[?], sto[?]. Ratio hæc est: Motus cæli, qui est generationis, atq; ut tam variæ species rerum naturalium emergant, causa efficiens[?], ipse circularis est. Itaq; res quoq; generatæ motum illum imitantur, atq; in orbem sese invicem consequuntur. Quemadmodum igitur, verbi causa, motus solis reparat tempora, menses, dies, horas, quæ sibi invicem perpetuo quodam circuitu succedunt: ita res novæ generatæ succedunt veteribus corruptis, perpetuo quodam ordine atque circulo. Corruptis hominibus succedunt alii recens generati homines, &c. Non autem corruptis hominibus succedunt plantæ, pisces vel huiusmodi, quæ series fieret progressu recto.
units.tr: More by circle and cycle than by straight progression. The reason is this: the motion of the heavens, which is the efficient cause of generation and of the emergence of so many varied species of natural things, is itself circular. Hence generated things also imitate that motion and follow one another in a circle. Just as, for instance, the motion of the sun renews the seasons, months, days and hours, which succeed one another in a perpetual circuit, so new things generated succeed old things corrupted, in a perpetual order and circle. Corrupted men are succeeded by other newly generated men, and so on. But corrupted men are not succeeded by plants, fish or the like, which would make a series by straight progression.

units.la: Cur quædam circulo atq; ambitu sem- per ipsa vicisim redeunt, quædam vero non ita redeunt?
units.tr: Why do some things always return to one another in a circle and cycle, while others do not return in this way?

units.la: Circulo atq; ambitu vicissim redire cernimus nubes & pluviam. Si namq; nubes est, sequitur pluvia: & rursus, ut pluat, necessum est ut nubes sit: quod ita fit perpetuo circuitu ac vicissitudine. Alia vero, ut homines & animalia, non ita ambitu quodam sibi succedunt. Nam etiamsi fit vir aliquis, qui possit esse pater: non propterea sequitur, alium quoq; hominē produci. Itaq; responsio ad quæstionē hæc esto: Quæ prioris sunt generis, magis imitatur motu circulare ipsius cæli, ideoq; circulo redeunt: quæ vero posterioris sunt generis, non perinde imitatur motum illum circularem, imò videntur quodammodo sese consequi progressu recto.
units.tr: We see clouds and rain return to one another in a circle and cycle. For if there is a cloud, rain follows; and again, for it to rain, there must be a cloud; and this happens by perpetual circuit and alternation. But others, such as men and animals, do not succeed one another in such a cycle. For even if a man comes to be who could be a father, it does not follow that another man is produced. So the answer to the question is this: those of the former kind imitate more closely the circular motion of the heavens itself, and therefore return in a circle; but those of the latter kind do not imitate that circular motion in the same way, and seem rather to follow one another by straight progression.

units.la: Redeúntne omnia similiter modo, an quaedam tantùm eodem numero, quaedam tantùm eadem specie?
units.tr: Do all things return in the same way, or do some return only in the same number and others only in the same species?

units.la: Quorum substantia mota ingenita & incorruptibilis est, hæc semper redeunt eodem numero: ut Sol, stellæ, &c. quorum vero substantia mota est generabilis corruptibilisque, ea specie tantùm eadem redeunt. Itaque non redeunt iidem numero homines, vel plantæ, sed iidem specie: & cum ex aqua fit aer, ex eodem aere iterum aqua, non redit eadem aqua numero, sed tantùm specie. Aqua enim illa corruptibilis erat, ac fieri potuisset, ut nulla iterum aqua inde produceretur. Tantùm de generatione & corruptione dixisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Those whose substance is ingenerable and incorruptible, being moved, always return in the same number, as the sun, the stars, and so on. But those whose substance is generable and corruptible return only in the same species. Thus men or plants do not return in the same number, but in the same species; and when air comes from water, and water again from the same air, the water does not return the same in number, but only in species. For that water was corruptible, and it could have happened that no water was produced from it again. Let it suffice to have said this much about generation and corruption.

units.la: LIBER QUARTUS, De meteoris.
units.tr: Book Four, On Meteors.

units.la: Hactenus satis dictum est de cœlo, quod se habet ut causa efficiens rerum naturalium: deinde de elementis (quæ una cum cœlo sunt corpora simplicia) quæ se habet ut rerum naturalium causa materialis: hinc insuper de generatione, in qua rerum naturalium explicatur causa formalis. Consentaneum est, nunc de ipsis rebus naturalibus, & & per naturam generatis, orationem instituamus. Cum autem corporum generatorum seu compositorum alia sint imperfecta, atq; in aere plerunq; locum habentia: alia uero perfecta, atque in terra aliquisq; constituta: uidemur recte facturi, si de imperfectis, & in aere constitutis, quae ipsa uocantur μετέωρα, primo loco differamus, postea descensuri ad composita perfecta.
units.tr: So far enough has been said about the heavens, which act as the efficient cause of natural things; then about the elements (which, together with the heavens, are the simple bodies), which act as the material cause of natural things; and further about generation, in which the formal cause of natural things is explained. It follows that we now take up discussion of natural things themselves, those that come into being by nature. Since some generated or compound bodies are imperfect and for the most part occur in the air, while others are perfect and established in the earth, we shall seem to be acting rightly if we first treat of the imperfect bodies situated in the air, which are themselves called meteora, and afterwards descend to the perfect compounds.

units.la: Quæ sunt μετέωρα?
units.tr: What are meteora?

units.la: Corpora composita imperfecta, uirtute solis & stellarum producta, atq; in sublimi aere apparetia: ut nubes, arcus cœlestis, uia lactea, cometæ, fulgura, tonitrua, uenti, &c. Μετέωρα ἀπὸ τῆς μετὰ τῇ ἀέ-ρω, aut ἄεω, quod est suspendo, pendeo, sustollo.[?] Itaque dicuntur μετέωρα, quasi supra & in sublimi suspensa: quamobrē Latini quidā uerterunt, sublimia.
units.tr: Meteora are imperfect compound bodies, produced by the power of the sun and the stars and appearing in the high air: such as clouds, the rainbow, the Milky Way, comets, lightnings, thunders, winds, and so on. The name meteora comes from the Greek μετὰ τῇ ἀέρι [meta tēi aeri, "in the air"], or from aeirō, which means to hang, to be suspended, to be lifted up. Hence they are called meteora, as if hung up and suspended on high; for which reason some Latin writers rendered them sublimia.

units.la: Quotuplicia sunt μετέωρα?
units.tr: How many kinds of meteora are there?

units.la: Quadruplicia. 1. Ignita: ut faces uolantes, hiatus, torres decidetes, cometæ, &c. de quibus Aristoteles à capite 4. lib. 1. usq; ad caput nonum.
units.tr: There are four kinds. (1) Fiery ones: such as flying torches, gaping fires, falling torches, comets, and so on. Aristotle deals with these from chapter 4 of book 1 to chapter 9.

units.la: 2. Aquea: ut nubes, pluuiæ, nix, grando: de quibus Aristoteles à lib. 1. cap. 9. ad 13. usq;.
units.tr: (2) Watery ones: such as clouds, rains, snow, hail. Aristotle deals with these in book 1, from chapter 9 to chapter 13.

units.la: 3. Flatuosa, quæ è flatu siue spiritu potissimùm proueniunt: ut uenti, tonitrua, fontes, &c. de quibus à cap. 13. lib. 1. usq; ad 2. lib. 3.
units.tr: (3) Windy ones, which arise chiefly from a blast or breath: such as winds, thunders, springs, and so on. Aristotle deals with these from chapter 13 of book 1 to book 2 and book 3.

units.la: 4. Ex refractione nata: cuiusmodi sunt area siue corona, arcus cœlestis, parelij seu geminati soles, uirgæ,&c.de quibus Aristoteles à 2.cap.li.3.ad finé usque lib.eiusdē. Nam quæ 4 libro ab Aristotele explicantur,alió pertinent,magisq; referenda sunt ad capita de generatione atq; interitu corporum mixtorum perfectorum,quàm ad Meteorologiam.
units.tr: (4) Those produced by refraction: of this kind are the halo or corona, the rainbow, the parhelia or double suns, rods, and so on. Aristotle deals with these from chapter 2 of book 3 to the end of the same book. For the things Aristotle explains in book 4 pertain to another subject, and are rather to be referred to the chapters on the generation and destruction of perfect mixed bodies than to Meteorology.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ meteororum?
units.tr: What are the causes of meteora?

units.la: 1. Causa efficiens propinqua & principalis est motus cœli,solis,aliorumq; siderum. Propterea mundus iste elemetaris supernis motionibus est propinquus & cõtinuus, ut illius uis uniuersa ab his regatur. Itaq; totius cœli ac solis calor educit è terra & aquis multiplices uapores,etc. Stellarũ autē uis atq; positus inducit alias atq; alias meteororum species.
units.tr: (1) The proximate and principal efficient cause is the motion of the heavens, the sun, and the other stars. Therefore this elemental world lies close to, and is continuously under, the heavenly motions, so that its whole power is governed by them. Thus the heat of the whole heaven and of the sun draws up many kinds of vapours from the earth and the waters, and so on. The power and position of the stars, however, bring about different kinds of meteora.

units.la: 2. Causa materialis remota, sunt elementa, quæ inter se mutuò commiscentur,& agedo patiendoq; subministrat unde res naturales fiant,atq; hæ rursus in illa resoluuntur. Causa materialis propinqua sunt ἀτμίδες,uapores,qui sunt calidi & humidi:& ἀναθυμιάσεις[?], exhalationes, quæ sunt calidæ & siccæ. Atq; ex illis quidem plurima μετέωρα aquea,ut nubes,pluuiæ,ros,nix, proueniunt: ex his uerò ignea, ut faces ardentes,ignes saltantes,uolantes,&c.
units.tr: (2) The remote material cause is the elements, which are mutually mixed together; by acting and being acted upon they supply the matter from which natural things come into being, and into which they are again resolved. The proximate material causes are the vapours (ἀτμίδες), which are warm and moist, and the exhalations (ἀναθυμιάσεις), which are warm and dry. From the former come most of the watery meteora, such as clouds, rains, dew, snow; from the latter come the fiery ones, such as burning torches, leaping and flying fires, and so on.

units.la: 3. Forma tam diuersa est ac multiplex, quàm meteora etiam ipsa diuersa sunt.
units.tr: (3) The form is as diverse and manifold as the meteora themselves are diverse.

units.la: Quis locus meteororum?
units.tr: What is the place of meteora?

units.la: Spacium illud, quod est inter orbem Lunæ ac terram istam medium: quod tamen in tria interualla[?],siue in tres regiones apte distinguitur.
units.tr: The space lying between the orb of the Moon and this earth in the middle, which is aptly divided into three intervals [?], or into three regions.

units.la: Prima est suprema,eademq; purior,necnon subtiliori referta aere,atq; calidior. In hac autem producuntur plurimum meteora ignea:ut cometæ,fulmina,&c.
units.tr: The first is the highest, and at the same time the purer, and filled with a finer and warmer air. In this region most fiery meteora are produced, such as comets, lightnings, and so on.

units.la: Secunda,infima,nobis uicina, denso ac crassiore aere referta, in qua gignuntur μετέωρα aquea : ut nubes,pluuiæ, atq; æstate ros,hyeme pruina: ille ui caloris,hæc uero frigoris.
units.tr: The second, the lowest, is near to us, filled with a dense and thicker air, in which watery meteora are generated: such as clouds and rains, and in summer dew, and in winter hoarfrost; the former by the force of heat, the latter by the force of cold.

units.la: Tertia,media inter has duas constituitur,eadeq; mixto aere referta: in qua locum iudicantur habere nix,grando,& aerea quædam meteora. Quamuis hanc tertiam regionem Aristoteles in præsenti capite non prorsus ita distinguit: usurpata tamen hæc est partitio omnibus recentioribus, ac sumpta quidem ex ijs quæ ab Aristotele explicantur lib. 1. Meteororum, cap.11.ac 12.ubi de grandine agit ex sententia Anaxagoræ.
units.tr: The third is set between these two, and is likewise filled with a mixed air; in it snow, hail, and certain airy meteora are judged to have their place. Although Aristotle does not quite distinguish this third region in this chapter, this division has been adopted by all the more recent writers, and it is taken indeed from what Aristotle explains in book 1 of the Meteorology, chapters 11 and 12, where he treats of hail according to the opinion of Anaxagoras.

units.la: Quæ est natura aeris,siue uniuersi eius spacij quod inter orbes cœlestes ac terram interponitur?
units.tr: What is the nature of air, or of the whole space that is interposed between the heavenly spheres and the earth?

units.la: Hanc quæstionem mouet Aristoteles occasione quæstionis præcedētis.Fuit autem de ea quæstione hæc quorundā ueterū opinio:Arbitrati sunt cœlū ipsum unà cū stellis naturæ esse igneæ, ideoq; toto illo orbium cœlestiū interuallo elementum ignis contineri:spacium autē inde ad nos usq; uniuersum solo impleri aere, atq; elemento aeris esse proprium. Atqui non potest hæc opinio subsistere.
units.tr: Aristotle raises this question on the occasion of the preceding question. Now some of the ancients held the following opinion on this matter: they thought that the heaven itself, together with the stars, is of a fiery nature, and therefore that the element of fire is contained throughout that whole interval of the heavenly orbs; and they thought that the space from there all the way down to us is filled entirely with air alone, and belongs to the element of air. But this opinion cannot stand.

units.la: Si superius illud spacium totum undiq; esset ignitum, necessario tantorum ignium ui omnia hæc inseriora absumerentur.
units.tr: If that upper space were wholly on fire on every side, then all these lower things would necessarily be consumed by the force of so great fires.

units.la: Si rursus ab orbibus cœlestibus ad terram usq; omnia plena erunt solo aere, tum aer sua amplitudine reliqua elementa superaret, nullaq; elementorum inter se existeret proportio: quæ tamen omnino necessaria est, ut secum inuicè agant & patiantur, unum transmutetur in aliud, atq; res naturales producant. Si namque non esset in illis proportio, tum quod amplius ac uastius foret, id elementa cætera sua ui semper superaret.
units.tr: Again, if from the heavenly orbs down to the earth everything were full of air alone, then the air, by its vastness, would surpass the other elements, and no proportion would exist among the elements. Yet such a proportion is entirely necessary, so that they may act and be acted upon by one another in turn, one be changed into another, and produce natural things. For if there were no proportion among them, then whatever was larger and vaster would always overpower the other elements by its force.

units.la: Respondetur ad quæstionem: Spacium illud, quod est inter infimum orbem lunæ ac terram, est corpus ab igne diuersum, & tamen nequaquam puro constans aere. Nam diuersæ differentiæ ei permixtæ sunt, ita ut parti eius superiori aer insit purus, sudus & syncerus: inferiori autem terram uersus crassus ac densus, quòd nimirum per hanc uagentur humidi ac crassi uapores, eò è terra atque aquis sublati, quiob suum pondus pensiles ibi manent.
units.tr: The answer to the question is this: the space that lies between the lowest orb of the Moon and the earth is a body different from fire, and yet by no means consists of pure air. For various differences are mixed in it, so that in its upper part there is pure, clear and unmixed air, while in the lower part, toward the earth, the air is thick and dense, because of course the moist and thick vapours, raised up from the earth and the waters, wander through this part, and since they are heavy they remain suspended there.

units.la: Obiectio.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Si totum illud interuallum est aer, ubi tunc locus erit elemento ignis?
units.tr: If that whole interval is air, where then will there be a place for the element of fire?

units.la: Responsio: Non debemus imaginari ignem aliquem nostro igni artificiali similem, qui elementi locum subeat: sed pro elemento ignis accipiemus superiorem illam partem spacij aerei, quæ orbibus cœlestibus proximè subiecta est. ea namq; tota undiq; immenso calore est oppleta, qui ibi prouenit ac dispargitur ex motu uehementi impendentiū orbium cœlestium, qui tam celer tantusq; est, ut calore maximum ibi excitet. Altera pars inferior aere tempe rato tota occupatur, sed alibi densiore, & alibi subtiliore, & alibi frigidiore, alibi calidiore: atque hæc proprie elementi aeris sortitur locum. Ergo recte hunc in modum elementis sua loca assignantur, ut supremus sit proximè sub orbe Lunæ ignis, sub igne aer, hinc aqua (cuius portio aliquota per aerē, portio alia circum & per terram diffunditur) infimo uero terra.
units.tr: Answer: We must not imagine some fire similar to our artificial fire, which takes the place of an element. Rather, by the element of fire we shall understand that upper part of the aerial space which lies immediately beneath the celestial spheres. For this whole part is filled on every side with immense heat, which arises there and is spread abroad from the violent motion of the overhanging celestial spheres; this motion is so swift and so great that it excites the greatest heat there. The lower part is entirely occupied by temperate air, though it is denser in some places, thinner in others, colder in some and warmer in others; and this is what properly holds the place of the element of air. Therefore the elements are rightly assigned their places in this way: the highest is fire, lying immediately beneath the orb of the Moon; beneath the fire is air; then water (one portion of which is spread through the air, another portion around and through the earth); and lowest of all is earth.

units.la: Cæterum in illa parte aeris inferiore intellige meteororum locum existere, atq; eam ipsam in tres regiones, ut dictum est, distribui.
units.tr: Moreover, understand that the place of the meteors exists in that lower part of the air, and that this same part is divided, as has been said, into three regions.

units.la: Quæ est causa efficiens instrumentalis, siue quomodo educitur materia meteororum ad locum aeris?
units.tr: What is the efficient, instrumental cause, or how is the matter of the meteors drawn up into the region of the air?

units.la: Per calorem qui terræ huic uicinus atq; undiq; circumfusus est, educuntur e terra & aquis subcale factis tum uapores, tum exhalationes, quæ sursum ad eum usq; locum, in quo produci diuersi generis meteora queant, attolluntur. Ac densiores quidem & humidiores ad regionem infimam, in qua ponderẽ suo prægrauatæ cõsistunt: subtiliores uerò & sicciores ad regionem supremā eluctantur: quidam uerò intelliguntur se continere in regione media.
units.tr: By the heat which is near to this earth and diffused all around it, vapours and exhalations are drawn up out of the earth and waters, made somewhat warm, and are lifted upward as far as that place in which meteors of various kinds can be produced. The denser and moister ones sink to the lowest region, where, weighed down by their own weight, they remain; but the thinner and drier ones struggle up to the highest region; while some are understood to remain in the middle region.

units.la: Vnde nascitur calor circum terras?
units.tr: Whence does the heat around the earth arise?

units.la: A' solis motu, qui & concitatior est, quàm reliquarũ stellarũ, & nobis propinquior. Sol namq; sui motus tum uehementia, tum celeritate continua, calorem in cœlo ingentem cõcitat. Deinde ab eodem superior pars aeris (quam elemento ignis cedere diximus) calore immeso undiq; impletur. Inde uerò ad aerem quoq; nobis uicinum calor dispergitur, sed frigore quodam à subiecta aqua accedente temperatus. Hinc autem & terra & aquæ incalescunt.
units.tr: From the motion of the sun, which is both more rapid than that of the other stars and nearer to us. For the sun, by the force and continual speed of its motion, stirs up immense heat in the heavens. Then from the sun the upper part of the air (which we said yields to the element of fire) is filled on every side with immeasurable heat. Thence the heat is spread also to the air nearest us, yet tempered by a certain coldness coming from the water beneath. Hence both the earth and the waters grow warm.

units.la: Neq; uerò Sol ipse uel stellæ sunt ignes, ut quìdam arbitrati sunt: sed motus siue agitatio illorum corporum causam caloris adsert. Itaq; Sol apparet quidem candidus, non tamen igneus.
units.tr: Nor indeed are the sun itself or the stars fires, as some have thought; rather, the motion or agitation of those bodies brings about the cause of heat. And so the sun appears indeed bright, but is not fiery.

units.la: Nunc de unoquoq; meteororum genere par est ordine dicamus.
units.tr: Now it is fitting to speak in order of each kind of meteor.

units.la: DE METEORIS ignitis.
units.tr: ON FIERY METEORS.

units.la: Quæ sunt meteora ignita?
units.tr: What are fiery meteors?

units.la: Væ ignem referunt, adeoq; ardent: ut stipulæ, capræ, lancea, faces, draco uolans, &c.
units.tr: Those which resemble fire and actually burn, such as straw-like streaks, goats, a spear, torches, a flying dragon, etc.

units.la: Quæ sunt communiter horum omnium causæ?
units.tr: What are the common causes of all these?

units.la: 1. Causa efficiens recte dicitur Sol terram calefaciens, atq; ex hac suo calore educens exhalationes, id est, spirationes, calidas & siccas, quæ deinde eiusdem solis ui altius subuchuntur.
units.tr: 1. The efficient cause is rightly said to be the sun, warming the earth and drawing from it, by its heat, exhalations, that is, warm and dry vapours, which are then lifted higher by the power of the same sun.

units.la: 2. Causa materialis sunt hæ ipsæ exhalationes.
units.tr: 2. The material cause is these same exhalations.

units.la: 3. Causa formalis: Eæ cum ad regionem calidam peruenerint, inter se agitantur, ac ueluti confricantur: tandem uero mutuo contactu accenduntur. Vt autem materia ipsa est dispositta in longum uel in latum, &c. ita hanc uel illam speciem meteori uisendam nobis præbent. Ac tamdiu quidè ardent, quamdiu adest idonea materia. Sed potest de singulis speciebus commodè reddi ratio.
units.tr: 3. The formal cause: when these have reached a warm region, they are driven about among themselves and, as it were, rubbed together, and at last catch fire from mutual contact. And just as the matter itself is spread out lengthwise or widthwise, and so on, so they present to us this or that kind of meteor to be seen. They keep burning as long as suitable matter is present. But an account of each kind can be given conveniently.

units.la: Exhibe aliquot species, & quomodo eæ generentur, declara?
units.tr: Set out some of the kinds, and explain how they are generated.

units.la: 1. Scintillæ seu stipulæ primo loco ab Aristotele enumerantur. harum materia est exhalatio subtilis, non satis compacta, atq; hinc inde in longitudinem ac latitudinem sparsa. Ideoq; sic accenditur, ut aliæ flammæ aliæ insequantur, non aliter quàm si stipulæ in agro subito ab iniecto igne corriperentur, eædemq; statim deficerent.
units.tr: 1. Sparks or straws are listed first by Aristotle. Their matter is a subtle exhalation, not sufficiently compacted, and scattered here and there lengthwise and widthwise. Hence it catches fire in such a way that one flame follows another, just as if straw in a field were suddenly seized by a fire thrown into it, and these would immediately die out.

units.la: 2. Capræ ex exhalatione globosa et inæquali, quæ in duas partes non longè ab inuicem distantes differènt est, fere ad eum modum quo solet duæ capræ cornua concussuræ in pedes erectæ consistere.
units.tr: 2. Goats arise from a globular and uneven exhalation, which is divided into two parts not far from each other, roughly in the way that two goats butting horns tend to stand upright on their feet.

units.la: 2.[?] Torris seu Ἀχλὸς[?], ubi exhalatio bene compacta una tantum parte accenditur.
units.tr: 2.[?] Torch, or achlys [Ἀχλύς], where a well-compacted exhalation catches fire on one side only.

units.la: 4. Stellæ discurrentes, ubi exhalatio longius diductá in multas easdemq; exiguas particulas disseminata existit, & latitudo & crassitudo consimiliter se habent.
units.tr: 4. Running stars arise where the exhalation is drawn out at length and scattered into many small particles; its breadth and thickness are similarly arranged.

units.la: Ex his facile potest de alijs eiusdem generis, ut de igne perpendiculari, lancea ardente, igne fatuo, igne lambente, Dracone uolante, similibusq;, quæ non ab Aristotele, sed ab alijs scriptoribus nominantur, iudicari.
units.tr: From these one can easily judge the others of the same kind, such as the upright fire, the burning lance, the will-o'-the-wisp, the licking fire, the flying dragon, and similar things, which are named not by Aristotle but by other writers.

units.la: In perpendiculo, exhalationis portio crassior in imo subsidet, subtilior sursum vergit in mucronem.
units.tr: In an upright fire, the thicker portion of the exhalation settles at the bottom, while the finer part rises upward into a point.

units.la: In lancea ardente, uel iaculo, exhalatio per omnia subtilis est, & in rectum diductá: sed alicubi paulo densior, alicubi rarior.
units.tr: In a burning lance or javelin, the exhalation is subtle throughout and drawn out in a straight line, but in some places a little denser, in others rarer.

units.la: In igne fatuo, siue Castore ac Polluce, exhalatio crassa est & pinguis, quæ leui flatu huc illucq; protruditur, & propter crassitiem sæpe visitur in locis humilioribus.
units.tr: In the will-o'-the-wisp, or Castor and Pollux, the exhalation is thick and fat, and is pushed hither and thither by a light breath; because of its thickness it is often seen in lower places.

units.la: Ignis lambens ad iubas equorum, ad vestes hominum exilit, quasi lambendo eas. producitur ex tenuibus exhalationibus, plerunque è sudoribus deductis.
units.tr: The licking fire leaps up around the manes of horses and the clothes of men, as if licking them. It is produced from thin exhalations, mostly drawn from sweat.

units.la: Draco volans prouenit ab exhalatione densa & inæquali, inter duas nubes, quarum altera calida, alda, altera frigida, collocata. cumq; media pars fit lata & bene compacta, exhibet ea imaginem trunci seu uentris: cū duæ exteriores partes magis sint attenuatæ atq; inæquales, fit ut hinc aliquid cernatur se habens ut caput, inde uero aliquid ut cauda. Fumus uero etiam à Dracone progreditur, propterea quòd exhalatio accensa incidit in uapores seu nubes frigidas. Vbi namq; humiditas ignitis admiscetur, solet fumus oriri.
units.tr: The flying dragon arises from a dense and uneven exhalation placed between two clouds, one warm and dry, the other cold. And when the middle part becomes broad and well compacted, it presents the image of a trunk or belly; while the two outer parts are more attenuated and uneven, so that on one side something is seen that resembles a head, and on the other something like a tail. Smoke also comes forth from the dragon, because the kindled exhalation strikes against cold vapours or clouds. For where moisture is mixed with fiery things, smoke is usually produced.

units.la: In summa, exhalationum dispositarum ad procreandum aliquod meteoron, quantitas, densitas, positus, diuersarum formarum causæ existunt.
units.tr: In sum, the quantity, density, and position of the exhalations, as they are arranged to produce some meteor, are the causes of the different forms.

units.la: Vnde fit, quòd quidā ignes, cum accenduntur, quieti subsistunt: quidam uerò quasi impetu quodam proijciuntur?
units.tr: Why is it that some fires, once kindled, remain still, while others are, as it were, thrown forward with some impulse?

units.la: Duobus modis cōtingit ignita μετέωρα accendi.
units.tr: Fiery meteors [μετέωρα] can be kindled in two ways.

units.la: 1. Exhalatio aliquādo inflammatur adfrictu seu collisione aeris undiq; æquabiliter, quod ad calorem attinet, temperati: ac tum quidem μετέωρον ipsum quictum manet.
units.tr: 1. Sometimes the exhalation is set alight by friction or collision with the air, which is evenly tempered on every side as far as heat is concerned; and then the meteor itself remains at rest.

units.la: 2. Aliquādo inflammatur exhalatio attritu quidem aeris circumfluentis, sed alicunde interim accurrente aere quodam denso & subfrigido. Qua igitur ex parte hic aduenit, ab ea exhalatio uiolenter propellitur adeoq; proijcitur.
units.tr: 2. Sometimes the exhalation is set alight by the friction of the air flowing around it, but meanwhile some denser and somewhat cold air rushes in from one side. So from whichever side this air arrives, the exhalation is violently driven out from that side and thrown forward.

units.la: Qui fit, quòd ignes quidam proij- ciuntur deorsum?
units.tr: Why is it that some fires are hurled downwards?

units.la: Omnis quidem ignis natura sursum enitítur: attamen meteora quaedam ignita proijciuntur deorsum, quòd supra exhalatione pendeant fumi quidam concreti, humiditatis & frigiditatis nonnihil in se habentes. Quamuis hic aliquàdo auxiliatur aliquo modo exhalationum pondus ac densitas.
units.tr: Every fire, by its nature, strives upward; yet some fiery meteors are hurled downward, because certain condensed vapours hang above the exhalation, containing something of moisture and cold. Although here the weight and density of the exhalations sometimes help in some way.

units.la: Qui fit, quòd quidam ignes post ac- censionem mouentur in di- uersas partes?
units.tr: Why do some fires, after they have kindled, move in different directions?

units.la: Mouentur in obliquum ac saltant quidam ignes duabus de causis. 1. A natura omnes eluctantur sursum, siue recta, siue in latus. 2. Vi autem mouentur deorsum, siue recta, siue in latus. Prouenit autem hæc uis à materia humida & frigida, supernè occurrente. Natura ac uis motus causa existunt.
units.tr: Some fires move obliquely and leap about for two reasons. 1. By nature all of them struggle upward, whether straight or to the side. 2. But they are moved downward, whether straight or to the side, by force. This force arises from the moist and cold matter that meets them from above. Nature and force are the causes of the motion.

units.la: Quae sunt causae phasmatum, ac diuer- forum colorum in sublimi apparentium?
units.tr: What are the causes of the phantoms and the various colours that appear on high?

units.la: Causa formalis: Duobus modis colores in exhalationes inducuntur. 1. Quando alicubi ignis siue lumen in sublimi existit, verum inter illud & nostrum aspectum exhalationes quaedam bene compactae suspensae hærent, tum quidem necesse est in ipsis ipsis exhalationibus inusitatos quosdam colores, in primis autem igneos apparere. Candela per cornu paulo spissius aut maculis respersum lucens, certum huius rei præbet argumentum. 2. Quando radij ignis sive luminis alicubi ex adverso existentis in corpus exhalationum congestarum refringuntur. verbi causa: Si ignis sit in occidente, facile huius radij refringentur, coloremque inducent in exhalationibus quæ pendent in plaga orientali. Itaque istiusmodi phasmata, ostenta, sive colores, non sunt simpliciter ignes, ut quidam suspicantur, verum ab ignibus inducuntur. Et qualitas permixtioque exhalationum efficit, ut modo purpurei, modo punicei colores appareant.
units.tr: Formal cause: Colours are induced in exhalations in two ways. (1) When a fire or light is somewhere on high, and between it and our sight certain well-compacted exhalations hang suspended, then unusual colours must appear in those exhalations themselves, chiefly fiery ones. A candle shining through a horn that is somewhat thick, or spotted, provides clear proof of this. (2) When the rays of a fire or light situated somewhere opposite are refracted in a mass of gathered exhalations. For example, if the fire is in the west, its rays will easily be refracted and will colour the exhalations that hang in the eastern region. So such phantoms, portents, or colours are not simply fires, as some suppose, but are induced by fires. And the quality and mixture of the exhalations causes purple colours to appear at one time and crimson colours at another.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ hiatuum seu chasmatum?
units.tr: What are the causes of gaping openings or chasms?

units.la: Causa materialis & formalis exhalationes multæ sunt conglobatæ, eædemque media quidem parte admodum crassæ: quamobrem nigrior ibi apparet, atque vulgo putatur hiatus seu vorago, foramen, rima. In parte vero exteriori circumquaque subtiles sunt ac tenues, quamobrem undique inflammatur. Quòd autè ex chasmatibus interdū torres excidunt, hac fit de causa: Coacervantur ibi multæ ac densæ exhalationes, quæ motu sive attritu vehementi (quæ excitari subinde contingit ab aere circumfluo, inflammantur: cumque superne supernè obuiet aliquid humidum & suffrigidum, detruduntur impetu quodam in terras.
units.tr: Material and formal cause: Many exhalations are gathered into a mass, and these are very thick in the middle, so that the middle appears darker there, and it is commonly thought to be a gulf, an abyss, a hole, or a cleft. But on the outer part all around they are fine and thin, so that they catch fire on every side. As for the fact that torches sometimes fall out of the chasms, this happens for the following reason: many dense exhalations gather there, and these are set on fire by a violent motion or friction (which is sometimes stirred up by the air flowing around them). When something moist and somewhat cold meets them from above, they are thrust down onto the earth with a certain force.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ cometarum?
units.tr: What are the causes of comets?

units.la: Variæ de his veterum fuerunt opiniones.
units.tr: There have been various opinions of the ancients about these.

units.la: 1. Anaxagoras & Democritus arbitrati sunt, tunc cometam fieri, quando contingit plures stellas planetarias invicem sibi coniungi: coniunctas enim tantum fulgorem præbere.
units.tr: 1. Anaxagoras and Democritus thought that a comet comes into being when several planetary stars happen to join together with one another, for when joined they give forth only a brilliance.

units.la: 2. Pythagorici dixerunt, unum esse aliquem planetam, qui quando vicinus est Soli, non fulget, impediente nimirum id ipsius Solis amplo splendore: quando vero abest à Sole, tum quasi cum fœnore radios proicit. Et cum raro contingat planetas multum à Sole disiungi, raro etiam cometæ apparent.
units.tr: 2. The Pythagoreans said that there is a certain one planet which, when it is near the Sun, does not shine, of course because the great splendour of the Sun itself hinders it; but when it is far from the Sun, then it throws out its rays as if with interest. And since it rarely happens that the planets are far separated from the Sun, comets also rarely appear.

units.la: 3. Hippocrates statuit, esse aliquem planetam, sed qui subiectas exhalationes nonnullas ad se trahit accenditq;.
units.tr: 3. Hippocrates held that there is a certain planet, which draws to itself and sets on fire some exhalations lying beneath it.

units.la: Refelluntur autem opiniones hæ simul omnes, atq; demonstratur, Planetas esse non posse eosdem qui comam assumunt. Primò: Planetæ semper obErrant sub signifero & intra tropicos: atqui cometæ cōspecti sunt sæpenumero extra tropicos. Secundò: Vno tantum planeta supra horizontem nostrum apparere, visi sunt interdum cometæ plures. Tertiò: Nonnunquam supra horizontem apparuerunt quinq; stellæ planetariæ (nam Solem & Lunā omnes semper excipiunt, negantq; crinem assume-re) & re) & interea uisus est etiam separatim cometa.
units.tr: But these opinions are all refuted together, and it is demonstrated that the planets cannot be the same bodies that take on a hair-like tail. First: the planets always wander beneath the zodiac and within the tropics, but comets have been seen very often outside the tropics. Second: only one planet appears above our horizon at a time, but sometimes several comets have been seen. Third: at times five planetary stars have appeared above the horizon (for they all always exclude the Sun and the Moon, and deny that they take on a tail), and meanwhile a comet has also been seen separately.

units.la: Tantum in genere de omnibus illis opinionibus pariter.De modo autem quo singuli exposuerunt à planetis illis flammas concipi, uberiore confutationem licet apud Aristotelem legere.
units.tr: This is enough, in general, to say about all those opinions alike. But concerning the manner in which each of them explained that flames are kindled from those planets, one may read a fuller refutation in Aristotle.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ cometarum ex sen- tentia Aristotelis?
units.tr: What are the causes of comets according to the opinion of Aristotle?

units.la: Causa efficiens: Motus in aere proueniens à motu cœli atq; orbium planetariorum.
units.tr: Efficient cause: Motion arising in the air from the motion of the heaven and of the planetary spheres.

units.la: Causa materialis: Densæ & pingues exhalationes, eæq; tanta mole ac frequentia congestæ, ut diu persistere flammasq; conceptas alere queant.
units.tr: Material cause: Dense and oily exhalations, gathered in such great mass and frequency that they can last a long time and feed the flames once kindled.

units.la: Causa formalis: Vbi materia arida & sicca coaceruata est semelq; accenditur,mox accedunt aliæ de nouæ exhalationes continenter & copiosæ: hæ autem posteriores formam adhærentis comæ, dum inflammantur,repræsentant.
units.tr: Formal cause: When dry and arid matter has been heaped together and is once kindled, other new exhalations immediately come in continually and abundantly; these later exhalations, as they catch fire, represent the form of an adhering hair.

units.la: Necessarium autem est, hoc pacto cōstituere nouas exhalationes accedentes,de his causis. 1. Nisi enim id fieret, tantus fulgor nequaquam procrearetur. 2. Figura non alia proueniret, quàm simpliciter circularis & undequaq; æqualis. 3. Non tamdiu consisteret.
units.tr: It is necessary to posit in this way that new exhalations come in, for these reasons: (1) unless this happened, so great a brightness would by no means be produced; (2) the shape would not be other than simply circular and equal on every side; (3) it would not last so long.

units.la: Quot sunt species cometarum?
units.tr: How many kinds of comets are there?

units.la: Materia quidem omniũ eadem est: uerùm huius uaria constitutio & collocatio diuersas figuras inducit.Aristoteles igitur duas enumerat.
units.tr: The matter of all of them is indeed the same, but its various constitution and arrangement induce different shapes. Aristotle therefore lists two kinds.

units.la: 1. Cometes generatim proprie dictus is est, qui circumquaq; hispidus & comas habens apparet.
units.tr: 1. The comet properly so called, in general, is the one that appears bristly all around and having hair.

units.la: 2. Γωνωνίας, cum inferiori ex parte imaginem exhibet prolixae barbae. Ab alijs plures species adduntur.
units.tr: 2. The γωνωνίας [bearded comet], which shows on its lower part the likeness of a long beard. Others add several more kinds.

units.la: 3. Ἀνούτιας, cum effigiem iaculi repraesentat.
units.tr: 3. The ἀνούτιας [javelin-like comet], which presents the likeness of a javelin.

units.la: 4. Χιφίας, cum brevior & in mucrone desinens ac pallens exprimit effigiem gladij.
units.tr: 4. The χιφίας [sword-like comet], which, shorter and ending in a point and pale, displays the likeness of a sword.

units.la: 5. Αἰονευς, qui disci habet speciem, & colorem ostendit electri.
units.tr: 5. The αἰονευς [disc-like comet], which has the form of a disc and shows the colour of amber.

units.la: 6. Γ.Θὸς, figura dolij ignescens, fumo interspersa.
units.tr: 6. The γ.θὸς [barrel-like comet], the figure of a cask glowing, interspersed with smoke.

units.la: 7. Κεράσυς, cui caesaries est diducta in modum cornu.
units.tr: 7. The κεράσυς [horn-like comet], whose hair is spread out in the manner of a horn.

units.la: 8. Λαμπαδίας, quando instar accensae facis.
units.tr: 8. The λαμπαδίας [torch-like comet], when it is like a lit torch.

units.la: 9. Ἵππος vel Ἱππεὺς, ubi equinae iubae figura.
units.tr: 9. The ἵππος or ἱππεὺς [horse or horseman comet], where there is the shape of a horse's mane.

units.la: Qui fit, quod quidam cometae loco mo- ventur, quidam vero stabiles fixiq; manent?
units.tr: Why do some comets move from place to place, while others remain fixed and stationary?

units.la: Quemadmodum materia ipsa dispositu est, ut moveatur aut quiescat: ita contingit ipsum quoq; cometam moveri aut quiescere. Etenim quae causae sper stantur motus & quietis in alijs ignitis meteoris, eadem & hic locum habent.
units.tr: Just as matter itself is disposed either to move or to rest, so the comet itself happens to move or to rest. The causes of motion and rest that are assigned in the other fiery meteors apply here as well.

units.la: Deprehensi aut sunt varij cometarum motus, quorum etiam diversae rationes reddi possunt.
units.tr: Various motions of comets have been observed, and different explanations can be given for them.

units.la: 1. Aliquado ab oriente in occidentem more aliorum astrorum tendunt. Nimirum vehemens motus cœli secum rapit partes uicinas, sicut uentus aquâ aut ignem protrudit.
units.tr: 1. Sometimes they travel from east to west, like the other stars. Clearly the strong motion of the heavens carries along the neighbouring parts with it, just as the wind pushes water or fire along.

units.la: 2. Aliquando liberè & nullo seruato ordine deuoluuntur modò huc, modò illuc, actì fortasīs impulsu rerum in circumfluo aere occursantium.
units.tr: 2. Sometimes they roll about freely, without any fixed order, now this way, now that, perhaps driven by the impact of things that meet them in the surrounding air.

units.la: 3. Fieri etiam potest, ut stellæ, inprimis planetariæ, quarum naturam participant, eos ad se aliquà uia alliciant.
units.tr: 3. It may also happen that the stars, especially the planets, whose nature the comets share, draw them to themselves in some way.

units.la: 4. Quid quòd ignis eò plerunque accurrit, ubi spes est inueniendi noui pabuli, siue ubi sparsa est idonea materia?
units.tr: 4. Or why would fire not usually run to where there is hope of finding fresh fuel, or where suitable matter lies scattered?

units.la: Contingit'ne stellas quoque, siue fi- xas, siue planetarias, comam accipere?
units.tr: Does it happen that stars too, whether fixed or planetary, take on a tail (coma)?

units.la: Non quidè proprie, quamuis interdum apparet aliquo modo id fieri. Quādo enim stella putatur comā accipere, certò non ipsa stella accèditur, sed exhalationes quædam procul subter stellam in aere suspensæ. Idq; eodem prorsus pacto, quo etiā arcæ seu coronæ procreantur, frequenter prope nos directè sub Luna: cōstant nāq; hæ uaporibus, in quos in medio suspensos refringūtur sideris radij. At uerò cometes nihil est aliud, quàm ipsamet exhalatio inflammata. Quantum igitur discrimen est inter coronam & cometā, tantum etiā distare intelligetur stella cui creditur coma adhærere, à uero cometa. Adhæc, stella speciè cometæ exhibens, aliò plerunq; mouctur, mouetur, quàm subiecta coma:[?] in cometa uerò talis separatio non conspicitur.
units.tr: Not properly, although it sometimes appears that this happens in a way. When a star is thought to take on a tail, the star itself is certainly not what is touched; rather, some exhalations suspended in the air far below the star are. This happens in exactly the same way that halos and coronas are produced, often close to us directly beneath the Moon: these consist of vapours in which the rays of the star are refracted as they are suspended in the middle. But a comet is nothing other than the exhalation itself, set on fire. So, just as great as the difference is between a corona and a comet, so great will it be understood to be the distance between the star to which a tail is believed to cling and the true comet. Moreover, a star that presents the appearance of a comet usually moves somewhere other than the tail that lies beneath it; but in a comet no such separation is seen.

units.la: Vtrum cometæ sint natura igniti?
units.tr: Are comets by nature fiery?

units.la: Maxime. Probatur à signo. Nam si quando cometæ aliqui extiterunt, secuti sunt eos magni flatus seu ueti, et ἀχυμοί[?], id est, squalores ex siccitate prouenientes: ac totus annus sequens sæpe uisus est uentis calidis & siccitate abundare.
units.tr: Most certainly. This is proved from the sign: for whenever comets have appeared, strong blasts or winds have followed them, and dry scorching squalor from drought; and the whole year after has often seemed to abound in hot winds and dryness.

units.la: Cur raró, cur nunquam plures simul, cur extra tropicos potius quàm intra, cometæ procreantur?
units.tr: Why are comets produced rarely, why never several at once, and why outside the tropics rather than within?

units.la: Non facilè tanta moles exhalationum, quanta ad productionem uel unius cometæ requiritur, potest conglobari: Solis nimirum & astrorum ui, deinde aeris motu eas dispellente. Deinde, intra tropicos, cum hic semper abundet calor (unde zonam torridam ibidem constituunt) exhalationes, priusquam coeant, dissipantur atq; absumuntur. Postremò, multa exhalationum materia sursum sublata ad circulum lacteum deuehitur.
units.tr: Such a great mass of exhalations, as is required for the production of even a single comet, cannot easily be gathered together: partly by the power of the Sun and the stars, and then by the motion of the air scattering them. Then, within the tropics, since heat always abounds there (for which reason they set up the torrid zone in that place), the exhalations are dissipated and consumed before they can come together. Lastly, much material of exhalations, raised upward, is carried along to the Milky Way.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ circuli lactei, seu uiæ lacteæ?
units.tr: What are the causes of the Milky Way, or the Galaxy?

units.la: Variæ fuerunt ueterum opiniones.
units.tr: The opinions of the ancients were various.

units.la: Pythagorici suspicatur, eam uiam olim inflammatam igne alicuius astri de cælo lapsi, aut forte ipsius Solis quondam ab imperito Phaethonte eò devecti: ab eo tempore vestigia lactei orbis esse relicta. Sed consistere hæc opinio non potest. Nam si ita res haberet, tum multo magis necessarium foret, inflammatum cerni totum iter Solis sub zodiaco, quo perpetuo obambulat. Quod tamen non fit: ut non dicamus, cœlum esse eius substantiæ, quæ nullo modo est inflammationis capax.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans suspected that this path was once set on fire by the fire of some star fallen from heaven, or perhaps by the Sun itself, once carried thither by the inexperienced Phaethon: and that from that time traces of the milky circle have remained. But this opinion cannot stand. For if things were so, it would be much more necessary for the whole path of the Sun beneath the zodiac, along which it wanders continually, to be seen as burning. Yet this does not happen, not to mention that heaven is of a substance that is in no way capable of being set on fire.

units.la: 2. Anaxagoras & Democritus viam lacteam cen [?] fuerunt esse cœtum quendam stellarum, quæ non illustrantur à Sole subter terram commeante: ideoq; lumen suum illæ ipsæ liberius, quàm cæteræ à Sole illustratæ, diffundunt. Atqui si ita esset, tum ut Sol infra terram moueretur, ita circulū lacteum oporteret moueri mutariq; supra terram. Constat namque, semper eodem loco & ad easdem stellas eam hærere. Deinde, cùm tanta sit Solis tum magnitudo, tum distantia sub exigua terræ mole, ut nullæ reuera in extimo cœlo stellæ existant, ad quas lumen à Sole non perueniat: nulla profecto est ratio, cur magis una parte cœli, quàm alia, talis lacteus fulgor siue candor appareat.
units.tr: 2. Anaxagoras and Democritus thought that the Milky Way is a certain company of stars which are not illuminated by the Sun, which passes beneath the earth; and so these stars shed their light more freely than the others, which are illuminated by the Sun. But if this were so, then just as the Sun moves beneath the earth, so the Milky Way would have to move and change position above the earth. For it is clear that it always clings to the same place and to the same stars. Furthermore, since the Sun is so great in size and so distant, beneath the small mass of the earth, that there are really no stars in the outermost heaven to which light from the Sun does not reach, there is surely no reason why such a milky glow or brightness should appear more on one part of the heavens than on another.

units.la: 3. Quidam lacteam viam dixerunt per reflexionem nostri visus ad radios Solis, qui ipsi refringuntur in exhalationib. in sublimi suspensis, gigni: quèadmodum antea dictū est, areas procreari sub Luna. Quod si daretur, tum necessum foret, ut quādo moto sole, moverentur in alias partes ipsi radij, simul etiam moueri deprehenderetur ipse lacteus circulus. Atqui istud non fit: manet enim semper eodem loco fixus. Igitur nullo pacto credendum est, quod refractio radiorum Solis, & uisus nostri reflectio, uiam lacteam procreet. Secundo, cernitur item circulus lacteus in aqua, quod sane fieri haud posset, si per refractionem radiorum Solis gigneretur. Quamuis infirma est hæc ratio, quando arcus cœlestis ex reflectione radiorum Solis natus, etiam conspicuus fit in aqua. Tertio, præterea Sole noctu longissimè à nobis subter terram remoto, qui fieri posset, ut uisus noster ab eo refringeretur.
units.tr: 3. Some have said that the Milky Way arises from the reflection of our sight onto the rays of the Sun, which are refracted in exhalations suspended on high, just as was said before concerning halos produced beneath the Moon. But if this were so, then whenever the Sun moved and its rays shifted into other parts, the Milky Way itself would necessarily be seen to move at the same time. Yet this does not happen: for it always remains fixed in the same place. Therefore it is in no way to be believed that the refraction of the Sun's rays and the reflection of our sight produce the Milky Way. Secondly, the Milky Way is also seen in water, which certainly could not happen if it were generated by the refraction of the Sun's rays. Although this argument is weak, since the heavenly arc produced by reflection of the Sun's rays is also visible in water. Thirdly, moreover, when the Sun is far below the earth at night, far removed from us, how could it happen that our sight is refracted by it?

units.la: Quæ nam sunt causæ uiæ lacteæ ex sententia Aristotelis?
units.tr: What are the causes of the Milky Way according to Aristotle?

units.la: Causa materialis: Exhalationes, sed subtiles, aridæ, & non satis compactæ, in locum ualde excelsum sublatæ. Causa formalis: Sicut exhalationes quædam inflammantur suspensæ subter stellam aliquam, ita ut stella ipsa credatur comam accipere: sicut item colorantur exhalationes sub Sole aut Luna, dum fiunt coronæ: ita exhalationes subtiles atq; aridæ, longo cœli tractu diffusæ, candorem lacteum in se recipiunt à multis & magnis stellis, sub quibus suspensæ hærèt. Confirmatur hæc ratio duobus argumentis.
units.tr: The material cause is exhalations, but thin, dry, and not tightly compacted, raised to a very high place. The formal cause is this: just as certain exhalations catch fire when suspended beneath a particular star, so that the star itself seems to take on a mane, and just as exhalations under the Sun or Moon are coloured when they form halos, so thin and dry exhalations, spread over a long stretch of the heavens, take on a milky whiteness from the many great stars beneath which they hang. This reasoning is confirmed by two arguments.

units.la: 1. Sub una stella cõtingit suspensas exhalationes, ut suprà dictum est, inflammari: quanto magis candorem accipiet sub pluribus simul collectis positæ?
units.tr: 1. Under a single star, suspended exhalations, as has been said above, catch fire. How much more will they take on whiteness when they are placed beneath many stars gathered together?

units.la: 2. Ipsarum stellarum quæ ibi sunt, magnitudo & multitudo plurimum ad id conferre potest. Argumento est, quòd qua parte plures maioresq; stellæ apparent, ea etiam candor magis visendus elucet.
units.tr: 2. The number and magnitude of the stars that are there can contribute greatly to this. The proof is that wherever more and larger stars appear, the whiteness also shines more visibly.

units.la: Dicet forte aliquis, exhalationes omnes intra tropicos & subzodiaco plerunq; consumi caloris uehementia: itaque circuli lactei, qui ex parte visitur intra tropicos, materiam non posse dici exhalationes. Responsio: Primùm quidè circuli lactei maxima pars extra tropicos conspicitur. Secundò, quæ pars intra tropicos existit, ea eiusmodi habet stellas, quæ sua virtute possint exhalationes tenues atque aridas ad se perpetuò attrahere, necnon suspensas retinere, ut talis color omni tempore ibi maneat. At propter tenuitatē & siccitatem illarum exhalationū candor tantum apparet. Si densiores et pinguiores essent, fortasis flammas conciperent ale rentq;. Et hæc hactenus de meteoris ignitis, quæ in superiore aeris regione gignuntur.
units.tr: Someone may perhaps say that all exhalations within the tropics and below the zodiac are for the most part consumed by the violence of the heat, so that the matter of the part of the Milky Way seen within the tropics cannot be called exhalations. Reply: first, the greater part of the Milky Way is seen outside the tropics. Second, the part that lies within the tropics has stars of such a kind that by their power they can continually draw to themselves thin and dry exhalations and hold them suspended, so that this colour remains there at all times. But because those exhalations are thin and dry, the whiteness appears only faintly. If they were denser and fattier, they would perhaps conceive flames and feed them. And so much for fiery meteors, which are generated in the upper region of the air.

units.la: DE METEORIS aqueis.
units.tr: ON AQUEOUS METEORS.

units.la: Quæ sunt meteora aquea?
units.tr: What are the aqueous meteors?

units.la: Quæ humida sunt & aquam referunt, atque in aquam plurimum resoluuntur: ut nubes, pluuiæ, nebulæ, ros, pruina, nix, &c. quæ procreantur in ima aeris regione.
units.tr: Those that are moist and resemble water, and for the most part dissolve into water: such as clouds, rains, mists, dew, hoarfrost, snow, and so on, which are produced in the lowest region of the air.

units.la: Quæ sunt communiter horum omnium causæ?
units.tr: What are the common causes of all these?

units.la: 1. Causa efficiens: Solis atque aliarum stellarum uis ac motus. 2. Causa materialis: Vapores ἀτμίδες, qui sunt halitus calidi & humidi, sursum è terra & aquis ui caloris cœlestis sublati. 3. Causa formalis: Vapores sursum evecti magna mole colliguntur in inferiore & nobis propinqua aeris regione, sensim vero calor in illis remittitur (dum videlicet is partim petit regionem sublimiorem, partim ab abundanti humido dispellitur:) itaq; opera frigoris vapores sese colligunt, ut (exempli gratia) crassæ & corpolentæ nubes cuadant, quæ aliquanto post frigore prævalente resolvuntur & liquantur, necnon pluvias nobis præbent.
units.tr: 1. The efficient cause: the power and motion of the Sun and the other stars. 2. The material cause: vapours [ἀτμίδες], which are warm and moist breaths, raised upwards from the earth and waters by the force of the heavenly heat. 3. The formal cause: vapours carried upwards gather in great mass in the lower region of the air, nearer to us; but gradually the heat in them abates (namely, partly because it seeks the higher region, partly because it is dispelled by the abundant moisture). So by the work of cold the vapours gather together, so that (for example) thick and dense clouds form, which a little later, when the cold prevails, dissolve and melt, and furnish us with rains.

units.la: Exhibe nunc aliquot species, & quo- modo eæ generentur, declara.
units.tr: Now set out some of the kinds, and explain how each is generated.

units.la: 1. Vapores sunt ipsi halitus, qui proximo nobis aere circumferuntur, atque è terra aquisq; educti, procreandorum meteororum aqueorum subministrant materiam, seq; habent ad nubes, ut nubes ad pluviam.
units.tr: 1. Vapours are the breaths themselves, which drift through the air near us, and, drawn up from the earth and waters, supply the matter for producing aqueous meteors; they stand to clouds as clouds stand to rain.

units.la: 2. Nubes est, quando eiusmodi vapor ita condensatur, ut aquæ naturam in se recipiat.
units.tr: 2. A cloud is formed when such a vapour is condensed so that it takes on the nature of water.

units.la: 3. Nebula est nubis spuma, adeoq; redundàs excrementum. Probatur id à signo. Nam ex collectis nebulis non sequitur pluvia, sed potius serenitas. Cæterùm cum ignita meteora, ut cometa, stellæ currentes; item meteora ex reflectione nata, ut iris, area, et raro & non diu appareant, hæc tamen aquea frequentissimè & perpetuo quasi circuitu conspiciuntur.
