Ratio hæc est: Cum Sol circulo quodam sine intermissione terram circumeat, fit ut semper vapores aliqui sursum evehantur, vel multi, vel pauci: & plerunq; qui interdiu attolluntur Solis calore, ijdem rursus noctu in terram delabuntur, ut semper terra mane humida appareat. Itaq; perpetua quædam agitatio atque vicissitudo in his aqueis meteoris observatur.
units.tr: 3. Mist is the foam of clouds, and so a superfluous excrement. This is proved by a sign: from gathered mists rain does not follow, but rather fair weather. Moreover, while fiery meteors, such as comets, shooting stars, and likewise meteors produced by reflection, such as the rainbow and the halo, appear rarely and not for long, these aqueous ones are seen very frequently and almost in perpetual cycle. The reason is this: since the Sun goes round the earth without interruption in a certain circuit, it comes about that some vapours are always being raised upwards, many or few; and for the most part those that are lifted up by day through the heat of the Sun fall back again to the earth by night, so that the ground always appears wet in the morning. Thus a certain constant agitation and alternation is observed in these aqueous meteors.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ roris ac pruinæ?
units.tr: What are the causes of dew and hoarfrost?

units.la: I. Causa efficiens utriusque est, calor Solis vapores sursum elevans.
units.tr: I. The efficient cause of both is the heat of the Sun, which raises the vapours upwards.

units.la: II. Causa materialis: Vapores è locis, præsertim uliginosis, paulo crassiores et graviores, quàm ij ex quibus cōstat pluvia, ijdemq; lento & mediocri calore educti. Ob quas duas causas, crassitiè, inquam, & caloris tenuitatem, fit ut non admodum altè scandant.
units.tr: II. The material cause: vapours from places, especially marshy ones, somewhat thicker and heavier than those of which rain consists, and drawn up by a slow and moderate heat. For these two causes, namely their thickness and the weakness of the heat, it comes about that they do not climb very high.

units.la: III. Causa formalis: Interdiu quidem vapores illi sensim attolluntur: at verò noctu, quādo accedit frigus, iterum demittuntur terrā versus, cui dum propinquant, in tenuem soluuntur liquorem. Verùm ut causa hæc formalis plenius intelligatur, operæprecium est annotare, quibus rebus ros & pruina differant, quibus item congruant.
units.tr: III. The formal cause: by day those vapours are gradually raised; but by night, when the cold comes on, they are let down again towards the earth, and as they approach it they dissolve into a thin liquid. But in order that this formal cause may be understood more fully, it is worth noting in what respects dew and hoarfrost differ, and likewise in what respects they agree.

units.la: 1. Pruina soluitur in liquorem, sed utcunq; induratum, frigore vero circumfusi aeris id efficiente: ros vero soluitur in liquorem mollem & fluidum.
units.tr: 1. Hoarfrost dissolves into a liquid, but one that is somehow hardened, the surrounding air producing this by its cold; dew dissolves into a soft and fluid liquid.

units.la: 2. Pruina fit hyeme, & in locis frigidis: ros fit æstate, & locis calidis.
units.tr: 2. Hoarfrost occurs in winter and in cold places; dew occurs in summer and in warm places.

units.la: 3. Quod ad materiæ constitutionem attinet, pruina prouenit ex vapore frigido, ros ex tepido.
units.tr: 3. As regards the constitution of the matter, hoarfrost comes from a cold vapour, dew from a tepid one.

units.la: 4. Pruina affinitatem habet cum niue, ros cum pluvia.
units.tr: 4. Hoarfrost has an affinity with snow, dew with rain.

units.la: 5. Pruina gignitur flante Borea, qui auget frigus: ros flante Austro, qui adfert temperiem.
units.tr: 5. Hoarfrost is produced when the North wind blows, which increases the cold; dew when the South wind blows, which brings mildness.

units.la: Convenit autem pruinæ cum rore:
units.tr: But hoarfrost agrees with dew in the following respects:

units.la: 1. Utrumq; meteorum fit noctu, quo tempore frigus ad condensandum & resoluendum idoneum est.
units.tr: 1. Both meteors occur by night, the time when the cold is suited to condensing and dissolving.

units.la: 2. Utrumq; fit cœlo sereno. Densis enim nubibus interpositis, non possunt vapores commodè eleuari.
units.tr: 2. Both occur when the sky is clear. For when thick clouds intervene, the vapours cannot conveniently be raised.

units.la: 3. Utrumq; fit sedatis ventis: nam venti vapores dispergunt.
units.tr: 3. Both occur when the winds are calm, for winds scatter the vapours.

units.la: 4. Utrumq; fit non longè à terra. Argumento est, quod in excelsis montibus non inueniuntur.
units.tr: 4. Both occur not far from the earth. The proof is that they are not found on high mountains.

units.la: Cæterum quod ad quintâ differentiâ attinet, ubi dicitur, Rorem fieri flante Austro: obseruanda est exceptio. Nam in ponto diuersum euenit, ac procreatur ros flante Borea, qui frigidus est. Causa uero hæc est: Ponto vastū mare opponitur, ideoq; & frigus ab aqua proveniens ibi dominatur: ex quo fit, ut flatus Austrini calor vix in pontum penetret. Atqui provenit ibi calor quidā intrò coactus per ἀντιπερίστασιν[?] (quasi dicas, contrariorum circumstantiam) à frigore undique circumambiente, & Borea prævalente. Itaque talis calor quando vi circumfusi frigoris excitatur, tum ros producitur.
units.tr: As for the fifth difference, where it is said that dew is produced when the South wind blows, an exception must be noted. For in Pontus the opposite happens, and dew is produced when the North wind blows, which is cold. The cause is this: the vast sea lies opposite Pontus, and so the cold coming from the water prevails there, with the result that the heat of the South wind can scarcely penetrate into Pontus. Yet a certain heat is produced there, shut in by the counter-standing [ἀντιπερίστασις] (as one might say, the circumstance of contraries), by the cold surrounding it on every side and the North wind prevailing. So when such heat is excited by the force of the surrounding cold, then dew is produced.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ nivis?
units.tr: What are the causes of snow?

units.la: 1. Causa materialis, vapores. Eadem plane materia est nivis, quæ & primæ: verum nivis materia altius subvehitur.
units.tr: 1. The material cause: vapours. The matter of snow is plainly the same as that of the earlier meteors, but the matter of snow is drawn up to a greater height.

units.la: 2. Causa formalis: Eodem pacto procreatur nix, quo pruina. Etenim proportio & ἀναλογία[?] magna est nivis cum pruina, sicut & pluviæ cum rore. Nix namq; & pruina gignuntur tantum tempore ac locis frigidis, sicut ros & pruina tempore ac locis subcalidis. Hæc autem, ut rectius iudicemus de causa nivis formali, sunt observanda discrimina: Pluvia sublimiore loco & ex crassiore provenit materia (nempe à magnis nubibus) eademq; longiore temporis spacio collecta: ros vero loco humiliore ex materia tenui, & tanquam ex nebulis, & sursum cuecta unius diei spacio. Ad eundem modum nix quoq; loco sublimiore ex materia corpulenta & paulatim collecta procreatur: pruina vero loco hu-miliore ex materia exili & celeriter è terris educta.
units.tr: 2. The formal cause: snow is produced in the same way as hoarfrost. For there is a great proportion and analogy between snow and hoarfrost, just as between rain and dew. For snow and hoarfrost are produced only in cold times and places, just as dew and hoarfrost are produced in times and places that are somewhat warm. Now, to judge more rightly about the formal cause of snow, the following differences are to be observed: rain arises in a higher place and from thicker matter (namely from great clouds), and that matter is gathered over a longer span of time; dew, on the other hand, arises in a lower place from thin matter, as it were from mists, and is drawn up within the space of a single day. In the same way, snow is produced in a higher place from dense matter gathered gradually; but hoarfrost in a lower place from slight matter and quickly drawn up from the earth.

units.la: Obiectio.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Quomodo intelligetur aliquis calor in nubibus, ex quibus nix, tempore frigidissimo dispersus, sicut existit in nubibus ex quibus fit pluuia?
units.tr: How is one to understand that there is some heat in the clouds from which snow comes, when the weather is most frigid, just as there is heat in the clouds from which rain comes?

units.la: Etenim calor quidem requiritur ad uapores colligendos & coiungendos, sicut ad resolutionem eorundem requiritur frigus. Responsio: Calor ille, per quem uapores paulo ante sursum sublati sunt, adhuc in nubibus hinc inde diffusus manet, qui & ibidem augetur aliturque, quando radij solis à terra eousq; reflectuntur. Calorem autem aliquatum ad niuis productionem requiri, ex eo cognoscitur, quod non nisi mediocri quadam aeris constitutione nix gignitur: quoniam nisi aliquantus fuerit calor, uapores aegre sursum pertrahentur: nisi etiā aliquantum fuerit frigus, uapores non congelabuntur. Etenim neque magno calore, neque in intensissimo frigore nix decidit.
units.tr: For heat is indeed required for gathering and joining vapours, just as cold is required for their dissolution. Answer: that heat, by which the vapours were lifted up a little while ago, still remains diffused here and there in the clouds, and it is also increased and fed there whenever the rays of the sun are reflected from the earth so far. Now, that some heat is required for the production of snow is known from this, that snow is produced only in a moderate condition of the air: for unless there is some heat, the vapours are drawn up with difficulty; unless there is some cold also, the vapours will not freeze. For snow falls neither in great heat nor in the most intense cold.

units.la: Quae sunt causae grandinis?
units.tr: What are the causes of hail?

units.la: Dictum est, ἀναλόγα[?] pluuiam & rorem, niuem & pruinam: uerum grandini nullum aliud μετέωρον eo pacto respondet. Quamobrem alia ratione, quàm proximè factum est, grandinis causas oportet inquiramus. Duae sunt de causis grandinis opiniones. Etenim incidunt nonnulla, ob quae non tam facile est pronunciare de grandine, quàm de meteoris præcedentibus.
units.tr: It has been said that rain and dew, snow and hoarfrost, are analogous; but no other meteor corresponds to hail in that way. Therefore we must inquire into the causes of hail by a different method from the one just used. There are two opinions about the causes of hail. For there arise some circumstances on account of which it is not as easy to pronounce about hail as about the preceding meteors.

units.la: 1. Grando est glacies, & interim cum glacies & nix non proueniat nisi hyeme & locis frigore horrentibus, grando tamen decidit autumno & uere atq; locis temperatis.
units.tr: 1. Hail is ice, and yet, since ice and snow do not arise except in winter and in places bristling with cold, hail nevertheless falls in autumn and spring and in temperate places.

units.la: 2. Cum grando è sublimi loco decidat,mirum est, unde ibi frigus ad congelandum: deinde,quomodo aquæ illic suspensæ maneant,donec congelentur.
units.tr: 2. Since hail falls from a high place, it is strange whence there is cold there to freeze it; then, how the waters remain suspended there until they are frozen.

units.la: 3. Quî potest etiam grando tanta magnitudine in aere consistere atq; ibi concrescere? Decidũt quidem magnæ guttæ pluuiarum, sed quæ inter cadendum ex multis ualde minutis coalescunt: atqui grandinem ita augeri,uerisimile non est. His igitur de causis alij aliter de grandine statuerunt.
units.tr: 3. How can hail also of such great size remain in the air and grow together there? Indeed large drops of rain do fall, but these, in falling, coalesce from many very small ones; yet it is not likely that hail is increased in this way. For these reasons, therefore, others have judged differently about hail.

units.la: Prima opinio Anaxagoræ est: secundum hunc causa materialis grandinis sunt nubes. Causa formalis: Condensantur nubes illæ per frigus, quod in media regione aeris semper acerrimum consistit. Etenim quando supernè imminet calor multò maximus, & rursus inferne calor ex refractione radiorum Solis ad terrã ualde magnus sursum uehitur, fit ut interuallo medio ingens frigus per ἀντιπερίστασιν[?] coaceruetur. Tanti igitur frigoris ui nubes, si quando ad eum usque locum attolluntur,in grandinem indurescunt. Facilè autem eosq; subuehuntur tempore calido,quale est uernum & autumnale.
units.tr: The first opinion is that of Anaxagoras: according to him, the material cause of hail is clouds. The formal cause: those clouds are condensed by the cold, which always stands most keenly in the middle region of the air. For when a very great heat is above, and again below, a very great heat rises up from the reflection of the sun's rays to the earth, it comes about that a huge cold is heaped up in the intervening space by reciprocal opposition. Therefore, if the clouds are at any time lifted up as far as that place, they harden into hail by the force of so great a cold. Moreover, they are easily carried up in warm weather, such as spring and autumn.

units.la: Atqui hæc sententia, præsertim de loco, Aristoteli improbatur, & quidem his de causis.
units.tr: Yet this opinion, especially concerning the place, is rejected by Aristotle, and indeed for these reasons.

units.la: Si grando æquè excelso loco gigneretur atque nix, oporteret grandinem ita cerni in montibus, sicut cernitur nix. Sed istud non fit: igitur grando adeò sublimi loco non procreatur.
units.tr: If hail were produced in as lofty a place as snow, hail would have to be seen on mountains just as snow is seen. But this does not happen; therefore hail is not produced in so high a place.

units.la: Crebrò propter terram animaduersæ sunt densæ nubes magno fragore inter se collidi, postquam collisione statim grando decidit. Igitur non ita sublimi loco gignitur.
units.tr: Often dense clouds have been observed colliding with one another with a great crash near the earth, immediately after which hail falls from the collision. Therefore it is not produced in so high a place.

units.la: Si adeò sublimi loco grando formaretur, non decideret ad nos forma inæquali & angulosa, neq; etiam tanta magnitudine: sed necessariò, dum per inferiorem aerem calidum labitur, rotunda ac par ua existeret. Ergo uerisimile non est, tam excelso loco grandinem procreari.
units.tr: If hail were formed in so lofty a place, it would not fall to us in an uneven and angular shape, nor of so great a size; but necessarily, while it slides through the lower warm air, it would be round and small. Therefore it is not likely that hail is produced in so lofty a place.

units.la: Secunda opinio est ipsius Aristotelis. Is uerò causam materialem grandinis eandem ponit cum Anaxagora, itemq; modum congelationis, sed de loco dissentit. Ait enim, etiam in inferiore aeris plaga frigus aliquando per ἀντιπερίστασιν ita imalescere, ut aqua congelari ibi facile queat. Nubes enim celeriter in propinquo aere ui frigoris resolui, & postquam aliquandiu ibi hæserint, mox magnos imbres magnasq; guttas decidere animaduertimus: eadem igitur ratione aqua quoque ibi aliquantulum hærere suspensa potest, mox uerò conglaciari ac decidere. Posse autem ibi celeriter aquam conglaciari, ex duobus signis colligi potest.
units.tr: The second opinion is Aristotle's own. He indeed posits the same material cause of hail as Anaxagoras, and likewise the same mode of freezing, but he disagrees about the place. For he says that even in the lower region of the air the cold sometimes grows so strong by reciprocal opposition that water can easily freeze there. For we observe that clouds are quickly dissolved in the nearby air by the force of cold, and after they have lingered there for a while, soon great showers and large drops fall; by the same reasoning, water also can hang suspended there for a little while, but then indeed freeze and fall. Moreover, that water can freeze quickly there may be gathered from two signs.

units.la: 1. Grandines subito & cum impetu ruunt, quamobrem probabile est subito quoq; concrescere.
units.tr: 1. Hailstones fall suddenly and with force; therefore it is probable that they also form suddenly.

units.la: 2. Decidunt magna & inæquali forma, quæ non contingeret, si lentius ac temporis progressu aliquo gignerentur. Deinde raro decidunt sine aliqua plu uia. Quia nimirum no potuit adeo cito omnis aqua congelescere, ideoq; necessario pars nondum concreta simul decidit.
units.tr: 2. They fall large and of uneven shape, which would not happen if they were produced more slowly and over some progression of time. Further, they rarely fall without some rain. Clearly, not all the water could freeze so quickly, and therefore of necessity the part not yet frozen falls together with it.

units.la: Verum enimuero quando Aristoteles tantum impugnat rationem Anaxagoræ de loco, omnes autem recentiores philosophi libeter cum Anaxagora aerem diuidunt in tres regiones, quarum media sit frigidissima: plures sane inuenias, qui de procreatione grandinis cum Anaxagora, quam cum Aristotele sentiunt.
units.tr: Indeed, when Aristotle only attacks the argument of Anaxagoras about the place, but all more recent philosophers gladly divide the air with Anaxagoras into three regions, of which the middle is the coldest, you will certainly find more who think about the production of hail with Anaxagoras than with Aristotle.

units.la: Cur grando non prouenit hyeme uel æstate, sed tantum Vere & autumno?
units.tr: Why does hail not occur in winter or summer, but only in spring and autumn?

units.la: In uere & autumno mediocris est calor per aerem diffusus, qui uapores idoneos commode sursum rapit. Deinde eo ipso tempore frigus no ita est dissusum undequaq; ut hyeme, non etiam ita exile ut tempore æstiuo, sed media quadam constitutione positu: quamobrem a circumfuso undiq; calore facile ita cogitur, ut cito perfici congelatio queat.
units.tr: In spring and autumn there is a moderate heat diffused through the air, which conveniently carries the suitable vapours upward. Then, at that same season, the cold is not spread everywhere as it is in winter, nor is it so thin as in summer, but is placed in a certain middle condition; for this reason it is easily compressed by the heat surrounding it on every side, so that the freezing can be quickly brought about.

units.la: DE
units.tr: DE

units.la: Quaenam sunt meteora flatuosa?
units.tr: What are the flatulent meteors?

units.la: Quae spirationum ac flatuum ui potissimum producuntur: cuiusmodi sunt fontes, flumina, uenti, terraemotus, tonitrua, fulmina, et cognatae his species.
units.tr: These are produced chiefly by the force of breathings and winds: such as springs, rivers, winds, earthquakes, thunder, lightning, and the species akin to these.

units.la: Quae sunt communiter horum omnium causae?
units.tr: What are the common causes of all these?

units.la: 1. Causa materialis partim uapores, ut ex quibus in terris gignuntur fontes ac flumina, dum illi in aquam resoluuntur: partim exhalationes, quemadmodum in uentis ac fulmine considerari id posse, ali quanto post docebimus. Haec diuersitas materiae in causa est, ut quaedam hoc genus meteora in aere gignantur, nonnulla uero etiam in terra.
units.tr: 1. The material cause is partly vapours, out of which springs and rivers are generated in the earth when these are dissolved into water; partly exhalations, as we shall teach a little later can be seen in the case of winds and lightning. This difference of matter is the reason why some meteors of this kind are generated in the air, and others indeed in the earth.

units.la: 2. Causa efficiens: Sol quidem tum uapores, tum exhalationes omnes ubique educit. Caeterum ad formam inducendam causa praecipua et tanquam instrumentalis sunt spiramina ac flatus, qui collectam materiam agitant. Etenim in omnibus huius ordinis meteoris spiraminum facultas sese exerit.
units.tr: 2. The efficient cause: the sun, indeed, draws up both vapours and exhalations everywhere. But for the forming of these, the chief cause, and as it were the instrumental cause, is the breathings and blasts, which stir the gathered matter. For in all meteors of this order the power of the breathings shows itself.

units.la: Quae sunt causae fontium ac fluminum?
units.tr: What are the causes of springs and rivers?

units.la: Tres de origine aquarum siue fontium ac fluminum leguntur opiniones.
units.tr: Three opinions are recorded concerning the origin of waters, that is, of springs and rivers.

units.la: I. Quidâ dixerunt, causam materialem aquæ esse aerem, sicut etiam materia existit uentorū. Etenim quod ad causam formale attinet, uentum esse aerem motum ac fluitantem: aquam uerò esse similiter aerem, sed cōsistentem. Quam ob causam, cum omnis aer sit unus idemq; aer, ijdem censuerunt omnem uentum esse unum eundemque uentum, & omnem aquam siue omnia flumina esse unam eandemque aquam & unum idemq; flumen. Verum huius opinionis absurditas per se manifesta est.
units.tr: I. Some have said that the material cause of water is air, just as the matter of winds is also air. For as regards the formal cause, wind is air in motion and flowing, but water is likewise air, only in a settled state. For this reason, since all air is one and the same air, they thought that every wind is one and the same wind, and that all water, or all rivers, are one and the same water and one and the same river. But the absurdity of this opinion is evident in itself.

units.la: II. Quidā imaginati sunt, in terra existere immensam aliquam uoraginē, ex qua tanquā publico penu fontes ac flumina aquarū dulcium hinc inde in omnes orbis partes deriuentur: sicut in humano corpore sanguis per uenas ab arce cordis in omnia membra emanat. Cū uerò ex his aquis semper ingens aquarū uis sursum educatur, rursumq; eadem in aquas recidat, eandē ubiq; aquā semper manere, nec ullam nouam procreari. Verum subsistere sententia hæc non potest. Si namque omnis aqua esset eadem aqua, sequeretur, aquam multò esse ampliorē uniuersa terra: quod absurdum est. Deinde, ubi immensa illa uorágo locum habet?
units.tr: II. Some have imagined that there is in the earth some immense abyss, from which, as from a common storehouse, springs and rivers of sweet water are carried off hither and thither to all parts of the world, just as in the human body blood flows through the veins from the citadel of the heart into all the members. But since a huge quantity of water is always drawn up from these waters, and the same falls back again into the waters, they thought that the same water always remains everywhere and that no new water is created. But this opinion cannot stand. For if all water were the same water, it would follow that the water is far greater than the whole earth, which is absurd. Next, where is that immense abyss situated?

units.la: III. Aristoteli placet, eodē pacto aquam gigni in terra, quo gignitur in aere. Ascendunt autem in acrem uapores multi ac densi, qui ibi in uastas nubes coeunt: paulatim uerò accedēte frigore, in aquā resolvuntur[?]. Eodem modo vapores & halitus multi colliguntur in terræ cauernis, ubi condensantur et crassescunt: tandem autem frigido aliquo spiramine interueniente, resoluuntur in tenues guttas sparsim appendentes, quæ temporis progressu continuè coalescunt, atque aquarum copiam efficiunt. Confirmatur hæc sententia aliquot rationibus.
units.tr: III. Aristotle holds that water is generated in the earth in the same way that it is generated in the air. Now many thick vapours rise into the air, and there gather into vast clouds; but as the cold gradually comes on, they are dissolved into water. In the same way, many vapours and breaths are collected in the caverns of the earth, where they are condensed and thickened; then, when some cold breath intervenes, they are dissolved into fine drops hanging here and there, which in the course of time continually coalesce and produce a quantity of waters. This opinion is confirmed by several reasons.

units.la: 1. Ab experimento in rebus artificialibus, qui ὑ-δραγωγίας[?], id est, aquæductus parare volunt, ita ducunt fossas, ut in eas excipiant aquam e terris defluentem, atque à sublimioribus semper ad inferiores partes decurrentem.
units.tr: 1. From experience in artificial things: those who wish to construct waterworks [ὑδραγωγίας], that is, aqueducts, dig channels in such a way that they catch the water flowing down from the lands and running always from higher to lower parts.

units.la: 2. Fontes & flumina plurimum ex montibus scaturiunt. Nam & montes plerùq; habet amplas cauernas, in quibus vapores colligi condensariq; compertum est. Quinetiam in ijsdē cauernis ex testudine & lateribus plurima aqua destillat, sæpe etiam aliqua in imo fluit vel consistit. Sunt deniq; montes acri atq; frigori omni ex parte expositi: quamobrem facilè frigus concipiunt, quo vapores condensantur & resoluuntur. Videre autem licet, omnes memorabiles fontes ac fluvios è montibus originem trahere:ut in Germania Rhenus, Danubius, Albis, Mosa, &c.
units.tr: 2. Springs and rivers for the most part gush out of mountains. For mountains generally have wide caverns, in which it is known that vapours are gathered and condensed. Moreover, in these same caverns much water drips from the vault and the sides, and often some water also flows or stands at the bottom. Finally, there are mountains exposed on every side to air and cold, and so they easily take on the cold by which vapours are condensed and dissolved. Moreover, one may see that all the famous springs and rivers take their origin from mountains, as in Germany the Rhine, the Danube, the Elbe, the Meuse, and so on.

units.la: Porrò multas passim in terra esse cauernas, quales diximus, ex eo cognosci potest, quòd alicubi ampli meatus subterranei & scrobes, atq; in his etiam aqua aliqua consistens inueniuntur: deinde, quòd non pauca sunt flumina, quæ cum longo interuallo apparent, tandem alicubi se abscondant in terræ uisceribus, & non multo post iterum emerguntiut [?] Lycus amnis in Asia, Erasinus in Argolica, Tygris in Mesopotamia.
units.tr: Furthermore, that there are many caverns of the kind we have described throughout the earth can be known from this: that in some places wide underground passages and pits are found, and in these some standing water as well; then, because there are not a few rivers which, after appearing for a long distance, at last hide themselves somewhere in the bowels of the earth and soon emerge again: the Lycus river in Asia, the Erasinus in Argolis, the Tigris in Mesopotamia.

units.la: Quas ob causas tum aquæ, tum terræ, interdum longo temporis pro- gressu locum mutant?
units.tr: For what reasons do waters and land sometimes change their place over a long progression of time?

units.la: Compertum est, quibus locis nunc mare est uel aliæ aquæ, ijsdem fuisse olim uastam terram: & uice uersa, ubi nunc terra est, ibi quondam fuisse aquas. Sic antiquitus tota Ægyptus urbe, quam Thebas uocant, constabat, teste etiam Homero: nunc uero latissimè patet, multis undiq; terris circumpositis, &c. Itaq; huius mutationis causæ dignæ sunt inquisitione.
units.tr: It is established that where there is now sea or other waters, there was formerly a vast land; and conversely, where there is now land, there were once waters. Thus in ancient times the whole of Egypt was occupied by the city which they call Thebes, as Homer also attests; but now it extends very widely, with many lands lying around it on every side, and so on. Therefore the causes of this change are worthy of investigation.

units.la: 1. Causa formalis: Quemadmodum plantæ & animalia à cœlo præcipuè accipiunt suæ conditionis & alterationis modum, ut primùm quidè quasi in iuuenta floreát, deinde robur ac magnitudinè tanquàm uirilem ætatem induant, tandem uero quasi senio languescát atq; extinguantur: ita terra & aqua calore atq; frigore à Solis siderumq; motu proueniêntibus uariè afficiuntur, ac terra quidem modò quasi in uirenti ætate humore undique perfunditur, modò uero quasi senio confecta arescit & siccatur: aquæ autem aliquando uno loco cedūt, moxq; alium locum nouum occupant.
units.tr: 1. The formal cause: just as plants and animals receive from the heavens, above all, the manner of their condition and alteration, so that first they flourish as if in youth, then they take on strength and size as if in manhood, and at last they languish and die as if from old age, so earth and water are variously affected by heat and cold arising from the motion of the sun and stars: and the land, at one time, as if in its green age, is drenched with moisture on all sides, while at another time, as if worn out by old age, it dries up and is parched; and the waters at one time give way in one place, and soon occupy another, new place.

units.la: 2. Causa efficiens: Calor uehemens & diuturnum, quo assiccatur omnia, ebibûtur aquæ, arescit terra: & frigus, quo humectantur & resoluuntur omnia, augentur aquæ, terra mollitur. Quo quidem pacto uariæ mutationes inducûtur à colore & frigore in plantis & animalibus: quinetiâ exempla licet uidere in multis terrarum partibus minoribus. Itaq; solis calore loca arescût: dum autè loca arescunt, præsocantur fontes: dum fontes præsocatur, minuuntur flumina, & paulatim aqua omnis disparet: mutatis autem fluminibus, necessariò sequitur mutatio quædam in ipso mari: cum autem mutatio hoc pacto fiat in aquis, intellige eodem pacto, quamuis ratione contraria, mutationem fieri etiam in terris.
units.tr: 2. The efficient cause: a vehement and lasting heat, by which all things are dried up, the waters are drunk up, and the land grows dry; and cold, by which all things are moistened and dissolved, the waters increase, and the land is softened. In this way various changes are brought about in plants and animals by heat and cold; and indeed examples of this may be seen in many smaller parts of the earth. Thus by the heat of the sun places grow dry; while places are drying up, the springs are dried up; while the springs are being dried up, the rivers are diminished, and gradually all water disappears; and when the rivers are changed, a certain change necessarily follows in the sea itself. And since change in the waters takes place in this way, understand that, by a similar process though in a contrary manner, change also takes place in the lands.

units.la: Qui fit, quòd eiusmodi magnæ mutatio- nes non facilè percipiuntur?
units.tr: How does it come about that changes of this kind of magnitude are not easily noticed?

units.la: Duæ sunt rationes. 1. Harum mutationum lenti sunt progressus, & non nisi admodum longo tempore perficiuntur. 2. Vita hominis breuis est, & plurimi intereunt, multi sedem mutant, priusquàm insignis mutatio facta deprehendatur. Sunt autè apud scriptores exempla eiusmodi mutationum non pauca obuia. Hom. li. 4. Odyss. asseruit, à Pharo insula in Aegyptum noctis & dici cursum nauigio fuisse, quod uniuersum spacium nunc continenti est adiunctum. Troianorum ætate regio Argiuorum palustris erat, paucosq; alere poterat, Myccnorum uero regio tunc erat bene culta: at nunc cōtraria sunt in illis omnia, &c. Vide Ouid.lib.ultimo Metamorph.Atq; hactenus hæc quidem ex Aristotelis sententia.
units.tr: There are two reasons. (1) These changes progress slowly and are accomplished only over very long periods. (2) Human life is short, and most people die, and many change their home, before a notable change is observed. There are, however, not a few examples of such changes to be found among the writers. Homer, in the fourth book of the Odyssey, asserts that a voyage of a night and a day ran from the island of Pharos to Egypt, whereas that whole stretch is now joined to the mainland. In the age of the Trojans the region of the Argives was marshy and could support only a few people, while the land of the Mycenaeans was then well cultivated; but now everything there is the opposite, and so on. See Ovid, in the last book of the Metamorphoses. So far these things are said according to the opinion of Aristotle.

units.la: Quænam est sententia aliorum de his mutationibus?
units.tr: What is the view of others about these changes?

units.la: Quida, imprimis qui sentiut mundū in tempore esse conditū, & in tepore debere finiri, iudicāt mutationes has ideo sic fieri, quod mūdus quotidie neluti senescat, atq; ad corruptionē totus vergat. Etenim debere hinc inde per partes sensim et tantisper immutari, dum ad vniuersi quoq; mutatione perueniatur. Verum Aristoteles, cui placet mundum esse æternum, hanc refellit opinione duabus rationibus.
units.tr: Some, above all those who hold that the world was created in time and must come to an end in time, judge that these changes happen in this way because the world is, as it were, growing old every day and tends wholly towards corruption. For it must be that, little by little and part by part, it is altered in this way until a change of the whole universe is reached as well. Aristotle, however, who holds that the world is eternal, refutes this opinion with two reasons.

units.la: 1. Manifestis experimentis aduertimus, quantum interdū una in parte vel terris vel aquis adimitur, tantum rursus alia in parte terris siue aquis accedere. Itaq; etiamsi modo hic, modo alibi, putetur aliquid corrumpi: certum tamen est, reuera nihil corrumpi, sed tantum loco mutari.
units.tr: (1) By plain experience we notice that as much as is sometimes taken away from earth or water in one place, just as much is added again to the earth or waters in another place. So although something may seem to be corrupted now here, now there, it is nonetheless certain that in truth nothing is corrupted, but only changed in place.

units.la: 2. Vt etiam alicubi portio aliquāta vel terræ vel aquæ consumeretur: at minime conficitur, aut mundū vniuersum paulatim debere propterea corrumpi, aut eo pacto ad corruptionem eius parari viam. Quantulæ enim sunt eæ partes, quæ nonnunquam subsidunt, ad reliquam vniuersi molem.
units.tr: (2) Even if some quantity of earth or water were consumed in one place, it would by no means follow either that the whole world must for that reason gradually be corrupted, or that a path to its corruption is thereby prepared. For how small are those parts which sometimes sink down, compared with the whole mass of the universe!

units.la: Itaq; Aristoteles exīstimat statuendū, quod quemadmodū inter anni vertentis partes alia est hyems,
units.tr: Therefore Aristotle thinks it must be laid down that, just as among the parts of the turning year one is winter,

units.la: x frigore & humiditate abundas: alia est æstas, calore & siccitate insignis: ita multorum seculorum curriculis aliquod incidit tempus, quod erga terram & hæc inferiora se habet in modu hyemis, quo ob iuges pluuias eueniunt in aliquibus mundi partibus alluuiones, atque notabiles mutationes terrarum. Quam ob causam certo tempore debuit euenire diluuium Deucalionis, &c.
units.tr: abounding in cold and moisture, and another is summer, marked by heat and dryness, so in the course of many ages there occurs a certain time which stands towards the earth and these lower things in the manner of winter, in which, because of continual rains, floods and notable changes of lands happen in some parts of the world. For this reason the deluge of Deucalion had to happen at a certain time, and so on.

units.la: Possunt autem ad huiusmodi mutationes multæ causæ adiuuantes & concurrentes obseruari: ueluti situs regionum (in regione enim plana & humili paulatim aquæ obtinebunt) aeris temperies, aspectus stellarum & planetarum, aquarum cursus & uiolentia, terrarum qualitas (ut mollities, concauitas) montium raritas uel frequentia, &c. Nam hæc proculdubio plurimum momenti adferunt, ut alicubi aqua incipiat paulatim supernatare, terra autem disparere: uel uice uersa, terra incipiat eminere atq; accumulari.
units.tr: Moreover, many causes that help and combine toward changes of this kind can be observed: for example, the situation of regions (for in a flat and low region the waters gradually gain the upper hand), the temperature of the air, the aspects of the stars and planets, the course and violence of waters, the nature of the land (such as its softness or hollowness), the scarcity or abundance of mountains, and so on. For these undoubtedly contribute very much, so that in one place the water begins gradually to cover the land, while the land disappears; or, conversely, the land begins to rise up and accumulate.

units.la: Quæ sunt causæ maris?
units.tr: What are the causes of the sea?

units.la: Variæ sunt de causis maris opiniones.
units.tr: There are various opinions about the causes of the sea.

units.la: I. Veteres Theologi gentilium, poetæ uidelicet, Hesiodus, Orpheus, &c. dixerunt, in terra existere quosdam abditos fontes, e quibus aqua uniuersa, atq; etiam uastum mare erumpit.
units.tr: I. The ancient theologians of the gentiles, namely the poets Hesiod, Orpheus, and others, said that certain hidden springs exist in the earth, from which all the water, and even the vast sea, bursts forth.

units.la: II. Quidam physici, ut Anaximander, atq; etiam Diogenes, opinati sunt, terram quondam fuisse undiq; diq[?]; aquis cinctam & inclusam, ucrùm calore solis partem aliquâ eductam sursum in aera, partem uerò absumptâ: ex eo autem quod reliquũ mansit, mare constitui. Argumeto esse dicebât, quòd mare perpetua asiccatione attenuetur atq; minus reddatur.
units.tr: II. Certain natural philosophers, such as Anaximander and also Diogenes, thought that the earth was once surrounded and enclosed on all sides by water; but that, when part of it was drawn up into the air by the heat of the sun and part was consumed, the sea was formed from what remained. As evidence of this they said that the sea is continually thinned by evaporation and becomes less.

units.la: III. Empedocles ratus est, terrâ fuisse intus aquis refertam: Solis autem calore eductos ex ea sudores, qui in unum collecti, uastum mare nobis præbent. quod comprobari eo uult, quòd mare perinde atq; sudor salsedine inficiatur.
units.tr: III. Empedocles reckoned that the earth was filled inwardly with water, and that sweats drawn out of it by the heat of the sun, collected into one, give us the vast sea; he wants this to be proved by the fact that the sea, just like sweat, is tainted with saltiness.

units.la: IIII. Quidam falsum mare dixerunt ob terram siccam admixtam, sicut lixiuium quoq; falsum est propter cineres per quos colatur.
units.tr: IV. Some have called the sea false because dry earth is mixed into it, just as lye is also false because of the ashes through which it is filtered.

units.la: V. Plato in Phædone constituit quandâ immensam uoraginem, cui nomen Tartaro, ex qua omnes aquarum fontes & flumina derivantur, & in quam rursus omnes aquæ recidunt, ut ita perpetua & indeficiens aquarum cõsistat moles. Ab hac igitur uoragine etiam mare ipsum ebulliret.
units.tr: V. Plato, in the Phaedo, posits a certain immense abyss, called Tartarus, from which all the sources and rivers of water are derived, and into which all the waters fall back again, so that such a constant and unfailing mass of water persists. Therefore the sea itself also boils up from this abyss.

units.la: Sed hæ opiniones propè omnes à uero quamlongissimè absunt, nec difficile est eas confutare.
units.tr: But almost all these opinions are very far from the truth, and it is not difficult to refute them.

units.la: Prima euertitur duabus rationibus. 1. Aquæ omnes è fontibus scaturientes, aut perpetuò rectà excurrunt, aut arte cohibetur, fiuntq; statariæ. Atqui de aquis marinis neutrum horum dici potest. Igitur non proueniunt è fontibus. Maior est manifesta ex aquarum differentijs. Minorem experientia comprobat.Nam neq; cernútur ab uno aliquo loco ad certu finem omnes excurrere, neq; etiá posset ut [?]ulla ratione tanta molcs quieta cotineri. Quód si quæ dá forte maria particularia uideantur ad unā metā tendere, atq; unum sese exonerare in aliud uicinum, proue nit sane id non ex fontibus unde oriuntur, sed uel ex terræ atq; litoru dispositione, uel ex multitudine & ui fluminum in id illabentium, uel ex terræ atq; alueorum inæquali profunditate.
units.tr: The first is overturned by two reasons. (1) All waters gushing from springs either flow straight on continually, or are checked by some art and become stagnant. But neither of these can be said of the waters of the sea. Therefore they do not come forth from springs. The major premise is clear from the differences among waters. The minor premise is confirmed by experience. For we do not see all of them running to one fixed end from a single place, nor could such a great mass be held still by any means. But if some particular seas perhaps seem to tend to one boundary and to discharge themselves into another neighbouring sea, this certainly does not happen from the springs from which they arise, but either from the arrangement of the land and shores, or from the number and force of the rivers flowing into them, or from the unequal depth of the land and of the channels.

units.la: 2. Si amplißimū mare ex fontibus ullis oriretur, haud dubiè etiam ubi minora sunt maria, quale est Hircanum & Caspium, ibi fontes aliqui conspicerentur. Sed istud nequaquam fit. Igitur intelligi nullo modo potest, mare illud amplißimum ex fontibus oriri.
units.tr: (2) If the most vast sea arose from any springs, then surely springs would be seen also where the smaller seas are, such as the Hyrcanian and the Caspian. But this by no means happens. Therefore it can in no way be understood that that most vast sea arises from springs.

units.la: Quod ad secundam opinionē attinet, complectitur ea aliquid uerisimile, uidelicet aquas quasdam educi sursum calore Solis. Verum absurda est persuasio, quòd aquæ ullæ à Sole absumantur, tanquam si Sol ijs aleretur ac pascceretur. Existimarunt enim quidā Platonici, Solem propterea & ab oriente in occidentē, & à tropico Austrino ad Septentrionalem perpetuò ferri, ut nouū undiq; pabulū semper hauriat. Cum enim immensus sit solis calor, necessario illū nouo humore subinde refici & conseruari, ne consumatur prorsus: quemadmodū ignis, ne consumatur, soueri ac refici debet noua subinde lignorum appositione. Sed multis rationibus perspicuis opinio hæc evertitur.
units.tr: As for the second opinion, it contains something probable, namely that certain waters are drawn upwards by the heat of the sun. Yet the belief that any waters are consumed by the sun is absurd, as if the sun were nourished and fed by them. For some Platonists have thought that the sun is therefore carried continually both from east to west and from the southern tropic to the northern, so that it may always draw in fresh nourishment on every side. For since the sun's heat is immense, it must needs be restored and preserved from time to time by new moisture, lest it be utterly consumed, just as fire, so that it may not be consumed, must be fostered and renewed from time to time by the addition of fresh wood. But this opinion is overturned by many plain reasons.

units.la: 1. Vapores qui attolluntur, non ascendunt ad locum usq; solis, sed tantum ad vicinam nobis partem aeris. quomodo igitur Sol ijs pascatur?
units.tr: (1) The vapours that are lifted up do not rise to the place of the sun, but only to the part of the air near to us. How, then, is the sun nourished by them?

units.la: 2. Non est apta coparatio Solis cum igne. Siquidem ignis excitatur e subiecta materia, & tamdiu durat, quamdiu materia idonea superadditur: neq; dicitur ignis ali, sed ex lignis fieri. Cæterum de Sole idem dici non potest: neq; enim ut ignis ex ligno, ita Sol fit ex vaporibus.
units.tr: (2) The comparison of the sun with fire is not apt. For fire is kindled from the matter beneath it and lasts as long as suitable matter is added on top; and fire is not said to be fed, but to be made from wood. But the same cannot be said of the sun: for the sun is not made from vapours as fire is made from wood.

units.la: 3. Ex causa formali: Sol educit vapores ex terra & aquis, sicut ignis educit vapores ex aqua calefacta. Atqui ignis, dum istud facit, nequaquam dicitur vaporibus illis pasci. Quare neq; Sol, quālibet multos attollat, alij ijsdem dicetur.
units.tr: (3) From the formal cause: the sun draws up vapours from earth and water, just as fire draws up vapours from heated water. But fire, while doing this, is by no means said to be nourished by those vapours. Therefore neither is the sun, however many it draws up, said to be fed by them.

units.la: 4. Si reliqua astra non pascuntur humoribus, profectò nec Sol ijs pascitur, cum omnium siderum pars sit & substantia.
units.tr: (4) If the other stars are not nourished by moisture, certainly neither is the sun fed by it, since it is a part and substance of the stars as a whole.

units.la: 5. Quanta portio omni tempore vaporū sursum attollitur, tanta denuò ad nos ex aere redit. Igitur falsum est, Solem aquis pasci. Quinetiam falsum esse liquet, quod quidam suspicati sunt, vapores sursum sublatos transire in naturam aeris. Quomodo enim istud fiat, quando iterum decidunt?
units.tr: (5) As great a portion of vapour as is lifted up at any time, so much again returns to us from the air. Therefore it is false that the sun is nourished by waters. Moreover, it is clear to be false what some have suspected, that vapours once lifted up pass over into the nature of air. For how could this happen, when they fall down again?

units.la: De tertia & quarta opinione erit dicendi locus, ubi separatim de salsedine maris disputabimus.
units.tr: We shall have an occasion to speak of the third and fourth opinions, where we shall discuss separately the saltiness of the sea.

units.la: Quinta opinio Platonis similiter facile refutatur.
units.tr: The fifth opinion, that of Plato, is likewise easily refuted.

units.la: 1. Absurdum est, ex Tartaro omnes aquas deriuari: quando si ita esset, necessum foret easdem aquas contrario motu ferri: quasdam nempe sursum, quae nimirum ad terrae superficiem irrigandam ascendunt: quasdam vero deorsum, quae rursus versus ipsum tartari centrum a terra descendentes refluunt. Atqui valde absurdum est istud astruere, maxime vero quod aquae ex imo scandant sursum, attestante id proverbio, quo ad significandum rem absurdam dicitur ἀνωποταμῶν, id est, sursum flumina. Igitur non est concedendum, quod ex tartaro aliquo aquae omnes profluant.
units.tr: 1. It is absurd to derive all waters from Tartarus. For if that were so, the same waters would necessarily have to move in opposite directions: some upward, to irrigate the surface of the earth, and others downward, flowing back from the earth toward the very centre of Tartarus. But it is very absurd to assert this, especially because waters climb upward from the depths, as the proverb attests, by which an absurd thing is called up-flowing rivers [ἀνωποταμῶν]. Therefore it must not be conceded that all waters flow out of some Tartarus.

units.la: 2. Plurima quotidie tum in aere, tum in terra, deinde etiam ex aere & ex terra aqua nova gignitur: quare verum esse nequit, omnem aquam ex tartaro scaturire. Item multa quotidie aqua evaporatur, attollitur in sublime & absumitur: quomodo igitur omnis in tartarum redeat?
units.tr: 2. Every day new water is generated both in the air and in the earth, and also from the air and the earth. So it cannot be true that all water wells up from Tartarus. Likewise, every day much water evaporates, is lifted up into the height and is consumed. How, then, does all of it return to Tartarus?

units.la: 3. Palam videmus fluvios omnes praecipuos dilabi in mare, & nequaquam per terrae cavernas ad tartarum ullum decurrere.
units.tr: 3. We plainly see that all the principal rivers flow down into the sea, and in no way run through the caverns of the earth to any Tartarus.

units.la: 4. Animadvertimus flumina increscere & augeri, non quod aquas accipiat e tartaro, sed quod in ea multi amnes fontesque corriuetur: rursumque decrescere & minui, non quod labantur in tartarum, sed quod vel calore caelesti aquae attollantur, vel praecipitentur in mare. Tantum de variis aliorum opinionibus. Nunc sententia ipsius Aristotelis audiamus.
units.tr: 4. We observe that rivers swell and grow, not because they take in water from Tartarus, but because many streams and springs flow into them; and again they shrink and diminish, not because they slip back into Tartarus, but because the waters are lifted up by the heat of the heavens or carried off into the sea. So much for the various opinions of others. Now let us hear the view of Aristotle himself.

units.la: Elementum aquæ omnium philosophantium consensu locum suum obtinet inter aerem & terram. Duas uero necesse est constituamus uniuersæ aquæ elementaris portiones: alteram corpulentam & crassam, alteram tenuem & subtilem. Ex his autem duabus illa quidem constituit mare, atque circumquaque terram ambit, utpote quæ ob pondus suum debet terræ proximè adhærere: illa uero subtilior dispargitur per uicinum aerem quaquauersum diffusa. Nec potest intelligi, quomodo aliter aqua elementaris inter aerem & terram locum sortiatur. Quod cum ita sit, manifestum euadit, quòd mare sit præcipua pars elementi, adeoq; principium aquarum omnium. Confirmatur hæc sententia ex eo, quòd omnia flumina ex mari ad nos profluunt, præterea iterum in mare exonerantur.
units.tr: The element of water, by the agreement of all philosophers, holds its place between air and earth. We must, however, posit two portions of the whole elemental water: one gross and thick, the other thin and subtle. Of these two, the former forms the sea and surrounds the land on every side, since on account of its weight it must cling closely to the earth; the latter, being finer, is spread abroad through the neighbouring air in every direction. Nor can we understand how elemental water could otherwise obtain its place between air and earth. This being so, it is clear that the sea is the principal part of the element, and so the principle of all waters. This view is confirmed by the fact that all rivers flow to us from the sea and, again, discharge themselves into the sea.

units.la: Obiectio. Quomodo aqua marina dicetur aqua elementaris, cum sit impotabi- lis & inepta humanis vsibus?
units.tr: Objection. How can sea water be called elemental water, since it is undrinkable and unfit for human uses?

units.la: Respondetur, Aquas maris esse duplices. quasdam molles, leues, subtiles, et plus habentes aereæ substantiæ, quàm terreæ: quasdam uero densas, poderosas, corpuletās[?], quib. multū terræ admixtū est. Ex his uero, quæ graviores sunt, manent eo loco, quo mare cernimus:quæ uerò leuiores sunt, subuchuntur sursum, nec non Solis calore ita resoluuntur & quasi coquuntur, humanis usibus aptæ ut fiant. Igitur mare omnium aquarum principium existit, atq; aqua elementaris agnosci debet.
units.tr: The reply is that sea waters are of two kinds: some soft, light and subtle, containing more of the substance of air than of earth; others dense, heavy and thick, with much earth mixed in. Of these, the heavier remain in the place where we see the sea; the lighter are drawn upward, and by the heat of the sun they are so dissolved and, as it were, cooked, that they become fit for human use. Therefore the sea exists as the principle of all waters, and it must be recognised as elemental water.

units.la: An mare semper fuerit, semperq; futurum sit?
units.tr: Has the sea always existed, and will it always exist?

units.la: Aristoteles quemadmodū mundum uniuersum, ita mare quoque arbitratus est initium quidem habuisse, atqui finem nunquam habituru. Quod autem mare semper consistat, neq; ulla ratione, omniū uerò minimè calore Solis, multas quotidie aquas abfumente, sit finiendum, quatuor cōfirmat rationibus.
units.tr: Aristotle, just as he thought the whole world had a beginning but will never have an end, so also held that the sea had a beginning but will never have an end. That the sea always persists, and that it cannot in any way be made to vanish, least of all by the heat of the sun, which consumes many waters every day, he confirms with four arguments.

units.la: 1. Quibus de causis aqua maris hucusq; ab initio inde constitit, quantumuis multi humores dulces ac potabiles sint calore Solis ex eo educti, ijsdem etiam posthac consistet.
units.tr: 1. For whatever the reason that the water of the sea has stood from the beginning until now, however many sweet and drinkable moisture is drawn out of it by the sun's heat, for the same reason it will continue to stand hereafter.

units.la: 2. Sicut semper aliqua aquæ portio in sublime attollitur, ita rursum semper aliqua defcēdit in mare: igitur mare nunquā assiccatione aliqua cōsumetur.
units.tr: 2. Just as some portion of water is always raised into the height, so again some portion always descends into the sea. Therefore the sea will never be used up by any drying-up.

units.la: 3. Solis latio uel aliquando interquiescet, uel erit perpetua. Si interquiescet, tum desinet uis exiccandi: quamobrem mare sempiternum consistet. Sin erit perpetua, tum sat erit Soli aquam tantum subtilem dulcemq; elicere, quam rursus ad nos demittat, quomodo hactenus semper solet facere. Igitur mare æternum manebit.
units.tr: 3. The sun's motion will either at some time cease, or it will be perpetual. If it ceases, then the power of drying up will cease, and so the sea will remain everlasting. But if it is perpetual, then it will be enough for the sun to draw up only the thin and sweet water, which it sends down again to us, as it has always done hitherto. Therefore the sea will remain eternal.

units.la: 4. Etsi cōtingat sæpenumero aquas alicubi defice re, nouasq; terras emergere: tamē minimē sequitur, mare aliquando defecturū. nam perpetua quadā periodo ita fit, ut quantū alibi aquæ absumitur, tantū alibi recentis aquæ iterum oriatur, nec non noua loca aquis cōtegantur. Itaq; aqua maris haud deficiet.
units.tr: 4. Even if it often happens that waters fail in one place and new lands emerge, it by no means follows that the sea will one day fail. For by a certain perpetual cycle it comes about that as much water is consumed in one place, so much fresh water again arises elsewhere, and new places are covered with water. Thus the water of the sea will never fail.

units.la: Atq; Aristoteles quidē ita. Cæterū nos ex religionis nostræ literis edocti sumus, mare & terram principiū habuisse, Genes. 1. Verūm eadē omnia, & tam cœlum quàm elementa semel igne cōflagratūra, atq; nouā facie nouasq; acceptura qualitates, 2. Pet. 3. codē fere pacto, quo homiñ & hominū corpora cōsumi oportet, ac postea nouas qualitates accipere.
units.tr: So much for Aristotle. But we, taught by the writings of our religion, know that the sea and the land had a beginning, Gen. 1. Yet all these things, both heaven and the elements, are to be consumed once by fire and to receive a new face and new qualities, 2 Pet. 3., in much the same way as men and their bodies must be consumed and afterwards receive new qualities.

units.la: Quam ob causam mare salsum est?
units.tr: Why is the sea salt?

units.la: Refert Aristoteles aliorum de hac quæstione opiniones, easdemq; confutat. Postea vero suū ipse profert iudicium.
units.tr: Aristotle reports the opinions of others on this question and refutes them. Afterwards he sets out his own judgement.

units.la: Prima opinio fuit dicentiū, omnia quondam suisse aquis obtecta: porrò uniuersam aquam dulcē calore Solis sursum sublatā, salsam vero relictā & mare efficere. Confutatur hæc opinio hoc pacto: Mare fuit salsum, antequā aliqua inde aqua sursum attolleretur, vel non. Si nō fuit ante salsum, sequitur, quòd vbi iterū aqua dulcis sublata in illud recidit, tū dulcescere totū mare rursus debeat. Si ante fuit salsum, restat adhuc, ut causæ inquirantur eius salsedinis.
units.tr: The first opinion was that of those who said that all things were once covered with water; that the whole water, sweet from the heat of the sun, was lifted up, and the salt left behind made the sea. This opinion is refuted in this way: either the sea was salt before any water was lifted up from it, or it was not. If it was not salt before, it follows that when the sweet water that was raised up falls back into it, the whole sea ought to become sweet again. If it was salt before, there remains the question of what causes that saltness.

units.la: Secunda opinio: Mare salsum est propter admixtionem xtione terræ, queadmodũ lixiuium falsum est propter admixtos cineres. Confutatur: Si mare falsum efficeretur ob admixtā terrā, at multò magis flumina ipsa virtute admixtæ terræ falsa fierent. Atqui ut demus in fluminibus plane diversum cuenire[?]. Igitur salsedo ab admixta terra mari nequaquā inducitur.
units.tr: The second opinion: the sea is salt because of the earth mixed into it, just as lye is salty because of the ashes mixed into it. Refutation: if the sea were made salt by the earth mixed into it, then rivers themselves, by the power of the same mixed earth, would become much more salt. But even granting that the opposite happens in rivers, it follows that saltiness is in no way induced into the sea by the earth mixed into it.

units.la: Tertia opinio, Empedoclis, astruentis mare esse sudorem terræ, æstu solis eductum, atq; ea ratione falsum effici, qua etiam sudor humani corporis salsus existit. Verum opinio hæc nullo nititur fundamento.
units.tr: The third opinion, that of Empedocles, asserts that the sea is the sweat of the earth, drawn out by the heat of the sun, and that it is made salt in the same way that the sweat of the human body is salty. But this opinion rests on no foundation.

units.la: 1. Resipit plane comentum quoddam poeticum.
units.tr: 1. It plainly smells of some poetic fiction.

units.la: 2. Non potest ostendi, quòd eodē modo generatur atq; emanct[?] aqua maris ex poris et interioribus partibus terræ, quo sudor vel etiam urina emanat ex poris & interioribus partibus humani corporis. Etenim sudoris & urinæ salsedo ex eo prouenit, quòd sensim defluant à crassa & superuacanea hypostasi ciborum, qui percoqui in corpore satis non possunt. Atqui nihil demonstrabitur, quod in terra sic se habeat, sicut in corpore humano se habent ciborum reliquiæ non percoctæ. Igitur non rectè dicitur, Mare propterea esse salsum, quòd è terra educitur, sicut sudor ex humano corpore.
units.tr: 2. It cannot be shown that the water of the sea is generated and emitted in the same way, from the pores and inner parts of the earth, as sweat or even urine is emitted from the pores and inner parts of the human body. For the saltness of sweat and urine comes from this: that they gradually flow off from the thick and superfluous residue of food, which cannot be sufficiently digested in the body. But nothing will be shown to be so in the earth as the remains of undigested food are in the human body. Therefore it is not rightly said that the sea is salt because it is drawn out of the earth, as sweat is from the human body.

units.la: 3. Si mare esset sudor terræ, tum oporteret sudorem hunc rariorem esse aquis cæteris, in terra relictis, quemadmodum in corpore humano sudor exiqua [?] quædam est portio ad reliquos humores eiusdem corporis. Atqui palàm videmus, aquas maris ampliores esse aquis relictis in terra. Igitur aqua maris dici sudor terræ nequit.
units.tr: 3. If the sea were the sweat of the earth, then this sweat would have to be thinner than the other waters left in the earth, just as in the human body sweat is a small portion compared with the remaining humours of the same body. But we plainly see that the waters of the sea are greater in quantity than the waters left in the earth. Therefore the sea water cannot be called the sweat of the earth.

units.la: 4. Si olim terra calefacta à Sole sudavit, cum esset adhuc humidior: multò quidem magis nunc sudaret, quando magis sicca est (siquidem cùm humida est, non proprie dicitur sudare, sed potius siccari.) Verùm quantumlibet terra evadat sicca, nusquam tamen sudare animadvertitur. Quamobrem falsum est, quòd aquæ maris existant terræ sudor. Ex his igitur manifestum evadit, opiniones hactenus enumeratas esse pro infirmis habendas.
units.tr: 4. If the earth once sweated when it was heated by the sun, while it was still more moist, then it would sweat much more now, when it is drier (for when it is moist it is not properly said to sweat, but rather to dry). Yet however dry the earth becomes, it is nowhere observed to sweat. Therefore it is false that the waters of the sea are the sweat of the earth. From these points it is therefore clear that the opinions listed so far must be regarded as weak.

units.la: Cæterum hæ demum causæ salsedinis putandæ sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, these causes are to be considered the causes of saltiness.

units.la: I. Statuendum est, in mari esse exhalationes aliquas calidas et siccas, ex quibus calor prodiens admodum est ad inducēdam salsedinē efficax. Etenim quod calidū est & siccum, huic rei valde est accommodum. Tales autem exhalationes ibi existere, hoc pacto probatur: Cū terra quæ mari substrata est, se habeat veluti cinis, & per se sit calida ac sicca (hoc enim sensu percipiunt, quicunq; vel exiguam molè arenæ maris coacervant) necesse est, à Sole atque astris inde calidas siccasq; exhalationes educi. qualis enim subiecta terra est, tales prodeunt aspirationes, è sicca siccæ, ex humida humidæ. Ab his igitur tam cum sursum attolluntur, quàm cum rursus in mare recidunt, non paruus calor mari undique inducitur.
units.tr: I. It must be laid down that in the sea there are certain hot and dry exhalations, from which the heat that emerges is very effective in bringing about saltiness. For what is hot and dry is especially suited to this matter. That such exhalations exist there is proved in this way: since the earth that lies beneath the sea is like ash, and is in itself hot and dry (people perceive this by sense, for whoever heaps up even a small mass of sea sand notices it), it is necessary that hot and dry exhalations are drawn up from it by the Sun and the stars. For whatever kind of ground lies beneath, such exhalations arise: dry from dry, moist from moist. Therefore, as these are lifted up, and again as they fall back into the sea, no small heat is brought to the sea on every side.

units.la: 2. Aquis maris inest nonnihil admixtum, quod similiter ad salsedinem producendam confert, nimirum terra calida & sicca in modum cinerum se habens. Atq; huiusmodi admixtionem plurimum momenti habere ad salsitudinem inducendam, diversis comprobari exemplis potest. Generatim namq; in omnibus sedimentis invenitur salsedo, propter res quasdam admixtas. Quod in urina & sudore, deinde & in lixivio cerni potest. Etenim duo illa cum defluant, secum trahunt nonnihil de hypostasi elementorum in corpore humano: lixivio autem permixti fuerunt cineres. Breviter igitur duæ res salsedinem in mari efficiunt: altera calor ab exhalationibus calidis & siccis inductus: deinde verò materia admixta, quæ excrementorum instar in eo colligitur.
units.tr: 2. The waters of the sea contain something mixed in, which similarly contributes to producing saltiness, namely earth that is hot and dry, resembling ashes. And that such a mixture has very great weight in bringing about saltiness can be shown by various examples. For in general saltiness is found in all sediments, on account of certain things mixed in with them. This can be seen in urine and sweat, and then also in lye. For when those two fluids flow away, they carry with them some of the sediment of the elements in the human body; and ashes were mixed into the lye. In short, then, two things produce saltiness in the sea: first, heat induced by hot and dry exhalations; and second, the mixed-in matter, which is gathered in it like excrement.
